In problems involving mechanical failure under load (compression/tension/shear), material 'strength' refers to a critical stress (units of pressure), not a force. The failure force must be obtained via F = σ × A, where A is the loaded cross-sectional area. The rule checks for any claim that the required/destructive force scales directly with 'strength' (e.g., F ∝ strength, F = k·strength, or F1/F2 = S1/S2) without explicitly stating the stress-to-force relation F = σ × A or without accounting for the cross-sectional area (A). It also checks that, when specimens are compared, the solution either (a) shows A is identical (same shape and size) to justify F ∝ σ, or (b) includes the area ratio: F1/F2 = (σ1/σ2) × (A1/A2). The rule further enforces dimensional consistency: force (N) must be derived from stress (Pa) times area (m²). If the solution equates or scales force with strength without mentioning area or the relation F = σ × A, it is flagged.

Statics and Elasticity.title: Avoid scaling failure force with total constituent count; use load-bearing cross-section
Statics and Elasticity.description: This rule checks for a common modeling error in scaling-law solutions for mechanical strength or failure force of specimens with fixed shape and size (e.g., cylinders under compression). The error is to scale the failure force F (or strength/stress σ) with the total number of microscopic constituents in the entire specimen volume (N ∝ V_sample / V_grain ∝ d^-3 for grain size d) rather than with the number of load-bearing contacts across the failure cross-section. What the verifier looks for: - The solution directly asserts or implies F ∝ N or σ ∝ N, where N is counted over the whole specimen volume (e.g., N ∝ 1/V_grain, N ∝ d^-3), without converting to a per-area load path count. - The solution uses phrases like "number of grains in the cylinder" or "same total volume" to justify strength scaling, and omits discussion of the failure plane/cross-sectional area or contacts per unit area. - The solution does not express F = σ A for fixed geometry, nor derive σ from a per-area micro-mechanism (e.g., contacts/bridges per area ∝ d^-2 times per-contact force scaling). - In granular/capillary cohesion contexts, the solution ignores that: contact density per area ∝ d^-2 and per-contact force often scales with grain size (e.g., ∝ d), so σ typically ∝ d^-1. The rule flags the above even if the final exponent accidentally matches the correct result, because the physical basis (volume-based counting) is incorrect for load transfer across a section. Acceptable modeling cues that avoid flagging: - Expressing failure force via stress and area for fixed geometry (F ∝ A σ), and deriving σ from the number of load-bearing contacts per unit cross-sectional area and the per-contact force. - Explicit mention of a failure plane/cross-section and counting load paths/contacts per area (∝ d^-2), combined with a justified per-contact force scaling. The rule is triggered when volume-based constituent counting is used to scale strength/force without transitioning to a per-area load-bearing argument.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Incompressible assumption violated by adiabatic/compressible reasoning
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: Checks for conceptual inconsistency where a solution invokes adiabatic/compressible effects or variable density after the problem (or the solution itself) has assumed negligible density variation/incompressible flow. Trigger conditions: (a) The problem statement or solution explicitly assumes constant density, negligible density change with height, or applies the incompressible Bernoulli equation; and (b) the solution later uses adiabatic/isentropic relations (e.g., p·rho^{-gamma}, pV^{gamma}, mentions of 'adiabatic', 'isentropic', 'compressible expansion', 'gamma'), or derives rho(z), or argues that velocity varies with height because of expansion/compressibility. Also flag if the solution mixes continuity for a constant-area duct with a given volumetric flow rate B (implying v = B/A constant) and simultaneously attributes a non-constant velocity profile to adiabatic expansion or variable density without explicitly redefining B as mass flow and justifying a departure from the stated assumptions. The rule detects keywords such as 'adiabatic', 'isentropic', 'compressible', 'gamma', 'p rho^-gamma', 'polytropic', 'expansion', 'rho(z)', or use of the ideal-gas law to vary density along the flow, when paired with earlier statements like 'incompressible', 'density change negligible', 'rho constant', or use of Bernoulli in its constant-density form. If both are present, flag an assumption-method mismatch and note that continuity (B = A v for constant A and stated volumetric flow) and incompressible Bernoulli should be used instead, without adiabatic expansion.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Misapplication of wall boundary conditions at non-boundary locations
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: Flag solutions that enforce impermeable-wall boundary conditions (no-penetration: v·n = 0) at points not on the wall. The no-penetration condition must be satisfied on the wall surface(s) only; it does not constrain the velocity at interior points or at singularities (e.g., vortex filaments) that are merely near the walls. In method-of-images arguments, images are chosen to enforce v·n = 0 on the boundary; this does not imply that the velocity at the real filament/source has zero normal components relative to the walls. Trigger when the solution claims statements such as 'the velocity components perpendicular to both walls are zero at the filament' or any equivalent inference applying wall boundary conditions at the filament or other interior locations. Also verify that superfluid/ideal flow boundary treatment distinguishes no-penetration from no-slip (no-slip does not generally apply); only v·n = 0 on the wall should be enforced. The rule checks that boundary conditions are applied on the correct geometric set (the boundary surfaces), not at interior points unless the object is explicitly at the boundary.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Detect extra layer-length factors in ΔP_i/L_i for two-layer Darcy flow
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: This rule checks algebraic steps in 1D Darcy flow through two layers in series (flow normal to layers) for improper handling of layer lengths when partitioning pressure drop. Context: two layers with permeabilities k1, k2 and thicknesses L1, L2; common flow rate Q; total pressure drop ΔP = ΔP1 + ΔP2; Darcy relations Q = (k1 A/μ)(ΔP1/L1) = (k2 A/μ)(ΔP2/L2). The correct expressions for the pressure partition are: ΔP1 = [(L1/k1) / (L1/k1 + L2/k2)] ΔP and ΔP1/L1 = [(1/k1) / (L1/k1 + L2/k2)] ΔP = [k2 / (k2 L1 + k1 L2)] ΔP (and symmetrically for layer 2). The rule verifies that any intermediate or final expression for ΔP1/L1 or ΔP2/L2 has a coefficient on ΔP with units 1/length and is algebraically equivalent to one of the correct forms above. It flags errors where an extra division by a layer thickness (e.g., an uncanceled L1) is introduced during substitution, producing coefficients with spurious products like L1·L2 in the denominator that do not cancel, or with dimensional inconsistency (coefficient units 1/length^2 or other non-1/length units). Specifically, the rule triggers if: (a) the parsed coefficient multiplying ΔP in ΔP_i/L_i contains L1·L2 (or higher powers of Li) in the denominator without an identical factor in the numerator, (b) the simplified form is not equivalent to k_j/(k_j L_i + k_i L_j) for i≠j, or (c) dimensional analysis of the coefficient yields units other than 1/length. The rule also raises a warning if such an inconsistent intermediate step appears even when the final k_eff or Q is correct, to highlight transient algebraic/units errors.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Boundary value claimed as optimal without model-based optimization
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: This rule flags solutions that declare an 'optimal' value equal to a stated constraint bound (upper or lower) without performing any optimization or using the governing physical relations. Applicable to problems that explicitly require choosing an optimal parameter (e.g., antenna length s, resonance condition, switching threshold) based on circuit or wave dynamics. The verifier checks: (1) whether the final chosen value exactly matches a constraint limit mentioned in the problem; (2) whether the solution derives or cites an objective/optimality criterion (e.g., quarter- or half-wavelength, resonance/impedance matching, instability threshold) and uses the relevant model equations; (3) whether the solution computes the dependent physical quantity that determines the optimum (e.g., oscillation frequency from circuit parameters R, C, and nonlinear element characteristics) and maps it to the target variable; (4) whether a monotonicity or boundary-optimality justification is provided (e.g., showing the objective is monotonic over the feasible interval). If the answer equals a bound and the solution lacks both a derived criterion and a calculation tying parameters to the optimum (or lacks monotonicity analysis), the rule marks a logic error: 'constraint bound taken as optimal without analysis.' This catches cases like setting s to the maximum allowed length solely due to the constraint, instead of determining s from wavelength/frequency or resonance determined by circuit parameters.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Missing/Incorrect validity interval for intersection-based quantities
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: This rule checks that any solution deriving quantities at the intersection of two shapes (e.g., rings/circles) whose relative position changes over time explicitly states and correctly applies the time (or parameter) interval over which the intersection exists. Specifically, for two identical circular rings of radius R in a vertical plane, initially coincident, with one ring in free fall under gravity, the center separation is d(t) = (1/2) g t^2. Intersection points exist only if d(t) ≤ 2R, which implies the valid time interval is 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 sqrt(R/g). The rule flags solutions that: (a) present expressions for intersection-based quantities (e.g., centripetal acceleration of intersection points relative to the fixed ring center) without specifying any validity interval; (b) specify a time interval but do not enforce d(t) ≤ 2R; or (c) provide an incorrect interval (e.g., t_max ≠ 2 sqrt(R/g)). This rule also applies to analogous problems where intersection existence requires an inequality (e.g., discriminant ≥ 0, distance ≤ sum of radii), and the solution must state and use the corresponding domain.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Continuity with non-zero source/sink must show flux change
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: Checks continuity statements in steady flows when a volumetric source/sink (e.g., uniform α, injection, losses) is present. If the problem specifies a non-zero source/sink per unit volume S(x) ≠ 0, the solution must not assert constant mass/particle flux along the flow or equate fluxes at two positions (e.g., φ(s1) = φ(s2)). The correct continuity condition is φ_out − φ_in = ∫_V S dV over the volume bounded by the two cross-sections; in 1D this is d(ρ v A)/ds = S A(s), and for uniform α it reduces to φ(s2) − φ(s1) = α · V_between. The rule flags solutions that: (a) claim flux is constant or set φ(s1) = φ(s2) despite a stated source/sink; (b) write ∇·(ρ v) = 0 or d(ρ v A)/ds = 0 when S ≠ 0; (c) omit the source term in the integrated continuity; or (d) use the wrong integration volume (e.g., total jet volume instead of the subvolume between s1 and s2) when relating flux difference to α. The rule passes when the solution explicitly includes the source term and correctly relates the flux difference to the integrated source over the appropriate region.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Volumetric source must be integrated to modify cross-sectional flux
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: Checks continuity/conservation equations that relate mass or particle flow rate through a cross-section (e.g., ṁ = ρ v A or N˙ = n v A) to sources/sinks. If a volumetric source term α (units: quantity per volume per time, e.g., M·L^-3·T^-1 or particles·L^-3·T^-1) is added/subtracted directly to a flow rate using only the cross-sectional area A(s), i.e., terms like α·A(s), the rule flags a dimensional inconsistency because α·A(s) has units quantity·L^-1·T^-1, not quantity·T^-1. The source contribution must be integrated over a volume between two stations: Δflow = ∫_{s1}^{s2} α(s) A(s) ds (or α·A·Δs when constant), or equivalently α·V for uniform α over a known volume V. For particle-number formulations, the rule also checks that any conversion between mass and particles uses the mean particle mass μ_pp, e.g., ΔN˙ = (α/μ_pp)·V. The rule permits derivative forms d/ds(ṁ) = α(s)·A(s) (or d/ds(N˙) = α_n(s)·A(s)) but flags expressions where α·A(s) appears added to ṁ or N˙ without an explicit integral over s or multiplication by a length/volume. It performs unit consistency checks: RHS must match the units of the LHS flow rate. Example of incorrect form to flag: ṁ(s2) = ṁ(s1) + α·A(s). Correct forms to accept: ṁ(s2) = ṁ(s1) + ∫_{s1}^{s2} α(s) A(s) ds; for constant α and A, ṁ(s2) = ṁ(s1) + α·A·(s2 - s1) = α·V.

Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.title: Continuity relation must include specified global volume V
Fluid Mechanics and Continuity.description: This rule checks that when a problem explicitly requests a continuity (mass or particle flux) relationship 'in terms of' a global volumetric quantity (e.g., the total jet volume V), the derived expression includes that quantity explicitly or via an equivalent integral representation. Implementation details: (1) Parse the problem statement to identify required variables that must appear in the final expression (e.g., V, 'total volume', 'V_jet'). (2) Inspect the student's final continuity equation(s) and supporting derivations to confirm that V appears as a symbol in the relationship or that an integral over the jet geometry that equals V is included (e.g., V = ∫ A(s) ds or ∫ dV). (3) If the solution uses only local geometric terms (such as A(s1), A(s2), A(s), or cross-sectional areas at specific positions) without incorporating the global volume V or its integral definition, flag the solution as a modeling mismatch. (4) Also flag cases where V is mentioned separately but does not actually enter the continuity relation (i.e., the equation does not depend on V). This rule is designed to catch errors where students ignore required global quantities and instead provide purely local expressions, contrary to the problem’s 'in terms of ... V' specification.

Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.title: Misplaced boundary condition for capillary surface: z(0)=0 instead of far-field z(∞)=0 and wall slope
Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.description: Checks boundary conditions in static capillary surface problems near a vertical wall/board. If the problem statement specifies that far away the free surface is horizontal at z=0 and gives a contact angle θ0 at the wall (x=0), the correct boundary conditions are z(∞)=0 (far-field height reference) and z'(0)=tan(θ0) (or z'(0)≈θ0 under small-slope approximation). Flag a solution if it imposes z(0)=0 without explicit and consistent redefinition of the height origin, or uses a height condition at the wall instead of a slope/contact-angle condition. Also flag if the far-field condition is omitted or incorrectly translated to a local condition at x=0. Accept solutions that either (i) use z(∞)=0 and z'(0)=tan(θ0), or (ii) explicitly shift the vertical reference (e.g., choose z(0)=0) but then correctly adjust the far-field condition to z(∞)=const≠0 and keep the contact angle as a slope at the wall. This rule targets unjustified or inconsistent boundary conditions that lead to incorrect modeling of the meniscus profile.

Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.title: Zero perpendicular velocity at symmetry plane (ice divide / centerline)
Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.description: This rule verifies that solutions invoking a mirror-symmetry plane or axis (e.g., an ice divide at x = 0, centerline, mid-plane) enforce the correct boundary condition: the velocity component normal to the symmetry plane must vanish at the symmetry location. For a symmetry plane at x = 0 in Cartesian coordinates, the condition is v_x(0, z) = 0 for all z (and more generally, the normal component v_n = 0 at the plane). The rule flags the following issues: (1) The solution explicitly assigns a nonzero value to v_x at x = 0, or implies it by stating v_x is uniform/constant in x with a nonzero value; (2) The solution omits the boundary condition v_x(0, z) = 0 while using symmetry arguments (e.g., ‘flow away from the divide’) or outflow only at ±L; (3) The solution fails to recognize that symmetry requires v_x to be an odd function of x, hence v_x(0) = 0. This check applies to incompressible or compressible flows alike when a geometric symmetry plane is invoked. Trigger examples: ‘ice divide at x = 0’ + ‘v_x independent of z’ + ‘v_x = const ≠ 0’; ‘centerline symmetry’ but v_x(0) ≠ 0. If any such condition is detected, the rule reports a boundary-condition violation due to neglected symmetry.

Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.title: Incompressible continuity requires balanced divergence terms
Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.description: Checks misuse of the incompressible continuity equation. For steady incompressible flow, the continuity equation enforces ∇·v = 0 (e.g., ∂v_x/∂x + ∂v_y/∂y + ∂v_z/∂z = 0; in 2D, ∂v_x/∂x + ∂v_z/∂z = 0). It is incorrect to conclude that one derivative term (e.g., ∂v_z/∂z) is approximately zero solely because another term (e.g., ∂v_x/∂x) is 'small but nonzero'. The terms must balance: each nonzero contribution must be offset by others so their sum is exactly zero (e.g., ∂v_z/∂z = −∂v_x/∂x). This rule flags solutions that: (1) write the continuity relation and then set one term to ≈ 0 due to the smallness of another term without showing it is identically zero; (2) set each divergence term to zero individually without additional justified constraints (symmetry, boundary conditions, or true independence implying the corresponding derivative is exactly zero with respect to its own variable). Acceptable reasoning must either (a) demonstrate a term is exactly zero from proper independence (e.g., v_x independent of x ⇒ ∂v_x/∂x = 0), or (b) explicitly balance nonzero terms to satisfy the zero-sum requirement.

Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.title: Velocity-Accumulation Dimensional Consistency and Surface Kinematic Boundary
Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.description: This rule verifies dimensional consistency when a velocity component (e.g., v_x, v_z) is expressed using the accumulation rate c in ice-sheet or similar flow problems. It flags any instance where a velocity is equated to c divided by a spatial increment, length scale, or spatial derivative (e.g., c/dx, c/Δx, c/∂x), because c has units of length/time (L/T) and dividing by length produces 1/T, which is not a velocity. The rule also enforces the kinematic surface boundary condition: at a flat upper surface with accumulation rate c, the normal component of velocity must equal c (up to sign), not c/length. Detection patterns include (but are not limited to): v_* = c / L, v_* ≈ c / (dx), v_* ~ c / (∂x), or using c multiplied by a dimensionless gradient operator without an explicit length scale restoring L/T. Any velocity expression whose right-hand side reduces to 1/T, T^-1, or a dimensionless quantity is flagged as dimensionally incorrect.

Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.title: Surface mass-balance must be per unit area (no extraneous dx/dA)
Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.description: Checks that the kinematic boundary condition at a free surface uses accumulation/ablation as an areal rate (units of length/time) without multiplying by geometric factors like dx or dA unless an explicit area integration is being performed. Triggers when a solution writes a mass-balance such as ρ·c = ρ·v_z(z=H)·dx, v_z(H) ∝ c·dx, or c·Δx, which incorrectly treats the accumulation rate c (m/s or m/yr) as a line or area-integrated flux. Correct usage: the boundary condition at the surface is v_z(z=H) = ±c (sign depends on convention; downward positive gives v_z = +c, upward positive gives v_z = −c), and at the bed v_z(z=0) = 0 (no penetration). Units consistency: c and v_z must both have L/T; any occurrence of c multiplied by a length or area (dx, dy, dA, width, thickness) in a pointwise boundary condition is flagged. Exception: geometric factors are permitted only when the equation explicitly represents an integral over a control surface, e.g., ∫_A c dA = ∫_A v_z dA, with both sides using the same area element. The rule also suggests verifying incompressibility application: ∂v_x/∂x + ∂v_z/∂z = 0 implies a linear v_z(z) profile under the stated separability assumptions, but the primary check is misuse of geometric factors in the surface mass-balance boundary condition.

Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.title: Incompressible glacier: vertical velocity profile and logarithmic age must be derived
Capillarity and Glacier Dynamics.description:
This rule verifies solutions for glacier/ice‐sheet age at the ice divide under incompressible flow with constant accumulation. It checks that the solver (1) derives the vertical velocity profile v_z(z) consistent with incompressibility and boundary conditions, and (2) integrates to obtain the age τ(z). Specifically:

- Preconditions this rule looks for in the problem statement or assumptions:
  - Incompressible ice (mass conservation: ∂v_x/∂x + ∂v_z/∂z = 0).
  - Accumulation rate c is constant at the surface.
  - Velocity independence: v_x independent of z; v_z independent of x (so ∂v_z/∂z is constant).
  - Boundary conditions at the divide: v_z(0) = 0 (no penetration at bed), v_z(H_m) = c (downward accumulation at surface; sign tolerance allowed).

- Required derivations the solution must include:
  1) An explicit vertical velocity profile v_z(z) that is linear in z and satisfies both boundary conditions. Accepted forms: v_z(z) = (c/H_m)·z or v_z(z) = −(c/H_m)·z depending on sign convention, with v_z(0) = 0 and |v_z(H_m)| = |c|. Equivalently, ∂v_z/∂z is a constant equal in magnitude to c/H_m.
  2) The age function τ(z) obtained by integrating the inverse vertical velocity from depth z to the surface: τ(z) = ∫_z^{H_m} dz'/v_z(z'). The final simplified form must be logarithmic in z, e.g., τ(z) = (H_m/c)·ln(H_m/z) up to sign/convention. Units must be time (e.g., years), with H_m/c dimensionally time.

- The rule flags a logic error if any of the following occur:
  - The solution invokes incompressibility but does not derive v_z(z) explicitly.
  - v_z(z) is not linear in z or violates v_z(0) = 0 and v_z(H_m) = c (up to sign).
  - τ(z) is not obtained via τ(z) = ∫_z^{H_m} dz'/v_z(z') or does not simplify to a logarithmic dependence (e.g., gives τ ∝ z, τ ∝ H_m − z, or a constant τ).
  - Misapplication of incompressibility leading to ∂v_z/∂z = 0 in this setup.
  - Dimensional inconsistency: τ not proportional to H_m/c or lacking time units.

- Allowed variations:
  - Sign conventions (upward positive vs downward positive) are accepted if boundary magnitudes and monotonicity are correct.
  - Equivalent algebraic forms of the logarithmic age (e.g., τ = −(H_m/c)·ln(z/H_m)).

This rule targets the common omission/logic error where the vertical velocity profile and subsequent age integral are not carried through or are derived with an incorrect functional form.

General Verification and Parameterizatio.title: Enforce requested-variable parameterization (no speculative redefinitions)
General Verification and Parameterizatio.description: This rule checks that the final expression is presented strictly in the variables requested by the problem and does not rely on speculative or inconsistent symbol redefinitions. Specifically: (1) Extract the set of required variables from instructions of the form "express your answer in terms of ..." (e.g., A_req = {P, ε, F'(r_h)}). (2) Build an allowed symbol set A = A_req ∪ {numeric constants, π, explicitly permitted physical constants if stated (e.g., c, G)}. If the problem text specifies a compound token like F'(r_h), treat it as an atomic allowed token; appearances of r_h outside this exact token are not allowed unless r_h itself is listed in A_req. (3) Parse the student’s final answer/expression and collect all free symbols and functions with their arguments; normalize whitespace and notation (e.g., F'(r_h), dF/dr|_{r_h}). (4) Fail if any symbol appears that is not in A (e.g., r_h appears freely when only P is allowed, or r is used instead of P). (5) Fail if both a required symbol is missing (e.g., P absent) and an unrequested stand-in is used (e.g., r_h or r present) without an explicit equivalence mandated by the prompt. (6) Fail if the solution introduces speculative or uncertain redefinitions of symbols (heuristic text scan for phrases like "I assume P = ...", "P might be ...", "probably", "guess", "let P be" when not supported by the prompt) or mixes notations (uses both P and r_h for the same quantity). (7) If the prompt requires F'(r_h) specifically, do not accept substitution by F'(P) unless the prompt explicitly states r_h ≡ P; allow r_h only inside the exact token F'(r_h) otherwise. This rule flags answers that do not express the result exclusively in the requested parameterization or that rely on unjustified/ambiguous symbol mappings.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Use tangential component (F·v̂) for speed/energy with anisotropic friction
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description:
This rule flags solutions that use the magnitude of the friction force |F| to compute deceleration or work in problems where friction is direction-dependent (anisotropic) and thus not generally collinear with the velocity. Checks:
- If the friction law is anisotropic (e.g., Fx = -(N/|v|) μx vx, Fy = -(N/|v|) μy vy with μx ≠ μy, or any stated direction-dependent μ), the change of speed and kinetic energy must be computed from the tangential component of friction, not from |F|.
- Flag statements like m dv/dt = -|F|, dv/ds = -|F|/m, dK/ds = -|F|, or W = -∫|F| ds when no projection onto the velocity direction is performed.
- Require the correct relations: dv/dt = (F · v̂)/m, dK/dt = F · v, dK/ds = F · v̂. For the common anisotropic model Fx = -(N/|v|) μx vx, Fy = -(N/|v|) μy vy, one must use F · v = -(N/|v|)(μx vx^2 + μy vy^2) and therefore dv/dt = -(N/(m |v|^2))(μx vx^2 + μy vy^2).
- Allow |F| to be used for speed/energy only if the solution explicitly shows F is parallel/antiparallel to v (e.g., isotropic Coulomb friction F = -μN v̂ or a scalar times v̂). Otherwise, using |F| overestimates dissipation by including components orthogonal to v that do no work on speed.
The rule triggers when a solution with anisotropic friction updates speed or energy using |F| instead of the tangential projection F · v̂.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Velocity–position angle mismatch in anisotropic friction with circular constraint
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description: Checks for misuse of the position/rod angle as the velocity direction when computing anisotropic friction components. Trigger conditions: (1) The problem or solution invokes anisotropic kinetic friction with component form F_x = -( |N| / |v| ) μ_x v_x and F_y = -( |N| / |v| ) μ_y v_y. (2) The motion is constrained by a rigid rod or a fixed-radius circular path, and an angle φ is defined as the rod orientation or the polar angle of the radius vector. Violation pattern: The solution sets v_x = v cos φ and v_y = v sin φ (or equivalently uses φ directly in friction components) where φ is explicitly the rod/position angle, without introducing a tangent-direction angle α. In circular motion the velocity is tangent, so its direction must satisfy α = φ ± π/2, implying v_x = v cos(α) = -v sin φ and v_y = v sin(α) = v cos φ (up to sign by rotation sense). Using v_x = v cos φ, v_y = v sin φ with φ as the rod/position angle misidentifies the velocity direction and yields an incorrect φ-dependence for friction and energy dissipation. Detection heuristics: flag if the text defines φ as a rod or position angle and later uses v_x = v cos φ, v_y = v sin φ (or substitutes φ directly into F_x, F_y) without a ±π/2 shift or explicit tangent relation; also flag if energy loss F·v or friction magnitude depends on cos^2 φ and sin^2 φ of the position angle rather than the tangent angle. Correction guidance: require defining α = φ ± π/2 for the velocity direction and computing v_x, v_y (and hence F_x, F_y) using α, not φ.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Require power-based (F·v) speed evolution under anisotropic friction
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description:
Checks solutions to problems that specify anisotropic kinetic friction (e.g., Fx = -(N/|v|) μx vx and Fy = -(N/|v|) μy vy with μx ≠ μy) for the correct treatment of speed evolution. Flags the common mistake of using a 1D scalar deceleration law m dv/dt = -|F| or dK/dt = -|F| |v| (i.e., assuming the friction force is exactly opposite to the velocity) instead of using the power F·v. The rule expects one of the following equivalent correct treatments:
- Power balance: dK/dt = F·v = -N |v| (μx cos^2α + μy sin^2α), where α is the angle between v and the primary X axis.
- Tangential acceleration: a_t = dv/dt = (F·v)/(m |v|) = -(N/m)(μx cos^2α + μy sin^2α); on a horizontal plane with N = mg, a_t = -g(μx cos^2α + μy sin^2α).
- Arc-length form: d(v^2)/ds = -2 g (μx cos^2α + μy sin^2α) for horizontal motion.
The rule triggers if:
- The solution collapses anisotropy into a single scalar law such as dv/dt = -μ g, m dv/dt = -|F|, or dK/dt = -|F||v|, without projecting F onto the velocity direction.
- The magnitude |F| is used to compute speed decay (e.g., treats |F| = N μeff and uses it directly in dv/dt or power) rather than using F·v or Ft = F·v̂.
- An "effective μ" is formed from μx and μy (e.g., μeff = sqrt(μx^2 cos^2α + μy^2 sin^2α)) and then used as if the friction were colinear with v.
Do not flag when the friction is isotropic (μx = μy) or the motion is explicitly and consistently constrained along a single primary axis (so that v is always along X or Y and the chosen μ matches that axis). Evidence of correctness includes explicit use of F·v, Ft = F·v̂, cos^2α/sin^2α weighting, or the stated differential forms above.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Verify work–energy setup for anisotropic friction under rotation
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description:
This rule checks solutions that use the work–energy theorem for a body constrained by a rotating rod on a horizontal plane with anisotropic friction defined by Fx = −(N/|v|) μx vx and Fy = −(N/|v|) μy vy. It flags errors where friction work is computed using the magnitude |F| or a single constant μ, instead of the directional projection F·v. Expected setup for an arc displacement ds = L dφ is dW = F·dr = −N (μx cos^2φ + μy sin^2φ) L dφ, leading to the energy relation v^2(φ) + g L [ (μx + μy) φ + (μx − μy) sin(2φ)/2 ] = v0^2 (with N = m g; equivalent rearrangements accepted).

The rule triggers if any of the following are detected:
- Work integral written as W = −∫ |F| L dφ, W = −∫ μ N L dφ with μ constant, or using an incorrect angular dependence (e.g., μx cosφ + μy sinφ, or √(μx^2 cos^2φ + μy^2 sin^2φ)).
- Final v^2(φ) expression lacks the sin(2φ) term or contains only a linear φ dependence.
- Incorrect coefficients: the linear φ term must have coefficient g L (μx + μy), and the sin(2φ) term must have coefficient g L (μx − μy)/2 (up to overall sign conventions and mass factors if not divided out).
- Small-angle consistency check: if a small-φ expansion is presented, dv^2/dφ at φ → 0 must equal −2 g L μx; deviations indicate misuse of the anisotropic friction projection or incorrect path length.

This rule is intended to catch the common mistake of using the friction magnitude in the work integral and to ensure the characteristic anisotropic angular dependence (linear φ plus sin 2φ term) appears in the v^2(φ) result.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Do not modify total normal force due to in-plane spin on a horizontal surface
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description: Checks solutions where a body slides on a horizontal surface while spinning about a vertical axis (ωr ≪ v) and ensures the total normal force is not altered by rotation. Flag as incorrect if the solution: (a) claims that the total normal force N depends on angular speed (e.g., N = mg + f(ω) or N = mg + m ω^2 r), (b) attributes a change in friction magnitude μN to a rotation-induced change in N via a 'centrifugal' effect, or (c) computes N by integrating dm·ω^2·r or similar horizontal fictitious/centrifugal forces. In such setups, with no vertical acceleration, the vertical force balance requires N = mg (or N = mg adjusted only for vertical components of other external forces or inclines). Rotation about the vertical axis may redistribute contact pressure around the ring but does not change the total normal force. Any change in the net friction force arises from the distribution and direction of local slip velocities v_rel = V + ω × r over the contact, not from a change in N. The rule allows N to vary only if the solution explicitly includes vertical acceleration, surface inclination/curvature causing vertical components, aerodynamic/other vertical forces, or geometric lift/tilt that alters vertical equilibrium. It also flags mixing of inertial-frame analysis with fictitious centrifugal forces to modify N in a purely horizontal, steady-contact case.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Do not alter total normal force using spin/centrifugal arguments in planar sliding with Coulomb friction
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description: Scope: Rigid body sliding on a flat horizontal surface under Coulomb friction (constant μ), with no vertical acceleration and small superposed rotation (ω r << v). The verifier checks that the total normal force N is determined by vertical force balance and is not modified by the body's spin. Checks performed: (1) Vertical equilibrium: Require N ≈ mg (or mg minus any explicitly modeled vertical forces) whenever the motion has no vertical acceleration and the surface is horizontal. Flag any dependence N = N(ω, v, r) introduced without vertical dynamics (e.g., adding ΔN terms due to rotation). (2) Centrifugal misuse: Flag use of centrifugal/centripetal arguments to change the total normal load in an inertial-frame contact problem on a flat surface. Internal rotational effects may redistribute pressure but must not change ∑p dA = N = mg. (3) Friction magnitude modeling: If the solution modifies the magnitude of the net friction force via F_fric = μ (mg + ΔN(ω,...)) to account for spin, flag as incorrect; spin should instead affect the distribution of frictional stress and frictional torque via the local slip velocity, not the total N. (4) Dimensional sanity: Flag any ΔN expression whose units are not force (e.g., terms like m ω^2 r^2 / v, m ω r, etc.). (5) Correct approach expectation: For spinning sliders, require that rotational effects be modeled by integrating local friction stresses over the contact (e.g., ring) using the local relative slip speed v_rel(φ) = |v + ω × r(φ)| to obtain net force/torque, while keeping ∫p dA = N = mg. (6) Allowed exceptions: Do not flag if the solution explicitly and consistently models scenarios that can change N (inclined/curved surfaces, vertical acceleration, aerodynamic lift, velocity-dependent normal load, or non-Coulomb friction with stated assumptions). The presence of terms labeled ‘centrifugal’ or explicit ΔN(ω,...) on a flat, horizontal, non-accelerating contact without such exceptions triggers this rule.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Dimensional and scaling check for friction/normal-force corrections under small rotation
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description: This rule verifies dimensional consistency and correct small-rotation scaling in expressions for the normal force N, its change ΔN, the friction force F_friction = μN, and its change ΔF when a sliding body (e.g., a curling stone) is given a small angular speed ω with ω r << v. The checker enforces: (1) Force units: Any claimed expression for N, ΔN, F_friction, or ΔF must have units of Newtons (kg·m·s⁻²). It flags terms like m·(ω² r² / v) (units kg·m·s⁻¹) or μ m·(ω² r² / v) as dimensionally incorrect for a force. (2) Presence of g in baseline friction: For horizontal sliding with gravity as the source of the normal force, the friction magnitude must scale as μ m g at leading order. If an expression for F_friction or ΔF contains only μ and m with no acceleration scale (e.g., no g or equivalent acceleration), it is flagged as missing g. (3) Correct small-rotation dependence: The leading-order correction due to rotation must be proportional to a dimensionless factor built from the small parameter ε = ω r / v (specifically O(ε²)), not linear in ε and not containing v to the first power in the denominator. The rule flags corrections that scale like μ m g·(ω r / v) or μ m·(ω² r² / v), and accepts forms like ΔF ≈ C·μ m g·(ω r / v)², where C is an O(1) numerical factor (exact C is not enforced). (4) Heuristic dimensional check of correction terms: For terms involving ω, r, and v, the verifier computes exponents p, q such that the factor is ω^p r^p v^q. To be dimensionless, p must equal 2 and q must equal −2 (or equivalent combinations yielding no net dimensions). Any non-dimensionless factor multiplying μ m g (or m times an acceleration) is flagged. This rule will catch errors like ΔN ≈ −m(ω² r² / v) and ΔF ≈ μ m(ω² r² / v), which have incorrect units, omit g, and use the wrong dependence on v.

Anisotropic Friction and Energy.title: Unjustified series expansion and fictitious-force reasoning in Coulomb friction with small rotation
Anisotropic Friction and Energy.description:
This rule flags solutions that claim a change in friction force due to rotation using series/binomial expansions or centrifugal-force arguments without a physically grounded derivation. It applies to rigid bodies sliding on a flat surface under Coulomb (velocity-independent) kinetic friction. The rule checks for the following:
- A series/Taylor/binomial expansion is applied to the friction force (or μN) without first defining an explicit analytic dependence F_friction(v, ω, …) or μ(v), and without introducing a dimensionless small parameter.
- The solution invokes 'centrifugal force' (or similar fictitious forces) to argue a redistribution of the normal force N in an inertial-frame analysis, when the body is simply sliding on a plane with no vertical acceleration or constraints that would alter N.
- The solution asserts that small rotation (ω r ≪ v) changes the magnitude of the net friction force without computing the local slip velocity around the contact (e.g., v_local(θ) = v − ω × r) and integrating the Coulomb friction density over the contact to obtain the net force/torque, or without a symmetry/first-order argument that the magnitude remains ≈ μN while torque is affected.
- The final simplification uses binomial/Taylor steps (e.g., (1 + ε)^n ≈ 1 + nε) that do not follow from any derived friction expression and lack a clear connection to physically relevant quantities (local slip speed distribution, contact pressure).
A solution is flagged if any of the above occurs, i.e., expansion without a defined function and small parameter, fictitious-force modification of N in an inertial analysis, or omission of the necessary contact-level integration/symmetry argument before concluding a changed friction magnitude.

Static and Kinetic Friction.title: Static friction must be solved as an unknown within |f| ≤ μN; do not set f = μN unless at impending slip
Static and Kinetic Friction.description: Checks that, in problems asserting rolling without slipping or static contact, the friction force is not incorrectly modeled as a constant f = μN (or f = μmg) or with a fixed direction by assumption. The verifier will: (1) Detect statements like “f = μN”, “f = μmg”, “friction equals μN”, or the use of kinetic friction while the text also claims no slip/rolling without slipping. (2) Require that static friction be introduced as an unknown f with sign to be determined, together with the inequality bound |f| ≤ μN (N possibly time/angle dependent), and that f be solved from force/torque balance and any rolling constraints (v_cm = rω, a_cm = rα). (3) Accept setting f = μN only if the solution explicitly justifies impending slip/limiting friction with a threshold argument (e.g., “at the verge of slipping”, “maximum static friction”, complementarity/slip condition). (4) Flag solutions that treat friction as constant in magnitude or direction throughout without deriving it from dynamics, especially when external forces/geometry imply f may vary with time/angle or change sign. (5) Require a post-check that the computed |f| stays ≤ μN over the assumed no-slip interval; if it exceeds μN, the model must switch to slipping/kinetic friction. This rule targets errors like setting f = μmg from the outset in rolling problems (e.g., a hoop pulled at its rim), where the correct static friction generally depends on the motion and may be zero initially or change sign.

Static and Kinetic Friction.title: Kinetic Friction Work Must Be Negative in Energy Balances
Static and Kinetic Friction.description:
Checks the sign of the kinetic friction work term in work–energy or energy conservation equations. The verifier searches for segments where mechanical energy is related across a leg of motion (e.g., from x=a to x=b) and a kinetic friction term appears (tokens such as μ, μ_k, f_k, W_f, friction, multiplied by m g or N and a displacement s, x, or Δx). For horizontal motion with normal force N = m g, the work done by kinetic friction over a positive path length L must be W_f = − μ_k m g L (negative) regardless of direction; friction cannot increase mechanical energy.

Detection criteria:
- Identify equations of the forms: (K_f + U_f) = (K_i + U_i) + W_nc, or ΔE_mech = W_nc, or E_available(start) ± (friction term) = E_required(end), etc.
- If the friction term appears with a positive sign contributing to energy (e.g., + μ m g L, + f_k L, or is added to available energy), flag an error. Valid forms include subtracting friction work (e.g., − μ m g L) or defining W_f explicitly negative.
- Specifically flag relations like 1/2 k x_max^2 = (energy at start) + μ m g x_max (or any positive friction term), which imply friction increases energy during the leg of motion.
- Accept equations where W_nc includes multiple non-conservative terms as long as the friction component is negative (e.g., W_nc = − μ m g L + other terms).

Rationale: Kinetic friction always dissipates mechanical energy; its work must reduce the mechanical energy available. Any positive friction work term in the energy balance indicates a sign error that can lead to incorrect amplitude/kinetic energy calculations.

Static and Kinetic Friction.title: Misapplied incline friction (μ ≥ tanθ) and wrong friction location in toppling analyses
Static and Kinetic Friction.description:
This rule flags solutions that (a) borrow the block-on-incline friction condition (e.g., μ ≥ tanθ, μ = tanθ, or references to the angle of repose) for contacts that are declared smooth, or (b) use the wrong contact to supply friction when analyzing tipping/toppling. Specifically, it checks for:

- Use of patterns like “μ ≥ tanθ”, “μ = tanθ”, “mu >= tan”, or “angle of repose” to determine motion/tipping when the problem states a smooth contact for that interface (e.g., chain–surface, rope–support, bead–wire). If the text contains both an explicit smooth-contact statement (keywords such as “smooth surface/contact”, “no friction”) and a friction law at the same interface (e.g., “f = μN” or “friction = μN”), flag.
- Application of a friction law f = μN at an interface that the problem states is smooth; e.g., a chain or rope on a smooth support, bead on a smooth track, etc. Detect via proximity of “smooth” to the named interface and subsequent use of “μN” for that interface.
- Tipping/toppling criteria expressed directly in terms of μ (or incline-type inequalities) without any moment/torque balance or geometric condition about the base/pivot (e.g., no mention of “moment”, “torque”, “pivot/edge”, “line of action”, “base width”, “normal reaction shift”). If toppling is concluded using only μ ≥ tanθ or similar, flag.
- Friction attributed to the wrong contact for resisting tipping (e.g., using chain–pillar friction to prevent/topple the pillar when that contact is smooth), while failing to analyze the pillar–ground friction which is the correct location for sliding resistance.

The expected correct approach for toppling is: determine when the resultant line of action passes through the base edge or when the net moment about the would-be pivot changes sign; the ground friction coefficient μ only appears to ensure no sliding occurs before tipping. Do not flag if the problem genuinely involves a rough incline where μ ≥ tanθ is the correct condition at that specific interface, or if μ is used solely to compare sliding vs tipping at the ground contact accompanied by a clear moment analysis around the base.

Static and Kinetic Friction.title: Incorrect fixed friction under no-slip or velocity-proportional conditions
Static and Kinetic Friction.description:
This rule flags solutions that incorrectly assign a fixed Coulomb friction magnitude (e.g., F = μN or F = μmg) when the contact is described as no-slip/static or when the problem specifies a different friction law (e.g., friction proportional to velocity). The rule checks for the following:
- The solution asserts equality F = μN (or F = μmg) at a contact while also stating or implying no slip, static friction, or walking/rolling without slipping, without demonstrating that the contact is at the threshold of slip (|F| = μ_s N) or that kinetic friction applies. Static friction should be modeled as an adjustable constraint force with |F| ≤ μ_s N; equality is only valid at impending or actual slip.
- The problem states that friction at a specific interface is proportional to velocity (linear drag), yet the solution uses a Coulomb model (μN) for that interface instead of f = -k v.
- The problem states no friction at an interface, yet the solution introduces any nonzero friction force at that interface.
- The solution introduces or uses a specific friction magnitude for an internal contact (e.g., child–slab) to determine system-level horizontal displacement or momentum balance in a closed system where the result should not depend on μ unless slip is proven. Internal friction should not be treated as an external horizontal force for the composite system.
The verifier should flag phrases/patterns such as: "F = μN", "F = μ mg", "assume constant friction μN", or use of μ in final displacement/momentum formulas in contexts that assert no slip or specify velocity-proportional friction. The expected correct modeling is: treat static friction as an unknown within bounds (no fixed value unless slip occurs) and use drag f = -k v when the problem specifies velocity-proportional friction.

Static and Kinetic Friction.title: Static friction must be a bounded reaction, not a fixed μ_s N
Static and Kinetic Friction.description:
Flag solutions that model static friction during no-slip (sticking) as a constant force equal to μ_s N rather than a reaction that adjusts up to its maximum. The correct modeling for a sticking contact is: (i) enforce zero relative motion at the contact (v_rel = 0), (ii) treat the static friction force F_s as an unknown satisfying |F_s| ≤ μ_s N and directed to prevent slip, and (iii) determine slip onset by checking whether the required friction magnitude reaches μ_s N (|F_required| = μ_s N). After slip begins, the kinetic friction magnitude should be μ_k N opposing the direction of slip.

Detection criteria (any trigger should flag):
- Textual assertions in the no-slip regime like "static friction equals μ_s N", "F_f = μ_s N when not sliding", or equivalent statements that set F_static to a fixed magnitude without an inequality or a threshold check.
- Equations or ODEs for a sticking phase that include a constant ± μ_s N term for the friction force, instead of solving for an unknown friction that enforces v_rel = 0 and checking |F_s| ≤ μ_s N.
- Absence of the inequality |F_s| ≤ μ_s N and of a stick/slip decision based on comparing the required friction to μ_s N; i.e., the solution never computes the friction needed to prevent slip nor verifies it against the static limit.

Expected correct structure:
- Sticking phase: impose v_rel = 0 (or x_dot equals the driver velocity), solve dynamics with F_s as an unknown reaction, verify |F_s| ≤ μ_s N; slip starts when the bound is met.
- Sliding phase: set |F_k| = μ_k N opposite slip direction.

This rule targets the common modeling error of treating static friction as always μ_s N during adhesion, which misrepresents the dynamics and the slip threshold.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Rolling-without-slip must use kinematic constraint; friction limit (f=μN) or T=μmg is not a valid substitute
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description:
This rule flags solutions that (a) equate the static friction force to its maximum value (f = μN) or set an applied horizontal force equal to μmg to claim 'rolling without slipping' or to locate a turning point in a rotational coordinate, and/or (b) omit the rolling-without-slip kinematic constraint. Detection criteria:
- If the solution claims or implies 'rolling without slipping' (phrases like 'no slip', 'rolls without slipping') but does not introduce the kinematic relation v_cm = r·ω (or a_cm = r·α with appropriate sign), flag.
- If the solution directly sets f = μN (or |f| = μN) without explicitly arguing impending slip or deriving f from Newton/Euler equations with the inequality |f| ≤ μN, flag.
- If the solution asserts a critical force condition like T = μmg (or T/(μmg) = 1) as the criterion for no slip or for a local extremum of an angle, flag unless it is clearly justified as a slip-threshold check after solving dynamics.
- For problems where a force is applied at a point that moves with the body (e.g., a constant horizontal tension at the rim of a rotating hoop), check torque expressions: if torque is treated as constant in time/angle and contains no θ-dependence (e.g., no sinθ/cosθ factor for the changing lever arm), flag any conclusions about local maxima/minima of θ based solely on constant-force equalities (like T = μmg).
Rationale: Rolling without slipping is enforced by the kinematic constraint (v_cm = r·ω or a_cm = r·α), not by equating forces to the friction limit. The friction limit |f| ≤ μN only saturates at impending slip. Conditions for an extremum in θ(t) must come from the time/angle-dependent torque and the friction inequality, not from setting T equal to μmg.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Include rotational inertia and rolling constraint for inner rolling cylinder oscillations
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description: When a uniform solid cylinder (mass m, radius r) rolls without slipping on the inner surface of a larger cylinder (radius R), the model must include both translational and rotational kinetic energy and enforce the rolling constraint. The correct small-oscillation dynamics about the bottom position uses: I = (1/2) m r^2, the no-slip constraint φ̇ = ((R - r)/r) θ̇, total kinetic energy K = (1/2) m (R - r)^2 θ̇^2 + (1/2) I φ̇^2 = (3/4) m (R - r)^2 θ̇^2, and potential U ≈ (1/2) m g (R - r) θ^2. This yields the linearized equation (3/2) m (R - r)^2 θ̈ + m g (R - r) θ = 0, natural frequency ω0^2 = 2 g / [3 (R - r)], and period T = 2π √[3 (R - r)/(2 g)]. The verifier should flag a modeling error if: (a) the rotational kinetic energy term is omitted or I is not used for a solid cylinder, (b) the rolling constraint linking the spin φ̇ and the orbital angle θ̇ is missing or incorrect, (c) the effective inertia in front of θ̈ is m (R - r)^2 (simple pendulum) rather than (3/2) m (R - r)^2, or (d) the reported period reduces to the simple pendulum form T = 2π √[(R - r)/g] (or equivalent) instead of T = 2π √[3 (R - r)/(2 g)]. Additionally, check that the final expression depends on R and r only through (R - r), consistent with the rolling constraint for a solid cylinder.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Normal force at circular rolling contact gives no torque about the body’s center
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description: Checks torque balances written about the rolling body’s own central axis in problems involving a circular rigid body (e.g., a cylinder or disk) in point contact with another circular surface under pure rolling. For such contacts, the normal reaction acts along the line joining the centers and passes through the rolling body’s center of mass; therefore, its moment about that center is zero. The rule flags solutions that include a nonzero torque term attributed to the contact normal (e.g., τ_N = N · (R − r) · sinθ or similar) when the torque is taken about the small body’s center. It also flags omission of the frictional torque (which should be ±f · r) when modeling the spin equation I·α = Στ about the center. Exceptions: do not flag if the solution explicitly computes torque about a different axis (not the small body’s center), if the contact geometry is non-circular or off-axis so the normal does not pass through the center (e.g., cam profile, asymmetric deformation), or if the model states distributed contact with a resultant normal having a known offset. Applies in both no-slip and slip cases (in slip, friction is kinetic but still the only contact force producing spin torque). The verifier should parse torque equations and associated axis statements; if an N term appears in Στ_about(center of the small body), or a lever arm for N about that center is treated as nonzero, raise a modeling error.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Incorrect rolling-without-slipping constraint on inner surface (frame-mixing)
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description: Checks kinematic constraints for a body rolling without slipping on the INNER surface of a cylinder. For a small cylinder of radius r rolling inside a larger cylinder of radius R, the correct no-slip relation between its spin about its own axis (φ) and the orbital angle of its center (θ) is r·φ̇ = (R − r)·θ̇ (equivalently φ̇ = ((R − r)/r)·θ̇, up to an overall sign). The rule flags the following violations: (1) Frame-mixing: φ̇ written with an additive term in the container’s angular velocity ω (e.g., φ̇ = ((R − r)/r)·θ̇ + ω, φ̇ = θ̇ + (R − r)/r·ω, or any φ̇ = a·θ̇ + b·ω with b ≠ 0) in the no-slip constraint. The container’s ω must not enter additively; the constraint must be stated in a single frame (typically the container frame), relating φ̇ solely to θ̇. (2) Use of absolute values in the constraint (e.g., |φ̇| = ((R − r)/r)|θ̇|), which drops the physically relevant sign and direction of rolling. (3) Incorrect geometric factor: using (R + r)/r, R/r, or φ̇ = θ̇ for inner rolling. (4) Setting the contact-point velocity to zero in the lab frame (e.g., v_contact(lab) = 0) rather than equating the velocities of the two contacting surfaces in the same frame. If any of these patterns are detected in the stated no-slip relation, flag a concept error: mishandled rolling constraint on inner surface.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Inconsistent use of moment of inertia about contact point in rolling dynamics
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description:
Checks for misuse or inconsistent use of the moment of inertia taken about the contact point (via the parallel-axis theorem) in rolling-without-slipping analyses. The rule flags solutions that: 
- Explicitly compute or reference I about the contact point (e.g., I_contact = I_cm + m r^2, commonly 3/2 m r^2 for a solid cylinder) and then mix this with center-of-mass rolling constraints (v_cm = ω r or a_cm = α r) without a consistent torque reference. 
- Use τ = I α with I_contact while summing torques about the center of mass, or include a nonzero friction torque in τ about the contact point while simultaneously treating the contact as the instantaneous center. 
- Treat the contact point as an instantaneous axis without stating or ensuring that the contact point is instantaneously at rest in an inertial frame; for rolling on a moving/rotating surface, using I_contact without introducing the necessary additional terms for rotation about a moving point (e.g., m r × a_P or equivalent transport/acceleration corrections) is flagged. 
- Mention I_contact (e.g., “I = 3/2 m r^2”) but then fail to use it consistently in subsequent equations, or switch back to I_cm without justification. 
Rationale: For rolling without slipping, a consistent approach is to write dynamics about the center using I_cm together with the no-slip kinematic relation. Using I about the contact point is valid only if equations are written about an instantaneous center that is fixed in an inertial frame and torques are summed about that point with proper treatment of moving-axis effects. This rule detects logical inconsistency and misuse that typically leads to incorrect equations of motion or oscillation periods.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Missing rotational inertia factor in period of rolling small oscillations
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description: Checks solutions to small-oscillation problems where a rigid body rolls without slipping (e.g., a cylinder or sphere on a circular track) to ensure the period T includes the rotational inertia correction required by the rolling constraint. Trigger conditions: the problem statement contains phrases like "rolls without slipping" and asks for the period of small oscillations about equilibrium; the final period is expressed as T = 2π √(L/g) with L a geometric length (e.g., R or R − r) and lacks the dimensionless factor √(1 + I/(m r^2)). Correct formulation: for a body of mass m, radius r, and moment of inertia I about its center, moving on a path of effective radius L (e.g., L = R − r for rolling inside a cylinder), the period must scale as T = 2π √(L/g) × √(1 + I/(m r^2)). Shape-specific checks: solid cylinder I = (1/2) m r^2 ⇒ factor √(3/2); solid sphere I = (2/5) m r^2 ⇒ factor √(7/5); hoop I = m r^2 ⇒ factor √(2). Flag as an error if the reported T omits this factor or uses a factor inconsistent with the object's stated geometry/inertia. Also flag if the derivation shows kinetic energy or equations of motion that include only translational terms (½ m v^2) while explicitly stating rolling without slipping, since the rotational term (½ I ω^2) must be present and leads to the same correction.

Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.title: Avoid energy-based v–ω relation for impact coefficient s in polygonal rolling
Rolling Dynamics and Constraints.description: This rule flags solutions that introduce conservation of mechanical energy to relate translational speed v and angular velocity ω before an edge-impact when the task is to find the coefficient s in ω_f = s ω_i for a non-circular body (e.g., a regular hexagonal prism). Energy is not conserved across the impact, and s must be obtained from angular momentum balance about the instantaneous contact edge (using the given I about the center and I' about the edge via the parallel-axis theorem) and appropriate impulsive kinematics. The rule triggers if any of the following are detected: (1) The solution invokes conservation of mechanical energy prior to the impact to derive a v–ω relation; (2) The solution uses a circular rolling constraint v = ω R for a polygonal cross-section, e.g., taking R = a or R = sqrt(3)/2 * a, without deriving the correct instantaneous geometry or constraints for edge contact; (3) The energy-derived v–ω relation is extraneous and not used to compute s. Correct verification expects angular momentum about the new contact point and the provided moments of inertia, not pre-impact energy relations.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Improper assumption of constant static friction and constant torque with changing geometry
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: This rule flags solutions that incorrectly assume (1) static friction is always at its limiting value and constant (f = μN) without establishing slip or verifying the inequality |f| ≤ μN, and/or (2) the torque from a force applied at a body-fixed point is constant despite a changing moment arm with the rotation angle θ. The rule targets rotating/rolling systems where a force has a fixed direction in the inertial frame but is applied at a point that moves with the body (e.g., a horizontal tension applied at the top of a rolling hoop). Detection heuristics: (a) the solution uses f = μN as an equality without an explicit slip/impending-slip argument or subsequent inequality check; (b) the torque from the applied force is written as τ = T r (or another constant) without any θ-dependent factor (e.g., no sinθ or cosθ dependence) when the geometry implies a varying lever arm; (c) the derived angular acceleration α is a constant function of parameters (T, μ, m, g, r, etc.) with no θ dependence in a setup where torque should depend on θ. If any combination of these patterns appears, flag as incorrect friction/torque modeling.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Unjustified switch to kinetic friction or fixed f=μN yielding spurious constant threshold
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description:
Flag solutions that determine a threshold for a local maximum in angle (or reversal of angular velocity) by (a) asserting kinetic friction or switching friction models without first proving slip onset, or (b) treating friction as f = μN identically (constant μmg) throughout without enforcing the static-friction bound |f| ≤ μN and checking when it is exceeded, and then (c) producing a simple constant threshold (e.g., T/(μmg) = 3/2 or 1.5) not derived from the equations of motion. The rule checks for the following red flags:
- Mentions of “kinetic friction,” “sliding friction,” or a separate μ_k (or a mid-solution ‘transition to kinetic friction’) when the problem provides a single μ and the solution does not explicitly demonstrate slip onset by requiring |f_required(θ)| > μN.
- Setting f = μN (or f = μmg) as an equality from the outset, used through the derivation without any inequality |f| ≤ μN, no case distinction for sticking vs slipping, and no check that the required static friction exceeds μN.
- Absence of a correct local-maximum condition for θ(t), e.g., no explicit use of dθ/dt = 0 (ω = 0) and sign change or ω(θ) analysis (energy/torque integral) to identify reversal, while still claiming a threshold.
- A final threshold for T/(μmg) reported as a small, simple constant (specifically flag values like 3/2 or 1.5, or a constant independent of any θ-dependent analysis) with no derivation tied to torque/ω(θ) and the static-friction limit.
If any combination of the above is detected—particularly a kinetic-friction switch without proof of slip and/or a fixed f = μN assumption leading to T/(μmg) = 3/2—the solution is flagged as conceptually incorrect for failing to apply the static-friction inequality and the correct reversal condition.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Local extremum requires zero velocity (or angular velocity), not zero force/torque
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: Detects the misuse of acceleration-level conditions (net force F=0, acceleration a=0, net torque τ=0, or angular acceleration α=0) as the criterion for a local maximum/minimum of a coordinate. For any claim that x(t) or θ(t) has a local extremum, the solution must set the first derivative to zero (v(t*)=0 for position or ω(t*)=0 for angle) and verify a sign change or second-derivative test (e.g., a(t*)<0 or α(t*)<0 for a local maximum). Flag the solution if it asserts an extremum occurs when τ=0 or α=0 (or F=0 or a=0) without explicitly setting ω=0 (or v=0) and checking a sign change/second-derivative condition. Additionally, if a constant-torque/constant-acceleration model is used, require that an extremum arises from ω crossing zero; merely noting that torque crosses or equals zero at an instant is insufficient and should be flagged.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Misclassifying θ̈ ∝ sinθ·θ̇ (or θ·θ̇) as linear/SHM under small-angle approximation
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: This rule verifies the correctness of linearization and classification of equations of motion that contain multiplicative state–velocity terms. It triggers if a solution derives or uses an equation of the form q̈ = k·f(q)·q̇ (common examples: θ̈ = k·sinθ·θ̇, θ̈ = k·cosθ·θ̇, ẍ = k·x·ẋ), and then: (a) applies small-angle/small-displacement approximations (e.g., sinθ ≈ θ, cosθ ≈ 1) and claims the resulting ODE is linear or first-order linear in the state, or (b) treats the system as simple harmonic motion (uses SHO terminology/solutions), or (c) solves it using linear time-invariant methods (e.g., assumes exponential/sinusoidal solutions with constant coefficients). The checker flags this because such equations remain nonlinear after small-angle approximations: products like q·q̇ or f(q)·q̇ are not linear in the dependent variable; linear ODEs cannot contain products of the state and its derivative, and their coefficients must depend at most on time. The rule also flags statements that interpret terms proportional to q̇ or q·q̇ as a restoring torque/force (implying oscillation) rather than (state-dependent) damping/anti-damping. Correct linearized second-order form near equilibrium must be q̈ + a(t) q̇ + b(t) q = g(t) with coefficients independent of q and q̇; any residual multiplicative q·q̇ indicates nonlinearity.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: No sinusoidal motion in purely dissipative rotational models
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: Flags solutions that assert oscillatory/sinusoidal time dependence (e.g., θ(t) ∝ sin/cos, V(t) ∝ sin/cos, use of a 'natural frequency') when the modeled dynamics include only dissipative torque proportional to angular velocity and no restoring torque or reactive energy storage. Specifically: if the governing equation inferred or stated is of the form I·θ¨ + γ·θ̇ = 0 (or more generally contains only θ̇ and no term ∝ θ, and no external periodic drive), the motion cannot be sinusoidal; the correct homogeneous response is monotonic/exponential decay of θ̇ and non-oscillatory evolution of θ. The rule also checks for contexts where the circuit is open and self-inductance is neglected (no L/C elements, no current), in which case magnetic torque due to induced current is absent; any claim of post-disconnection sinusoidal rotation or sinusoidal V_PQ(t) without a justified restoring mechanism (gravity, spring, inductive inertia, LC resonance, or an explicit periodic drive) is marked as a modeling error.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Unjustified constant angular velocity assumption for a constraint
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description:
This rule flags solutions that assume a constant angular velocity (ω = const) for a constraining link (e.g., rod, string) without explicit justification from the problem statement or an identified external driver, especially when dissipative forces (e.g., friction) are present and the motion is governed by v = L dφ/dt. Checks performed:

- Context detection: If the problem involves a point mass constrained by a rod/link of fixed length L and includes friction (isotropic or anisotropic) that causes speed to decay, then v is not constant and, via v = L dφ/dt, ω should generally vary unless an external actuator enforces ω.
- Assumption scan: Detect phrases or steps asserting or implicitly using constant angular velocity, such as "assume ω is constant", "constant angular speed", "φ = ω t", "uniform rotation", or using a time integration that presumes ω is fixed.
- Consistency check: If the solution elsewhere uses energy dissipation or variable-speed relations (e.g., friction work, v decreasing, v = L dφ/dt) while also assuming ω = const without specifying an external torque/power maintaining ω, flag a contradiction.
- Problem-statement alignment: Do not flag if the problem explicitly states the rod is externally driven at constant ω or prescribes ω(t), or if the student introduces and uses an external driving torque/power to justify constant ω.
- Unnecessary parameter introduction: If ω is introduced as a constant and later abandoned (not used in final derivation), or replaced by v = L dφ/dt without a consistent transition, flag as an unnecessary/misleading assumption.

Rationale: In constrained systems with friction and no specified driver, ω is a dynamical variable tied to v via v = L dφ/dt; assuming ω = const biases the analysis and can yield incorrect or inconsistent results. The correct approach is to use the kinematic relation directly and derive ω from the dynamics or energy balance.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Incorrect assumption that static friction acts purely perpendicular to velocity (constant speed during turning)
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: This rule flags solutions to turning/reorientation problems on low-friction surfaces (e.g., ice) that (a) treat the horizontal friction force as the only available control force with magnitude bounded by μN, and simultaneously (b) assert that friction acts purely perpendicular to the velocity so that the speed (or kinetic energy) remains constant while changing direction. Typical indicators include statements like: 'friction provides the centripetal acceleration', 'friction is perpendicular to velocity, so it does not change speed', 'static friction does no work', or use of a_c = v^2/R with v held constant, combined with F_fric = μ m g as the sole horizontal force. In such settings, unless an additional propulsive force or explicit constraint is provided to enforce constant speed, static friction can point in any horizontal direction up to magnitude μN and generally has a tangential component that does work on the center of mass, changing the speed. For minimum-time reorientation with bounded |F| and only friction available, the optimal maneuver uses the full friction magnitude with a nonzero tangential component, reducing speed during the first part of the turn and increasing it later to satisfy the final speed constraint (e.g., speed dips below the initial value during a 90° turn). The rule should trigger when a solution: 1) assumes constant speed throughout the turn without additional forces or constraints to justify it; 2) models friction solely as a centripetal force or strictly perpendicular to velocity over the entire maneuver; or 3) claims static friction does no work on the moving person/object. The verifier should require either (i) an explicit justification for constant speed via other forces balancing the tangential component, or (ii) a work-energy/optimal-control argument acknowledging that friction may (and in minimum-time problems should) have a tangential component that changes speed. Absent such justification, flag the solution as a conceptual error.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Unjustified circular-path time for minimal-direction change
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: Flags solutions to minimal-time direction-change problems (constant speed, bounded acceleration/friction) that compute time as arc length of a circular segment divided by speed without a valid optimality justification. Typical pattern: use the friction limit to set a_max = μ g, infer a circular trajectory via centripetal acceleration v^2/R = a_max to get R, set arc length s = θ R for a heading change (e.g., θ = π/2), and conclude t = s/v. The rule triggers when: (1) time is obtained via t = s/v from a geometric arc (phrases like 'arc length', 'quarter circle', 'path length', 'circumference'); (2) centripetal acceleration and radius are used (e.g., R = v^2/a, v^2/R) to justify the path; and (3) there is no explicit argument that the chosen trajectory is both feasible under the acceleration bound and time-optimal (e.g., no discussion that acceleration direction is a control variable, that |a| should be held at the bound and perpendicular to velocity to maximize angular rate ω = a⊥/v, or derivation of t from velocity-vector rotation t = Δθ/ω). The rule targets the logic error of inferring minimal time from geometric path length rather than from the bounded-acceleration control required to reorient the velocity vector, even if the numerical result coincides with the correct formula.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Disallow phantom elastic potential energy terms (rope/pulley not elastic)
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description:
Checks energy-method setups to ensure elastic potential energy is assigned only to declared elastic elements (springs) and not to inextensible ropes or inertial components.
- Parse the problem statement to identify the set of elastic elements and their stiffnesses (e.g., springs with constants k, 2k). Record the count and labels of springs.
- Inspect the user’s potential energy U expression. Verify that U_elastic is a sum of quadratic terms 1/2 * k_i * x_i^2 only for the identified springs; flag any additional quadratic elastic term not mapped to a declared spring or elastic component (e.g., a rope or pulley).
- If the rope is described as inextensible/massless (or otherwise non-elastic), ensure no term of the form 1/2 * K_rope * x^2 appears; flag such terms as modeling errors.
- Ensure rotational components (e.g., pulley with moment of inertia) appear only in kinetic energy, not in potential energy. Flag any 1/2 * I * ω^2 mistakenly placed in U.
- Cross-check effective stiffness: for symmetric motion where both springs extend by the same displacement y, the total elastic potential must equal 1/2 * k * y^2 + 1/2 * (2k) * y^2 = (3/2) * k * y^2. Flag any effective stiffness exceeding the sum implied by the declared springs (e.g., an incorrect (7/2) * k * y^2 arising from a fictitious third spring).
- Also verify coordinate mapping consistency: if the solution asserts x1 = x2 = y by symmetry, ensure no additional independent x3 appears without a corresponding physical spring.
This rule triggers when the energy method includes fictitious elastic terms (e.g., a third 1/2 * 2k * x^2 term for a rope) or otherwise inflates the elastic potential beyond what the physical springs justify.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Misuse of terminal velocity with time-varying viscous drag in thin-film sliding
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: Flags solutions that invoke a constant-coefficient terminal-velocity model for viscous sliding when the drag coefficient b(t) = η A(t) / Z is time- or position-dependent due to changing contact area. This rule applies to plate/slide problems with a lubricating film where the overlap area A decreases or otherwise varies during motion. It checks for the following patterns: (1) The solution treats A as a fixed full-plate area (e.g., A = L·W) instead of a function of overlap length/position/time, or never expresses A = W·ℓ(t/x). (2) The equation of motion is written as m dv/dt = mg − b v with constant b, or the solution introduces a constant terminal speed v_t = mg/b and/or an exponential approach v(t) = v_t (1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = m/b, despite geometric/time dependence of A. (3) The solution uses phrases such as "terminal velocity", "reaches steady speed after a long time", or presents a constant τ without justifying that b is constant. (4) In thin-film (lubrication) regimes, inertia is retained without a timescale check (e.g., estimating τ_inertial = m Z /(η A) and comparing to motion times), and no quasi-static force balance mg = η (A/Z) v(t) is applied. The rule expects either an instantaneous force balance with A(t) explicitly modeled or a justified constant-area scenario; otherwise, it flags the misuse of terminal velocity and constant-drag assumptions.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Incorrect use of radius of gyration (k) as a geometric distance
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: This rule checks for misuse of the 'radius of gyration' by equating it to a geometric distance or using it as a rolling/contact radius. The radius of gyration for a specified axis must be defined by k = sqrt(I/M), where I is the moment of inertia about that axis and M is the mass. It depends on mass distribution and the chosen axis, not merely on distances like center-to-edge, circumradius, inradius, or contact radius. The rule flags a solution if any of the following are detected: (1) The phrase 'radius of gyration' (or synonyms: 'gyration radius', 'radius of inertia') or the symbol 'k' is explicitly set equal to a geometric dimension (e.g., 'k = a', 'k equals distance from center to edge/vertex', 'k equals the pencil radius', 'k equals the contact radius'). (2) The equation I = M r^2 is used with r described as a geometric distance (e.g., center-to-edge, circumradius, inradius, distance to contact point) without deriving r from I/M, i.e., without stating that r is k = sqrt(I/M) for the relevant axis. (3) k is used interchangeably with the rolling radius in kinematic relations (e.g., v = ω k) or impact geometry without first computing k from I and M or citing a correct known formula for k for the specified axis. (4) The radius of gyration is invoked without specifying the axis of rotation. The rule passes if the solution introduces the axis and defines k via k = sqrt(I/M), or uses a correct known expression for k for the shape and axis (derived from its moment of inertia), and does not conflate k with purely geometric distances.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Incorrect static vertical force balance during rotating rod motion
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description: Checks for the misuse of static vertical force balance (e.g., N = mg or N = mg cosθ) in problems where a rigid rod pivots/falls about a contact point on horizontal ground. In such dynamic scenarios, the center of mass has vertical acceleration, so ΣF_y ≠ 0 and the normal force must satisfy N − mg = m a_y. For a uniform rod of length ℓ pivoting about its bottom end, the CM vertical acceleration is a_y = −(ℓ/2)(θ'' sinθ + θ'^2 cosθ). The rule flags a solution if, while analyzing a rotating/tilting/falling rod (mentions of θ varying, nonzero θ' or θ'' or use of torque/rotation equations), it contains any of the following: (1) Equations setting N = mg cosθ or N = mg; (2) Statements asserting ΣF_y = 0 or "no vertical acceleration"; (3) Treating the normal force as a component of weight (e.g., using mg cosθ as the ground normal) or computing friction f_s = μ_s N with N obtained from static balance in a dynamic rotation context. The correction requires using N − mg = m a_y with the appropriate kinematics of the center of mass.

General Misconceptions and Assumptions.title: Core vs crust volume/mass assignment consistency
General Misconceptions and Assumptions.description:
