Checks that, for a spherical (or nearly spherical) body partitioned into an inner core (interior) of radius R_int and an outer crust (shell) extending to an outer radius R_out, the volumes and masses are assigned to the correct regions.

The verifier will:
- Identify symbols used for radii: outer radius (e.g., R_out, R, R_avg, R_surface, R_e for spherical approximation) and interior/core radius (e.g., R_int, r_core).
- Accept the spherical approximation where R_out is taken as an average/surface radius when flattening is small.

Required geometry relations:
- Interior/core volume: V_core = (4/3)π R_int^3
- Crust/shell volume: V_crust = (4/3)π (R_out^3 − R_int^3)

Mass assignment (single density ρ):
- M_core = ρ · V_core
- M_crust = ρ · V_crust

Flag as an error if any of the following are detected:
- The interior/core volume is computed as the shell volume: V_core = (4/3)π (R_out^3 − R_int^3).
- The crust/shell volume is computed as the inner solid sphere: V_crust = (4/3)π R_int^3.
- Masses are assigned with these swapped volumes (e.g., M_crust = ρ · (4/3)π R_int^3 while M_core = ρ · (4/3)π (R_out^3 − R_int^3)).

Additional consistency checks:
- If distinct densities are used (ρ_core, ρ_crust), verify that each density multiplies the correct region volume (ρ_core with V_core, ρ_crust with V_crust).
- If moments of inertia are later derived from these assignments, warn if a solid-sphere inertia is applied to the crust or a thin-shell inertia is applied to the core, indicating region-role reversal.

This rule is intended to catch the common core–crust reversal where the interior is mistakenly treated as the shell and the crust as the inner sphere.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Account for friction-shifted equilibria in spring–block systems with Coulomb friction
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description: This rule checks whether a solution to a spring–mass problem on a horizontal surface with dry (Coulomb) friction correctly identifies and uses the friction-shifted equilibria and piecewise dynamics. Specifically, the verifier will: (1) Require the force model during motion to be stated as F_net = -k x - sgn(v)·μ m g (or equivalent piecewise form), and at rest to apply static friction |F_s| ≤ μ_s m g with the condition for impending motion |k x| = μ_s m g. (2) Require explicit identification of the dynamic equilibrium positions at x = ±(μ m g / k) (locations where acceleration is zero for each direction of motion under kinetic friction), and recognition of the static “dead zone”/rest interval |x| ≤ μ_s m g / k. (3) Require that the term “equilibrium position” be interpreted correctly in the presence of friction (i.e., not assumed to be x = 0 as in the frictionless case) and that turning points and maximum displacements be referenced relative to the appropriate shifted equilibrium for the current direction of motion. (4) For oscillation/amplitude questions, expect acknowledgment that the amplitude decreases linearly by 2·(μ m g / k) per half-cycle under kinetic friction, or an equivalent energy-based argument that is consistent with the shifted equilibria. The rule will flag solutions that: (a) treat the equilibrium position as x = 0 without discussing friction-induced offsets, (b) omit the ±(μ m g / k) shift entirely when interpreting motion or computing return displacements, (c) fail to use a piecewise force law tied to the sign of velocity, or (d) compute displacements/energies as if the system were frictionless except for a single work term, with no reference to the dynamic/static equilibrium structure. Note: Computing kinetic energy at x = 0 via energy minus friction work can be acceptable for that specific part, but the solution must still demonstrate awareness of the shifted equilibria when the problem references an equilibrium position or amplitude evolution.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Linear amplitude decrement with Coulomb friction in mass–spring oscillations
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description: Applies to a horizontal mass–spring system with constant kinetic friction (force magnitude F_f = μ m g) and initial release from x = d. Under sliding conditions (μ_s > μ), the turning-point amplitudes decrease linearly by 2 μ m g / k per half-cycle. The correct first return maximum displacement to the right is x_max = d − 4 μ m g / k. The verifier checks: (1) Energy accounting per half-cycle uses W_f = μ m g × (path length), with friction opposing motion in each leg; (2) The left turning amplitude satisfies 1/2 k A_left^2 = 1/2 k d^2 − μ m g (d + A_left) and simplifies to A_left = d − 2 μ m g / k; (3) The right turning amplitude follows A_right = A_left − 2 μ m g / k, giving x_max = d − 4 μ m g / k; (4) The derived x_max is linear in d and μ m g / k (equivalently d − 4 F_f / k) and has correct monotonicity: decreases with μ, m, g and increases with k, with x_max < d; (5) Dimensional consistency: 4 μ m g / k has units of length. Flag a calculation/modeling/sign error if the solution produces a quadratic or square-root expression for x_max that does not reduce to the linear relation above, if x_max ≥ d, if friction work is not equal to μ m g times total travel, or if the amplitude decrement per half-cycle is not 2 μ m g / k.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Mischaracterizing Coulomb (sliding) friction as viscous damping with exponential decay to x=0
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description:
This rule checks solutions to problems that specify Coulomb/sliding friction (friction force of constant magnitude independent of speed, typically F_f = μ N opposing motion or using sign(v)) for incorrect qualitative behavior borrowed from viscous damping. It flags the following errors:

Trigger condition:
- The problem or the student's model includes sliding/Coulomb friction, e.g., terms like F_f = μ N, F_f = −μ N·sign(v), a sign(v) term, or text indicating friction independent of the magnitude of velocity.

Flag as incorrect if any of the following appear in the solution:
1) Exponential decay or viscous-damping classifications: The solution asserts or uses forms characteristic of viscous damping, such as x(t) ∼ e^{−bt}(A cos ω t + B sin ω t), mentions a damping ratio ζ, or labels the motion as underdamped/overdamped/critically damped, or otherwise claims exponential decay of amplitude for a system modeled with Coulomb friction.
2) Incorrect final state at x = 0: The solution claims that the mass necessarily comes to rest at x = 0 without addressing the static-friction threshold, i.e., without recognizing that the motion will stick once |x| ≤ μ N/k (for a mass–spring on a horizontal surface), and the final rest position can be anywhere in that interval depending on phase/history.
3) Missing stick–slip and shifted equilibria during slip: For a mass–spring with Coulomb friction, the slip dynamics are piecewise harmonic about shifted equilibria x_eq = ±(μ N)/k (depending on velocity sign) with amplitude decreasing linearly per half-cycle. Flag if the solution instead treats the dynamics as a single equilibrium at x = 0 during motion, or describes a smooth single-ODE viscous-like decay without sign-dependent switching, or claims exponential decay of amplitude.

Notes for verifier implementation (text cues to search):
- Presence of phrases like "exponential decay", "e^{-bt}", "under/over/critical damping", "damping ratio", or explicit linear viscous term c v in the solution when the friction model was given as Coulomb.
- Claims like "x → 0 as t → ∞" for Coulomb friction without mention of a sticking interval |x| ≤ μ N/k or static friction.
- Absence of any mention of sign-dependent force, stick–slip, or shifted equilibria in a Coulomb model combined with viscous-damping solution forms.

Rationale: Coulomb friction yields piecewise sinusoidal motion about x_eq = ± μ N/k with linear amplitude decay per half-cycle and eventual sticking within |x| ≤ μ N/k; it is not equivalent to viscous damping and does not generically produce exponential decay to x = 0.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Missing static friction (stick-slip) regime in Coulomb friction modeling
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description: This rule flags solutions that model dry (sliding/Coulomb) friction solely as F_f = -μN·sign(v) without handling the static friction condition at v = 0 and the associated stick-slip behavior. The checker looks for the following patterns and omissions: (1) Friction is written as F_f = -μN·sign(v) (e.g., -μmg·sign(v) on a horizontal plane) and used universally in the equation of motion m x¨ = ΣF, with no piecewise definition for v = 0. (2) No explicit static friction inequality is stated, i.e., absence of a condition of the form |F_tangential_applied| ≤ μ_s N implies v = 0 and friction adjusts within |F_f| ≤ μ_s N to prevent motion; and |F_tangential_applied| > μ_s N implies slip with |F_f| = μ_k N opposing impending motion. (3) The coefficient μ is treated as a single constant without distinguishing static (μ_s) and kinetic (μ_k), or without clarifying behavior at rest even if μ_s = μ_k (the direction at v = 0 must oppose impending motion to satisfy the inequality). (4) For mass–spring on a horizontal surface, the solution lacks an explicit stick region/dead band: |kx| ≤ μ_s N (equivalently |x| ≤ μ_s N/k), and/or concludes a unique final equilibrium at x = 0, ignoring that any x in [-μ_s N/k, μ_s N/k] can be a valid rest position. (5) Equilibrium or steady-state analysis sets v = 0 and keeps the sign(v) friction term without addressing its undefined sign at zero velocity, or uses continuous ODE integration with the sign(v) term across v = 0 without switching regimes. If any of these are detected, the solution is flagged for missing the static friction regime and misrepresenting the qualitative behavior (e.g., incorrect claim that the mass settles at x = 0 rather than within the stick band).

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Dry-friction oscillator: per-cycle work must use current amplitude; ΔA = 2 μN/k
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description:
Scope: Applies to mass–spring systems on a horizontal surface with sliding (Coulomb) friction modeled as F_f = -μN·sign(v) (with N = mg on a horizontal plane). The rule verifies energy-based or turning-point analyses over successive half-cycles.

What this rule checks:
- The work done by Coulomb friction over a half-cycle must be computed from the distance traveled between turning points: W_half(n) = μN [A_n + A_{n+1}], where A_n and A_{n+1} are successive turning-point amplitudes. Consequently, the per-cycle work W_cycle(n) = 2 μN [A_n + A_{n+1}] decreases as amplitude shrinks.
- The turning-point energy relation is used correctly: (1/2)k A_{n+1}^2 = (1/2)k A_n^2 − μN (A_n + A_{n+1}). Equivalently, the amplitude decrement per half-cycle is constant: ΔA = A_n − A_{n+1} = 2 μN / k, until the stall condition is reached.

Flag as error if any of the following are detected:
- The work by friction per cycle or half-cycle is taken as a constant based on the initial amplitude (e.g., W_cycle = 4 μN A0, W_half = 2 μN A0) and reused for all cycles, without updating A.
- The solution states or implies a constant per-cycle energy loss independent of the current amplitude (e.g., uses A0 in every cycle) for Coulomb-friction oscillations.
- The amplitude update across half-cycles is omitted or inconsistent with ΔA = 2 μN/k (e.g., exponential decay or geometric progression appropriate to viscous damping is used instead).

Pass criteria:
- The solution derives or uses A_{n+1} = A_n − 2 μN/k per half-cycle and, if computing work, uses W_half(n) = μN (A_n + A_{n+1}) or an equivalent decreasing per-cycle work expression tied to the current amplitude.

Rationale: In Coulomb-friction oscillations, the travel distance between turning points is A_n + A_{n+1}, so the frictional work per half-cycle decreases as the amplitude shrinks. Using the initial amplitude A0 for every cycle (e.g., W_friction = 4 μmg A0) overestimates the loss and yields incorrect dynamics.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Incorrect turning-point modeling in spring–mass with kinetic friction
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description: Checks solutions for 1D mass–spring motion with constant kinetic friction (Coulomb friction) released from x = d > 0. Correct dynamics: the mass initially moves left, passes x = 0 with leftward velocity, reaches a left turning point at x_left = -(d - 2 μ m g / k), then returns right. Energy is reduced by μ m g per unit distance traveled, causing the oscillation amplitude to decrease by 2 μ m g / k each half-cycle. The first right turning point is x_right = +(d - 4 μ m g / k), provided μ_s > μ and spring force at turning points exceeds static friction (as ensured by the given inequality). Flag the following modeling errors: (a) treating the crossing at x = 0 as the start of the rightward excursion and using K(0) (computed from motion d → 0) as the initial energy to find the next right turning point; (b) predicting the first right turning displacement as d - 2 μ m g / k (only accounting for one half-cycle loss); (c) writing an energy balance for 0 → x_right that uses K(0) without subtracting the additional friction work on the 0 → x_left leg; (d) any claim that the mass immediately proceeds to the right turning point after crossing x = 0 on the first pass. The verifier should expect amplitude reduction per half-cycle of 2 μ m g / k and the sequence of turning points: first left at d - 2 μ m g / k (on the negative side), then first right at d - 4 μ m g / k.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Amplitude in stick–slip driven oscillator must depend on driver speed, mass, spring, and friction difference
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description:
Applicability: Use this rule when the problem describes a mass–spring system driven by a plate moving at constant speed u, with normal load N and two friction regimes (static μ1 and kinetic μ2 where μ2 < μ1). The model includes parameters m, k, u, N, μ1, and μ2. Checks: 
- Extract the final expression for the amplitude A. If A does not contain u or does not contain m while both parameters are present in the model, flag an error: amplitude missing driver speed or mass. In stick–slip driven oscillators, the amplitude must depend on the driving speed and inertia. 
- If A uses only a single friction coefficient (only μ1 or only μ2) and does not involve the difference Δμ = μ1 − μ2 or an explicit conditional dependence on stick vs slip, flag an error: friction regime dependence omitted. 
- If A is of the form C·(μ N)/k (for any constant C) and is independent of u and m, flag as suspicious amplitude form: amplitude cannot be determined solely by static or kinetic friction and spring stiffness in a speed-driven system. 
- If the solution derivation switches from using μ2 to μ1 (or vice versa) in the final answer without a stated regime change or condition (e.g., the transition point between sticking and slipping), flag an error: inconsistent friction coefficient usage. Rationale: For periodic stick–slip under constant-speed driving, the amplitude depends on u, m, k, and the friction contrast (μ1 − μ2), and cannot be reduced to a function of μ and N alone.

Friction in Oscillatory Systems.title: Stick–slip threshold must be applied in friction-driven oscillator analysis
Friction in Oscillatory Systems.description: Applies to problems that specify distinct static and kinetic friction coefficients (μ1 > μ2) for a contact that drives a mass–spring system. The verifier checks that the solution explicitly uses the stick–slip transition criterion rather than assuming static friction is a fixed force. Required elements: (1) Static friction is treated as an adjustable force with magnitude ≤ μ1 N (not set equal to μ1 N during sticking), and the no-slip condition is stated as |F_required| ≤ μ1 N. (2) The slip onset is identified by the equality |F_required| = μ1 N. For the specific mass–spring driven by a plate moving at constant speed u, the solution must recognize that during stick the block’s velocity equals u, its acceleration is zero, and the required tangential force to maintain stick is the spring force F_required = k x; hence the transition is at |k x| = μ1 N. (3) During slip, the friction force magnitude is taken as μ2 N with sign opposing the relative motion, and the dynamics are written accordingly (e.g., m x¨ + k x = ± μ2 N). (4) The amplitude A is derived from these thresholds, showing dependence on μ1, μ2, N, and k (and noting u’s role via the stick phase), rather than ignoring the stick–slip mechanism. The rule flags solutions that: set F_static = μ1 N during stick without stating it is a variable up to μ1 N; omit the inequality/equality transition conditions (|F_required| ≤ μ1 N → |F_required| = μ1 N); fail to identify F_required = k x in the sticking phase with v_block = u; or present an amplitude independent of μ1, μ2, N, and k.

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Torque from a force applied at a body-fixed point must depend on orientation
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description:
Checks for the incorrect modeling of torque as constant when a force is applied at a fixed material point of a rotating rigid body and the force direction is fixed in the inertial frame. In such cases, the lever arm relative to the chosen axis changes with the body's orientation, so the torque must depend on the angle (e.g., θ).

What the rule checks:
- Context trigger: The solution involves a planar rigid body with a defined orientation variable (e.g., θ(t)) and an external force F applied at a point located a distance r ≠ 0 from the rotation axis. The point of application is attached to the body (body-fixed), while the force direction is stated or implied to be fixed in the lab frame (e.g., a constant horizontal or vertical pull, a constant wind force, etc.).
- Correct physics requirement: The torque contribution from that force about the axis must be τ(θ, t) = (r × F)·k, whose magnitude is r F sin φ(θ, t), where φ is the angle between the radius vector from the axis to the point of application and the force direction. Therefore, unless the line of action passes through the axis or special symmetry applies, τ must depend on θ (typically as sinθ or cosθ).
- Violation pattern: The solution assigns a constant torque magnitude equal to rF (e.g., τ = Tr) or any sign-fixed constant for that force, with no dependence on θ (or time) in a scenario where the point of application rotates with the body while the force direction does not. Examples to flag include: "τ_T = Tr", "I θ¨ = Tr − ...", or any torque term from the applied force that lacks θ dependence despite the above context.

Concrete example (this problem): A string applies a constant horizontal tension T at the material point initially at the hoop's top. The radius vector to that point rotates with the hoop, so the torque is τ_T(θ) = −T r cos θ (for CCW positive). Modeling τ_T as a constant ±Tr is incorrect and should be flagged.

Exceptions to avoid false positives:
- Do not flag if the force line-of-action rotates with the body in such a way that the perpendicular moment arm remains constant (e.g., a tangential force always tangent to a rim due to a string wrapped around it that turns with the body). In such cases, a constant torque may be correct.
- Do not flag if the force passes through the rotation axis (r⊥ = 0) or if geometry explicitly yields a constant perpendicular lever arm.

Implementation hints:
- Identify presence of θ(t) and an external force described as constant in direction in the lab frame (e.g., "constant horizontal T").
- Detect modeling of torque terms as constants of the form rF, Tr, or ±c without θ dependence for forces applied at body-fixed points at radius r.
- If the text mentions attachment to a specific point on the rim/edge/top/edge of a rotating body and a constant-direction force, require θ-dependence in the torque term. If absent, raise a modeling error with a suggested correction: τ(θ) = rF sin(φ(θ)).

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Rigid-body point-velocity sign analysis under off-center impulse
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule checks for incorrect assumptions about the direction of the rotational (ω × r) contribution relative to the translational center-of-mass (COM) velocity when computing the velocity of a point on a rigid body immediately after an impulse is applied at an offset from the COM. The verifier scans solutions to problems where a lateral impulse P is applied at a point located a distance from the COM (e.g., a rod of length 2ℓ with COM at ℓ above the bottom, impulse applied at height h). Correct analysis requires: (1) determining the sign of the induced angular velocity from the angular impulse L_z = (r_imp-from-CM) × P, which for the rod is proportional to (h − ℓ)P and thus ω_z ∝ sgn(h − ℓ); and (2) computing the point velocity using v_point = v_C + ω × r_point, so that the component along the impulse direction can be opposite to v_C depending on geometry. The rule flags solutions that: (a) unconditionally state that the rotational contribution at a specific point (e.g., the top end A) is in the same direction as the COM translational velocity without evaluating the sign via the cross product or the (h − ℓ) factor; (b) combine magnitudes as v_A = v_C + ω d (e.g., d = ℓ) without a sign or conditional dependence on h; or (c) present |v_A| = v_C + ω d as a magnitude expression without acknowledging that the correct magnitude is |v_C ± ω d| with the sign set by sgn(h − ℓ) via the right-hand rule. The rule accepts solutions that explicitly include the sign through a cross-product calculation, use a sgn(h − ℓ) factor, or write the magnitude as |v_A| = |v_C − ω ℓ| (or equivalently |v_C + sgn(h − ℓ) ω ℓ|), reflecting that the rotational term aligns with v_C only if the impulse point is above the COM (h > ℓ) and opposes it if h < ℓ. This rule generalizes to any rigid-body impulse problem where point velocities are formed by combining COM translation with rotation; unconditional same-direction claims for the rotational term are considered conceptual errors.

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Moment of inertia for two point masses connected by a massless rod
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description: When the system is explicitly described as two identical point masses m connected by a rigid rod of length ℓ whose mass is negligible, and rotation is about the center of mass around an axis perpendicular to the rod, the correct moment of inertia is I = m ℓ^2 / 2 (equivalently, I = 2 m (ℓ/2)^2 or I = μ ℓ^2 with μ = m/2). The verifier should flag solutions that: (1) use uniform-rod formulas such as I = (1/12) M ℓ^2 (about the rod’s center) or I = (1/3) M ℓ^2 (about an end), (2) include the rod’s mass in I despite the rod being stated as massless, or (3) give any expression for I proportional to m ℓ^2 with a coefficient different from 1/2 when m denotes the mass of each point particle. This rule targets modeling errors where the inertia of a point-mass dipole is incorrectly replaced by that of a continuous rod.

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Correct rotational kinetic energy for a two-mass dipole (I = μℓ^2)
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description: Checks that the rotational kinetic energy for a rigid two-point-mass dipole (dumbbell) rotating about its center of mass uses the correct moment of inertia. Applicability: two point masses m1 and m2 connected by a massless rod of length ℓ (ℓ is the full separation between masses), rotation about the center of mass with angular speed ω. Expected relations: I_expected = μ ℓ^2, where μ = (m1 m2)/(m1 + m2). Thus E_rot_expected = (1/2) I_expected ω^2. Special case (equal masses m): I_expected = m ℓ^2 / 2 and E_rot_expected = (1/4) m ℓ^2 ω^2. The rule flags errors if any of the following are detected: (a) the solution sets I = (m1 + m2) ℓ^2 or, in the equal-mass case, I = m ℓ^2 or I = 2 m ℓ^2; (b) the solution states E_rot = (1/2) m ℓ^2 ω^2 for equal masses when ℓ is defined as the rod length (full separation); (c) the coefficient of m ℓ^2 ω^2 in E_rot for equal masses is not 1/4; (d) the solution misinterprets ℓ as the radius to each mass (leading to I = 2 m ℓ^2) despite the problem defining ℓ as the distance between the masses. As a consistency cross-check, the rule also verifies that the translational kinetic energy of the center of mass uses the total mass: E_trans = (1/2) (m1 + m2) v_CM^2 (for equal masses: E_trans = m v_CM^2), and flags use of m or μ in place of (m1 + m2). The rule is insensitive to electromagnetic details (B-field) because the moment of inertia depends only on the mass distribution.

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Explicit accounting for imposed rotation ω in small-oscillation analysis
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description:
Checks that when a problem specifies a system constrained to rotate at a constant angular velocity (ω), the solution explicitly incorporates ω into the equations of motion or provides a clear derivation showing that ω does not affect the small-oscillation period. The rule triggers if ω is introduced and then omitted without justification, or if the final period is independent of ω but the solution does not demonstrate why.

Pass criteria (any one is sufficient):
- The solution works in the co-rotating frame and includes centrifugal (m ω^2 r_eff) and, where applicable, Coriolis terms in the equation of motion; identifies the shifted equilibrium due to ω; linearizes about that equilibrium; and shows that ω-dependent terms cancel from the small-oscillation frequency.
- The solution works in the inertial frame and incorporates the rotation of the constraint (e.g., moving contact point/geometry) so that ω appears in the kinematics/dynamics; then shows by derivation that ω only shifts the equilibrium and does not enter the linearized frequency.
- The solution explicitly states and proves that the equilibrium position depends on ω (e.g., via an effective potential or force balance) and that the second derivative (stiffness) at equilibrium is ω-independent, yielding a period independent of ω.

Fail conditions (any one triggers an error):
- ω is mentioned in the problem setup but is absent from the equations of motion, energy, or constraint relations, and no explanation is provided for its irrelevance.
- The final expression for the small-oscillation period omits ω without an explicit derivation demonstrating ω-independence (e.g., no equilibrium shift analysis and no cancellation shown).
- In a rotating-frame approach, pseudo forces (centrifugal/Coriolis) are not included or discussed, or the equilibrium about which linearization is performed is not adjusted for ω.

Scope notes: This rule targets small-oscillation problems with externally imposed constant rotation. It does not require ω to appear in the final period if the solution shows, step-by-step, why ω cancels or affects only the equilibrium position. It is acceptable to use either inertial or rotating frames, but the chosen approach must make the role of ω explicit and justify its absence from the final frequency, if applicable.

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Reject geometric-only h ≤ R(1−2/π) tipping condition; require torque about pivot with chain-induced lateral force and ground reaction shift
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule verifies the correctness of toppling criteria for a rigid pillar on rough ground with a smooth (frictionless) chain sliding over a curved top. It checks that the solution derives the toppling threshold from a moment (torque) balance about the impending pivot edge at the base, with the ground reaction shifting to that edge (normal at the opposite edge vanishes), and includes all relevant forces: (i) the pillar’s weight acting at its own COM, (ii) the chain’s weight acting at its instantaneous COM, (iii) the lateral (horizontal) and vertical components of the normal reaction transmitted by the smooth chain–pillar contact along the curved surface, and (iv) the ground reaction decomposed into normal and friction consistent with the roughness coefficient μ. The rule flags solutions that: (1) present a final toppling condition purely in geometric form h ≤ k·R (or h/R ≤ k) with a constant k≈0.36, specifically containing 1−2/π, or use the wrong inequality direction (e.g., h ≤ … where increasing h would incorrectly be said to promote tip), (2) omit the chain-induced horizontal push on the pillar in the moment balance, (3) treat the ground reaction as a single fixed upward normal at the base without shift to an edge at impending tip, (4) exclude μ entirely from the stability/slip-vs-tip discussion without justifying independence via required friction checks, or (5) misplace friction by applying f=μN at the chain–pillar interface despite it being smooth (frictionless). Acceptable solutions must either include μ explicitly in the tipping/sliding conditions or argue why the tipping threshold is independent of μ by comparing required ground friction to μ. They must also base the threshold on ΣM_about_pivot=0 at the instant of impending toppling and account for the chain’s contact-induced horizontal force on the pillar. Any occurrence of an h ≤ R(1−2/π)-type threshold, or absence of these elements, triggers a failure under this rule.

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Falling rod friction onset must use pivot torque, energy, and COM acceleration (μ_s ≈ 0.35 at 30°)
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description:
Checks solutions for a uniform rod of length ℓ and mass m falling about a non-slipping bottom end on rough ground at θ = 30°. The correct dynamic framework is:
- Use torque about the ground contact: τ = mg(ℓ/2) sin θ = I_end θ'', with I_end = (1/3) m ℓ^2. From this, θ'' = (3g/2ℓ) sin θ. Flag if I_end is not used (e.g., using I_C alone without the parallel-axis correction), or if τ uses cos θ instead of sin θ.
- Use energy conservation to get the angular speed vs angle: θ'^2(θ) = (3g/ℓ)(1 − cos θ). Flag if this relation is missing, has incorrect coefficients (e.g., missing the factor 3), or wrong dependence on cos θ.
- Compute center-of-mass acceleration components relative to the pivot: a_x = (ℓ/2)(θ'' cos θ − θ'^2 sin θ), a_y = −(ℓ/2)(θ'' sin θ + θ'^2 cos θ). Flag if centripetal/tangential terms are omitted or signs are incorrect (e.g., using only mg components to infer accelerations).
- Relate contact forces to COM accelerations: H = m a_x, N = mg + m a_y. Do not accept N = mg or H expressed solely via weight components (e.g., H = mg sin θ) in this dynamic scenario. At the onset of sliding, enforce f_s = μ_s N ⇒ μ_s = |H|/N.
- Numerical check at θ = 30°: The expected coefficient is μ_s ≈ 0.35. Accept if μ_s is within [0.33, 0.37]. Flag if μ_s is far outside this range (e.g., μ_s ≤ 0.30 or μ_s ≥ 0.40). Explicitly flag the incorrect value μ_s = 3/16 ≈ 0.1875.
- Pattern-based flags: solutions that resolve mg into components along/perpendicular to the rod and use those directly for torque or friction without rotational dynamics; using I_C instead of I_end; assuming static force balance (N = mg, H = μ_s N) without accounting for COM acceleration; or deriving μ_s from trigonometric ratios of mg components (e.g., μ_s = tan θ).

Torque and Rotational Dynamics.title: Incorrect sin/cos assignment when resolving a force into components relative to a rod/axis
Torque and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule checks the consistency of trigonometric components when a force (e.g., gravity mg) is resolved into parts parallel and perpendicular to an axis (such as a rod) under a stated angle convention. It specifically targets the common modeling error of swapping sin and cos. Verification steps: (1) Detect statements that define components like F_parallel, F_along, or 'parallel to the rod/axis', and F_perpendicular, F_normal, or 'perpendicular to the rod/axis' for a force vector. (2) Identify the angle definition (e.g., 'θ is the angle between the rod and the vertical' or 'θ is the tilt from vertical'). If θ is defined as the angle between the axis and the vertical (the direction of gravity), then the angle between the force vector and the axis is θ, and the correct components are |F| cos θ (parallel) and |F| sin θ (perpendicular). If the solution instead sets parallel = |F| sin θ and perpendicular = |F| cos θ under this convention, flag a modeling error. (3) If the angle is defined from the horizontal (φ), then the angle between gravity (vertical) and the axis is 90° − φ, and the correct components become |F| sin φ (parallel) and |F| cos φ (perpendicular); flag if a swap occurs. (4) Apply limit checks regardless of naming: at 0° tilt from vertical, the parallel component must equal |F| and the perpendicular component must be 0; at 90° tilt, the parallel component must be 0 and the perpendicular component must equal |F|. If the provided formulas fail these limits, flag an inconsistency. (5) The rule should trigger even if the erroneous components are not used later in the solution, as they indicate an incorrect angle convention or decomposition.

Angular Momentum and Conservation.title: Angular momentum non-conservation must be attributed to torques, not dissipation
Angular Momentum and Conservation.description:
This rule verifies explanations of angular momentum non-conservation in atmospheric or geophysical flows (e.g., Hadley circulation). It flags solutions that misattribute the loss of angular momentum to 'dissipation' by turbulence or to intrinsic properties (density/inertia, moisture) instead of external torques. The check consists of:

- Trigger conditions:
  - The text states or implies that turbulence, viscosity, or mixing 'dissipates', 'destroys', 'consumes', or 'loses' angular momentum (e.g., phrases like 'turbulence dissipates angular momentum', 'angular momentum is dissipated', 'momentum loss due to turbulence'), without concurrently framing turbulence as momentum transport/exchange that produces torques via stresses.
  - The explanation for non-conservation fails to mention external torques or stresses (surface friction/drag, turbulent/eddy stresses, pressure/stress torques) when discussing the lower branches/boundary layer.
  - The explanation attributes non-conservation to air density/inertia ('air is denser lower down so inertia slows rotation') or moisture content, with no reference to torques or momentum exchange.

- Required elements for a correct explanation:
  - Explicit recognition that angular momentum changes only under external torques; in the lower atmosphere these arise from surface friction (boundary layer drag) and turbulent/eddy stresses that exchange momentum between layers and with the surface.
  - Turbulence described as momentum transport/mixing producing effective (Reynolds) stresses and torques, not as a mechanism that intrinsically dissipates angular momentum (contrast with energy dissipation).

- Detection method (text-based):
  - Search for dissipation-related keywords in proximity to 'angular momentum' (dissipate/dissipation/destroy/consume/loss) and flag unless nearby terms include 'torque', 'stress', 'friction', 'drag', 'eddy', 'momentum exchange', or 'transport'.
  - Search for claims blaming 'density', 'inertia', or 'moisture/humidity' for angular momentum non-conservation without any mention of torque/stress; flag as concept error.
  - Validate that at least one correct torque source is named when explaining non-conservation along lower branches (e.g., surface friction/drag, turbulent/eddy stresses).

The rule aims to catch the common conceptual error of treating angular momentum like a dissipative quantity and to ensure explanations correctly attribute non-conservation to torques from frictional and turbulent stresses.

Angular Momentum and Conservation.title: Misuse of angular momentum conservation in planar sliding without rotation
Angular Momentum and Conservation.description: Flags solutions that invoke conservation of angular momentum as a necessary step in problems where bodies are constrained to slide without rotation and the interaction is along the line of centers. Detection criteria: (1) Problem context includes keywords such as "frictionless sliding", "can only slide", "no rotation", or describes symmetric setups with a push from the center (e.g., frog at the center of a circular leaf). (2) The solution states or uses "conservation of angular momentum" (e.g., "L is conserved", "sum of external torque is zero implies angular momentum conservation") to derive velocities or work, rather than recognizing that the relevant conserved quantity is linear momentum in the horizontal direction. (3) There is no explicit rotational degree of freedom or off-center impulse/force causing a torque; initial angular momentum is zero by symmetry (e.g., push from the center of a symmetric platform). The rule should not trigger if angular momentum is mentioned only to note it is zero and irrelevant or if the problem explicitly includes rotation (e.g., off-center push, spinning, rolling, or nonzero external torque). When triggered, the verifier should prompt: "Angular momentum conservation is unnecessary/misleading here; use linear momentum conservation in the horizontal direction to relate the bodies' velocities and determine work."

Angular Momentum and Conservation.title: Absolute angular momentum of air parcels must include zonal wind and latitude dependence
Angular Momentum and Conservation.description: This rule checks solutions in atmospheric dynamics contexts (e.g., Hadley circulation, tropical circulation, angular momentum about Earth's spin axis) for misuse of the rigid-body formula L = m r^2 ω to represent an air parcel's angular momentum. It flags the following patterns as errors: (a) defining angular momentum of an air parcel about Earth's axis using only Earth's spin rate (ω or Ω) without including the parcel's zonal wind u, e.g., statements like 'L = m r^2 ω' with ω identified as Earth's angular velocity, or 'per unit mass L = r^2 ω', and (b) omitting the latitude geometry (r = a cos φ) by using r = a or no cos φ dependence. In such contexts, the correct specific absolute angular momentum is M = (Ω a cos φ + u) a cos φ (equivalently M = Ω a^2 cos^2 φ + u a cos φ). The rule triggers when: keywords indicate atmospheric circulation (e.g., 'Hadley', 'tropical circulation', 'upper/lower branch', 'air parcel', 'about the Earth's spin axis') AND an angular momentum expression uses only Ω (or Earth's angular velocity) without a u term, or uses r^2 ω without subsequent inclusion of u and cos φ. The rule does not trigger if the solution explicitly defines absolute angular momentum with both Ω and u and includes the cos φ factor, or if the context is rigid-body rotation unrelated to atmospheric parcels.

Angular Momentum and Conservation.title: Incorrect use of momentum/COM conservation under external horizontal friction
Angular Momentum and Conservation.description: This rule flags solutions that apply conservation of total linear momentum or a fixed center-of-mass (COM) condition to a chosen system while the problem explicitly introduces external horizontal forces (e.g., slab–ground friction, velocity-proportional drag). Detection criteria: (1) The problem or the solution text indicates nonzero external horizontal friction/drag acting on the system (phrases like "with friction", "friction proportional to velocity", or any external horizontal force on the slab). (2) The solution asserts momentum conservation or COM invariance for the same system, e.g., statements such as "no external horizontal force", "total momentum conserved", "p_final = p_initial", "dp/dt = 0", "COM stays fixed", or uses relations like m*x_child + M*x_slab = constant (often set to 0) to determine displacements/velocities. (3) The solution reuses frictionless COM-based results (e.g., deriving slab displacement from m*x_child + M*x_slab = const together with a relative displacement constraint) in a frictional case, or concludes the same displacement as the frictionless case without modeling the external impulse F_ext or COM equation M_total*a_COM = F_ext. Exception: Do not flag if the solution explicitly expands the system to include the Earth/ground and accounts for the Earth's momentum/impulse or motion (i.e., external impulse is modeled within an enlarged isolated system). The rule is intended to catch logical inconsistencies such as using COM constraints derived for isolated systems in scenarios where external friction is present.

Angular Momentum and Conservation.title: Angular momentum decomposition at impact for hexagonal prism
Angular Momentum and Conservation.description: This rule verifies the decomposition of angular momentum used to compute the coefficient s = ω_f / ω_i during the impact of a solid, regular hexagonal prism on an inclined plane when contact occurs at a vertex (edge of the cross-section). It checks that the initial angular momentum about the impending contact point (edge) is correctly written as L_i = L_trans + L_rot, with: (1) L_trans = M r v sin(φ), where r = a (center-to-vertex distance for a regular hexagon), v = a ω_i (rolling kinematic relation immediately prior to impact), and φ = 30° (geometric angle between r and the COM velocity at impact for a hexagon), yielding L_trans = (1/2) M a^2 ω_i; (2) L_rot = I ω_i with I = (5/12) M a^2 (given). Therefore, L_i must equal (11/12) M a^2 ω_i. The rule then checks that conservation of angular momentum about the impact edge uses I' = (17/12) M a^2 (given) for the post-impact rotation, implying s = L_i / I' = (11/12) / (17/12) = 11/17. The verifier flags solutions that: use an incorrect coefficient for L_trans (e.g., 1/3 instead of 1/2), sum to an incorrect L_i coefficient (not 11/12), or report s ≠ 11/17 when I and I' are as stated. Exceptions are allowed only if the solution explicitly justifies a different contact geometry or kinematic relation (e.g., a different φ or v–ω relation); otherwise, deviations are treated as calculation errors.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Torque from friction at sphere–plane contact must be nonzero and use vertical lever arm
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: Checks torque calculation about the center of a sphere slipping on a horizontal plane. In this geometry, the contact-point lever arm relative to the center is vertical: r_contact = -R * z_hat. The kinetic friction force is horizontal: f_k = -μ_k * N * u_hat with N = mg, so r_contact ⟂ f_k. Therefore the torque is τ = r_contact × f_k = μ_k * m * g * R * (z_hat × u_hat) ≠ 0. Flag an error if the solution: (a) sets the lever arm r along the slip/force direction (e.g., r = -R * u_hat or any horizontal vector), (b) concludes τ = 0 via (u_hat × u_hat) = 0 or any r ∥ f_k argument, or (c) reports τ = 0 while f_k ≠ 0 and the ground is horizontal. The expected nonzero torque has magnitude μ_k * m * g * R and direction z_hat × u_hat; the lever arm must be vertical. This rule targets the conceptual mistake of equating the lever arm direction with the bottom-point velocity/force direction instead of the geometric center-to-contact vector.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Torque from kinetic friction must be r × F = μ_k m g R (z × u)
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: For a sphere slipping on a horizontal plane, the kinetic friction at the contact is F_f = -μ_k N u with N = mg, and the lever arm from the center to the contact is r_c = -R z. The rotational equation must use the torque  = r_c × F_f = μ_k m g R (z × u), so I d/dt = . Flag solutions that: (a) set I d/dt parallel to ±u (i.e., torque colinear with the slip direction), (b) replace the cross product with a scalar product such as  = ±R |F_f| u or any expression lacking the r × F structure, (c) omit the factor R or mg in the torque magnitude when expressing , or (d) use the wrong cross-product order yielding  = μ_k m g R (u × z) (sign error), or produce a torque not lying in the xy-plane and perpendicular to u. This rule verifies that the rotational dynamics are derived with  = μ_k m g R (z × u) and I d/dt = .

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Stick-at-separation impulse for spinning solid sphere: v_after must be (2/7) R ω0
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: Checks the tangential impulse-momentum reasoning for a homogeneous solid sphere (I = 2/5 m R^2) that is dropped with zero initial horizontal COM speed and nonzero spin ω0, contacting a rough horizontal plane. In the case where slipping ceases before the end of the impact (stick at separation), the solution must: (1) enforce the kinematic no-slip condition at separation v_after = R ω_after, (2) use only the tangential frictional impulse J_t to change both horizontal linear momentum and spin (normal impulse produces no torque about the center for a sphere), via m v_after = J_t and I ω_after = I ω0 − R J_t, and (3) combine these to obtain v_after = (I R ω0)/(I + m R^2). For a solid sphere (I = 2/5 m R^2) this simplifies to v_after = (2/7) R ω0 in magnitude. The rule flags solutions that: • Omit or misapply the no-slip-at-separation condition v_after = R ω_after. • Attribute the angular impulse to the normal impulse instead of the tangential frictional impulse (e.g., using R N in ΔL rather than R J_t). • Derive an incorrect post-impact horizontal speed such as v_after = (2/5) R ω0 or any expression not equal to (I R ω0)/(I + m R^2) for the stick-at-separation case (sign differences are tolerated, magnitudes are checked). This rule targets the connection between frictional impulse and the coupled linear/angular changes that determine the horizontal speed after the first impact, which directly affects the horizontal flight distance to the second impact.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Spinning sphere impact: require 2/7 inertia factor and friction/regime dependence in horizontal distance
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: This rule verifies final expressions for the horizontal distance traveled between the first and second impacts for a homogeneous solid sphere (I = 2/5 m R^2) dropped from height h with initial spin ω0 and contacting a rough floor. The correct structure arises from the frictional impulse coupling translation and rotation and must include: (1) the inertia-derived coefficient 2/7 multiplying R·ω0 (not 2/5), (2) a dependence on the stated slip/impact parameter (e.g., a dimensionless c encoding slip duration/impulse, or the kinetic friction coefficient μ_k for the slipping case), and (3) the free-fall time scale √(2h/g) (equivalently √(2gh)/g). Flag the solution if any of the following are true: (a) the coefficient on R·ω0 is 2/5 (or any value ≠ 2/7), indicating misuse of rotational inertia in the impulse/rolling relation; (b) the final distance expression omits any explicit dependence on the problem’s friction/regime parameter (c or μ_k) despite the problem distinguishing slipping vs non-slip phases; (c) the time-scale factor is not proportional to √(2h/g) (or √(2gh)/g). This catches errors like producing d ∝ (2/5) R ω0 √(2h/g) instead of the required form d ∝ (2/7) R ω0 × (2c √(2h/g)).

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Correct toppling criterion: pivot at base edge and include all external forces
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description:
This rule verifies that a solution uses the correct criterion for the onset of toppling (tipping) of a rigid body resting on a horizontal surface. It flags solutions that: (a) determine toppling by setting the sum of torques of weights to zero (e.g., τ_p + τ_other weights = 0) or by balancing only gravitational torques; (b) compute moments about the base center rather than about a bottom edge; (c) equate 'net torque = 0' without specifying that the normal reaction shifts to a single edge (reaction at the opposite edge becomes zero) or that the resultant line of action exits the base footprint; or (d) omit applied/contact forces from interacting bodies (e.g., chains, strings, external loads) when forming the tipping moment balance.

Pass conditions:
- At incipient toppling, the ground reaction is explicitly stated to act at one bottom edge (opposite edge reaction is zero), or equivalently, the line of action of the resultant external force is stated to reach the boundary of the support base.
- The torque (moment) balance used to identify the tipping condition is taken about that edge and includes all relevant external forces on the body: its own weight, external loads, and any contact forces from attached or contacting bodies (not just weights).
- If friction is discussed, it is not misused as a fixed f = μN to compute a horizontal moment without acknowledging that the contact reaction is distributed and collapses to the edge at tipping.

Fail/flag conditions (any one triggers a flag):
- The toppling condition is written as the sum of torques of weights equals zero, or only weights appear in the criterion with no mention of ground reaction shift to an edge.
- The pivot for the tipping condition is taken at the center of the base (or an arbitrary point) instead of the bottom edge, with no justification tied to reaction shifting.
- The criterion is stated solely as 'net torque = 0' for motion onset without reference to the base of support/edge reaction.
- External/contact forces from interacting bodies (e.g., a chain on top) are omitted from the torque balance used to decide tipping.

This rule is triggered in problems that mention toppling/tipping/overturning for bodies on a support surface and ensures the solution checks the correct edge-pivot/line-of-action condition rather than an incorrect torque-of-weights balance.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Torque of vertical forces must use horizontal lever arm (no vertical height × sinθ)
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: This rule verifies torque expressions for vertical forces (e.g., weight mg) about a pivot in planar problems. For any vertical force, the torque magnitude about a pivot equals F multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. In 2D with gravity vertical, this perpendicular distance is the horizontal offset of the center of mass (x-distance), not a vertical height multiplied by a trigonometric factor. The rule flags torque formulas that erroneously compute torque of mg as mg × (vertical length) × sinθ or mg × f(θ) × sinθ where f(θ) represents a vertical coordinate or arc-length-related quantity. Detection criteria: (1) Identify torque terms τ, M, or T involving mg (or m*g) and a trigonometric factor sin(·) or cos(·). (2) If the lever arm is expressed using symbols commonly denoting vertical measures (e.g., y, h, height, R when used as vertical radius/height, or any sum of vertical dimensions) multiplied by sin(·)/cos(·), and no explicit horizontal distance (x, x_COM, r_perp-to-vertical, or an expression clearly equal to the horizontal offset) is present, flag as incorrect. (3) Specifically flag patterns like τ = m g (h/… + …R…) sinθ, τ = m g (R − …cosθ) sinθ, or any mg × (vertical function of θ) × sinθ used as the torque. (4) Allowable forms include τ = m g × (horizontal distance to the weight’s line of action), or τ = m g r sinφ only when φ is explicitly the angle between r and the vertical force and r sinφ is demonstrated to equal the horizontal offset. Rationale: For a vertical force, the lever arm is purely horizontal; using vertical heights with sinθ/cosθ to construct the lever arm is conceptually incorrect and often yields wrong torque. The rule will mark such expressions as errors and recommend: compute torque as τ = m g × (horizontal distance from the pivot to the center-of-mass line of action), with sign determined by rotation sense.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Contact lever arm must align with plane normal, not slip direction
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: For a rigid sphere of radius R on a horizontal plane (xy-plane), the position vector from the center of mass to the contact point is r_c = -R * n_hat, where n_hat is the plane's unit normal (e.g., +ẑ upward, so r_c = -R ẑ). This lever arm is fixed by geometry and does not depend on the slip direction or the instantaneous velocity of the bottom point. Verification checks: (1) If a solution defines the lever arm r_c using the slip/relative-motion direction (e.g., r_c = -R û) or includes tangential components (x̂ or ŷ) in a horizontal-plane setup, flag as a modeling error. (2) For kinetic friction f_k acting at the contact (tangent to the plane), ensure the torque τ_f = r_c × f_k is nonzero when f_k ≠ 0; its magnitude should be R|f_k| and it should not be set to zero by claiming r_c ∥ f_k. Flag any step that makes τ_f = 0 because r_c was taken parallel to the friction direction. (3) In problems that specify a plane normal n_hat (e.g., ẑ), require r_c = -R n_hat (or equivalent). Any dependence of r_c on û or on the tangential velocity is invalid and should be reported.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Detect self-referential unit-vector definitions in contact kinematics
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: This rule flags circular or ill-posed definitions of the slip-direction unit vector at a contact point (e.g., a rolling/slipping sphere on a plane). Specifically: (1) If the solution defines the unit vector hat{u} for the contact/slip direction using an expression that itself contains hat{u} (e.g., hat{u} = normalize(v - R (omega × hat{u}))) or any RHS that depends on hat{u}, mark as an error due to self-reference. A unit vector must be defined as the normalization of a nonzero vector that does not include itself. (2) If the contact-point velocity vector u is defined using hat{u} on the RHS (e.g., u = v - R (omega × hat{u})), flag as incorrect kinematics. The correct rigid-body kinematics at a contact point is u = v_cm + omega × r_cp, where r_cp is the position vector from the center of mass to the contact point determined by geometry and independent of hat{u}. For a sphere on a horizontal plane with the center at height R, r_cp = -R ẑ, so u = v_cm + omega × (-R ẑ) = v_cm - R (omega × ẑ). (3) If the kinetic friction direction is used as hat{u} in f_k = -μ_k N hat{u}, require that hat{u} be defined as u / |u| where u is computed from the correct kinematics independent of hat{u}. The rule detects patterns such as 'ω × û' appearing inside the definition of u or û, or any equation of the form û = normalize(… û …). The intent is to ensure that contact kinematics use geometry-based position vectors (e.g., ±R ẑ for a sphere on a plane) and that unit-direction vectors are not self-referential.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Correct contact-point position vector for a sphere on a horizontal plane
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: Checks the kinematic and torque modeling for a uniform sphere contacting a horizontal plane (xy-plane). For any use of the rigid-body point-velocity relation u = v + ω × r (where u is the velocity of the bottom contact point, v the COM velocity, and ω the angular velocity), the position vector from the COM to the contact point must be r = -R ẑ, i.e., fixed along the plane normal and independent of slip direction. The rule flags solutions that set r to -R û (unit vector along the slip/contact velocity), to any time-varying horizontal direction, or to any expression with x/y components or dependence on û, v, or ω. It also checks torque modeling: the friction torque about the COM must use τ_fric = r × f_k with r = -R ẑ; using r aligned with û or any horizontal vector is incorrect. This rule catches errors where the contact-point geometry is mis-specified (e.g., r = -R û) leading to wrong u and τ.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Disallow friction at declared smooth contacts and misuse of μ on wrong interface
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: This rule flags solutions that introduce tangential (frictional) forces at contacts explicitly stated to be smooth/frictionless, or that apply a given coefficient of friction μ to the wrong interface. Detection steps: (1) Parse the problem statement to extract contact descriptions: identify interfaces labeled as smooth/frictionless/no friction and interfaces for which a friction coefficient (e.g., μ) is specified (e.g., 'friction between the pillar and the ground is μ'). (2) In the student solution, scan free-body diagrams, force lists, and equations for friction terms (keywords/structures such as 'friction', 'f', 'f_fric', 'kinetic/static friction', and formulas like f = μN, μ_s N, μ_k N, or a tangential force described as opposing motion along a surface). (3) If an interface is marked smooth in the problem, any introduction of a tangential contact force on that interface (including f = μN or generic 'friction along the surface') is an error; only a normal reaction is allowed there. (4) If μ is specified for a particular interface (e.g., body–ground), verify that any friction forces using μ are attached only to that specified interface. Using μ to define friction on a different interface (e.g., chain–pillar when that contact is declared smooth) is an error. (5) Also flag torque/rotation analyses that include moments due to such forbidden friction forces. (6) Guard against false positives by allowing non-contact dissipative forces (e.g., air drag) if explicitly identified and not tied to the smooth contact, and by checking that the μ symbol in the solution is indeed used as a friction coefficient. Typical violation to catch: the problem states the chain–pillar contact is smooth and μ refers to pillar–ground, but the solution introduces a friction force f = μN along the pillar acting on the chain and uses it to derive conditions like μ ≥ tanθ.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Smooth curved contact must be modeled as distributed normal forces (no direct weight or single-point N)
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: Applies when one body rests or slides in smooth contact along a curved surface of another body (e.g., a chain on a semicircular cap). Verification checks: (1) The interaction force between the contacting bodies must be a distributed normal reaction along the contact; modeling it as a single normal force N at one point over an extended arc is invalid unless a derived resultant of the distribution is explicitly justified. (2) The weight of the upper body (e.g., the chain) must not be applied directly to the lower body to compute torque or tipping moments; only the resultant of the contact normal distribution contributes to the lower body's moment. Flag if a solution uses m_chain*g with a lever arm to compute the pillar’s tipping moment without deriving the contact resultant. (3) If the interface is stated as smooth, tangential friction at that interface must be zero; flag any use of f = μN at the chain–pillar interface. (4) On curved interfaces, the normal distribution generally has horizontal components; tipping analysis must account for these components via the resultant of the distributed normals. Flag if the analysis considers only vertical forces or ignores the horizontal component from the curved contact when assessing toppling. This rule detects modeling errors where contact mechanics are replaced by direct application of the other body's weight or oversimplified to a single-point reaction.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Invalid single-parameter center-of-mass for a chain on a composite support
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: Trigger when a solution treats a uniform chain draped over a composite support (e.g., a semicircular cap of radius R atop a rectangular body of height h) as if its configuration and center of mass can be described by a single angle or by the centroid of a semicircular arc alone. The correct approach requires: (1) partitioning the chain into segments that follow the support (left down-hanging/side segment, top arc segment on the semicircle, right down-hanging/side segment), (2) enforcing the total-length constraint and the endpoint-height constraint (both ends at height h/2) to relate the segment lengths and angular spans on the cap, and (3) computing the chain’s center of mass as a length-weighted sum of segment centroids or via an explicit line integral over the contact path. Flag the solution if any of the following are detected: - The center-of-mass expression depends only on R and a single angle θ (e.g., y_c = R − (R/π) cos θ or similar) without any dependence on h or separate segment lengths. - A single angle θ is used to describe the entire chain configuration without defining left/right arc angles and vertical/side lengths, and without a length constraint L_left + L_top + L_right = const. - The rectangular portion (height h) is ignored in the geometry or in the CoM expression, despite the end-height condition at h/2. - The chain’s CoM is equated to the centroid of a semicircle or a semicircular arc without adding contributions from the down-hanging segments. - No explicit enforcement that the chain ends are at height h/2 and that the path is continuous at the arc–side junctions. This rule is intended to catch conceptual mischaracterizations of the chain’s geometry and center of mass for composite-support draping problems.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Missing tension forces in free-body when a body is supported by rope/pulley
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: This rule verifies that solutions include all constraint forces in the free-body diagram (FBD) and equations of motion for a body connected to a rope/pulley. It targets the common modeling error where rope tensions are omitted from the force balance of the body. Checks: (1) Detect references to a rope/pulley attached to the analyzed body (keywords: rope, string, cable, pulley, tension; plus parameters like R, M, pulley inertia). (2) Inspect the FBD/equations for the body: the vertical force balance must include tension terms (e.g., T, T1, T2) at each rope attachment point, in addition to spring forces and weight. If the body is suspended by two rope segments, the bar should have two upward tensions unless explicitly justified otherwise. (3) If a torque equation for a massive pulley is written (e.g., τ = (T2 − T1)R, Iα = τ), the body’s EoM must also include the corresponding tensions; omitting them indicates inconsistent coupling. (4) Flag patterns where the net restoring force is modeled using only springs and gravity (e.g., mg balanced by kx + k'x, or m y¨ = −(k1 + k2) y) while the problem states the body is additionally supported or constrained by a rope/pulley. (5) Allow omission only if the solution explicitly demonstrates that rope forces on the body cancel by geometry or are internal to another subsystem and do not act on the body (rare), or if tensions are eliminated via a clear constraint/kinematic relation and combined dynamics (e.g., expressed as an effective stiffness/mass with derivation). (6) Strengthen the flag if pulley inertia (I = 1/2 M R^2, R, M) is mentioned but no tension terms appear in the body’s force balance. This rule catches modeling errors like treating the bar’s dynamics with springs only (kx + 2kx) and ignoring rope tensions and their coupling, leading to incorrect equations such as m y¨ = −3k y without tension contributions.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Misuse of Newton’s second law on massless connectors and improper pulley coupling
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: This rule flags solutions that treat massless, inextensible connectors (rope or spring segments) as independent dynamical elements by applying Newton’s second law to them or by assigning them an 'effective mass'. Typical erroneous forms include equations like T − kx = m_eff * a, T1 − kx = m_eff * y¨, T2 − 2kx = m_eff * y¨, or equating a spring force directly to a pulley inertia term such as kx = (I/R^2) * y¨ (e.g., kx = (1/2) M * y¨). For a massless rope segment, F = m a does not apply with nonzero m; tension along any straight massless segment is uniform, and the net force on such a segment must be zero. Any tension difference can only arise across a rotating pulley and must be related through the torque equation I * α = (T2 − T1) * R with the kinematic constraint α = a/R (no slip). Valid equations of motion should be written for massive components (e.g., the bar: sum of external forces = m_bar * y¨) and for the pulley via torque balance, not for the rope/spring segments themselves. The rule triggers if the solution assigns mass or effective mass to the rope/spring, applies F = m a to rope segments, or bypasses the torque relation by directly tying spring force to the pulley’s rotational inertia.

Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.title: Parallel-axis consistency: center-to-edge distance for a hexagonal prism
Contact Mechanics and Lever Arms.description: Checks that the distance used between the centroidal axis and an edge axis (center-to-edge/apothem/lever arm) is consistent with the given moments of inertia via the parallel-axis theorem. Detection logic: (1) Identify a regular hexagonal prism with side length a and given moments of inertia I about the central axis and I' about an edge axis. (2) Compute the required shift distance d_required from the parallel-axis theorem: d_required^2 = (I' - I) / M. For the provided values I = (5/12) M a^2 and I' = (17/12) M a^2, d_required = a. (3) Parse the student solution for any stated or implied center-to-edge distance used in kinematics/impact/torque (terms like 'apothem', 'inradius', 'center-to-edge distance', 'pivot shift', lever arm to the edge contact). (4) If the student uses d_est such that d_est^2 ≠ (I' - I) / M (beyond a small tolerance), flag an error. Specifically flag common misstatements like d_est = a/√3 or d_est = (√3/2) a when used as the center-to-edge distance in this context, because the given I and I' imply d_required = a. (5) Also check consistency in downstream uses: if the lever arm for torque, angular momentum, or impact calculations is taken as a/√3 (or any value not matching d_required) for edge contact, flag the step as geometrically inconsistent. Rationale: For this problem, the parallel-axis relation determines the effective center-to-edge distance; using an incorrect apothem leads to wrong kinematics and angular momentum results.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Swapped radial (normal) and tangential components in polar coordinates
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description:
This rule checks whether a solution mislabels the radial ("normal") and tangential components when decomposing a vector (e.g., electric field, force, velocity, acceleration) in plane polar coordinates. In polar coordinates, the radial (normal) direction must be along r̂ (parallel to the position vector r), and the tangential direction must be along θ̂ (perpendicular to r). The rule flags the following patterns:

- Textual misdefinitions:
  - Statements asserting that the normal (or radial) component is perpendicular to r (or aligned with θ̂), e.g., "En is perpendicular to r", "normal along θ̂".
  - Statements asserting that the tangential component is parallel to r (or aligned with r̂), e.g., "Eτ is parallel to r", "tangential along r̂".

- Symbolic label swaps:
  - Equalities mapping En to Eθ (or n̂ to θ̂) and/or Eτ to Er (or τ̂ to r̂), e.g., En = Eθ, Eτ = Er, n̂ = θ̂, τ̂ = r̂.
  - Decompositions that imply the above, such as writing E = En θ̂ + Eτ r̂, or defining the normal basis vector to be θ̂ and the tangential basis vector to be r̂.

- Consistency check with standard basis:
  - If a solution defines E = Er r̂ + Eθ θ̂ but then interprets En as Eθ and Eτ as Er (or any equivalent swapped mapping), flag.

The rule should be applied to any vector decomposition in 2D polar coordinates where "normal" is used to mean radial (along r̂). It should not flag cases where "normal" is explicitly defined relative to the trajectory curvature (n̂ along the principal normal to the path), unless the solution also claims to be using polar (r, θ) components. The rule reports an error when any of the above misdefinitions or mappings are detected.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Swapped radial (n̂) and tangential (τ̂) unit vectors in polar decomposition
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description:
Purpose: Detect solutions that misassign the radial and tangential unit vectors when decomposing vectors (e.g., electric field) in 2D polar coordinates, leading to En and Eτ being swapped.

Trigger context:
- The solution works in plane polar coordinates (r, θ) or cylindrical polar in a plane, and introduces components labeled as normal (En) and tangential (Eτ), or unit vectors n̂ and τ̂.
- The problem statement indicates that normal means radial (along r̂) and tangential means transverse/azimuthal (along θ̂), i.e., n̂ = r̂ and τ̂ = θ̂.

Checks:
1) Unit-vector definition check:
   - Scan for explicit unit vector identifications. Flag if any of the following are found:
     • τ̂ = r̂ (or τ̂ ≡ e_r, \hat r)
     • n̂ = θ̂ (or n̂ ≡ e_θ, \hat θ, \hat\theta)
   - Accept only the mapping n̂ = r̂ and τ̂ = θ̂ (synonyms allowed: e_r, \hat r for r̂; e_θ, \hat θ, \hat\theta for θ̂; tangential/transverse/azimuthal for θ̂; normal/radial for r̂).

2) Projection/operator check:
   - If components are obtained by projection, ensure:
     • En = E · r̂
     • Eτ = E · θ̂
   - Flag as an error if instead:
     • En = E · θ̂, or
     • Eτ = E · r̂.

3) Component-label consistency check (when explicit projections are not shown):
   - If a vector V is expressed as V = V_r r̂ + V_θ θ̂, then the correct identification is En = V_r and Eτ = V_θ.
   - Flag if the solution assigns En = V_θ and Eτ = V_r (possibly with identical functional dependence), indicating a label swap.

4) Textual synonym handling:
   - Treat the following as equivalent labels during parsing:
     • Radial: radial, normal, n, n-hat, \hat n, e_n.
     • Tangential: tangential, transverse, azimuthal, theta-direction, τ, tau-hat, \hat τ, e_τ, e_theta, e_θ.
   - Treat r̂ synonyms: r-hat, \hat r, e_r. Treat θ̂ synonyms: theta-hat, \hat θ, \hat\theta, e_theta, e_θ.

5) Context safeguards to avoid false positives:
   - Apply the rule only when the problem explicitly uses polar (r, θ) basis for decomposition relative to the position vector, not a general Frenet–Serret frame along an arbitrary trajectory. If a Frenet–Serret normal/tangent is explicitly used (t̂, n̂ along the path curvature), do not apply this rule.

Error condition:
- Raise an error if any of the checks (1)–(3) indicate that the radial and tangential directions were interchanged (e.g., τ̂ assigned to r̂, n̂ assigned to θ̂, En computed from θ̂, Eτ from r̂, or En/Eτ expressions matching V_θ/V_r, respectively). The error indicates a mislabeling of components relative to the standard polar basis.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Polar component sign consistency with axis orientation
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description: This rule verifies that the signs of field or force components defined as 'normal' (En, E_n) and 'tangential' (Eτ, E_t) in polar/spherical coordinates are consistent with the stated axis orientations. The verifier will: (1) Determine the canonical basis directions from the problem statement (r̂ is outward radial; θ̂ increases counterclockwise). (2) Parse the student's definitions of component axes (e.g., 'normal inward', 'toward origin', or arrows indicating −r̂; 'tangential opposite to increasing θ', or arrows indicating −θ̂). (3) Compute or reference the canonical component expressions for the field in r̂ and θ̂ (for an electric dipole aligned with the axis: E_r = (2 p cosθ)/(4π ε0 r^3), E_θ = (p sinθ)/(4π ε0 r^3) with p = qd). (4) Map the expected components to the student's axes: if En is along −r̂, expected En = −E_r; if Eτ is along −θ̂, expected Eτ = −E_θ; if axes align with r̂ and θ̂, no sign flip is required. (5) Compare the student's En/Eτ expressions: if the student presents En/Eτ with the same sign as E_r/E_θ while the axes are defined along −r̂/−θ̂ (or vice versa), flag an error for inconsistent sign convention. This rule also applies generally to any vector decomposition where component axes are reversed relative to the canonical basis; if the problem does not specify axis orientation, the rule does not trigger to avoid false positives.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Validate angular acceleration and linear–angular mapping
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description: Check consistency of rotational kinematics and torque relations involving angular acceleration. The rule enforces that angular acceleration α is the second time derivative of angular displacement: α = d²θ/dt² (i.e., α = θ¨), and must not include geometric factors like radius R. Flag any occurrence of α defined as θ¨/R, ω˙/R, or any expression putting 1/R with purely angular quantities. Verify the no-slip kinematic mapping between linear and angular motion: a_t = R α and α = a_t / R; flag incorrect mappings such as a_t = α, a_t = θ¨, α = a_t R, or y¨ = θ¨ (missing the factor R) when relating a translating element to pulley rotation. In torque balance τ = I α, ensure α refers to angular acceleration (θ¨) and that reduction to linear variables is done via a_t = R α (e.g., substituting α = y¨/R is acceptable, but substituting α = θ¨/R is not). Dimensional check: α must have units s⁻²; flag any expression for α that carries length units (e.g., s⁻²/m or m·s⁻²) unless it appears as part of the correct relation a_t = R α or α = a_t / R. This rule catches confusion between α and θ¨, and misuse of R in angular acceleration definitions that leads to downstream errors in torque/force relations.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Include correct sin(angle) in translational angular momentum about a new contact point
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description: This rule checks computations of the translational contribution to angular momentum about a point that is not the instantaneous center of rotation. It targets impact/pivot-change scenarios (e.g., a rolling polygonal prism transitioning contact from one edge to the next) where students often assume the center-of-mass velocity v_CM is perpendicular to the position vector r_new from the center of mass to the new contact point. Checks performed: (1) When angular momentum about a point P is evaluated just before impact, verify that the translational term is written as L_trans = M |r_CM→P| |v_CM| sin(phi), where phi is the angle between r_CM→P and v_CM. Flag an error if the expression is simplified to M v R (i.e., sin(phi) implicitly set to 1) without justification that r_CM→P ⟂ v_CM. (2) If the body was rolling without slipping about an old contact point O_old prior to impact, infer that v_CM ⟂ r_CM→O_old, not necessarily r_CM→O_new. Require the solver to account for the geometry relating r_CM→O_old and r_CM→O_new. (3) For a regular N-gon transitioning to the next supporting edge, enforce phi = 90° − Δ with Δ = 2π/N, so sin(phi) = cos(Δ). For a hexagon (N = 6), this yields phi = 30° and sin(phi) = 1/2. Flag if the solution omits this factor or uses sin(phi) = 1. (4) Accept equivalent correct treatments (e.g., component-wise cross product or explicit dot/cross evaluation) that produce the same sin(phi) factor. (5) Also flag if the perpendicular assumption is justified using the old contact geometry for the new contact (i.e., conflating r_new with r_old). This rule is triggered whenever an impact/pivot-change angular momentum balance about the new contact point is used and the translational term lacks or mis-evaluates the required sin(angle) factor.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Rigid-body COM acceleration must include tangential and centripetal terms
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description: This rule verifies the correctness of center-of-mass (COM) acceleration expressions in planar rigid-body rotation about a fixed contact point (e.g., a rod tipping with its bottom end not sliding). It checks that the COM acceleration components include both the tangential (α r) and centripetal (−ω^2 r) contributions with proper projection onto the chosen axes. Specific check for the tipping rod with θ measured from the vertical: if the COM position is x_c = (ℓ/2) sin θ, y_c = (ℓ/2) cos θ, then the correct accelerations are a_x = (ℓ/2)(θ'' cos θ − θ'^2 sin θ) and a_y = −(ℓ/2)(θ'' sin θ + θ'^2 cos θ). The rule flags solutions that: (1) use a_x = (ℓ/2) θ'' sin θ or any expression missing the −(ℓ/2) θ'^2 sin θ term; (2) mis-project the tangential term by using sin θ instead of cos θ for a_x when x_c = (ℓ/2) sin θ; (3) provide COM acceleration components containing only θ'' (no θ'^2 term) for a rotating body. General implementation guidance: parse the student's COM acceleration expression in terms of θ, θ', θ'', and verify it equals the second time derivative of the COM position used in the solution (or equivalently satisfies a = r θ'' (perpendicular to the link) − r θ'^2 (along the link)). If the centripetal term is absent or the trigonometric projection is inconsistent with the stated geometry, flag a conceptual kinematics error. This rule helps catch underestimation of required friction or forces due to missing −ω^2 r contributions.

Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.title: Missing angular speed or centripetal term in rotating rigid body contact-force analysis
Polar Coordinates and Angular Motion.description: This rule flags solutions that compute friction or normal force for a rigid body rotating about a non-slipping contact point at a specified angle without accounting for velocity-dependent acceleration. Specifically, it detects when a solution: (1) derives only the angular acceleration (θ'' or α) from torque balance but never derives the angular speed θ' (ω) as a function of angle (e.g., via energy conservation), and then proceeds to evaluate contact forces or a friction coefficient; (2) writes the normal force N using only static components (e.g., N = mg cosθ) or similar expressions without including the centripetal contribution m r ω^2 for the center-of-mass radial acceleration; (3) performs ΣF = m a for the center of mass without any ω^2 term in the radial direction; (4) determines μ_s at the onset of sliding using f_s = μ_s N with N computed from static balance or torque-only equations, i.e., omitting velocity-dependent load. The rule expects, for rotating rods/pendulums with a fixed/no-slip pivot, the presence of either: (a) an explicit ω(θ) or θ'^2(θ) relation obtained from energy or dynamics (e.g., I_p ω^2 = 2 m g r (1 − cosθ), or θ'^2 = (3g/ℓ)(1 − cosθ) for a uniform rod about its end), and (b) centripetal acceleration terms for the COM such as a_n = (ℓ/2) ω^2 included in force balance. If neither an ω(θ) relation nor ω^2 terms appear when computing contact forces/friction at a given angle, the solution is flagged as a logic error for neglecting velocity-dependent dynamics required at that configuration.

Velocity and Frame Transformations.title: Use ω × r with the object's radius in rotating-frame velocity transformations
Velocity and Frame Transformations.description: This rule verifies correct modeling of velocity transformations between an inertial frame and an Earth-fixed (ground) rotating frame. The physically correct relation is v_rot = v_inertial − ω × r, where ω is Earth's angular velocity and r is the object's position vector from the rotation axis.
