Equivalent algebraic rearrangements that simplify to a difference are acceptable and should not be flagged.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Vector field direction must reflect source sign
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description: When verifying superposition of electric or magnetic fields from point sources (charges or monopoles), ensure the direction of each contribution includes the sign of the source and the correct orientation of r̂ (from source to observation point). The correct vector form is F ∝ q·r̂/r² (E for charges, B for monopoles). Flag solutions that: (a) assert all contributions point in the same axial direction (e.g., +z) without stating that all sources are positive; (b) treat negative sources as producing outward fields; or (c) sum magnitudes only (|q|) and assign a common direction. Specifically for z-axis evaluations (e.g., z > d with sources at z=0 and z=d), a negative source must contribute along −z at points beyond it, while a positive source contributes along +z. Any omission or misassignment of these directional signs is a concept error.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Electrostatic dipole field components must be 1/r^3 and consistent with vector form
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description:
Scope: Static (electrostatic) point dipole in 3D vacuum, no time variation, and radiation effects neglected. Expected field: E(r) = (1/(4π ε0 r^3)) [3 (p·r̂) r̂ − p]. In spherical/polar components with dipole aligned along the polar axis (ẑ): E_r = (1/(4π ε0)) (2 p cosθ / r^3) and E_θ = (1/(4π ε0)) (p sinθ / r^3). Both components scale as 1/r^3.

The rule flags the following issues:
- Any dipole field component given with an r-dependence other than 1/r^3 (e.g., 1/r^2 or 1/r), unless the solution explicitly models a 2D line-dipole or a time-varying/radiating dipole (exceptions below).
- Labeling the total vector expression (1/(4π ε0 r^3))[3(p·r̂) r̂ − p] as a single component (e.g., calling it E_r) or introducing an E_θ with a different power of r than the vector form.
- Presenting mixed or inconsistent component formulas such as E_θ ∝ (p·r̂) θ̂ / r^2, or any E_θ with 1/r^2 scaling, which is incompatible with the electrostatic dipole field.
- Inconsistency between a provided vector form and component forms: if both are given, the projected components must satisfy E_r = (1/(4π ε0 r^3)) · 2(p·r̂) and |E_θ| = (1/(4π ε0 r^3)) · |p − (p·r̂) r̂| = (1/(4π ε0 r^3)) · p sinα, where α is the angle between p and r̂. Any mismatch is flagged.
- Dimensional inconsistency: expressions like (1/(4π ε0)) · p / r^2 for a 3D electrostatic dipole field are dimensionally incorrect and should be flagged.

Exceptions to avoid false positives:
- If the solution explicitly states a 2D electrostatics model (line dipole) where different r-scaling may appear, or explicitly treats a time-dependent dipole with radiation terms (1/r far field), this rule does not apply.

Implementation notes: Trigger when the solution mentions a dipole field and provides E_r and/or E_θ, or the canonical vector form. Check that (i) all components scale as 1/r^3; (ii) the vector-to-component mapping is consistent; and (iii) components are not mislabeled or mixed with incorrect unit powers.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Correct potential energy of a point charge in a dipole field (avoid U = q E·r)
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description:
This rule flags solutions that compute the electrostatic potential energy of a point charge in a non-uniform field (e.g., a dipole field) as U = q (E · r) or U ≈ q E r cosθ instead of using the scalar potential. The correct relation is U = q Φ, with Φ obtained from Φ(r, θ) = -∫ E · dl (and E = -∇Φ). For a fixed electric dipole with moment p in SI units, the scalar potential is Φ(r, θ) = (1/(4π ε0)) (p cosθ)/r^2, so U(r, θ) = q Φ(r, θ). The rule checks the following:

- Pattern misuse: If the solution explicitly sets potential or potential energy as Φ = E · r, U = q (E · r), or U = q E r cosθ in a spatially varying field (dipole), flag as a conceptual error (confusing local field with potential, failing to integrate).
- Dipole functional form: If the stated Φ or U for a dipole depends on r with any power other than r^-2, or lacks the angular factor cosθ, flag. Expected: Φ ∝ (p cosθ)/r^2 and U ∝ q p cosθ / r^2.
- Gradient consistency: If both Φ and E are given, verify E = -∇Φ. For a dipole, this implies E_r = (1/(4π ε0)) (2 p cosθ)/r^3 and E_θ = (1/(4π ε0)) (p sinθ)/r^3. If the solution instead ties Φ to E via Φ ≈ E_r r (yielding an extra factor of 2) or any non-integrated relation, flag.
- Coulomb constant factor: In SI-like derivations, require the presence of k = 1/(4π ε0) (or ke) in Φ and U. If ε0 or SI constants appear elsewhere and k is omitted in Φ/U, flag as missing factor. Allow omission only if the unit system is explicitly declared such that k = 1 (e.g., Gaussian or Heaviside-Lorentz units) and used consistently.
- Sign convention: Ensure U = q Φ (and Φ defined so that E = -∇Φ). If a solution uses U = -q Φ without redefining Φ accordingly, flag.

Implementation hints for a verifier:
- Look for text/math patterns like: "U = q (E·r)", "U = q E r", "Φ = E·r", or "U ≈ q E r cosθ".
- If a dipole is mentioned, check that Φ contains the cosθ/r^2 dependence and (1/(4π ε0)) (or declared k). If U or Φ is proportional to 1/r^3 or directly to E without integration, flag.
- If both E and Φ are provided, numerically/analytically differentiate Φ and compare to E to confirm E = -∇Φ; mismatch (e.g., factor 2) should be flagged.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Verify Coulomb constant and r-dependence in dipole field/potential (SI units)
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description: This rule checks solutions that use the electrostatic field or potential of an electric dipole to ensure correct SI-form constants and dimensional consistency. It triggers when terms involving a dipole moment p, position r, and angle θ are present for an electrostatic calculation (e.g., E, V, U for a dipole, energy conservation used to obtain velocity). The rule validates the following: (1) Presence of the Coulomb constant: In SI units, the dipole potential and field must include k_e = 1/(4π ε0). Accepted forms: explicitly 1/(4π ε0) or a symbol k_e defined as 1/(4π ε0). If the solution declares CGS/Gaussian units unambiguously, absence of k_e is allowed; otherwise, missing k_e is flagged. (2) Correct functional forms: The dipole potential must scale as V(r,θ) = (1/(4π ε0)) (p·r̂)/r^2. The dipole field must scale as E(r,θ) = (1/(4π ε0))(1/r^3)[3(p·r̂) r̂ − p]. Component-wise, both radial and tangential components of E must scale as 1/r^3; any component scaling as 1/r^2 is flagged. The numeric factor 3 must appear in the field expression (vector or components); missing or misplaced factors are flagged. (3) Potential energy and energy conservation: Potential energy of a charge in the dipole field must be U = q V with V as above, thus containing 1/(4π ε0). If energy conservation is used to compute velocity (e.g., ½ m v^2 + U = const), the resulting v^2 must have dimensions of m^2/s^2. Expressions where U ∝ q p / r^2 without k_e, or any velocity derived from such a U, are flagged for dimensional inconsistency. (4) Dimensional check: The rule performs a unit sanity check that E scales as p/(ε0 r^3) (units V/m), V as p/(ε0 r^2) (units V), and U = qV (units J). Any mismatch (e.g., E ∝ p/r^3 without 1/(4π ε0), giving C/m^2) triggers an error. (5) Equivalence handling: The rule accepts algebraically equivalent representations (e.g., using p cosθ for p·r̂) and symbolic constants defined once. It allows consistent use of CGS/Gaussian units only if the unit system is explicitly declared; otherwise, SI is assumed and missing k_e is treated as an error. This rule is intended to catch omissions or misuses of 1/(4π ε0) and associated numeric factors in dipole-related energy and velocity calculations.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Dipole potential and test-charge potential energy consistency
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description: Applies when a solution uses the scalar potential V of an ideal point electric dipole and the potential energy U of a test charge q in vacuum (polar/spherical coordinates). The rule enforces: V(r,θ) = (1/(4π ε0)) (p cos θ)/r^2 (equivalently V = (1/(4π ε0)) (p·r̂)/r^2), and U(r,θ) = q V(r,θ). The verifier should flag the following: (1) U is expressed without the factor q (e.g., U = (1/(4π ε0)) (p cos θ)/r^2). (2) An unconditional minus sign is introduced in V or U (e.g., V = -(1/(4π ε0)) (p cos θ)/r^2 or U = -(1/(4π ε0)) (p cos θ)/r^2) without an explicit, correct justification tied to the sign of q or to the chosen orientation of the dipole moment p relative to θ. (3) Dimensional inconsistency: the expression labeled as U has dimensions of voltage rather than energy (missing q). The rule accepts algebraically equivalent forms of V (p·r̂/r^2) and requires U = q V. Any deviation from these relations or units should be reported as a conceptual error.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Closed-form requirement for radial velocity v_{n2} in dipole systems
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description: This rule flags solutions that fail to provide the requested normal/radial velocity component v_{n2} in a closed form tailored to the dipole problem. The verifier checks the final expression(s) for v_{n2} and triggers an error if any of the following are true: (1) The expression retains unresolved auxiliary variables such as θ̇ (angular speed), v_t (tangential speed), L (angular momentum), generic total energy E, or generic potential U(r,θ), instead of eliminating or expressing them in terms of the system’s parameters and specified initial conditions; (2) The dipole-specific field/potential is not substituted (e.g., leaving placeholders like E_n, E_t, or U(r,θ) rather than using φ(r,θ) = (1/(4πϵ0)) p cosθ / r^2 and U = qφ); (3) The final v_{n2} depends on free/undefined quantities and is not expressed solely in terms of permitted parameters (m, q, dipole moment p, ϵ0), coordinates (r, θ), and explicitly stated valid invariants/initial conditions; (4) The scenario contradicts stated non-conservation (e.g., relying on conserved angular momentum in a setup where angular momentum is not conserved) or fails to provide an alternative relation to eliminate θ̇. If the final v_{n2} expression includes any of {θ̇, v_t, L, E, U, E_n, E_t} without explicit elimination/substitution or linkage to given data, or lacks dipole-specific substitution, the solution is marked as incomplete and non-responsive to the problem’s request for a closed form.

Dipole Fields and Potentials.title: Discrete dipole (±Q, d) must map to p = Q d and correct dipole scaling
Dipole Fields and Potentials.description:
Trigger this rule when a problem specifies a fixed electric dipole constructed from discrete charges ±Q separated by a distance d, but the solution switches to a point-dipole moment p without explicitly relating p to the given parameters or uses incorrect r-dependence for dipole quantities.

This rule checks:
- Parameter mapping: If the problem statement provides ±Q and d (and does not provide p), any introduction of a dipole moment p must include the definition p = Q d (with appropriate vector direction if needed), and p must be substituted back so that final expressions are in terms of the given parameters (Q, d, and any other stated quantities). Solutions that retain an undefined p, or mix p with Q and d simultaneously in final results, are flagged.
- Correct far-field formulas: If the point-dipole approximation is used, ensure the correct r and θ dependence is applied (up to unit-system constants):
  • Potential: V(r, θ) ∝ (p cosθ)/r^2.
  • Field: E_r ∝ (2 p cosθ)/r^3 and E_θ ∝ (p sinθ)/r^3.
  Using V ∝ p/r^3, E ∝ p/r^2, or other incorrect powers of r is flagged.
- Approximation justification: If the solution replaces the exact two-charge potential V = k Q (1/r_+ − 1/r_−) with the point-dipole form, it must state or imply the far-field condition (r ≫ d) or otherwise justify the dipole approximation. Absence of such justification is flagged when switching models.

Flags when:
- p appears in derivations or final answers without an explicit definition p = Q d given the problem’s parameters.
- Final answers are expressed in terms of p despite the problem providing Q and d (unless the problem explicitly permits/asks for p).
- Both p and (Q, d) appear in the same final expression without substitution.
- The dipole potential/field uses the wrong r-dependence for a point dipole.

Exceptions:
- Do not flag if the problem explicitly gives p or requests answers in terms of p.
- Do not flag if the solution uses the exact two-charge expressions consistently (no need to introduce p).
- Allow different unit-system constants (e.g., k = 1/(4π ε0)); focus on parameter mapping and power-law dependence in r.

Electromagnetic Momentum and Density.title: EM momentum density must be S/c^2 (not S/c)
Electromagnetic Momentum and Density.description:
Checks that the linear momentum density of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is expressed with the correct power of c. The correct vector relation is p_V = S/c^2, which is equivalent to p_V = (E × B)/(μ0 c^2) = ε0 (E × B). The rule flags solutions that:
- Express momentum density as p_V = S/c (missing one factor of c), or equivalently p_V = (E × B)/(μ0 c).
- Omit the c^2 in any expression proportional to the Poynting vector (e.g., p_V ∝ S) without the 1/c^2 factor.
- Fail a dimensional check: momentum density has units kg/(s·m^2); S/c has units kg/(s^2·m) and is inconsistent, while S/c^2 is consistent.
Accepted correct forms include any of the following (vacuum only):
- p_V = S/c^2
- p_V = (E × B)/(μ0 c^2)
- p_V = ε0 (E × B)
The rule should recognize common notations for momentum density (p_V, g) and for the Poynting vector (S), and verify algebraic equivalence under c^2 = 1/(μ0 ε0). It triggers a warning/error when the found expression is proportional to S/c rather than S/c^2.

Electromagnetic Momentum and Density.title: EM momentum density must be S/c^2 = ε0 (E × B), not along E or B alone
Electromagnetic Momentum and Density.description: Checks student expressions for the electromagnetic linear momentum density (p_V, g, or similar). The correct vector form in vacuum is g = p_V = S/c^2 = (1/μ0 c^2)(E × B) = ε0 (E × B), i.e., parallel to E × B (the propagation direction). The rule flags solutions that: (1) give a momentum density vector proportional to E or B alone (e.g., ε0 E E⃗, ε0 E^2 Ê, k E⃗, k B⃗), or explicitly state it is along E or B; (2) omit the cross product between E and B in the final vector expression for momentum density; (3) use B = E/c to eliminate B and produce an expression in terms of E only for momentum density; (4) equate momentum density to u/c or u/c^2 without tying it to S or the propagation direction (i.e., missing E × B); (5) use an incorrect prefactor when a cross product is present (prefactor must be ε0 or 1/(μ0 c^2)); (6) present a magnitude depending only on E^2 or B^2 (e.g., ε0 E^2) with direction Ê or B̂ instead of the vector E × B. Unit sanity check heuristic: flag if the proposed result has units of energy density (J/m^3, e.g., ε0 E^2) or field magnitude times permittivity (ε0 E) rather than N·s/m^3 (same as S/c^2). Acceptable forms that should pass: g = S/c^2, g = (1/μ0 c^2)(E × B), g = ε0 (E × B), and textual statements that the momentum density is parallel to E × B and proportional to S with factor 1/c^2.

Electric Fields and Conducting Wires.title: Conducting wire: Piecewise electric field domain (E=0 inside, 1/r outside)
Electric Fields and Conducting Wires.description: Checks derivations that use Gauss's law for a charged conducting wire in electrostatic equilibrium. Expected: a piecewise statement of the electric field with E(r<r0)=0 inside the metal and E(r>=r0)=lambda/(2*pi*epsilon*r) outside (using epsilon0 in vacuum or epsilon for a medium), and explicit mention of the boundary at the wire radius r0. Also expected: correct use of Gauss surfaces where Q_enc=0 for a cylindrical Gaussian surface with radius r<r0 (no enclosed surface charge) and Q_enc=lambda*L for r>=r0. Flags solutions that present E=lambda/(2*pi*epsilon*r) without specifying the domain r>=r0, that imply or state a nonzero field inside the conductor, that set Q_enc=lambda*L for a Gaussian surface with r<r0, or that omit the role of r0 entirely. If a sketch is provided, it should not show field lines inside the conductor and should reflect a constant potential inside. Do not trigger if the problem explicitly specifies a nonconducting (insulating) wire with a stated volume charge distribution or a non-electrostatic (time-varying) situation.

Electric Fields and Conducting Wires.title: Line-charge electric field magnitude consistency (power-of-ten check)
Electric Fields and Conducting Wires.description: Checks numerical evaluations of the electric field around a long straight charged wire computed via Gauss's law for large errors due to mishandled powers of ten. The expected magnitude outside the wire is E(r) = λ / (2π ε0 r), where λ is the linear charge density and ε0 ≈ 8.854×10^-12 C^2·N^-1·m^-2. The verifier should: (1) Detect that the solution uses a cylindrical Gaussian surface and a line charge model. (2) Extract λ from the problem/solution (e.g., λ = 4.4×10^-11 C·m^-1) and use ε0 unless the solution specifies a different value. (3) Compute the coefficient k = λ / (2π ε0); for λ = 4.4×10^-11 C·m^-1, k ≈ 0.79. (4) For any stated radii r (e.g., r0 = 1×10^-6 m, b_max = 1×10^-4 m) at which the solution reports numerical E values, compute E_expected = k / r. (5) Compare reported E_reported to E_expected via ratio R = E_reported / E_expected. (6) If R is outside [1/3, 3], flag a magnitude inconsistency; if R ≤ 0.1 or R ≥ 10, flag as likely power-of-ten error. Example target values for λ = 4.4×10^-11: E(1×10^-6 m) ≈ 7.9×10^5 N/C; E(1×10^-4 m) ≈ 7.9×10^3 N/C. Reported values like 8.0×10^4 N/C or 8.0 N/C would be flagged. This rule specifically catches errors where the analytic form is correct (E ∝ 1/r) but numerical substitutions produce wrong orders of magnitude due to exponent mishandling.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Misapplication of angular momentum conservation when moment of inertia changes
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: Checks solutions that invoke conservation of angular momentum in rotational systems to ensure they do not equate final and initial angular speeds when the moment of inertia changes between states. The rule triggers when: (1) The solution references conservation of angular momentum (e.g., uses L = I*omega, "no external torque"), and (2) There are indicators that the mass distribution/geometry or coupling changes between initial and final states (e.g., mentions crust and interior coupling, star-quake, friction equalizing angular velocities, shape/flattening factor epsilon, change in radius, mass redistribution, collapse/expansion, decoupled parts becoming locked). The rule flags the following patterns: - Directly setting omega_f = omega_0 (or omega_f = omega_i) solely because friction equalizes angular velocities or because there is no external torque. - Writing I_total*omega_0 = I_total*omega_f and canceling I_total to conclude omega_f = omega_0 when context indicates I changes (different geometry, radius, or coupling) or when different subsystems are combined. - Using the same inertia symbol I on both sides without primes/subscripts while earlier text implies a change in shape/size/composition, or computing distinct inertias for components but then replacing them with a single identical I in the conservation step. To avoid a flag, the solution must either: (a) explicitly use L_i = L_f with I_i*omega_i = I_f*omega_f, computing or justifying I_i and I_f; or (b) explicitly and plausibly justify that I_i = I_f (e.g., rigid body with unchanged geometry and mass distribution) before canceling I. Heuristics/keywords that increase confidence: "friction equalizes", "coupling/locked", "star-quake", "flattening factor/epsilon", "equatorial vs polar radius", "radius changes", "average radius", "liquid interior". Typical symbolic patterns to detect: omega_f = omega_0; w_f = w_0; I*omega_0 = I*omega_f; L conserved -> omega conserved. The rule is lenient if the solution clearly states and maintains a constant moment of inertia assumption consistent with the problem context; otherwise, it reports a logic error for conflating angular momentum conservation with angular velocity conservation.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Correct moment of inertia for square wire frame about in-plane central axis
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule verifies the moment of inertia used for a homogeneous square wire frame (loop) of side length l and total mass m, rotating about an axis lying in the plane of the frame that passes through the center (through the midpoints of two opposite sides) and is parallel to one side. For this geometry, the correct moment of inertia is I = (m l^2) / 6. Derivation (for reference): model the frame as four slender rods of mass m/4 each; two rods parallel to the axis each contribute (m/4)(l/2)^2 = m l^2 /16, totaling m l^2 /8; two rods perpendicular to the axis each contribute (m/4)(l^2/12) = m l^2 /48, totaling m l^2 /24; sum = m l^2 (1/8 + 1/24) = m l^2 /6. The verifier should: (1) Trigger when the solution describes a square wire frame/loop with uniform mass on the sides and an in-plane axis through the midpoints of opposite sides (or equivalently, an axis through the center parallel to one side). (2) Check the moment of inertia value used for rotational dynamics. (3) Flag a calculation error if the solution uses any k != 1/6 in I = k m l^2, especially common incorrect values such as 1/3 (rod about end), 1/12 (single rod about center), 1/8, or values appropriate to a solid plate instead of a wire frame. (4) Optionally cross-check downstream results: if the linearized equation of motion or natural frequency ω uses the incorrect I (e.g., producing a factor of 3 instead of 6 in coefficients proportional to BI/m for this setup), flag the result as inconsistent with I = m l^2 / 6. The rule does not apply to solid square plates or to axes not in the plane or not through the center.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: No torque from forces applied at the chosen pivot point
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: Checks rotational-equilibrium/dynamics equations for improper inclusion of torque from reaction forces applied at the pivot (moment reference) point. Physics principle: The torque of a force about a point lying on the force’s own line of action is zero. Therefore, when moments are taken about a contact/pivot point, any forces applied at that same point (e.g., a ground normal or ground friction at the bottom contact of a rod/ladder) must contribute zero torque and should not appear with a nonzero lever arm in the torque sum. Detection logic: (1) Identify the point about which torques are summed (from text like "about the bottom end/hinge," or from use of an end-pivot moment of inertia such as I_end = (1/3) m l^2, or notation τ_about A = I_A α). (2) Identify forces whose application point coincides with that pivot (e.g., ground normal N and static/kinetic friction f at the bottom contact; hinge reactions at a wall hinge). (3) Inspect the torque equation about that point; flag if any torque term includes these pivot reactions with a nonzero moment arm (patterns such as N·l cosθ, N·R, f·l sinθ, or any symbolically nonzero distance from the pivot). (4) Do not flag if the torque balance is explicitly taken about a different point (e.g., center of mass with I_cm = (1/12) m l^2), where such forces legitimately produce torque. Example caught: In a leaning rod problem taking moments about the bottom contact, terms like N·l cos(θ) or f_s·l sin(θ) are incorrectly included; they must be zero because the forces act at the pivot.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Enforce rolling-without-slipping and gyroscopic coupling in fast-rolling ring/disk models
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: Scope: Any solution modeling a ring/hoop/wheel/disk rolling on a plane near upright orientation, especially with 'rolling without slipping', 'fast rolling', 'gyroscopic stability', or 'minimum speed for stability'. Checkpoints: 1) Nonholonomic rolling constraint: The solution must explicitly impose v_contact = 0 (no slip), or an equivalent velocity relation linking the center-of-mass velocity to angular velocities and orientation (e.g., v_cm = ω × r_contact→CM). Treating δx, y, θ, φ (or similar) as independent generalized coordinates without these velocity constraints is incorrect. 2) Translational–rotational coupling: The kinetic energy or kinematics must exhibit mixed terms arising from the rolling constraints (coupling between CM motion and rotations). A separable T = (1/2) m v_cm^2 + (1/2) I ω^2 with no cross-velocity terms, or equations of motion that decouple translation and rotation, should be flagged. 3) Gyroscopic terms in linearized EOM: For small oscillations about a steady rolling state, the linearized equations must contain skew-symmetric (gyroscopic) terms proportional to the steady speed or spin (e.g., terms linear in V, φ̇, or ω) that couple tilt and spin/yaw. Absence of such terms indicates missing nonholonomic coupling. 4) Frequency and stability dependence on speed: The small-oscillation frequency Ω and the stability criterion must depend on the steady speed V (or spin rate). If Ω is independent of V, or V_min is not obtained from the characteristic equation including gyroscopic terms, flag the solution. 5) Method: The derivation must use Lagrange–d'Alembert with nonholonomic constraints or correctly substitute the rolling kinematic relations into velocities before forming T and the equations of motion; applying unconstrained Euler–Lagrange on independent variables for this system is a modeling error. The verifier should flag solutions failing any of these checks.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Ring EOM must use correct principal moments and include gyroscopic coupling
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: For rigid-body rings/hoops in fast rolling or spinning scenarios, verify that the solution: (1) explicitly identifies principal moments of inertia with respect to the actual small-angle motion axes (for a thin ring of radius R and mass m: I_normal = m R^2 about the symmetry axis normal to the ring plane, and I_diameter = m R^2 / 2 about any diameter in the plane), rather than using generic I or I_φ without axis specification; (2) relates these moments to the chosen small-angle coordinates (e.g., θ, φ) and the geometry; (3) enforces the kinematic no-slip constraint linking CM speed V and spin when applicable (e.g., V ≈ R ω) and retains lowest-order cross terms involving V or spin (terms linear in V or ω multiplied by small angles/rates); (4) includes gyroscopic/Coriolis-type coupling in the kinetic energy or equations of motion (non-diagonal inertia or terms linear in V or spin that couple translational and rotational DOFs), rather than treating T_trans and T_rot as fully decoupled quadratic forms; and (5) produces a stability threshold V_min that depends on the inertia distribution/geometry (R, relevant I) rather than being independent of them. Flag solutions that: (a) introduce unspecified generic moments of inertia, (b) present diagonal, decoupled EOM with no terms linear in V or spin, or (c) derive V_min or Ω without dependence on the ring’s correct moments/geometry.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Rolling ring small-oscillation frequency must include V-dependent gyroscopic term
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule verifies the small-oscillation frequency for a high-speed rolling ring oscillating near the vertical plane. In this context (CM approximately along x-axis with constant speed V; small y, θ, φ), the lowest-order linearization must produce a frequency that depends on V due to gyroscopic stabilization. Specifically, the correct leading-order result is Ω^2 = (8 V^2)/(3 R^2) − (2 g)/(3 R). The rule flags errors when: (a) Ω is reported as √(g/R) or any expression independent of V; (b) the Ω^2 expression lacks both terms proportional to V^2/R^2 and g/R; (c) the numerical coefficients in Ω^2 differ from 8/3 and 2/3 at lowest order; (d) the stability threshold V_min is not computed from Ω^2 ≥ 0, i.e., V_min must equal √(g R)/2. It also checks that the derivation retains the lowest-order V-dependent coupling terms arising from rolling constraints and gyroscopic effects; omitting these terms indicates an incorrect linearization.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Mislabeling azimuthal speed as the normal component of velocity
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: Flags solutions that equate the "normal component of velocity" (e.g., v_n, v_normal) to the azimuthal/tangential polar-coordinate speed (e.g., r*theta_dot, v_theta, omega*r) in contexts where "normal" and "tangential" are defined relative to the trajectory (Frenet frame). Detection criteria: (1) The solution text references path-based normal/tangential components (keywords: E_n, E_t, a_n, a_t, "normal to trajectory", "tangential to trajectory"), and (2) assigns v_n or v_normal to expressions like r*theta_dot, r*dtheta/dt, v_theta, or omega*r. In Frenet kinematics, velocity is tangent to the path, so the normal component of velocity is zero; only acceleration has a normal component. Correct usage in polar coordinates is v_r = r_dot and v_theta = r*theta_dot (tangential), while for trajectory-based components v_n = 0 and v_t = sqrt(r_dot^2 + (r*theta_dot)^2). The rule catches this misinterpretation to prevent computing or identifying v_n as the azimuthal speed.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Misapplied dynamic angular-momentum analysis in static geometry tasks
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: Checks for a modeling mismatch where the problem requests a static geometric quantity (e.g., average radius, flattening, or similar) under stated approximations (e.g., equal densities, ignore interior shape change, use data from a figure) but the solution introduces time-evolution dynamics or conservation laws. The rule flags a solution if: (1) The problem text contains cues like 'average radius', 'flattening factor', 'use data from Fig.', 'assume equal densities', or 'ignore shape change' and does not mention temporal change or dynamics; AND (2) the solution uses dynamic frameworks such as conservation of angular momentum/energy or time-evolution constructs (e.g., 'initial/final angular velocity', 'ω0/ω1', 'spin-up', 'spin-down', 'period change', 'conservation of angular momentum', torques, frictional equalization) or introduces unprompted events (e.g., 'star-quake'); AND/OR (3) the solution fails to reference or apply the stated approximations (equal densities, ignore interior shape change) or to use the provided figure/data, while focusing on temporal evolution instead of computing the requested static geometric quantity. This rule is intended to catch misdirection where conservation-law dynamics are applied to a purely geometric estimation task.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Instantaneous radial length change: do not conserve mechanical energy; conserve angular momentum about pivot
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description:
Purpose: Detect the misuse of mechanical energy conservation across quick/impulsive changes of the distance to a pivot (variable-length pendulum/swing), such as standing/squatting on a swing or reeling a mass in/out. Rationale: During an instantaneous radial change, the interaction/constraint force acts along the rod and does work because there is radial displacement; therefore the mechanical energy of the point mass is not conserved through the event. The correct invariant for the instant is angular momentum about the pivot (exact if the external torque about the pivot is zero, e.g., at the bottom; approximately conserved if the change is impulsive elsewhere).

Flag if any of the following are found across a transition where the radius r changes (e.g., A→A′ or B→B′ in swing problems):
- The solution sets E_after = E_before for the person/point mass without including a nonzero work term from the constraint/actuator (e.g., muscle/rod/string), or states that kinetic energy/speed is unchanged solely by energy conservation.
- The solution asserts K_after = K_before or v_after = v_before at the instant of radial change based on energy conservation alone.
- The solution treats the constraint force as doing no work because it is a 'constraint', despite nonzero radial displacement during the change.

Pass conditions (do not flag) if the solution instead: (a) applies conservation of angular momentum about the pivot (m r^2 ω = const) during the instantaneous radial change, noting that at the lowest point gravity’s torque about the pivot is zero, or (b) explicitly includes the work done by the constraint/actuator during the radial change in the energy balance and does not set E_after = E_before unless that work is shown to be zero by valid reasoning.

Typical trigger phrases/contexts: 'quickly squat/stand', 'instantaneous change of length', 'shorten/lengthen string/rod', 'variable-length pendulum', 'reel in/out', combined with equations like E_A = E_A′, K_A = K_A′, or v_A = v_A′ when r changes.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: No tangential speed from instantaneous radial change at turning point
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule checks for misuse of energy conservation and violation of angular-momentum constraints when a pendulum/swing length is changed instantaneously at an extreme point. Trigger conditions: (a) The solution identifies a highest/lowest point (turning point) where tangential speed is zero (v = 0, ω = 0) and thus angular momentum about the pivot is zero; (b) An instantaneous change of the radial distance (e.g., standing/squatting changing the COM distance r → r + Δr) is performed at that same angle with no external torque about the pivot (force along the radius only); (c) The solution then derives a nonzero tangential speed immediately after the change (v' > 0, ω' ≠ 0), typically by equating total mechanical energy before and after the instantaneous change (E_before = E_after) or by writing mgΔh = (1/2) m v'^2 at the same angular position. The rule flags: (1) Any claim that kinetic energy remains the same (or zero) at the turning point while also computing a nonzero tangential speed right after the radial change; (2) Any derivation that produces nonzero tangential velocity immediately after a purely radial, torque-free, instantaneous length change when the initial angular momentum is zero; (3) Application of energy conservation across the instantaneous internal actuation step to create tangential kinetic energy at the same angle. Rationale: With zero angular momentum and no external torque about the pivot, angular momentum must remain zero during an instantaneous radial change, so tangential speed cannot be created (ω' = 0). Mechanical energy may change due to work by the radial force, but it cannot instantaneously produce tangential kinetic energy when L = 0. Exceptions: Do not flag if the solution explicitly includes an external torque during the change (off-radial impulse, applied moment) or treats a finite-time process with nonzero torque that can change angular momentum.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Improper conservation of angular momentum about COM during impulsive collision
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description: This rule checks the use of angular momentum conservation in problems involving an impact/collision (keywords: collision, impact, impulsive, inelastic, perfectly inelastic, contact with ground/wall/floor). It flags solutions that: (1) claim angular momentum is conserved about the center of mass during the impulsive interval without explicitly justifying that the net external impulsive torque about the COM is zero (e.g., the impulse acts through the COM or all impulsive torques cancel). In typical ground/wall contacts, the contact impulse does not pass through the COM, so conservation about the COM is invalid. (2) compute angular momentum about the COM and incorrectly include a translational term like r_cm × m v_cm (e.g., using m v (l/2) or adding m v r terms) alongside I_cm ω; about the COM, H_COM must be I_COM ω only. (3) equate pre- and post-impact angular momentum using L = I ω with ω tied to v_CM during the collision while external impulses at a contact point exist; this is incorrect unless the chosen origin is one where the net external impulsive moment is zero. The rule expects that any conservation of angular momentum during an impulsive collision be performed about a point/axis with zero net external impulsive moment (commonly the instantaneous point of contact), with gravity treated as negligible over the short collision duration. If the solution uses COM as the reference or mixes translational and rotational terms incorrectly for COM, or omits justification for zero impulsive torque about the chosen origin, the rule should flag it as a logic error.

Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.title: Validate rigid-body angular momentum expression and origin specification
Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics.description:
This rule verifies that total angular momentum for a rigid body is formed correctly and about a clearly specified origin. It flags expressions that incorrectly add a term like m*v*r as a scalar to I*ω without using a cross product or a perpendicular component, and without stating the reference point. Specifically:
- Require the solution to state the origin/axis about which angular momentum is computed before writing L = ...
- If using I_cm (moment of inertia about the center of mass), require L_total = I_cm*ω + r_cm × (m*v_cm). If the translational term is missing, flag. If a scalar term m*v*r (e.g., m*v*(l/2)) is added without a cross product or perpendicular-component explanation, flag.
- If using I_about_origin (via the parallel-axis theorem), allow L_total = I_origin*ω and require that no additional translational term r_cm × (m*v_cm) is added to avoid double counting. If both I_origin*ω and a translational term are included, flag.
- Ensure the translational contribution is expressed as a vector cross product r × p or, in planar motion, as m*v_perp*r with the perpendicular component explicitly identified; if m*v*r is used without sin(theta) or v_perp, flag.
- Check dimensional and conceptual consistency: treating L as a scalar sum I*ω + m*v*r without origin specification, vector direction, or perpendicular component is flagged.
This rule will catch errors such as L_final = I*ω_final + m*v_final*(l/2) and similar formulations that ignore the cross product, the choice of origin, or the parallel-axis theorem.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: No spontaneous motion from frictionless static equilibrium
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks for modeling errors where a frictionless piston or mass initially in static equilibrium (net force = 0) is claimed to move simply by being 'released' or 'allowed to move freely' without any external perturbation. The verifier should: (1) Detect that the solution establishes initial equilibrium (e.g., p_gas*A = p_atm*A + W) with constant external parameters (p0, W, A), implying zero net force and no acceleration if nothing else changes. (2) If the solution then asserts a change of state (e.g., a different final height/volume or α ≠ 1) triggered only by a release, flag an error unless an explicit disturbance is introduced (such as adding/removing load, changing external pressure, heat input, or removing a constraint) and its energy/force effects are accounted for. (3) Flag the use of pV^γ = constant to model an irreversible process initiated solely by release; pV^γ = const applies to quasi-static (reversible) adiabatic paths and cannot justify spontaneous motion from an already balanced frictionless configuration. Expected outcome without disturbance: the system remains at the initial state (α = 1). Any deviation must be justified by a nonzero net force or a time-varying boundary condition and consistent energy balance.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: No horizontal component of gravity in ground-fixed force balance
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule verifies that, in a ground-fixed Cartesian frame (x horizontal, y vertical), the gravitational force mg is not treated as having a horizontal component. Specifically, it checks that ΣF_x does not include any terms proportional to mg (e.g., mg sinθ or mg cosθ), and that horizontal contact forces (such as ground friction) are not directly equated to a 'horizontal component of gravity' like f_s = mg sinθ. The rule allows mg to appear in ΣF_y and in torque expressions (e.g., τ_g = mg * lever arm * sinθ) about a pivot. It also allows decompositions of mg along rotated axes only if the axes are explicitly defined as rotated (e.g., along an incline) and are not mislabeled as the ground-fixed horizontal direction. Trigger examples: (1) An equation labeled as horizontal force balance contains mg sinθ or mg cosθ; (2) A statement sets ground friction f_s equal to mg sinθ in a detachment/toppling analysis on level ground; (3) Any occurrence of mg in ΣF_x without a clearly declared, rotated coordinate system. The rule flags such uses as logical errors because gravity acts purely vertically in the ground-fixed frame, contributing zero to ΣF_x.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Leaning rod detachment angle must be independent of friction coefficients
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: Scope: Problems where a uniform rod/ladder leans against a wall and the top end loses contact (detachment). The student is asked to find the detachment condition/angle (e.g., θ_d, θ2). Check: (1) The derived detachment angle/condition must be obtained from the wall normal force becoming zero (N_wall = 0) and rigid-body dynamics, not from equating ground static friction to its limit. (2) The reported detachment angle (θ_d) or its cosine/sine must not contain the ground or wall friction coefficients (μ_s, μ_k). Flag if θ_d (or cosθ_d, sinθ_d) depends on μ_s or μ_k, e.g., expressions like cosθ_d = 1/(2 μ_s). (3) Flag if the solution sets f_s = μ_s N_ground prior to or at detachment without explicitly stating that the ground contact is at imminent slip at that instant. Reference: For a uniform rod with no bottom slip, the correct detachment result is friction-independent and evaluates to a constant (commonly cosθ_d = 2/3 or θ_d = arccos(2/3)). Accept any equivalent constant independent of μ. Exception: Do not flag if the problem explicitly states the bottom contact is at the threshold of slip at the detachment instant ("imminent/limiting friction"), in which case μ may appear in slip-related conditions; however, detachment must still be enforced via N_wall = 0 rather than by Coulomb equality at the ground. Implementation hints: Detect context via keywords {rod, ladder, leaning, wall, detaches, loses contact}. Parse final/intermediate expressions for θ_d (aliases: θ2, theta_detach) and check symbol dependency on μ_s or μ_k. Also scan for uses of f_s = μ_s N without an accompanying "imminent slip" statement. Flag message: "Detachment angle of leaning rod should be independent of friction; using μ to compute θ_d (e.g., cosθ_d = 1/(2 μ_s)) is a modeling error. Use N_wall = 0 and rigid-body dynamics; for a uniform rod with no bottom slip, cosθ_d = 2/3."

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Missing inter-body contact forces in multi-body equilibrium
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: Checks multi-body statics solutions for omission of interaction forces at explicit contact interfaces. Applicability: Problems that involve two or more rigid bodies in contact (e.g., rods, blocks) with an interface described in the prompt, especially when a contact/friction coefficient (e.g., μ_c) is given. Required modeling: For each body that touches another body, the free-body analysis must include the contact forces at the interface—at minimum a normal force, and a tangential (friction) force if friction is possible—on both bodies (action–reaction pair). Verification steps: (1) Parse the problem for inter-body contact cues (keywords like "contact", named interface points, or coefficients such as μ_c). (2) Inspect the solution’s force listing/FBD and equilibrium equations for variables representing the interface forces (e.g., N_c, F_c, f_c) applied to each body. (3) Ensure those forces appear in both translational balances (ΣF_x, ΣF_y) and, when moments are taken, their torque contributions about a chosen point. (4) Flag an error if the solution omits these contact forces for any body, or if it asserts equalities that implicitly exclude them (e.g., setting horizontal balance to N_wall = f_ground or vertical balance to N_support = mg without additional interface terms when an inter-body contact exists). (5) Also flag if μ_c is referenced by the problem but the solution never introduces a friction variable at the interface or a constraint involving μ_c. Rationale: Omitting inter-body contact forces yields incorrect equilibrium equations and invalid relationships between wall and ground reactions.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Consistent contact/friction modeling (no unspecified friction; correct normals; include inter-rod contact forces)
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks that the contact and friction model used in a solution matches the problem statement. It flags: (a) any introduction of friction at contacts not specified as frictional, (b) any use of the wrong friction coefficient at a contact, (c) nonzero tangential (friction) forces at contacts declared smooth, (d) omission of inter-body contact forces between rods in equilibrium equations, and (e) unjustified assignments of a contact normal equal to the body’s weight. Specifically for problems stating: A is on horizontal ground with coefficient μ_A; B and D are on smooth vertical walls; and the AB–CD contact has coefficient μ_c. The rule fails if the solution: 1) defines or uses a friction force at any contact other than A or the AB–CD interface (e.g., f_C ≤ μ_A N_C), or uses μ_A at the AB–CD interface instead of μ_c; 2) includes any tangential/friction force at B or D (smooth-wall contacts must have zero tangential force); 3) omits the AB–CD contact force components (normal and possible friction) in the equilibrium equations or FBDs for either rod (Newton’s third-law pair must appear on both rods with equal magnitude and opposite direction); 4) sets a contact normal on CD (e.g., N_C) equal to mg without justification when multiple supports/contacts exist or when the contact is not a horizontal support (normal = mg is only valid for a single horizontal support carrying all weight). This rule is intended to catch modeling errors such as introducing ground-like friction at C, misusing μ_A away from A, ignoring AB–CD interaction forces, or equating a contact reaction to the rod’s weight inappropriately.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Component equilibrium omits inter-body contact force contributions
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks whether a solution's force-component equilibrium (ΣFx = 0 or ΣFy = 0) for a given rigid body includes all external contact forces that the problem statement specifies. In multi-body contact problems, every contact (with ground, walls, and other bodies) can exert a reaction that generally has components along both axes unless explicitly eliminated by smoothness and geometry. The rule flags cases where the student equates two forces in a component balance (e.g., N_wall = f_ground) while the problem indicates at least one additional contact that could contribute to that component (e.g., an AB–CD interface with nonzero or unspecified friction μ_c), and the solution does not include that contact force or justify its component being zero. Specifically: if the problem lists a contact between bodies with μ_c > 0 (or unspecified), the equilibrium for each body touching that interface must include the normal and friction at the contact resolved into components. Omitting these and asserting a two-term equality is a logical error unless the solution explicitly argues, based on smoothness and geometry, that the contact force has no component along the axis. The rule aims to catch statements like “Horizontal equilibrium: N_B = f_A” for rod AB when an AB–CD contact exists, by detecting incomplete free-body accounting of contact forces in the component equations.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Include inter-body contact forces and friction in multi-body statics
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: Checks solutions to multi-rigid-body equilibrium problems that specify a frictional inter-body contact (e.g., between two rods) alongside external supports. The rule verifies: (1) All contacts from the problem statement are represented with reaction forces in the free-body analysis—specifically, the inter-body contact must include both a normal force and a tangential (friction) force, and support contacts use appropriate reactions (smooth walls: no tangential reaction; rough ground: normal plus friction). (2) Coulomb static friction constraints are applied at each rough contact: |f| ≤ μ N, including the inter-body contact with the given μ_c. (3) Force and moment balance for each body explicitly couples through the inter-body contact forces (equal and opposite across bodies), rather than treating support frictions in isolation. (4) Any derived condition or final relation for geometric variables (e.g., an angle α) depends on the specified inter-body friction coefficient μ_c when the problem includes it; flag as a conceptual error if the result omits μ_c or depends only on unrelated supports (e.g., only μ_A). The rule triggers when the solution lacks inter-body contact forces, fails to use μ_c in equilibrium or inequality constraints, or attempts to bound variables using only isolated support friction without coupling through the contact.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Missing inter-contact forces in equilibrium of multi-contact rods
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description:
This rule checks solutions for rigid bodies with multiple contacts (ground, wall, and an inter-rod contact with friction) to ensure all contact forces are included in force and torque balances. Trigger conditions:
- The problem statement specifies a contact between two rods with a given friction coefficient (μ_c). If the solution does not introduce variables for both the normal and tangential (friction) components at this inter-rod contact, flag an error.
- Vertical force balance for a rod sets the ground normal equal to the weight (e.g., N_A = mg) while the setup includes any potential vertical interaction at the inter-rod contact; such an equation indicates omission of vertical components from the inter-rod force.
- Horizontal force balance equates wall normal to ground friction (e.g., N_B = f_A) without accounting for horizontal components from the inter-rod contact force.
- Torque balance about a contact point yields a wall reaction of the form N_wall = (mg cos θ)/(2 sin θ) (or structurally similar ratios involving only mg and geometry), with no terms arising from the inter-rod contact force; this indicates missing torque contributions.
- Final angle/inequality conditions (e.g., cot θ ≤ k μ_A or cot α ≤ k μ_A for some constant k) that do not involve μ_c are flagged, since the inter-rod friction coefficient must influence the equilibrium condition.
The rule is intended to catch incorrect torque relations and force balances that arise from omitting contact forces and misapplying geometry in multi-contact equilibrium problems.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Do not set a single support normal equal to mg when other contacts can carry vertical force
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks vertical force balance statements for each rigid body in multi-contact equilibrium problems. It flags solutions that set a single support normal equal to the weight (e.g., N = mg, N_A = mg) while the body has other contacts or constraints that can transmit vertical force components. Detection logic: (1) Identify each body's vertical equilibrium equation (sum of forces in the vertical direction, or explicit statements like N = mg). (2) From the problem setup and the solution's force list, determine whether the body has any additional interactions that can produce vertical components: inter-body contacts with nonzero friction coefficient (μ > 0), friction at any contact point, oblique contact normals, tension/compression in members at nonzero angles, or any external forces with vertical components. (3) If such interactions exist and the vertical equilibrium is written as N_support = mg or omits vertical components from these other contacts, flag the solution. (4) Do not flag if the solution explicitly demonstrates that all other potential vertical components are zero (e.g., friction coefficient at the contact is zero, the contact is smooth with no tangential force, the line of action is horizontal, or geometry eliminates vertical components). Example of a violation: For a rod on the ground that also touches another rod at a frictional interface (μ_c > 0), writing N_A = mg ignores the vertical component that the inter-rod contact can carry; the correct balance must include the vertical component of the AB–CD contact reaction. This rule also catches analogous errors such as setting N = mg for a block pulled by a rope at an angle or for a body on an inclined/oblique member without accounting for vertical components of those interactions.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Require lever-arm/line-of-action justification for zero torque about pivot
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks justifications for conservation of angular momentum about a pivot during an impulsive collision. It flags solutions that assert zero external torque about the pivot using imprecise direction-only arguments (e.g., 'tension exerts no torque because it acts along the string') without referencing the correct criterion. The correct criterion is: a force has zero torque about a chosen point if its point of application is at that point (lever arm is zero) or its line of action passes through that point (r × F = 0 due to colinearity). The rule triggers when: (1) the student concludes angular momentum is conserved about a pivot; and (2) the justification for zero torque mentions only that a force acts 'along the string/radius/connection' or relies solely on force direction, without explicitly stating that the force’s line of action passes through the pivot or that the lever arm is zero. It also flags misstatements that attribute zero torque to a force because of its direction while incorrectly identifying the point of application (e.g., claiming a force at the pivot has zero torque due to direction rather than zero lever arm). Acceptable explanations must explicitly connect zero torque to lever arm being zero or the line of action passing through the pivot, and should recognize that pivot reactions have zero torque about the pivot and that tension in a string gives zero torque about the pivot because its line of action goes through the pivot. If these conditions are not met, the justification is marked conceptually inconsistent.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Unjustified inclusion of external forces/potentials
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description:
Checks that the forces and potential energy terms used in the model match those specified or implied by the problem statement. If the problem restricts interactions to gravity and rolling constraints (e.g., a rigid ring rolling under gravity with small oscillations), then the model should include only gravitational potential (e.g., U = m g y or m g h) and constraint effects (which are non-conservative and do not appear in U). The rule flags inclusion of electromagnetic or other unrelated interactions unless explicitly introduced by the problem. Detection cues include:
- Potential energy terms involving electric or magnetic quantities (e.g., U = qV, U = k_e q1 q2 / r, magnetic vector potential A, or terms with epsilon_0, mu_0).
- Force expressions containing qE, q v × B, Coulomb or Lorentz force, or keywords: electric, magnetic, charge, field, Coulomb, Lorentz.
- Introduction of parameters not present in the problem (q, E, B, k_e, epsilon_0, mu_0) without justification. The rule passes if such terms are absent or the problem explicitly includes them; otherwise it raises a modeling error for unjustified forces/potentials.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Incorrect floor normal when mass is internally suspended
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description:
Checks problems where a box/container of mass M rests on a horizontal floor with friction and an internal mass m is attached to the box via a string/rod (e.g., a pendulum at angle θ with tension T). Flags solutions that model the floor normal force on the box as N = (M + m) g, N = Mg + mg, or use friction limits μ(M + m)g, ignoring that the internal mass’s weight is transmitted to the box via the joint force. Correct modeling requires the floor normal to equal the box’s weight plus the vertical component of the attachment force on the box (and any other external vertical loads), e.g., N = Mg + T cos θ when the box has no vertical acceleration. Detection criteria:
- Context includes: (i) a box on a horizontal surface with friction; (ii) an internal mass m suspended/attached to the box (string/rod), with an angle θ and/or tension T referenced.
- Any equation or statement sets N to (M + m) g or Mg + mg, or sets friction to μ(M + m) g, without including a vertical component of the attachment force (e.g., T cos θ) acting on the box.
- N or friction is modeled independent of θ (e.g., constant Mg + mg) while θ ≠ 0 is discussed.
- Specifically flags use of mg (from the internal mass) inside N when there is no contact of m with the floor/box base and no explicit joint-force vertical component in N.
Allowed forms (examples): N = Mg + T cos θ; N − Mg − T cos θ = 0; N = Mg + F_attach,vertical. Disallowed forms (examples): N = (M + m) g; N = Mg + mg; f_max = μ(M + m) g, unless accompanied by a justified joint-force substitution that reduces to an equivalent expression. The rule also checks special angles: at θ = 90°, N should reduce to Mg (not Mg + mg). This rule aims to prevent treating the internal mass’s weight as directly supported by the floor instead of through the attachment’s vertical force component.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Static friction at threshold: forbid using Ma or a = μ_s N/M before sliding
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks solutions involving a body that is at rest with static friction and is described as 'just begins to slide', 'on the verge of motion', 'threshold of sliding', or 'impending motion'. It flags the following modeling errors: (1) Using Newton’s second law ΣF = M a for the friction-limited body at the threshold, e.g., writing T sin(θ) − f_s = M a_box or directly setting a_box = f_s(max)/M, a_box = μ_s N / M, or a_box = μ_s g. (2) Treating the body’s acceleration as nonzero while static friction is still in effect, except immediately after the threshold; at the threshold condition itself, static friction still applies and acceleration should not be used to determine f_s. The correct condition at impending motion is: static friction magnitude equals its maximum, f_s = μ_s N, and the net horizontal force on the friction-limited body balances this static friction at that instant (ΣF_horizontal = 0 for that body just before motion; at the threshold, use f_s = μ_s N to relate applied horizontal forces). The verifier should flag any step that computes acceleration from μ_s N or μ_s g, or that substitutes Ma for the friction-limited body instead of using f_s = μ_s N at the stated threshold angle or condition.

Static Equilibrium and Forces.title: Detect inconsistent force balance and contradictory algebra in accelerating systems
Static Equilibrium and Forces.description: This rule checks for logical inconsistencies when analyzing dynamics (non-zero acceleration) problems. It flags solutions that simultaneously apply static equilibrium component balances and non-zero acceleration, or that yield mutually contradictory expressions for the same quantity. Specifically: (1) If the solution asserts a static vertical balance like "T cos(theta) = mg" or any component sum = 0 while also using non-zero acceleration (e.g., a = g sin(theta) for a swinging pendulum), the rule flags this as misuse of equilibrium in an accelerating system. (2) It collects all derived expressions for a target quantity (e.g., tension T) and checks for consistency; if two or more expressions (such as T = mg/cos(theta) and T = mg) are implied under the same conditions (e.g., theta = 60°), and they cannot be simultaneously true (e.g., would require cos(theta) = 1 at theta ≠ 0), the rule flags a contradiction. (3) It scans algebraic steps for impossible numeric equalities arising from these inconsistencies, such as sqrt(3) = 3 or sqrt(21) = 6, or deducing cos(60°) = 1, and flags them. The verifier should substitute given angle values and known trig identities to test whether the set of student equations has a consistent solution; absence of a consistent solution or presence of contradictory equalities triggers this rule.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: SHO about equilibrium: require offset term and correct initial conditions
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description:
This rule verifies consistency when solving spring–mass motion under a constant force (e.g., gravity) by checking proper use of the equilibrium offset and initial conditions. It targets errors where the equilibrium shift is computed but then omitted from the time-dependent solution or misused as the oscillation amplitude. The rule triggers if any of the following are detected: 
- An equilibrium extension x0 is introduced (e.g., k x0 = total weight) but the subsequent equation of motion is written as homogeneous in x, (M_total) x'' + k x = 0, without explicitly redefining the coordinate y = x − x0; in such cases, the final solution must include an additive offset +x0 (i.e., x(t) = x0 + A cos(ω t + φ)). If x(t) is purely oscillatory about zero (no +x0), flag.
- After defining x0, the solution uses x(t) = −x0 cos(ω t) or sets the amplitude A = x0, indicating that x0 was treated as the oscillation amplitude rather than the static offset; flag.
- Initial conditions are applied to x instead of the shifted variable y = x − x0. For scenarios where the system is held at the old equilibrium and then an additional mass m is added at release, verify y(0) = x(0) − x0 = −(m g)/k and y'(0) = 0. If y(0) is set to 0 or −x0, flag.
- Consistency check: If ω = sqrt(k/M_total) is used (implying SHO about equilibrium), the mean of x(t) over time must equal x0. If the provided x(t) has zero mean (no offset) while x0 was computed, flag.
This rule allows correct alternatives where the coordinate is explicitly defined relative to equilibrium from the start (never introducing x0) and all initial conditions are consistently applied to that shifted coordinate.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: SHM Linearization Restoring-Sign Consistency
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: Checks for sign consistency when linearizing the equation of motion near equilibrium and subsequently asserting simple harmonic motion (SHM). Detection logic: (1) Identify a defined perturbation variable (e.g., Δq = q − q_eq, δq, or similar). (2) Parse any linearized second-order ODE of the form d^2q/dt^2 = C·Δq or d^2Δq/dt^2 = C·Δq, where C is taken as a constant near equilibrium. (3) Verify that the sign of C matches the claimed behavior: for SHM about a stable equilibrium, the restoring acceleration must oppose displacement, i.e., d^2Δq/dt^2 = −|C|·Δq, and ω^2 = |C| > 0. (4) Flag inconsistency if the solution derives d^2q/dt^2 = +C·Δq (C > 0) and then immediately writes the SHM form d^2Δq/dt^2 + C·Δq = 0, or claims oscillatory motion/frequency ω = sqrt(C) without addressing the required negative sign (i.e., without showing C < 0 or redefining Δq with opposite sign). (5) Ensure the equivalence d^2Δq/dt^2 = d^2q/dt^2 is respected: flipping sign between consecutive lines without explicit justification is flagged. Example trigger: a derivation yielding d^2 y/dt^2 = (γ g / y_i)·Δy followed by d^2Δy/dt^2 + (γ g / y_i)·Δy = 0 or ω^2 = γ g / y_i; this indicates a sign inconsistency because stable SHM requires d^2Δy/dt^2 = −(γ g / y_i)·Δy. The rule applies to any coordinate and perturbation variable; it ignores cases where the perturbation is explicitly defined with opposite sign (e.g., Δq = q_eq − q) and the sign is handled consistently.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Correct spring-constant indexing for forces in a linear molecule (1D chain)
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: This rule verifies that the Hookean force expressions (or equivalent equations of motion) for a linear chain of N masses m_i connected by N−1 springs with constants k_1...k_{N−1} are modeled with the correct spring-constant indexing and without double-counting at the endpoints. It expects the chain topology where spring k_j connects atom j to atom j+1, and no external springs or fixed supports. Checks: (1) For interior atoms i = 2...N−1, the force must be F_i = −k_{i−1}(x_i − x_{i−1}) − k_i(x_i − x_{i+1}) = k_{i−1} x_{i−1} − (k_{i−1}+k_i) x_i + k_i x_{i+1}. The rule flags if: (a) the same spring constant is used for both neighbors (e.g., F_i = −2 k_i x_i + k_i x_{i−1} + k_i x_{i+1}); (b) coeff(x_i) equals −2·k_i (or −2·k_{i−1}) instead of −(k_{i−1}+k_i); (c) coeff(x_{i−1}) equals k_i instead of k_{i−1}; (d) coeff(x_{i+1}) equals k_{i−1} instead of k_i. (2) For the first atom i = 1, the force must be F_1 = −k_1(x_1 − x_2) = −k_1 x_1 + k_1 x_2. The rule flags if: (a) an extra −k_1 x_1 term is added (double-counting), yielding −2 k_1 x_1 + k_1 x_2; (b) any term with k_0 or a second spring on atom 1 appears. (3) For the last atom i = N, the force must be F_N = −k_{N−1}(x_N − x_{N−1}) = −k_{N−1} x_N + k_{N−1} x_{N−1}. The rule flags if: (a) an extra −k_{N−1} x_N term is added (double-counting), yielding −2 k_{N−1} x_N + k_{N−1} x_{N−1}; (b) any term with k_N or a second spring on atom N appears. Implementation notes: Parse the user’s force/EOM expressions into linear combinations of x_{i−1}, x_i, x_{i+1} with coefficients that are symbolic functions of k_j. Compare coefficients to the expected pattern above; flag on any mismatch. This rule catches modeling errors where the left/right spring constants are incorrectly indexed or endpoint forces are double-counted.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Internal-force relationship vs per-particle SHM misuse
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: Checks that, in an isolated multi-mass spring system (e.g., a linear molecule with only inter-atomic springs and no external forces/anchors), a requested 'relationship among the forces' is expressed as an internal-force cancellation statement rather than per-particle equations of motion. Pass conditions (any one suffices): (a) explicit net internal force vanishes on the whole system, e.g., Σ_i F_i = 0; (b) pairwise internal forces cancel, e.g., F_{i→j} = -F_{j→i}; (c) center-of-mass/momentum statements equivalent to (a), e.g., dP/dt = 0, a_CM = 0, X_CM linear in time, or Σ_i m_i x_i = M X_CM = constant (for small oscillations about equilibrium). Fail conditions: the solution presents only per-particle dynamics (e.g., F_i = m_i a_i, F_i = -m_i ω^2 x_i, or solely Hooke-law forces on individual masses) and labels this as the 'relationship among the forces' without including any of the internal-cancellation/CM invariants above. Additional indicator of omission: failure to acknowledge/allow the translational (ω = 0) mode when discussing normal modes. Exceptions/guards: Do not apply if the problem includes external forces, fixed/anchored ends, walls, driving, damping, or fields; if such terms are detected, skip this rule. Implementation hints: Look for keywords/phrases such as 'sum of forces is zero', 'internal forces cancel', 'equal and opposite', 'Newton’s third law (internal)', 'center of mass', 'momentum conserved', 'Σ m_i x_i = const', 'a_CM = 0', or 'ω = 0 mode'. Flag if those are absent while phrases like 'F_i = m_i a_i', 'F_i = -m_i ω^2 x_i', or only individual Hooke-force expressions are used to answer a prompt asking for a relationship among forces.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Correct indexing of spring constants in linear-chain normal-mode equations
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: This rule verifies the equations of motion/normal-mode eigenvalue equations for a 1D linear molecule (N masses m_i connected by N−1 springs with constants k_1,…,k_{N−1}). It flags the common mistake of using the same spring constant k_i for both the left and right springs of atom i and of replacing the diagonal spring coefficient by 2·k_i instead of the sum of the neighboring spring constants. Checks performed: (1) Interior atoms (2 ≤ i ≤ N−1): The correct force balance is m_i x_i'' = k_{i−1}(x_{i−1} − x_i) + k_i(x_{i+1} − x_i). Under the normal-mode ansatz x_i(t) = A_i e^{iωt}, the algebraically equivalent forms are k_{i−1} x_{i−1} + k_i x_{i+1} − (k_{i−1} + k_i) x_i = −m_i ω^2 x_i or [(k_{i−1}+k_i) − m_i ω^2] x_i − k_{i−1} x_{i−1} − k_i x_{i+1} = 0. Flag an error if the interior equation uses k_i on both neighbor terms (x_{i−1} and x_{i+1}) and a diagonal coefficient 2·k_i (e.g., k_i x_{i−1} + (2 k_i − m_i ω^2) x_i + k_i x_{i+1} = 0), unless the solution explicitly and correctly assumes a uniform chain k_j ≡ k for all j. (2) Boundary atoms: i = 1 must use only k_1: m_1 x_1'' = k_1 (x_2 − x_1) ⇒ k_1 x_2 − k_1 x_1 = −m_1 ω^2 x_1. i = N must use only k_{N−1}: m_N x_N'' = k_{N−1} (x_{N−1} − x_N) ⇒ k_{N−1} x_{N−1} − k_{N−1} x_N = −m_N ω^2 x_N. Flag an error if boundary equations contain −2 k_1 x_1 or −2 k_{N−1} x_N or use mismatched spring indices. (3) Mass/frequency term placement: Ensure the inertial term appears as −m_i ω^2 x_i (or equivalently moved to the LHS) and is not mixed into neighbor coefficients. The rule triggers when the problem statement provides distinct spring constants k_1,…,k_{N−1} (nonuniform chain) and the solution’s coefficients do not map to k_{i−1} for x_{i−1}, k_i for x_{i+1}, and (k_{i−1}+k_i) for x_i for interior atoms, or when boundary equations include spurious duplicate spring contributions.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Require COM conservation and zero-frequency translational mode in isolated mass–spring systems
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: Purpose: Detect solutions that ignore the center-of-mass (COM) consequence of internal forces and omit the translational zero-frequency normal mode in an isolated molecule (masses connected by springs, no external forces or fixed supports). When to apply: Problems modeling a finite chain of masses m_i connected by springs k_i with only internal (spring) forces, analyzing longitudinal motion/normal modes. Checks: (1) Momentum/COM statement: The solution should explicitly acknowledge that the sum of internal forces is zero (∑F_i = 0), implying total momentum conservation and d^2 X_CM/dt^2 = 0, or equivalently that the COM coordinate M X_CM = ∑ m_i x_i is constant (or moves uniformly). Accept any of: mentions of “center of mass”, “COM”, “momentum conserved”, “no external force”, “d^2 X_CM/dt^2 = 0”, “∑F_i = 0 implies P=const”. (2) Zero-frequency translational mode: The solution should identify a normal mode with ω = 0 in which all atoms translate together (mode shape u_i = const). Accept mentions of “ω = 0”, “zero frequency”, “translational mode”, or listing a frequency set that includes 0. (3) Vibrational-mode COM constraint: For non-translational vibrational modes, the solution should note or enforce ∑ m_i u_i = 0 (or ∑ m_i x_i = const, often set to 0 by choosing origin), indicating vibrations about a fixed COM. (4) End-force consistency (symptom of COM violation): For an isolated chain, end-atom force laws must involve only their single adjacent spring: F_1 = k_1 (x_2 − x_1) and F_N = −k_{N−1} (x_N − x_{N−1}). Flag if end equations include standalone wall-like restoring terms (e.g., −k_1 x_1 or −k_{N−1} x_N) without an external support, or if forces are double-counted leading to −2 k_1 x_1 + k_1 x_2, etc. Flagging criteria: Raise an error if (A) none of the COM/momentum/ω=0 indicators in (1)–(3) are present, or (B) the solution asserts or implies that all normal modes have nonzero frequency, or (C) end-atom force expressions include unsupported wall terms as in (4). This rule targets the conceptual oversight that internal forces cannot accelerate the COM; hence one normal mode is translational (ω=0), and other modes are vibrations about a fixed COM.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Disallow constant-acceleration modeling in mass–spring systems with applied force
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description:
This rule checks solutions for incorrect modeling of a mass attached to a linear spring (Hooke's law) when a constant external force is applied. Specifically, it flags cases where the acceleration is treated as constant (e.g., a = F/m) or kinematic equations for uniform acceleration are used, while the spring is engaged. The correct equation of motion during the forcing interval is m*x'' = F - k*x (or equivalently x'' + (k/m) x = F/m), implying acceleration depends on displacement and is not constant.

The rule triggers when:
- The problem context includes a spring with constant k connected to the moving mass, and an external force F acts along the spring axis for a finite time.
- The solution asserts a = F/m, uses F = m a with only the applied force F (omitting the spring force -k x), or applies constant-acceleration kinematic formulas (e.g., x = x0 + v0 t + 0.5 a t^2, v = v0 + a t) during a period where the spring is stretched/compressed.

Expected correct modeling:
- Include the spring force in the net force: m*x'' = F - k*x during the forcing interval, and m*x'' + k*x = 0 after the force is removed, with continuity of x and v at the switch.
- Recognize the shifted equilibrium x_eq = F/k and that the motion under constant F is oscillatory about x_eq, not uniformly accelerated.

Allowed exceptions (must be explicitly justified in the solution):
- k = 0 (no spring), or the spring is slack/not engaged so -k x = 0 throughout the interval.
- A limiting argument confined to an infinitesimal time where x ≈ 0 and the spring force is rigorously demonstrated negligible; this cannot be used to determine a finite duration.

Detection patterns to flag:
- Statements like "a = F/m" without a spring term in a spring–mass context.
- Use of phrases "constant acceleration" or "uniform acceleration" for the forced motion with a spring present.
- Application of constant-acceleration kinematics while k ≠ 0 and displacement is nonzero.

If any flagged pattern appears without a valid exception, the solution fails this rule.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Incorrect use of static equilibrium (x = F/k) to infer zero velocity in driven SHM
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: This rule flags solutions that set the displacement x = F/k (force balance F = kx) to determine the instant when the mass is momentarily at rest for a mass–spring system with a constant applied force. In the equation m x'' + k x = F, x = F/k is the static equilibrium under the applied force; crossing this position corresponds to maximal speed in the shifted SHO, not zero velocity. Correctly, if the constant force is switched on at t = 0 with initial conditions x(0) = 0 and v(0) = 0, the motion is x(t) = (F/k)(1 − cos(ωt) ) and v(t) ∝ sin(ωt) with ω = √(k/m), so v = 0 at t = n π/ω (n integer). The rule triggers when a solution: (a) equates net force to zero (F = kx) to claim the object stops or uses x = F/k to find the stopping time; (b) states that the object 'returns to the equilibrium position' at t = π/ω while the constant force remains applied; or (c) conflates static equilibrium with turning points. The verifier should check that rest instants under sustained constant force occur at t = n π√(m/k) and that x = F/k is a crossing point with maximal speed, not a rest condition.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Force-removal rest condition must include zero velocity and zero post-removal net force
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: Checks solutions to problems where an external force is applied for a duration and then removed (e.g., a mass-spring system with a constant force). If the requirement is that the object be at rest at the instant the force is removed, the solution must enforce both: (1) instantaneous velocity at removal is zero, and (2) the net force immediately after removal is zero (so acceleration is zero and the object does not start moving again). In a linear mass-spring with constant force F, starting from x=0 and v=0, the applied force shifts the equilibrium to x=F/k while it is on; after removal, the equilibrium reverts to x=0. Solutions that set the removal time to an odd half-period, Δt = (2n+1)·π√(m/k), using only the v=0 condition, are flagged, because at that instant the displacement is x=2F/k and the post-removal spring force −kx is nonzero, causing immediate acceleration. The rule accepts times that satisfy both conditions, e.g., Δt = n·2π√(m/k), or any t_stop for which v(t_stop)=0 and x(t_stop) equals the post-removal equilibrium (x=0 for no external force). This rule also flags reasoning that equates 'at rest at removal' solely with v=0 without verifying zero net force after the force is turned off.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Consistent small-oscillation linearization and constraint-respecting EOM
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: This rule verifies that equations of motion (EOM) for constrained rolling or oscillating systems are derived consistently from a well-defined model and that the linearization to lowest order in small quantities is respected.
