The solution must: (1) start from a clear Lagrangian or Newton–Euler formulation with stated constraints (e.g., rolling without slipping, near-vertical plane, CM moving at approximately constant speed V) and show how the EOM follow (Euler–Lagrange or force/torque balance); (2) when the text states 'retain terms to the lowest order of small quantities,' include only first-order terms in the declared small variables and their derivatives; mixed products of small quantities (e.g., y·θ, ẏ·θ̇, θ̈·y) are considered higher order and must be omitted unless an explicit scaling argument is provided that makes such products first order; (3) avoid free-fall CM equations like ÿ = −g when constraints imply near-constant height or small oscillations about equilibrium—gravity must enter via potential energy leading to linear restoring terms, not an unbalanced constant acceleration; (4) ensure coefficients in the linearized EOM are time-invariant and depend only on parameters such as V, g, geometry, and inertias, consistent with the assumption of constant forward speed; and (5) prohibit ad hoc mixed terms or forms not traceable to the stated model. The rule flags solutions that present inconsistent EOM (e.g., ÿ = −g under near-vertical rolling) or include higher-order/mixed terms without derivation despite a claimed first-order linearization.

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.title: Unjustified harmonic time-dependence in linearized EOM
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) and Oscilla.description: Flag solutions that assume sinusoidal (cosine/sine) time dependence for small variables without deriving an appropriate linearized equation of motion that supports oscillations. The checker should: (1) Detect statements like "assume x(t) = A cos(Ωt)" or "lowest-order small quantities vary as cos(Ωt)". (2) Verify that, for each variable with assumed harmonic form, the derived linearized ODE is homogeneous and contains a restoring term, e.g., x¨ + ω² x = 0, or a standard damped oscillator x¨ + 2ζω x˙ + ω² x = 0, or a coupled linear system M q¨ + C q˙ + K q = 0 with a positive-semidefinite mass matrix M and positive-definite stiffness K leading to purely imaginary eigenvalues ±iΩ. (3) If the equation is of the form x¨ = 0 (free drift), x¨ = constant (e.g., gravity only), first-order in time, or includes nonzero forcing terms without a balancing stiffness (M q¨ + K q = F(t)), then sinusoidal time dependence is unjustified and should be flagged. (4) Check the sign of the effective stiffness: if ω² ≤ 0 (zero or negative), or eigenvalues are real (exponential) rather than imaginary, harmonic motion is not supported—flag the assumption. (5) Require explicit identification of an equilibrium and linearization about that equilibrium; if equilibrium/linearization is omitted and harmonic forms are imposed, flag. Example triggers: assuming δx(t) ∝ cos(Ωt) when δx¨ = 0, or y(t) ∝ cos(Ωt) when y¨ = −g. This rule aims to prevent using a harmonic ansatz before establishing restoring dynamics from the equations of motion.

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Plumb-line tilt must be derived from the horizontal component of centrifugal acceleration (vector-sum model)
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description:
This rule verifies modeling of the vertical deviation of a plumb line on a rotating Earth. It enforces that the plumb line aligns with the direction of the resultant effective acceleration (true gravity plus centrifugal), not via a force balance along the plumb line or by equating radial gravity to the full centrifugal magnitude. The rule checks the following:
- The solution must decompose the centrifugal acceleration at latitude λ into components: radial component ω^2 R cos^2(λ) (reduces the radial gravity) and horizontal equatorward component ω^2 R sin(λ) cos(λ) (produces the tilt).
- The tilt angle α must be obtained from the ratio of these components, e.g., tan(α) = [ω^2 R sin(λ) cos(λ)] / [g0 − ω^2 R cos^2(λ)]. For small angles, the acceptable approximation is α ≈ (ω^2 R / g0) sin(λ) cos(λ).
- It flags errors where the entire centrifugal term ω^2 R cos(λ) is used as the tilting (horizontal) component, or where equations of the form mg cos(α) = m ω^2 R cos(λ) or mg_eff cos(α) = m ω^2 R cos(λ) appear (indicative of balancing forces along the plumb line or using the wrong component).
- It flags formulas for α(λ) that lack the sin(λ) factor (e.g., α ∝ cos(λ) only), or any derivation that maximizes α at λ = 0° (equator) or λ = 90° (pole) rather than at λ = 45° (where sin(λ) cos(λ) is maximal).
- It requires that the stated maximum deviation occur at λ = 45° and, if a numerical value is provided, be consistent with α_max ≈ (ω^2 R) / (2 g0) under the small-angle approximation.
Rationale: The plumb line aligns with the net effective gravity vector; the tilt is set by the horizontal (equatorward) component of the centrifugal acceleration relative to the net radial component. Using the full centrifugal magnitude or balancing forces along the plumb line leads to incorrect latitude dependence and maximum location.

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Plumb-line deflection: missing sin(λ) projection in centrifugal component
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description:
Checks solutions for the vertical deviation of a plumb line due to Earth's rotation. The correct small-angle relation is tan(α) ≈ (ω^2 R / g0) sin(λ) cos(λ) = (ω^2 R / 2 g0) sin(2λ). This rule flags conceptual errors where the latitude dependence from projecting the centrifugal acceleration onto the local horizontal is omitted.

It performs the following checks:
- Formula check: If a student gives tan(α) or α proportional to (ω^2 R / g0) times a function of latitude f(λ), verify f(λ) equals sin(λ) cos(λ) (or equivalently 0.5 sin(2λ)). Flag if f(λ) is only cos(λ), only sin(λ), or any form lacking the sin(λ) cos(λ) product, e.g., tan(α) = (ω^2 R cos(λ))/g0.
- Boundary conditions: Evaluate the provided f(λ) at λ = 0° (equator) and λ = 90° (pole). Correct physics requires α(0°) = α(90°) = 0. Flag if the expression yields nonzero values at either boundary.
- Maximum location: The deviation attains its maximum at λ = 45° (since sin(λ) cos(λ) is maximized there). Flag if the stated latitude of maximum is not 45°, or if the implied maximum from the given f(λ) occurs at a different latitude (e.g., f(λ) = cos(λ) implies a maximum at 0°).
- Projection reasoning: If the solution uses the full centrifugal magnitude ω^2 R cos(λ) as the horizontal component without the necessary sin(λ) factor from geometrical projection onto the local tangent plane, flag as a concept error.

This rule is specific to plumb-line/vertical deviation problems under Earth's rotation and catches overestimates of α caused by omitting the sin(λ) factor.

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Require justified angular dependence and correct periodicity in heading deviation models
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description: When verifying solutions that determine headings where a deviation δθ is maximal under small parameters (e.g., K_b, K_s ≪ 1), check the modeling assumptions for δθ(θ). The solution must either derive δθ(θ) from governing equations or cite a standard model consistent with the physical effect described (e.g., compass deviation components). Flag an error if: (1) the student asserts an ad hoc first-harmonic form δθ = a sin(θ) + b cos(θ) (or equivalent) without justification when the context implies quadrantal dependence (sin(2θ), cos(2θ)); (2) the computed extrema are based on that unjustified first-harmonic form (e.g., θ = arctan(a/b)), yielding periodicity inconsistent with the known effect; (3) a Taylor expansion with respect to θ is used to locate maxima/minima without specifying or deriving δθ(θ). For compass deviation with small coefficients, correct periodicity for quadrantal terms is 2θ (maxima near 45° + n·90°), while semicircular terms are sin(θ), cos(θ) and must be justified by the problem context. Flag any mismatch between the modeled periodicity and the stated physical source of error, or missing derivation/reference for the assumed δθ(θ).

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Centripetal acceleration must use total speed and circle constraint
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description: Checks solutions where a point is constrained to move on a circle of radius R (e.g., bead on a ring, intersection point of overlapping circles) and a centripetal acceleration about the circle’s center is derived. The rule verifies that the centripetal acceleration magnitude is expressed as a_c = v^2 / R (or equivalently a_c = R * (dθ/dt)^2) using the total speed v computed from both velocity components consistent with the geometric constraint x^2 + y^2 = R^2. It flags solutions that compute a_c from a single component (e.g., a_c = v_y^2 / R, a_c = (g t/2)^2 / R) or that neglect the coupling implied by the circle constraint (x ẋ + y ẏ = 0), which requires v^2 = ẋ^2 + ẏ^2 = ẏ^2 * (R^2 / x^2). For overlapping-ring intersection problems with vertical center separation s(t), the rule expects the use of x^2 = R^2 − s(t)^2/4, y = s(t)/2, ẋ = −[s(t) ṡ(t)]/(4 x), ẏ = ṡ(t)/2, leading to v^2 = ṡ(t)^2 R^2 / [4 (R^2 − s(t)^2/4)] and a_c = ṡ(t)^2 R / [4 (R^2 − s(t)^2/4)]. Any derived expression that reduces to a_c = ṡ(t)^2 / (4 R) or a_c = g^2 t^2 / (4 R), lacking the geometry-dependent denominator, is flagged as incorrect.

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Incorrect lateral velocity/acceleration from projecting forward speed with steering angle
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description: This rule flags modeling errors in front-steered, no-slip wheeled vehicle problems (bike/tricycle/car) where the steering angle θ(t) of the front wheel is misused to obtain lateral motion by projecting the forward speed v onto a fixed lateral axis. In a nonholonomic vehicle with rear wheels aligned to the body, the CoM velocity is constrained to lie along the body axis; steering changes path curvature, not by creating an instantaneous lateral component v_y = v sinθ. Correct kinematics use the bicycle model: yaw rate ψ̇ = v · tan(θ) / L, curvature κ = tan(θ)/L, and lateral (centripetal) acceleration a_y = v² · tan(θ) / L (≈ v² · θ / L for small θ). Flag solutions that: (1) set v_y = v sin(θ) or derive a_y by differentiating v sin(θ), e.g., a_y = v cos(θ) · θ̇; (2) equate heading rate ψ̇ to θ̇ or use a_y = v · θ̇; (3) compute a_y from θ without introducing wheelbase L or equivalent turn radius R = L / tan(θ); (4) treat θ as the direction of motion relative to global axes rather than a steering angle affecting curvature. The expected formulation for lateral acceleration must depend on v² and either tan(θ)/L or 1/Rturn, not on θ̇ alone nor a simple sine projection.

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Incorrect use of wheel spin ω in CoM lateral acceleration
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description: Flags derivations of a vehicle/tricycle center-of-mass (CoM) lateral acceleration that incorrectly combine the wheel's spin (ω) with the steering angle (θ) as if describing rim-point kinematics. Under pure rolling, ω should enter only via translational speed v = r·ω; lateral acceleration of the CoM must be based on path curvature/yaw rate (e.g., a_lat = v^2/R, a_lat = v^2·κ, or a_lat = v·dψ/dt). Trigger conditions: (1) The expression for lateral acceleration (e.g., a_y) contains ω^2 multiplied by the wheel radius r and a trigonometric function of θ, such as r·ω^2·sin(θ) or r·ω^2·cos(θ); (2) The expression includes terms like r·ddot(θ)·cos(θ) (or similar) directly contributing to a_y, indicative of rim-point acceleration components; (3) ω appears directly in a_y (especially as ω^2) rather than only through v = r·ω. If any of these patterns are detected, flag a conceptual error: mixing wheel spin with steering geometry for CoM dynamics. Acceptable forms explicitly derive a_lat from curvature/yaw rate and use ω only to compute v.

Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.title: Lateral acceleration must use curvature (v^2/R) or v^2 tan(theta)/L, not v*d(theta)/dt
Circular Motion and Centrifugal Effects.description: Scope: Solutions computing lateral (centripetal) acceleration for wheeled vehicles/tricycles/bicycle-model kinematics at constant forward speed with a steering angle theta(t). Detection logic: 1) Identify that the task is to find lateral acceleration (a_y, a_lat). 2) Detect use of a_y expressed as the product of forward speed and the time derivative of the steering angle: patterns like 'a = v * dθ/dt', 'a = v * θ̇', or 'a = (ω r) * θ̇' where v = ω r. 3) Detect if the maximum lateral acceleration is obtained from the maximum of θ̇ (e.g., taking cos-term maximum for θ(t)=A sin(Ω t)), without converting steering angle to curvature or yaw rate. 4) Check for absence of curvature-based formulas: no occurrence of v^2/R, a_y = v^2 κ, a_y = v ψ̇ with ψ̇ = v κ, or a_y = v^2 tan(θ)/L (or small-angle approximation a_y ≈ v^2 θ/L). Rule: Flag as incorrect if a_y depends linearly on v and θ̇ (v*θ̇) rather than quadratically on v via curvature (v^2/R or v^2 tan(θ)/L). Rationale: For steady-speed turning without slip, lateral acceleration is centripetal: a_y = v^2/R = v^2 κ. In the bicycle/tricycle kinematic model, κ = tan(θ)/L and yaw rate ψ̇ = v κ, so a_y = v ψ̇ = v^2 tan(θ)/L. Using v*θ̇ confuses steering-rate with yaw-rate and yields a jerk-like term tied to changing steer angle, not the centripetal acceleration of the CoM. Exception: Do not flag if θ explicitly denotes the heading (yaw) angle of the CoM (ψ), i.e., the solution clearly states θ(t) ≡ ψ(t) (path heading), in which case a_y = v * ψ̇ is correct and ψ̇ must be derived from path curvature or geometry, not directly from steering mechanics. Action on trigger: Report that lateral acceleration must be computed from curvature (v^2/R or v^2 tan(θ)/L) and that maximizing a_y should be done at maximum |θ| (or |tan θ|), not at maximum |θ̇|, unless θ is proven to be the yaw angle.

Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.title: Closed ring: use circumference extension ΔL = 2π(R − a), not radius change
Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.description: Checks derivations involving an elastic ring (closed circular loop) with natural radius a and stiffness k. The rule verifies that Hooke-type relations for elastic energy and tension use the change in circumference ΔL = 2π(R − a), rather than the change in radius R − a. It flags solutions that write elastic energy or tension as U_e = (1/2) k (R − a)^2 or T = k (R − a) without an explicit and correct redefinition of the stiffness to absorb the 2π factor (e.g., k' = k (2π)^2 or k_eff = EA/L0 with L0 = 2πa). Acceptable forms include U_e = (1/2) k (ΔL)^2 with ΔL = 2π(R − a) and T = k ΔL = 2πk(R − a). The rule also checks consistency statements: if k is defined as force per unit circumference extension (N/m), tension must be T = k ΔL and energy U_e = (1/2) k (ΔL)^2; using ΔR directly without the 2π factor leads to incorrect scaling and should be flagged.

Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.title: Trigonometric bounds and physical domain validation in angle optimization
Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.description: This rule verifies that any angle computed or optimized via trigonometric relations (e.g., using cos α, sin α, tan α) respects mathematical bounds and physical domains. It flags logic errors when: (1) a derived expression or extremum condition yields cos(·) or sin(·) values outside [-1, 1] (e.g., cos λ ≈ 9.85), (2) the solution attempts to maximize/minimize an angle by optimizing a surrogate (such as minimizing cos α) without ensuring monotonicity over the stated domain, and the resulting condition implies out-of-range trigonometric values, and (3) the optimized parameter representing an angle or latitude lies outside its physical range (e.g., latitude λ not in [−90°, 90°]). For equilibrium-based derivations (e.g., plumb line deflection), the rule evaluates the provided trigonometric relation f(λ) numerically across the admissible λ range using given constants and checks that the implied trigonometric quantities remain bounded; any violation indicates an incorrect equilibrium relation or invalid optimization step.

Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.title: Area vector magnitude must be the geometric area (angle-independent)
Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.description: This rule checks definitions of the area vector and magnetic dipole moment in current-loop problems within magnetic fields. It flags solutions that make the area vector (or dipole moment magnitude) depend on the loop’s orientation angle (e.g., include sinθ or cosθ factors) instead of keeping the geometric area constant and placing the angular dependence in the torque or energy expressions. Specifically, it verifies that: (1) The area vector is defined as A⃗ = A n̂ with A equal to the geometric area of the loop (e.g., l^2 for a square, πR^2 for a circle), independent of any orientation angle. (2) The magnetic dipole moment is defined as m⃗ = I A n̂ without any angular factor multiplying A or I. (3) The torque and energy use the correct angular dependence: |τ| = I A B sinα and U = −I A B cosα, where α is the angle between the loop’s normal n̂ and the magnetic field B. The rule flags expressions such as: A = l^2 sinθ n̂, A(θ) = A0 cosθ, m⃗ = I (A sinθ) n̂, or any statement implying that the magnitude of A⃗ varies with orientation. It allows torque expressions like τ = I A B sinθ only if θ is explicitly the angle between n̂ and B. It also prompts a check that the defined angle is the correct one (if the given angle is between the loop’s plane and B, then α = 90° − given angle; if between the normal and B, then α equals the given angle), but it does not flag angle-definition issues unless the area vector magnitude is made angle-dependent. This rule is intended to catch the specific misconception where students write A = l^2 sinθ n̂ or similar, incorrectly attributing the sinθ factor to the area vector rather than to the torque (or energy) formula.

Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.title: Specify angle reference when pivot/length changes (pendulum with pin)
Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.description: Checks that any angular coordinate (e.g., θ) used in height/energy/centripetal expressions is explicitly tied to a specific pivot and length, especially when a pin/peg changes the effective pivot and string length. The rule flags solutions that: (1) introduce an angle θ without stating whether it is measured from the vertical about the original pivot (O) or the new pivot at the pin (A); (2) use h = L(1 − cos θ) or v^2 = 2gL(1 − cos θ) after the string catches on a pin/peg (i.e., after a change in effective radius), unless θ is explicitly defined about pivot O and restricted to the pre-contact segment; (3) switch to the effective length (1 − α)L without redefining θ or clearly stating that θ is now measured about the new pivot A; or (4) mix quantities from different pivots (e.g., using r = L in tension/centripetal terms while using h based on (1 − α)L, or vice versa) without piecewise segmentation and redefinition. Acceptance criteria: The solution must either define distinct angles for each segment (e.g., θ_O for motion about O before contact and φ_A for motion about A after contact), or clearly state that θ is redefined at the moment of contact and then consistently use the matching radius (L before, (1 − α)L after) in all energy/height/centripetal expressions. This rule applies generally to problems with constraint/pivot changes (e.g., pegs, variable length, re-hinged systems) and aims to prevent conceptual inconsistencies arising from ambiguous angle references.

Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.title: Require geometric justification of height drop when pivot/length changes (pin/peg pendulum)
Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.description:
This rule checks energy-based solutions in pendulum problems where a pin/peg changes the effective pivot or length mid-motion. If conservation of energy is used to compute speed/tension at a point after the pivot changes, the solution must explicitly justify the gravitational height drop (delta h) with correct geometry. The rule flags solutions that: 
- Assert delta h = L or E_initial = mg L without explaining why the vertical drop from the initial horizontal release to the lowest point about the pin equals the original string length. An acceptable justification is a two-segment argument: descend alpha*L from O to the pin at A, then (1 - alpha)*L from A to the new lowest point, giving alpha*L + (1 - alpha)*L = L. 
- Use h = L(1 - cos theta) without identifying the correct pivot and effective length (e.g., using the original L instead of the post-pin length (1 - alpha)*L) or without specifying theta relative to the appropriate pivot. 
- Omit phase segmentation (before vs. after pin contact) or another equivalent geometric derivation (e.g., computing vertical coordinates relative to the same reference) to connect the initial horizontal position to the final position about the pin. 
The rule requires explicit, consistent geometric reasoning for delta h that matches the stated pivot and length at each phase. If such justification is missing or inconsistent, the solution is flagged as a logic error in the energy calculation.

Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.title: Incorrect lever-arm projection in torque when angle is measured from the vertical
Trigonometry and Geometric Consideration.description: This rule checks torque calculations for rods or line segments when the angle variable is explicitly defined with respect to the vertical (e.g., 'angle with the wall'). In such cases, the perpendicular lever arm must use the correct projection of the geometry: for a rod of length l making angle θ with the vertical, the coordinates of the far end relative to the pivot are (horizontal = l·sinθ, vertical = l·cosθ), and for the center of mass they are (horizontal = (l/2)·sinθ, vertical = (l/2)·cosθ). Therefore: (1) A horizontal force (e.g., normal from a vertical wall) contributes a torque equal to F × vertical offset, i.e., F·l·cosθ (or F·(l/2)·cosθ if applied at the center), and using sinθ here is incorrect. (2) A vertical force (e.g., weight mg or normal from the ground) contributes a torque equal to F × horizontal offset, i.e., F·(l/2)·sinθ (or F·l·sinθ for an endpoint), and using cosθ here is incorrect. The verifier should parse torque expressions of the form F * length * trig(angle) and identify the force direction (horizontal vs vertical) together with the angle’s reference (vertical). It then verifies that the trig function matches the perpendicular distance: horizontal force → cos(angle_to_vertical); vertical force → sin(angle_to_vertical). The rule flags torque equations where the mapping is swapped (e.g., N_B·l·sinθ for a horizontal wall force, mg·(l/2)·cosθ for a vertical weight) or where both horizontal and vertical forces use the same trig function under an angle defined to the vertical. The same check applies for any rod with angle α to the vertical: horizontal force must pair with cosα, vertical force with sinα. If the angle is instead defined to the horizontal, the expected mapping inverts (horizontal force → sin, vertical force → cos); the verifier should use the declared angle reference to select the correct mapping before checking.

Kinetic Energy.title: Kinetic energy must depend only on velocity (no strain/modulus in KE integrand)
Kinetic Energy.description: Scope: 1D longitudinal motion of a thin elastic rod (no bending, homogeneous, isotropic). In such systems the kinetic energy density is (1/2)·ρ·v^2, where v = ∂u/∂t, and the total kinetic energy is T = (1/2) ∫ ρ A (∂u/∂t)^2 dx (or an equivalent expression in terms of ε̇ only, e.g., T = (1/2) m (L^2/3) ε̇^2 for uniform strain u(x,t) = ε(t) x). This rule checks expressions labeled as kinetic energy T or kinetic energy density and flags the following issues: - The integrand contains spatial derivatives of displacement in any multiplicative way with time derivatives, e.g., terms like (∂u/∂x ∂u/∂t), (∂u/∂x)^2, ε·ε̇, or ε^2 within kinetic energy. - The kinetic energy includes material stiffness parameters (e.g., Young’s modulus E) or strain ε without time derivative, which belong to elastic potential energy, not kinetic energy. - Specific erroneous pattern: T written as (1/2) ρ A ∫ (∂u/∂x ∂u/∂t)^2 dx (or any variant where ε multiplies ∂u/∂t or ε̇). The rule passes when the kinetic energy is expressed purely in terms of velocity squared (∂u/∂t)^2 or, for uniform strain fields, solely in terms of ε̇ (no factors of ε or E). Rationale: Kinetic energy depends only on the velocity field; strain and elastic moduli appear only in potential (strain) energy.

Kinetic Energy.title: Kinetic energy of uniformly strained rod: final formula completeness and variable conformity
Kinetic Energy.description: Checks solutions to the thin elastic rod kinetic energy task for the following: (1) A complete, explicit final expression for kinetic energy T/K is present (e.g., starts with 'T =' or 'K =') and does not end mid-derivation, with ellipses, dangling equals, or unfinished integrals. (2) The final expression is written solely in terms of the requested variables m (mass), L (length), and the strain-rate ε̇ (time derivative of tensile strain), with no extraneous parameters such as ρ (density), A (cross-sectional area), u(x,t), ΔL, x, or unresolved integrals. (3) Proper elimination of ρ and A via m = ρ A L is performed; any residual appearance of ρ or A in the final answer is flagged. (4) Correct dependence for a uniformly strained, bending-prevented rod is enforced: T must scale as m L^2 ε̇^2 with a dimensionless numerical coefficient of 1/6, i.e., T = (1/6) m L^2 ε̇^2. Deviations in the coefficient or use of ε instead of ε̇ are flagged. (5) Dimensional consistency of the final formula (energy units: mass × (length/time)^2) is verified. This rule catches incomplete derivations, mid-expression termination during elimination (e.g., stopping at T = (1/2) ρ A ∫(ε̇^2 x^2) dx), missing final formula, failure to substitute m = ρ A L, inclusion of extraneous variables, and incorrect numerical factors.

Kinetic Energy.title: Turning-point velocity and kinetic energy consistency on constrained motion
Kinetic Energy.description: Checks solutions for internal consistency of velocity components and kinetic energy at a declared maximum height or turning point when the particle is constrained to move on a smooth curve/surface (e.g., z = f(x), parabolic bowl). The rule triggers when the context includes a geometric constraint and the solution references an extremum along the path ("maximum height", "turning point"). It enforces that at a turning point along the constraint the tangential speed is zero, hence the total kinetic energy is zero at that instant. Flags the following contradictions: (1) Claiming nonzero kinetic energy (or "purely vertical kinetic energy") at the turning point while also setting a component velocity to zero that would eliminate the stated kinetic energy (e.g., saying v_x = 0 and then v_z = 0 but still asserting nonzero KE). (2) Mixing projectile-apex logic with constrained motion: stating v_z = 0 while v_x ≠ 0 (or vice versa) at the maximum height along a surface defined by z = f(x), which implies nonzero tangential speed at a turning point; this is inconsistent with constrained turning points. (3) Using a nonzero kinetic term in the energy balance to compute the maximum height for a constrained turning point where speed must be zero. The rule is satisfied if the solution sets tangential speed to zero and uses purely potential energy at the extremum; it is violated by any simultaneous claims that imply nonzero kinetic energy or mutually inconsistent velocity component statements at that point.

Kinetic Energy.title: Final kinetic energy at impact must be nonzero in flight-phase energy balances
Kinetic Energy.description:
This rule flags solutions that incorrectly set the kinetic energy at the instant just before impact to zero when performing a work–energy balance over the flight (pre-collision) phase. It targets problems involving impact/hitting the ground where no collision modeling is included, especially with drag/air resistance.

Checks performed:
- Context detection: The solution text references impact-related phrases (e.g., "impact", "hits the ground", "point of impact", "just before impact") and models only the flight phase (no explicit collision impulse/impact model).
- Non-conservative forces present: Mentions of drag/air resistance/terminal velocity or an explicit work of non-conservative forces term are present, indicating dissipative flight dynamics.
- Erroneous zero final KE: The solution either (a) explicitly states/uses v_f = 0 or KE_f = 0 at impact, or (b) computes dissipated energy E_diss without a final kinetic energy term when the final speed should be nonzero.
- Algebraic omission pattern: Flags energy balances of the form E_diss = (K_i + U_i) - U_f (missing K_f), particularly when the initial and final heights are the same (e.g., object "falls back to the ground"), which implies E_diss = K_i and hence KE_f was implicitly set to zero.

Indicators that trigger the rule:
- Phrases such as "final kinetic energy is zero at impact", "v_f = 0 at impact", "KE_f = 0 at impact", or equivalent.
- Expressions like E_loss/E_diss = 1/2 m v0^2 (with no KE_f term) when the object ends the flight at the ground, or energy balance written as E_diss = (K_i + U_i) - U_f without a +K_f term.
- Use of terminal velocity/drag while concluding a zero speed at impact in the flight phase.

Exceptions (do not flag if any apply):
- The solution explicitly models a collision and clearly states the energy accounting includes the collision that brings the object to rest (post-impact), or the problem explicitly says the object comes to rest upon contact and the dissipated energy explicitly includes collision losses.
- The problem states the object is brought to rest by a non-flight mechanism before impact (e.g., tether, catcher) and the solution’s domain excludes free-flight impact.

Rationale and correction:
- For flight-phase work–energy with non-conservative forces: W_nc = (K_f + U_f) - (K_i + U_i). With drag, W_nc < 0, so E_diss = -(W_nc) = (K_i + U_i) - (K_f + U_f). Unless otherwise stated, right before impact K_f = 1/2 m v_impact^2 > 0. Setting K_f = 0 is a conceptual error unless a collision to rest is modeled. The rule prompts the solver to include K_f explicitly in the energy balance.

Kinetic Energy.title: Correct expansion of translational kinetic energy around constant drift
Kinetic Energy.description: Checks the algebraic and order-of-smallness consistency when translational kinetic energy is expanded about a constant CM speed V with a small correction δv (e.g., δẋ). Specifically: (1) Identify T_trans written as 1/2 M |V + δv|^2 or equivalent component-wise form. (2) Require the expansion to yield exactly 1/2 M V^2 + M V·δv + 1/2 M |δv|^2; flag if the cross term coefficient is not M (e.g., 1/2 M V·δv). (3) If the solution states 'retain lowest order of small quantities', allow dropping the quadratic term 1/2 M |δv|^2 only if all other second-order terms are consistently dropped; flag inconsistent truncation (e.g., dropping 1/2 M |δv|^2 while keeping other O(δ^2) terms). (4) If the cross term M V·δv is omitted, require an explicit justification that it is a total time derivative (M V·δx) and thus does not affect Euler–Lagrange equations; flag omission without such justification. (5) Verify canonical momentum consistency: if quadratic terms are kept, ∂T/∂(δv) must equal M V + M δv; discrepancies indicate a mis-expansion. Applies to scalar or vector forms and any coordinate component (x, y, z).

Energy Conservation.title: Total dissipation equals initial minus final mechanical energy (not just mgh)
Energy Conservation.description: For problems with non-conservative forces (e.g., quadratic drag) asking for energy dissipated over the entire motion or until impact, verify that the dissipated energy is computed as E_diss = (K_i + U_i) − (K_f + U_f). Flag solutions that: (a) equate total dissipation to E_initial − mgh using an intermediate height (e.g., the apex) when the requested interval is from launch to impact, (b) omit the final kinetic term K_f at impact, or (c) use only the gravitational potential change ΔU_g to represent total dissipation. Additionally, if the initial and final heights are the same (e.g., launch and impact at ground level), ensure ΔU_g = 0 in the total-energy balance; any formula for total dissipation that reduces to E_diss = E_initial − mgh under these conditions is a logic error. This rule catches the common confusion between the upward-segment loss (valid: E_up ≈ E_initial − mgh when K_top ≈ 0) and the total loss over the full trajectory (required: E_total = E_initial − E_final).

Energy Conservation.title: Energy conservation: verify potential sign, continuity, and ΔU consistency
Energy Conservation.description: This rule checks the use of conservation of energy when a potential energy U(x) is derived from a given (possibly piecewise) force F(x). Requirements: (1) The potential must satisfy F(x) = -dU/dx in every region of definition. Flag an error if F = +dU/dx is implied by the student’s U(x). (2) For piecewise forces, each segment’s U(x) must satisfy F = -dU/dx and the integration constants should make U(x) continuous at the boundary unless a physical discontinuity is explicitly justified. (3) The potential difference must match the work integral: ΔU = U(x_f) - U(x_i) should equal -∫_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) dx. Flag a logic/sign error if U(x_i) = U(x_f) (or ΔU ≈ 0) while F ≠ 0 along the path, or if the two computations of ΔU disagree. (4) For start-from-rest cases, verify that 1/2 m v_f^2 = U(x_i) - U(x_f) ≥ 0. Flag an error if the computed U leads to v_f^2 ≤ 0 or v_f = 0 in a situation where the conservative force does nonzero work along the path. These checks catch incorrectly signed potentials, mischosen constants that nullify energy change, and inconsistent energy balances in piecewise fields.

Energy Conservation.title: Conserve energy only between immediate endpoints of a conservative segment after an instantaneous configuration change
Energy Conservation.description:
This rule checks for misapplication of mechanical energy conservation across the wrong states in multi-stage problems that include instantaneous configuration changes (e.g., a swing rider quickly standing/squatting, variable-length pendulum steps, impulsive constraint changes). It enforces that for each conservative motion segment (no external nonconservative work), the energy equality must reference the immediate pre- and post-states of that segment, not an earlier state prior to a quick change. The rule performs the following checks:

- Segment boundary alignment: If the solution defines stages with an instantaneous change (e.g., A → A' where length changes l → l+d, or a note like "quickly stands/squats"), then for the subsequent conservative segment (e.g., A' → B) any pure energy conservation statement must be written as E(A') = E(B). If the student instead writes E(A) = E(B) (skipping over A'), the step is flagged unless additional work/energy terms bridging A → A' are explicitly included.

- Parameter/geometry consistency: In conservative segments, quantities used to compute gravitational potential differences or speed-from-height (e.g., v^2 = 2 g Δh) must be computed using the configuration parameters appropriate to the segment's start state. After a length change at A → A', the height at the start of the A' → B segment must reflect the new length (e.g., l+d), not the old length (e.g., l). Using a height drop h or geometry derived from the wrong configuration (pre-change instead of post-change) is flagged.

- Kinematic consistency: When using v = sqrt(2 g Δh) or equivalent, Δh must be the vertical drop between the correct endpoints of the conservative segment (e.g., A' to B). Using Δh from A to B while claiming conservation over A' → B is flagged.

- Exception handling: If the student explicitly includes nonconservative work/impulse or internal work across the instantaneous-change step (e.g., a work term accounting for standing/squatting) and then conserves energy across a larger interval consistently, do not flag.

This rule catches errors like: "From A' to B the student sets E_B = E_A and uses v_B = sqrt(2 g h_A)", by requiring E_B = E_A' and Δh computed from the A' configuration. It also applies to similar multi-stage problems with instantaneous parameter changes followed by conservative motion.

Energy Conservation.title: Incomplete multi-stage energy/transition derivation
Energy Conservation.description: Flags solutions to multi-stage mechanics problems (e.g., variable-length swing/pendulum) that do not carry the derivation through all specified stages and transitions as requested. The rule is triggered when the problem statement defines discrete labeled stages or points (e.g., A, A', B, B', C) and asks for energies, height changes, or energy changes per stage/transition. The checker parses the problem for stage labels and expected outputs, then verifies that the solution: (1) explicitly identifies every defined stage and provides a corresponding mechanical energy expression/value for each (e.g., E_A, E_A', E_B, E_B', E_C) in terms of the problem variables; (2) handles every transition between stages (e.g., A→A', A'→B, B→B', B'→C) by stating the governing principle (such as mechanical energy conservation where applicable, or angular momentum/impulse considerations during rapid length changes) and computes the post-transition energy; (3) reaches the final stage requested by the problem and reports the final requested quantity (e.g., energy change for each stage, final height/energy at C). The rule also detects premature termination or truncation via cues like missing later-stage labels present in the problem, absence of computed E for the last required stage, or textual markers such as '...', '(truncated)', or unfinished sections. If any stage or required energy/change is missing, undefined, or the solution stops before the final stage/result, the solution is flagged as incomplete.

Energy Conservation.title: Misuse of mechanical energy conservation with contacts, friction, or inelastic events
Energy Conservation.description: Flag solutions that equate gravitational potential energy loss directly to kinetic energy (e.g., statements like "PE = KE", "mgh = KE_total", or setting mg·Δh = (1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 I ω^2)) over a motion segment that includes sliding/toppling contact, friction, vibrating supports, or an inelastic collision, without explicitly accounting for non-conservative work or justifying why it is zero. Trigger conditions: (1) The problem text includes any of: friction, sliding/toppling, contact with wall/floor, vibration/time-dependent support, or inelastic/perfectly inelastic collision; AND (2) the solution applies conservation of mechanical energy from an initial configuration to pre-impact or post-impact state without a non-conservative work term. Acceptable justification requirements: The solution must identify all non-conservative interactions (e.g., kinetic friction at contacts, work by moving/vibrating constraints, plastic deformation/heat in inelastic collision) and argue that their net work is zero over the chosen interval (e.g., static friction at a stationary contact with no slip, constraints do no work because point of application has zero displacement along the force direction, or the interval excludes the collision). If such justification is absent, or if an inelastic collision is within the interval of energy conservation, or if sliding with kinetic friction is present, mark as a modeling error. Example patterns to detect: using mg(l/2) → KE at the moment just before ground impact for a rod that slid against a wall/floor; using energy conservation across a perfectly inelastic collision to obtain post-collision speed. The rule enforces that energy methods must include non-conservative work terms or be restricted to intervals where mechanical energy is demonstrably conserved.

Energy Conservation.title: Disallow mechanical energy conservation across inelastic collisions
Energy Conservation.description: This rule flags solutions that treat mechanical energy (potential + kinetic) as conserved across an inelastic collision to determine post-impact velocities or angular speeds. Detection criteria: (1) The scenario explicitly mentions an inelastic collision (e.g., "inelastic", "perfectly inelastic", or coefficient of restitution e=0 or e<1). (2) The solution equates total mechanical energy immediately before impact to total mechanical energy immediately after impact (patterns such as "energy is conserved during the collision", "KE_before = KE_after", "PE_before = KE_after", or using mgΔh = 1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 I ω^2 to solve for v_final or ω_final at the instant after impact). (3) The post-impact speed/rotation is derived solely from energy equality without including energy loss, work by impulsive non-conservative forces, or restitution. Exceptions: Energy conservation may be used for the pre-impact fall or motion in intervals without collisions; separate pre-impact energy analysis is allowed if followed by momentum/impulse methods for the collision. Non-violation: If the solution explicitly includes non-conservative energy loss terms (e.g., KE_after = KE_before − ΔE_loss with ΔE_loss > 0 consistent with e<1) or relies on linear/angular momentum about appropriate points during the impulsive event, it should not be flagged. Purpose: Prevent unphysical results such as computing post-impact velocities/ω from pure energy conservation in perfectly inelastic collisions, where mechanical energy decreases due to dissipation.

Force and Potential Energy.title: Sign consistency for attractive central force in 1D
Force and Potential Energy.description: This rule verifies that the direction (sign) of a gravitational/attractive central force is consistent with the chosen coordinate axis in one-dimensional motion. It applies when the problem states the force is attractive toward a fixed point (origin/center) and the coordinate x increases away from that point. Checks: (1) Force sign: For x > 0, the force component must be negative (points toward the origin); for x < 0, it must be positive. If x is defined as a nonnegative distance from the origin, the force must carry an overall negative sign for all x > 0. In piecewise definitions, each branch must preserve this sign. Example: F(x ≥ a) should be − m μ a^2 / x^2, and F(0 ≤ x ≤ a) should be − m μ x / a; using positive signs in these expressions is flagged. (2) Continuity at boundaries: At the interface (e.g., x = a), the signed force should be consistent across branches (equal magnitude and same inward direction), e.g., F(a−) = F(a+) = − m μ. (3) Energy/ODE consistency: If the solution uses m v dv/dx = F(x) or F = − dU/dx, the integrals must reflect the inward attraction: as x decreases toward the origin under attraction, v^2 should increase and remain nonnegative. Integrations that yield a negative v^2 or show acceleration away from the origin are flagged as sign errors. The rule triggers when a student treats the attractive force as positive along +x (e.g., F = + m μ a^2 / x^2 or F = + m μ x / a for x > 0), or otherwise violates F = − dU/dx for an attractive potential.

Force and Potential Energy.title: Force sign consistency in 1D integration (m v dv/dx)
Force and Potential Energy.description: Checks for incorrect sign of the force when deriving speed via m v dv/dx = F(x) or the work–energy integral in 1D motion. Applicable to problems where the force direction is specified or implied (e.g., attractive gravitational force toward the origin). The verifier inspects the student’s setup and integration over an interval [x_target, x_start] with given initial speed v(x_start). It asserts: (1) If the coordinate x increases away from the origin and the force is attractive toward the origin, then F(x) must be negative for x > 0 when substituted into m v dv/dx = F(x). (2) Using the initial condition (e.g., v(x_start) = 0), the integrated expression for v^2(x) must yield nonnegative values at all points reached by the motion and must not decrease when moving down the potential (for attraction, v^2 should increase as x decreases). (3) The integration constant computed from the initial condition must produce physically consistent kinetic energy; specifically, evaluating v^2 at any intermediate boundary (e.g., a piecewise switch point) must be ≥ 0. The rule flags an error if: the student uses a positive sign for F where a negative sign is required by the stated force direction, the derived v^2 at a boundary is negative (indicating nonphysical kinetic energy), or the work integral ∫ F(x) dx from x_start to x yields negative kinetic energy in a context where speed must increase. This catches errors like deriving (1/2) v^2 = C − k/x with C chosen so that v^2(x_boundary) < 0, which is symptomatic of a force sign mistake.

Force and Potential Energy.title: Potential energy from force: sign convention and piecewise continuity
Force and Potential Energy.description:
This rule verifies that a potential energy function U(x) derived from a force F(x) uses the correct sign convention and is continuous across piecewise-defined regions. It is triggered when a solution computes U(x) from a stated F(x) or uses energy conservation with a force-derived potential. Checks performed: 
- Sign convention: Confirm that U'(x) = -F(x) on each domain. Compute the derivative of the student's U(x) and compare to -F(x). If U'(x) equals +F(x) (global sign error) or deviates by a sign on any interval, flag an error. 
- Proper integral definition: If the student writes U(x) via an integral (e.g., "U = - ∫ F dx"), verify the correct use of limits: U(x) = U(x_ref) - ∫_{x_ref}^{x} F(x') dx. Flag misuse of indefinite integrals that results in wrong sign or missing constants. 
- Reference level consistency: Identify the stated reference (e.g., U(∞) = 0 or U(a) specified). Check that the student's U(x) satisfies the reference condition on the applicable domain (e.g., for inverse-square gravitational-like F ∝ 1/x^2 with U(∞) = 0, U(x) → 0 as x → ∞ and U(x) is negative). Flag if the chosen reference is contradicted by the expression (e.g., U(x) = +C/x when U(∞) = 0 is required). 
- Piecewise continuity: For piecewise F(x), verify that U(x) constructed on each segment is continuous at each boundary point (e.g., x = a) unless a physical discontinuity is explicitly justified. Compute U_left(boundary) and U_right(boundary) from the student's expressions; if |U_left - U_right| exceeds tolerance, flag "Potential energy discontinuous at boundary". 
- Direction/sign of F: If the problem context implies a direction (e.g., attractive gravitational force toward the origin), ensure the signed F(x) used in U'(x) = -F(x) reflects that direction. If the student has used the magnitude of F(x) without sign, leading to U'(x) = +F(x), flag a sign error. 
- Energy conservation consistency check (optional sanity): Using the student's U(x), verify that energy differences used to compute speeds are physically sensible (e.g., starting from rest, the kinetic energy gain equals U(initial) - U(final); if this yields negative kinetic energy or imaginary speed due to sign errors, flag). 
This rule will catch errors such as computing U(x) with the wrong sign from a given F(x), failing to enforce U(∞) = 0 for inverse-square segments, and introducing discontinuities at piecewise boundaries by choosing inconsistent constants of integration.

Force and Potential Energy.title: Negative squared speed indicates setup/sign error, not physical impossibility
Force and Potential Energy.description: This rule checks derivations where the speed is obtained from integrating Newton’s second law in 1D (e.g., m v dv/dx = F(x)) or from energy/work relations, producing an expression for v^2(x). The verifier will: (1) Locate any expression of the form v^2 = f(x) (or 2K/m = f(x)) and evaluate its sign over the physically reachable interval defined by the initial condition and intended endpoint. (2) If v^2(x) < 0 at any point that lies on the proposed trajectory (including at region boundaries in piecewise-defined forces), it flags a violation. A negative v^2 is non-physical and indicates a setup error such as an incorrect force sign, wrong integration limits, or misuse of the constant of integration, rather than a physical barrier. (3) For attractive forces toward decreasing x (e.g., gravity toward the origin), the rule checks that the sign of F(x) is consistent with the coordinate direction: F(x) should be negative when x increases away from the attractor, and v^2 derived from m v dv/dx = F(x) or from v^2 = (2/m)(W + C) must remain ≥ 0 along the path. (4) In piecewise force problems, the rule enforces continuity of energy at the boundary: the v^2 computed at the boundary must be non-negative; interpreting a negative v^2 at the boundary as meaning the particle cannot reach it is flagged as a logical error. The rule advises rechecking force direction, potential/work signs, integral limits, and constants of integration whenever v^2 becomes negative.

Force and Potential Energy.title: Continuity of potential for piecewise conservative forces
Force and Potential Energy.description:
Checks that, for a one-dimensional piecewise position-dependent force F(x) (i.e., conservative in 1D), the potential energy constructed in each region is made continuous at the interface(s). Common student error: integrating F(x) separately on each side of a boundary and assigning different integration constants so that U_left(b) ≠ U_right(b) at the matching point b, which is unphysical for a conservative force and breaks energy conservation.

Trigger conditions:
- The problem or solution defines a force F(x) piecewise over intervals separated by one or more boundary points b (e.g., x ≥ a and x ≤ a) and F depends only on position.
- The student constructs potentials U_i(x) (or equivalent energy relations v^2/2 + U_i(x) = const) independently in each region.

Verification steps:
1) Identify region boundaries b where the force definition changes.
2) For each region i, compute (or parse from the student's work) the potential U_i(x) as U_i(x) = -∫ F_i(x) dx + C_i (up to an additive constant C_i).
3) For each boundary b, evaluate the one-sided limits U_left(b) and U_right(b) using the student’s chosen constants. If |U_left(b) − U_right(b)| > tolerance (e.g., numerical epsilon or symbolic non-equality), flag an error.
4) If the student uses energy conservation across multiple regions, verify that a single continuous U(x) (or a single energy constant) is used across the boundary. Detect segmented energy constants or mismatched potential zeros that imply a discontinuity at b.

Exceptions:
- Skip continuity enforcement if the force model explicitly includes an impulsive (Dirac delta) term at the boundary or a non-conservative/time-dependent interaction is stated; otherwise, continuity is required in 1D.

Error message:
"Potential energy is not continuous at the region boundary (U_left(b) ≠ U_right(b)). Integration constants must be chosen so that U is single-valued across interfaces for conservative forces. Match constants at the boundary and recompute energy/velocity."

Potential Barriers and Constraints.title: Strict inequality for crossing a repulsive potential barrier
Potential Barriers and Constraints.description: This rule checks whether a solution uses the correct strict inequality when determining if a particle can enter or pass through a region bounded by a repulsive potential barrier. In classical mechanics/electrostatics, crossing a barrier requires total energy E strictly greater than the barrier height V_max along the approach path; equality (E = V_max) implies zero kinetic energy at the boundary (a turning point) and no entry. The verifier should: (1) identify that the barrier is repulsive (e.g., for electrostatics, Q1·Q2 > 0; the field at the boundary points opposite to the approach; potential reference V(∞) = 0); (2) find the stated crossing condition, such as ½ M v^2 >= ΔU, E >= V_max, or v >= sqrt(2 ΔU / M); (3) if a non-strict comparator (>= or =) is used to claim entry/passage/penetration, flag a conceptual error and require a strict inequality (>, v > ...). Example: for a positively charged particle approaching a positively charged thin spherical shell of radius R with small holes, the correct pass-through condition is ½ M2 v^2 > k Q1 Q2 / R, i.e., v > sqrt(2 k Q1 Q2 / (M2 R)). Note: This rule does not apply to escape from attractive potentials (e.g., gravity), where equality corresponds to asymptotic escape and '>=' may be acceptable.

Hydrostatics and Torque.title: Consistency of depth variable and moment arm in hydrostatic torque integrals
Hydrostatics and Torque.description:
Checks that, in hydrostatic moment/torque calculations on a vertical gate, the coordinate used for pressure depth is consistent with the lever arm to the stated axis of rotation. Specifically:

- Context: A planar vertical gate of width W with water depth h on a given side. Pressure is modeled as P(y) = ρ g y when y is measured downward from the free surface on that side, or P(y) = ρ g (h − y) when y is measured upward from the bottom. The torque about an axis must be M = ∫ P(y) r(y) dA, where r(y) is the perpendicular distance from the area element to the chosen axis.

- Correct lever arm mapping:
  - If y is measured from the free surface and the axis is at the bottom (distance h below the free surface), then r(y) must be (h − y), not y.
  - If y is measured from the bottom and the axis is at the bottom, then r(y) = y and P(y) = ρ g (h − y).
  - If the axis is at the top (free surface) and y is measured from the free surface, then r(y) = y and P(y) = ρ g y.
  - In all cases, r(y) must equal the geometric distance from the element to the stated axis, consistent with the chosen coordinate origin.

- Detection heuristics (any one triggers a flag):
  1) The solution defines P(y) = ρ g y (or equivalent) with y explicitly stated as depth from the free surface, the axis is explicitly at the bottom, and the torque integrand uses r(y) = y (e.g., torque written as ∫ ρ g y · W · y dy or proportional to ∫ y^2 dy).
  2) For a uniform-width vertical gate of height h, the reported torque about the bottom for one side evaluates to (ρ g W h^3)/3 (or any coefficient implying ∫ y^2 dy only), instead of the correct (ρ g W h^3)/6 that arises from ∫ y(h − y) dy. (Accept equivalent correct expressions obtained via centroid methods.)
  3) The text states the same variable y is both “depth from the free surface” for pressure and the “moment arm about the bottom” without redefining the origin or transforming to r = h − y.

- Two-sided gates: When computing net torque from depths h1 and h2 on opposite sides about the same bottom axis, each side must use its own consistent r(y) relative to the same physical axis. The rule flags if either side multiplies P(y) = ρ g y (y from that side’s free surface) by r(y) = y about the bottom, instead of r(y) = h_i − y.

- Accepted alternatives: No flag if the solver redefines the coordinate from the bottom (P = ρ g (h − y), r = y) or uses resultant-force/center-of-pressure methods yielding the correct moment about the axis.

- Purpose: Prevents the common error of overestimating torque by using the same depth variable for pressure and moment arm when the axis is at the opposite edge of the plate.

Hydrostatics and Torque.title: Hydrostatic torque about bottom hinge: lever arm must be (h − y), not y
Hydrostatics and Torque.description:
Checks computations of the torque (moment) on a vertical rectangular lock gate due to hydrostatic pressure when the axis of rotation is at the bottom edge. The correct elemental moment uses the lever arm from the bottom, i.e., (h − y), for a pressure strip at depth y below the free surface. Expected results: per side τ(h) = (1/6) ρ g W h^3; net torque magnitude τ_net = (1/6) ρ g W (h1^3 − h2^3). The rule flags common errors where the lever arm y is used instead, leading to τ(h) = (1/3) ρ g W h^3 and τ_net = (1/3) ρ g W (h1^3 − h2^3). Detection logic:
- If the torque integral is of the form ∫ y^2 (ρ g W) dy or ∫ y (ρ g y W) dy with pivot explicitly at the bottom, flag as incorrect lever arm; the integrand should include (h − y)(ρ g y W).
- If the final torque per side is proportional to ρ g W h^3 with coefficient 1/3 instead of 1/6, flag as wrong torque magnitude due to lever arm error.
- For two-sided problems, if the net torque is expressed as c · ρ g W (h1^3 − h2^3), verify c = 1/6 (magnitude); if c = 1/3, flag.
- Alternative correct formulations (e.g., using resultant force F = (1/2) ρ g W h^2 acting at depth y_cp = (2/3) h so that lever arm to bottom is h − y_cp = h/3) are accepted; if y_cp is taken as h/2 or lever arm as y_cp from bottom, flag.
- Sign conventions are not enforced; only magnitudes are checked.
Scope: Vertical rectangular gates/plates with negligible thickness, constant width W, water density ρ, gravity g, bottom hinge/axis specified. This rule targets misapplication of the lever arm in torque integrals leading to a factor-of-two error.

Hydrostatics and Torque.title: Cubic consistency for floating sphere cap height (checks factor 4 and constant term)
Hydrostatics and Torque.description:
This rule verifies the correctness of the cubic equation derived for the height h of the spherical cap of a floating sphere (radius R, densities ρ_m and ρ_w) above the fluid surface under static equilibrium. It targets common mistakes such as missing the factor 4 or using an incorrect constant term. Applicability: solutions that model a sphere partially submerged in a fluid and derive a cubic in h using Archimedes’ principle and the spherical cap volume.

Expected physical/model relations:
- Archimedes’ principle: V_sub = (ρ_m/ρ_w) * (4/3)π R^3.
- Geometry (cap in air of height h): V_cap = (π/3) h^2 (3R − h).
- Volume relation: V_cap = V_total − V_sub = (4/3)π R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w).

From these, the correct cubic (after canceling common factors and rearranging to one side) must be algebraically equivalent to:
  h^3 − 3 R h^2 + 4 R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) = 0
The rule checks algebraic equivalence up to overall sign and term order.

Verification steps:
1) Attempt to extract the user’s polynomial in h (degree ≤ 3) that relates h, R, and the density ratio ρ_m/ρ_w for the cap-height equilibrium. Normalize to a monic h^3 coefficient if present.
2) Confirm the h^2 coefficient equals −3 R (or equivalently 3 R if the equation is multiplied by −1). Flag if the coefficient deviates from ±3R.
3) Confirm the constant term equals 4 R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) up to overall sign. Accept algebraically equivalent forms such as −4 R^3 (ρ_m/ρ_w − 1). Reject forms missing the factor 4 or using just R^3 (ρ_m/ρ_w) or R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) without the factor 4.
4) Optionally check domain consistency 0 ≤ h ≤ 2R; flag if the derived relation precludes any solution in this physical range.

Failure patterns flagged by this rule include (non-exhaustive):
- h^3 − 3 R h^2 + (ρ_m/ρ_w) R^3 = 0 (missing factor 4 and wrong constant expression).
- h^3 − 3 R h^2 + R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) = 0 (missing factor 4).
- Any cubic where the constant term is not proportional to 4 R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) up to sign.

If the extracted equation does not match the expected coefficients under these checks, the rule reports an error: "Incorrect cubic for cap height: check spherical cap volume V_cap = (π/3) h^2 (3R − h) and buoyancy balance V_sub = (ρ_m/ρ_w) (4/3)π R^3; constant term should be 4 R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w)."

Hydrostatics and Torque.title: Numeric determination and correct cubic for spherical cap height h_c,N
Hydrostatics and Torque.description:
This rule verifies that when a problem asks to 'determine the height h_c,N' of the spherical cap of a floating sphere (melon) under specified conditions, the solution provides a numeric value and uses the correct buoyancy–geometry relation. The checker performs the following:

1) Numeric requirement: The final answer for h_c,N must be a single numeric value (with units of length) obtained by substituting the given parameters from the referenced conditions (e.g., Task 3b). Leaving h_c,N as an implicit root or as an unsolved polynomial equation is flagged.

2) Correct governing equation: If an intermediate implicit equation is presented, it must encode Archimedes’ principle and spherical cap geometry exactly as ρ_w (V_sphere − V_cap(h)) = ρ_m V_sphere, with V_sphere = (4/3)π R^3 and V_cap(h) = π h^2 (R − h/3). Equivalently, after canceling π, the cubic in h must be (1/3) h^3 − R h^2 + (4/3) R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) = 0. Any alternative cubic or mismatch in coefficients/terms (e.g., missing h^3 term, wrong signs, or incorrect dependence on densities) is flagged as a logic/formulation error.

3) Physical admissibility: The reported h_c,N must satisfy 0 ≤ h_c,N ≤ 2R and be consistent with the density ratio: for 0 < ρ_m/ρ_w < 1, the chosen root must lie in [0, 2R] and be unique/physically relevant. Violations are flagged.

4) Condition compliance: The solution must reflect the stated assumptions (e.g., negligible friction and negligible water motion) and not introduce extraneous parameters. If the problem references prior task conditions (Task 3b), the parameter values from that task must be used, and a numerical h_c,N must be computed.

5) Reporting: Units must be provided; significant figures should be compatible with given data. Failure to compute and present the numeric height or providing only an unsolved cubic is marked as non-compliance.

Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.title: Initial relative velocity must be zero at release in the platform frame
Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.description: Checks solutions that analyze motion in the frame of a moving platform (e.g., elevator, vehicle) for incorrect initialization of the object's relative velocity when the object is released/detaches/drops from the platform. If the object was mechanically attached and moving with the platform up to the release instant, then its initial velocity relative to the platform at t = 0 must be v_rel0 = 0 unless the problem explicitly states a throw/kick/projection relative to the platform. The rule flags cases where: (1) v_rel0 is set equal to the platform's absolute speed at release (a common error), or any non-zero value without explicit justification; (2) the relative displacement equation s_rel = v_rel0·t + (1/2)·a_rel·t^2 includes a non-zero v_rel0 term while the text indicates simple release; (3) the narrative claims 'relative to the elevator' (or similar) but uses the platform's absolute speed as the object's initial relative speed. As a consistency aid, the rule also checks that, for vertical motion under gravity, the relative acceleration magnitude in the platform frame is |a_rel| = g + |a_platform,vertical| (sign according to the chosen axis), so the time to traverse a fixed elevator gap should come from s_rel = (1/2)·a_rel·t^2 without a v_rel0 term when there is no launch. Exceptions: non-zero v_rel0 is allowed only if the solution explicitly states the object is given an additional velocity relative to the platform at release or if the analysis is performed entirely in an external inertial frame (in which case v0 is the platform's absolute velocity, but the solution should not call it 'relative to the platform').

Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.title: Equate object and moving boundary positions in impact problems
Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.description: This rule verifies correct modeling of contact time when an object detaches from a moving/accelerating system (e.g., an elevator) and later contacts a part of that system (floor/ceiling). The impact time must be obtained by equating the inertial-frame positions of the object and the moving boundary: y_obj(t) = y_bound(t), where y_obj(t) = y0_obj + v0_obj*t + 0.5*a_obj*t^2 and y_bound(t) = y0_bound + v_platform*t + 0.5*a_platform*t^2. Alternatively, in the accelerating platform frame, the relative motion must use initial relative velocity v_rel0 = 0 and include the pseudo-acceleration: a_rel = g − a_platform (with consistent sign convention), so for an upward-accelerating platform the magnitude is g + a_platform; the drop across a fixed internal gap H is H = v_rel0*t + 0.5*a_rel*t^2 = 0.5*(g + a_platform)*t^2. Flag solutions that: (a) treat the boundary as stationary in space by setting the object's displacement equal to the initial gap H (e.g., y_obj(t*) = −H) without modeling y_bound(t); (b) compute time using only free-fall distance H = 0.5*g*t^2 or y = v0*t − 0.5*g*t^2 when the platform has nonzero velocity/acceleration; (c) in the platform frame, omit the pseudo-acceleration or use an incorrect sign/magnitude for a_rel (e.g., using g − a_platform for an upward-accelerating platform without proper sign handling); (d) produce different impact times in different frames. The verifier should check for inclusion of boundary motion terms (v_platform*t and 0.5*a_platform*t^2) or, equivalently, the correct relative-acceleration formulation. Absence or mis-signing of these elements indicates the error.

Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.title: Rigid accelerating rocket: proper separation must be constant
Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.description: This rule checks solutions that use the equivalence principle or accelerating (Rindler) frames for a rigid rocket. It flags modeling errors where the proper separation d between two fixed points in the rocket (e.g., emitter and receiver at opposite ends) is stated or treated as time-dependent in the rocket’s frame. Specifically, it triggers when: (a) the solution asserts that d decreases/increases due to the rocket’s acceleration, (b) d(t) is introduced to compute frequency shifts, or (c) a relative velocity v ≈ gΔt between endpoints in the ship’s frame is used to produce a Doppler shift. For a Born-rigid rocket, the endpoints remain at rest in the rocket frame with constant proper separation; the frequency shift should be attributed to the effective gravitational field (gravitational redshift) or, equivalently, to kinematic effects accumulated over the light-travel time in an inertial frame, not to a changing d. The rule also flags the inconsistent assumption that all points of a ‘rigid’ rocket share identical proper acceleration, which would imply changing separation; Born rigidity requires different proper accelerations along the rocket. Valid treatments should give a first-order shift Δf/f ≈ ±(g d / c^2) and avoid attributing the shift to shrinking or growing distance within the rocket frame.

Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.title: Work in penetration problems must use relative displacement when the target moves
Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.description: Flags solutions that equate the projectile’s kinetic energy loss directly to W = F_avg * L with L taken as the target’s length/penetration depth, when the target is free to move during contact (finite mass, low-friction surface). In such cases the target accelerates while the projectile decelerates, so the projectile’s ground-frame displacement under the resistive force exceeds L. Correct modeling requires using the relative displacement between projectile and target: L = ∫(v_projectile − v_target) dt, with their velocities evolving under equal and opposite forces (a_projectile = −F_avg/m_projectile, a_target = +F_avg/m_target). The rule triggers if: (a) ΔK_projectile is set equal to F_avg * L without an explicit relative-motion relation (such as L = ∫ v_rel dt or L = v_rel_avg * t) or without adding the target’s displacement to the projectile’s ground-frame displacement, or (b) the computed F_avg matches a value obtained by assuming L equals the projectile’s displacement (e.g., F_avg = (3/8) m v0^2 / L for the m–2m, v_out = v0/2 case). For the specific configuration m projectile, 2m target, and v_out = v0/2, consistency under constant average force gives L = (5/16)(m v0^2)/F_avg, hence F_avg = (5 m v0^2)/(16 L). Any solution that does not incorporate target motion in the work–displacement relation should be flagged.

Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.title: No post-exit relative-motion displacement term after separation
Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.description: This rule verifies that, in penetration/exit scenarios (e.g., a bullet passing through a block), the solution does not compute any additional displacement or time interval for the block based on the projectile–block relative velocity after the projectile has exited. Once the projectile leaves the target, the internal interaction force between them is zero; they evolve independently under external forces only. The block’s motion after exit must be determined solely from its velocity at the instant of exit and any specified external forces (e.g., friction). Flag solutions that: (a) define a post-exit time t' using relative speed between projectile and block, such as t' = d / (v_projectile_exit − v_block_exit) or similar; (b) add an extra displacement term for the block proportional to t' or to the projectile’s post-exit velocity (e.g., x_extra = v_block_exit · t'); (c) assume or state that the projectile 'stops immediately' at exit without physical basis while also using it in relative-motion timing; or (d) attribute any continued block motion to interaction with the projectile after separation. Rationale: After exit, the projectile moves away and no further interaction occurs; any displacement derived from post-exit relative motion (e.g., spurious terms like L/3) is a logic error.

Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.title: Momentary rest does not imply static equilibrium
Relative Motion and Frames of Reference.description: This rule flags solutions that incorrectly infer force balance (net force = 0, a = 0, or F_spring = F) from the statement that the object is momentarily at rest (v = 0). Checks include: (1) Using v = 0 or "turning point" to set ΣF = 0, a = 0, or equate opposing forces (e.g., kx = F) without separately establishing a = 0. (2) In mass–spring problems, asserting kx = F at the instant v = 0 under a constant external force, instead of recognizing that at turning points acceleration is nonzero (a = −ω^2 x) and net force is not zero. (3) When a problem requires the object to remain at rest after removing an external force, ensuring the solution enforces both v = 0 and zero restoring force (e.g., x = 0 for a spring), not just v = 0. For the forced SHO m x'' = F − kx with initial x(0) = 0, v(0) = 0, times with v = 0 occur at t = nπ/ω; only at t = 2πn/ω does x = 0 so the object can remain at rest after force removal. Any reasoning that equates forces or sets a = 0 solely because v = 0 should be flagged.

Periodic Motion and Sampling.title: Require T and g dependence in stroboscopic free-fall conditions
Periodic Motion and Sampling.description: This rule targets problems involving vertical 1D free-fall under constant gravity with perfectly elastic bounces and observations (photos) taken at fixed time intervals T, especially when the statement implies the ball appears at the same position in each photo. In such settings the motion has a natural period P that depends on g and the fall height H (e.g., P = 2√(2H/g)), and stroboscopic equality of positions requires a commensurability condition between T and P (e.g., T = (p/q)P) or equivalently H ∝ g T^2 times a rational factor. The rule flags solutions that provide a final constraint or expression for H (or any parameter determining the period) that: (a) omits both T and g entirely, or (b) shows T and g cancel completely without an explicit, justified limiting condition, or (c) is dimensionally inconsistent for H. Examples of violations include expressions like H = m^2 h_A or H given solely in terms of other lengths and integers with no T or g, when the problem setup includes fixed-interval stroboscopic observation. To pass, the final condition must explicitly involve T and g through combinations such as √(H/g), g T^2, or a rational multiple/ratio relating T to the motion period.

Periodic Motion and Sampling.title: Same-position photos in vertical bounce must use Δ(y), not just full period
Periodic Motion and Sampling.description:
Checks solutions for the vertical free-fall with elastic bounce (initial rest at height H) photographed at equal intervals T. The ball passes any height y in (0, H) twice per cycle (downward then upward), and the time between these two occurrences is Δ(y) = 2 * sqrt(2 * (H - y) / g). Correct reasoning for "same position in every photo" must consider Δ(y), not only the full period P = 2 * sqrt(2H / g). The rule flags solutions that:
- Imply or state that identical positions at each photo require T = P or integer multiples of P only, without considering Δ(y).
- Do not derive or use Δ(y) = 2 * sqrt(2 * (H - y) / g) for the two-pass same-height interval.
- Fail to obtain the continuous family of observed heights h_A from T via h_A = H - (g * T^2) / 8 for 0 < T <= P (with special cases: T = P -> h_A = 0, T = P/2 -> h_A = 3H/4).
- Provide only discrete positions (e.g., top or bottom) or restrict T to specific fractions of P without giving the general dependence h_A(T).

Periodic Motion and Sampling.title: Complete case enumeration for repeated positions under periodic sampling (bounce in gravity)
Periodic Motion and Sampling.description: This rule verifies that a solution to problems involving a ball in vacuum undergoing 1D vertical motion under gravity with an elastic bounce at the bottom and photographed at equal time intervals T considers the full set of conditions under which the ball appears at the same position in every photo. Specifically, the solution must: (1) derive or explicitly state the oscillation period P of the motion starting from rest at height H, with P = 2 * sqrt(2H/g); (2) enumerate boundary photo positions y_A = 0 (bottom) and y_A = H (top) as valid cases where identical positions occur in every photo, and correctly link them to sampling via T = P (or integer multiples of P) producing repeated top or bottom positions; and (3) include the general interior case 0 < y_A < H, showing that identical positions can also occur when T equals the intra-cycle symmetric time between the two passes at the same height y within a period, with a correct expression equivalent to Δ(y) = 2 * [sqrt(2H/g) - sqrt(2(H - y)/g)], and noting that T = Δ(y) (or integer multiples thereof) yields the same position in every photo. The rule flags solutions that only compute free-fall time/impact speed without connecting T to P or Δ(y), or that ignore any of the special cases (bottom y_A=0, top y_A=H) or the interior-case family 0<y_A<H. It also requires mapping the observed repeated-position condition to possible pairs (H, y_A) via T = P or T = Δ(y), ensuring completeness of the solution set.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Misuse of horizontal v0 as tangential speed in constrained motion on a curved surface
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: This rule checks for modeling errors when applying conservation of energy to a particle constrained to move on a curved surface (e.g., a parabolic bowl z = k x^2). The error occurs when the solution treats an 'initial horizontal velocity v0' as the tangential speed at the starting point and uses E0 = (1/2) m v0^2 + m g z0 without ensuring that the initial velocity is aligned with the surface tangent. Trigger conditions: (1) The context indicates constrained motion on a surface (mentions such as 'parabolic bowl', 'track', 'surface', or an explicit relation like z = f(x) or z = k x^2). (2) The solution invokes conservation of mechanical energy and sets the initial energy with a kinetic term using v0 directly (e.g., E0 = (1/2) m v0^2 + m g z0) or equivalent, where v0 is described as 'horizontal' or given in a global direction not guaranteed to be tangent. (3) The starting height z0 is not explicitly at the bottom or the solution does not state that the tangent is horizontal at the start (no claim such as x0 = 0, slope dz/dx|_{x0} = 0, 'bottom of the bowl', or 'tangent is horizontal'). (4) The solution does not project the initial velocity onto the tangent (no use of v_t = v0 cos(phi) or an explicit computation of the tangential component) and does not justify an impulsive adjustment consistent with energy accounting. If all conditions are met, flag the solution: using a horizontal v0 as the tangential speed violates the constraint unless the start is at a point with horizontal tangent; conservation of energy should use the tangential component of the initial speed or explicitly place the start at the bottom where the tangent is horizontal.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Energy analysis on frictionless constrained motion must justify (in)dependence on geometry
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: This rule checks solutions that use conservation of mechanical energy to determine maximum height for a particle constrained on a smooth (frictionless) surface (e.g., a parabolic bowl z = k x^2). It flags three related logical issues: (1) Unused-geometry step: If a step claims to incorporate the surface geometry (mentions z = k x^2 or a curvature parameter k) but no subsequent equation actually uses k or relates x and z, the step is logically empty and should be flagged. (2) Missing no-work justification: If the solution’s energy analysis omits an explicit statement that the constraint (normal) force does no work (i.e., frictionless surface, force perpendicular to displacement), yet concludes that the maximum height depends only on mg z and not on k, the independence from geometry is not justified and should be flagged. Require presence of terms/phrases such as “normal force,” “constraint force,” “does no work,” or “frictionless” when geometry independence is asserted. (3) Spurious k-dependence: If the final maximum-height expression derived solely from conservation of mechanical energy (kinetic + gravitational potential mg z) includes the geometric parameter k, this is inconsistent because the constraint force does no work; flag such dependence. Detection cues: the solution includes keywords like “conservation of energy,” “mechanical energy,” “maximum height,” variables v0, z0, g, and mentions of geometry (e.g., “parabolic bowl,” “z = k x^2,” “curvature k”). Then check whether (a) a geometry step is present but k is not used thereafter, (b) independence from k is claimed without the no-work justification, or (c) k appears in the final height when only energy is used. Report one or more errors: “Geometry not actually used,” “Missing no-work/constraint justification for geometry independence,” or “Incorrect k-dependence in energy-only height result.”

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Incorrect assumption of constant horizontal velocity on curved frictionless constraints
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: Flags solutions to problems where a particle moves on a curved, frictionless track or surface under gravity (e.g., parabolic bowl, circular track, z=f(x) or z=f(y)) and the solution assumes a velocity component (typically horizontal) remains constant.
