Checks: - Detect explicit claims such as 'vx is constant', 'horizontal velocity remains unchanged', 'no horizontal force so px is conserved', or equations setting vx(t)=v0 away from the initial point, when a normal/contact force is present. - Detect use of energy conservation while holding a velocity component fixed as height changes (e.g., kinetic energy at higher z computed with 1/2 m v0^2, or v=v0 despite increasing potential energy). - Detect maximum-height arguments that null only the vertical component (e.g., vz=0) while keeping vx unchanged, instead of recognizing that the speed and direction along the constraint change. Rationale: On curved frictionless constraints, the normal force does no work but can change the direction and components of velocity; only total mechanical energy is conserved. As the particle climbs, speed generally decreases and velocity components vary with the geometry of the constraint. Exceptions: Do not flag free-flight projectile motion (no contact forces) or motion along a straight path with no external force in the component direction, where vx can be constant. Trigger conditions: Presence of a curved constraint indicated by keywords such as 'parabolic bowl', 'track', 'surface', 'normal force', or an explicit relation z=f(x) or z=f(y), combined with any claim of a constant horizontal (or tangential) velocity component.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Missing loss-of-contact condition on curved surface (N=0 / v^2κ = g·n)
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: This rule verifies that, in problems involving a particle constrained on a smooth curve z(y) under gravity (e.g., a parabolic bowl z = y^2/(2k)), the solution explicitly models loss of contact when the initial speed exceeds the critical value (v0 > vh or “critical speed” mentioned). The rule flags solutions that compute the maximum height using conservation of energy alone without introducing and using a detachment condition. Required checks: (1) The solution must state and use a loss-of-contact criterion: normal force N = 0, or equivalently that the required normal (centripetal) acceleration equals the normal component of gravity, such as v^2/R = g cos(α), v^2 κ = g / sqrt(1 + (z')^2), or N = m(g / sqrt(1 + (z')^2) − v^2 κ). Here κ is the curvature of the curve along the path, with an acceptable explicit form κ(y) = z''(y) / (1 + (z'(y))^2)^(3/2) and R = 1/κ; α is the local slope angle with tan(α) = z'(y) and cos(α) = 1 / sqrt(1 + (z')^2). (2) The detachment location y* must be determined by solving the loss-of-contact condition together with the speed along the surface (e.g., from energy: v(y)^2 = v0^2 − 2 g (z(y) − z0), for frictionless motion). (3) After detachment, the motion must be treated as free-flight (projectile) with initial state given by the tangent velocity at y*, and the maximum height must be computed from this ballistic phase. The rule flags an error if any of these elements are omitted or if the gravitational normal component is not projected correctly (e.g., missing the 1 / sqrt(1 + (z')^2) factor). This check is triggered by the presence of phrases like “v0 > vh”, “critical speed”, “loss of contact”, or by contexts where contact may be lost due to insufficient normal force, and it ensures that modeling accounts for the transition from constrained motion to free-flight.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Max height after loss of contact is z0 + v0^2/(2g), independent of bowl parameter
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: Scope: Problems involving a frictionless particle sliding in a parabolic bowl z = y^2/(2k) with a stated/assumed loss-of-contact condition when v0 > vh, where vh = sqrt(g k). Check: If the solution treats the case v0 > vh (explicitly or implicitly), it must: (1) transition from constrained motion to free-flight projectile motion after separation, and (2) yield a maximum height z_max satisfying z_max - z0 = v0^2/(2 g), i.e., z_max = z0 + v0^2/(2 g). This result must be independent of the bowl parameter k and any geometric coordinates of the surface. Flag as a conceptual error if any of the following are detected: - The final expression for z_max contains k (or depends on surface geometry) when v0 > sqrt(g k). - The solution continues to enforce the surface constraint beyond the separation point (e.g., using the track equation to determine the apex) when v0 > sqrt(g k). - The maximum height is not equal to v0^2/(2 g) above z0 (e.g., extra factors, missing 1/2, dependence on k, or incorrect g dependence). - Misuse of the critical speed (e.g., using vh ≠ sqrt(g k)) to justify a k-dependent maximum height. Implementation notes: Apply this rule only if the problem or solution states v0 > vh or an equivalent inequality implying loss of contact. Accept algebraic equivalents such as z_max - z0 = v0^2/(2 g) or z_max = z0 + v0^2/(2 g); constant mass factors must cancel. Reject answers in which symbol k appears in the final z_max for the v0 > vh case.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Unjustified Complementary Angle Assumptions Between Independent Bodies
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: Checks for logically unsupported angle relations (e.g., θ + α = 90°, α = 90° − θ, sin α = cos θ, cos α = sin θ, cot α = tan θ) asserted between orientation angles that belong to different rigid bodies or contacts. Trigger: The solution introduces a complementary-angle identity linking two angles that reference distinct objects (e.g., two rods or two separate contacts with wall/floor). Validation: Search for explicit prior geometric constraints that mandate complementarity or perpendicularity, such as (a) the angles are acute angles of the same triangle with a stated right angle, (b) the bodies are declared perpendicular or share a rigid right-angle bracket or hinge, or (c) both angles are defined at the same vertex with a known right angle. If none of these justifications are present, flag a logic error. Rationale: In statics problems with multiple rods contacting a wall/floor, each rod’s angle with the wall is independently determined by equilibrium; wall smoothness, friction coefficients, or mere contact do not impose α + θ = 90°. This rule prevents incorrect simplifications like α = 90° − θ or cot α = tan θ without geometric basis.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Angle condition must depend on inter-contact friction μ_C and given angle θ
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: Checks statics solutions for multi-body contact systems (e.g., two rods) where an inter-body friction coefficient (μ_C) is specified and a reference angle for one body (θ) is given. When the problem asks for an equilibrium condition on another angle α, the final equation/inequality for α must include dependence on both μ_C and θ. The verifier will: (1) detect from the problem statement that μ_C (rod-rod contact friction) and θ (angle of rod AB) are given; (2) extract the student's final condition for α; (3) verify that the final expression contains μ_C and θ as parameters. If either μ_C or θ is missing without an explicit, correct justification (e.g., a demonstrated cancellation from properly written equilibrium equations or a declared special case consistent with the problem), the solution is flagged. The rule also scans the derivation for inclusion of the inter-contact friction force in force/torque balances; if the rod-rod contact friction is never used, it is flagged as a conceptual omission. Typical violations include conclusions such as tan(α) ≥ 1/(2 μ_A), or any α-condition depending only on ground friction μ_A while omitting μ_C and θ. This rule helps catch oversimplifications that ignore required parameter dependencies arising from inter-contact friction and the given geometry.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Verify stability threshold V_min from Ω^2(V) and correct √(gR)/2 prefactor
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: This rule checks the correctness of the minimum speed for stability (V_min) in small-oscillation analyses where the angular frequency Ω depends on a translational speed V. It targets errors arising from an incorrect Ω expression or misuse of the stability criterion. The verifier will: (1) Ensure the stability condition is formulated with Ω^2 ≥ 0 (not Ω ≥ 0). (2) Recompute the stability threshold by solving Ω^2(V) = 0 and selecting the smallest positive real root as V_min*. (3) Validate dimensional consistency that V_min scales as √(g R) when gravity g and a length scale R appear in the model. (4) For the rolling ring near a vertical plane (the given context), verify the correct numerical prefactor: V_min must equal (1/2)√(g R). If the submitted V_min equals √(g R) or otherwise deviates from the 1/2 factor, flag a factor-of-two error. (5) Consistency check: substituting the claimed V_min into the submitted Ω^2(V) should yield zero; if it does not, flag an inconsistency in the derived Ω or threshold computation. This rule catches mistakes such as using Ω ≥ 0 instead of Ω^2 ≥ 0, sign errors in linearization, and missing numerical coefficients that lead to incorrect stability thresholds.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Linearization around equilibrium must eliminate constant forces
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: Checks small-oscillation derivations for proper equilibrium cancellation. Scope: solutions that analyze small oscillations (e.g., "linearize", "around equilibrium", "small vertical oscillations") and form an equation of motion m·q¨ = F_total(q). Requirements: (1) Identify the stated or implied equilibrium coordinate q_eq via a balance like F_total(q_eq) = 0 (e.g., buoyancy equals weight). (2) Verify that the linearized net force is written as ΔF ≈ (∂F_total/∂q)|_eq · δq, with no constant term. Concretely, after invoking equilibrium, the equation of motion for the perturbation δq must not contain standalone constants (e.g., mg, constant buoyant offsets) that do not depend on δq. (3) Evaluate the student's F_total at q_eq; if F_total(q_eq) is carried into the linearized EOM as a nonzero constant term or is "informally canceled" without explicitly subtracting the equilibrium values before linearization, flag an error. (4) Buoyancy-specific check: if F_total(q) = F_buoy(q) − W, ensure that the linearized EOM uses F_buoy(q_eq + δq) − W ≈ (∂F_buoy/∂q)|_eq · δq, and does not retain W or mg in the final linearized force. (5) Accept forms like m·δq¨ = −k_eff·δq with k_eff = −(∂F_total/∂q)|_eq; reject forms like m·δq¨ = mg − ρ_w g V_sub(q_eq) + α·δq or m·δq¨ = mg + k·δq. Rationale: At equilibrium, constant forces cancel; retaining them in the linearized force law yields an incorrect and confusing EOM.

Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.title: Improper simultaneous maximization of time-dependent factors
Constrained Motion and Contact Condition.description: Flags solutions that obtain the maximum of a time-dependent product or sum by independently setting each constituent factor to its own maximum (or minimum) at the same instant without proving that those extrema occur simultaneously. The rule targets expressions of the form a(t) = f(t) g(t) (or sums involving multiple time-varying terms), especially with periodic/trigonometric components or nested functions (e.g., cos(φ(t)) and cos(ψ(t)), sin(φ(t)) and cos(ψ(t)), or θ(t) and θ̇(t)). It checks for the pattern max[a(t)] = max[f] · max[g] or the verbal/implicit step “set sin(...) = 1 and cos(...) = 1 at the same time” or “take θ at its peak and θ̇ at its peak simultaneously.” To pass, the solution must justify simultaneity by either: (1) explicitly solving for the extremum of the composite expression (e.g., da/dt = 0 with verification of a maximum), or (2) proving alignment/functional dependence that guarantees the extrema coincide (e.g., identical phase and monotonic mapping, or a tight inequality bound with an attainable equality condition). If no such justification is provided, or if the factors depend on the same variable through different functions/frequencies/phases or via a derivative (e.g., cos(θ(t)) and θ̇(t)), the rule reports a logic error. Example application: for a_y(t) = v cos(θ(t)) θ̇(t), claiming the maximum by setting cos(θ) = 1 and θ̇ = max without demonstrating that those occur at the same t is flagged.

Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.title: Uniform axial strain and linear velocity field for non-bending rod
Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.description: Applicable when the problem specifies a very thin homogeneous rod with constant cross-section, prevented from bending, and stretched symmetrically from both ends (or equivalently, axial motion with symmetry). The rule verifies that the solution enforces the kinematic constraints implied by the setup and reduces the kinetic energy to depend only on m, L, and the strain-rate dot(ε). Checks performed: (1) Modeling: The axial strain must be uniform along the rod, i.e., ε(x, t) = ε(t); solutions that retain position-dependent ε(x, t) or arbitrary u(x, t) without asserting uniformity are flagged. (2) Symmetry/zero-momentum: The velocity field must be linear in position about the rod’s center, v(x, t) = dot(ε) (x − L/2), or an equivalent origin choice (e.g., v = dot(ε) x with origin at the center) that ensures ∫ v dm = 0; solutions using constant v, arbitrary v(x), or failing to impose zero net momentum are flagged. (3) Energy form: The kinetic energy must be computed as T = (1/2) ∫_0^L ρ A v^2 dx and simplified to T = (m L^2 / 24) [dot(ε)]^2; any dependence on E, spatial profiles, ρ or A separately (instead of m), or leaving T as an unsimplified integral is flagged. (4) Output variables: The final T must be expressible solely in terms of m, L, and dot(ε); inclusion of additional material parameters in the kinetic energy indicates a modeling error. This rule catches failures to apply the uniform-strain and symmetry constraints needed to express T in the requested variables.

Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.title: Continuous rope through frictionless guides: account for all loaded segments and correct elongation mapping
Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.description:
Scope: Problems with a single elastic rope running through frictionless carabiners/pulleys, anchored at one end and attached to a climber at the other. The rope has multiple taut segments (e.g., ground-to-carabiner length H and carabiner-to-climber length L) made of the same material and cross-section. Check the following modeling requirements and flag violations:

1) Uniform tension and strain across segments: Under frictionless guides and a continuous rope, each taut segment carries the same tension T. With uniform rope (same E and A), stress is equal in each segment, so strain is equal: ε = T/(EA). Flag if the solution assigns different tensions or strains to segments without friction or material changes.

2) Strain energy must include all loaded segments: The elastic energy is stored in every segment under tension. For a uniform rope, the total loaded length is (H + L), and the effective axial stiffness is k_eff = EA/(H + L). Correct energy expressions must integrate over the entire loaded length, e.g., U = ∫ (σ ε/2) dV over both segments, or equivalently U = (1/2) T · Δl_total with Δl_total = ε (H + L). Flag if the solution computes strain energy using only the climber-side segment length L (e.g., k = EA/L or U ∝ L only) while other segments are clearly taut.

3) Correct kinematic mapping of fall distance to rope elongation: The climber’s additional fall distance due to rope stretch equals the elongation of the climber-side segment only: Δy_climber = Δl_lower = ε·L. The total rope extension is Δl_total = ε (H + L) and is not equal to the climber’s displacement. Flag if the solution equates the climber’s fall distance to the total rope extension, or uses an unphysical relation such as ΔL = H − L or any difference of the geometric segment lengths to represent elastic elongation.

4) Consistency checks: When energy balance or force-displacement relations are used, ensure that terms involving EA, stiffness, or strain reference the sum of all taut lengths (H + L) when computing total rope energy or effective stiffness, and reference only L when relating the climber’s displacement to rope stretch. Flag if this consistency is violated.

This rule detects modeling errors where only one segment’s stretch is considered, where elongation is tied to geometric differences like H − L, or where tension/strain is not treated uniformly across segments in a continuous, frictionless rope system.

Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.title: Require energy balance and correct tension relation in elastic fall with acceleration limit
Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.description: This rule checks solutions to problems where an elastic rope (with a given or referenced stress–strain curve) arrests a fall under a specified maximum acceleration. The rule flags two classes of errors: (A) using only a local force balance to determine the allowable fall length without a work–energy analysis, and (B) incorrect sign or form in the force balance relating tension and acceleration. Specifically: (1) If the solution attempts to compute the maximum safe rope length L (or fall distance) solely from Newton’s second law at an instant (e.g., sets mg − T = m a_max or similar) and does not equate the gravitational potential energy lost during the fall to the elastic energy stored in the rope (via integrating stress vs. strain or referencing the area under the stress–strain curve), flag the solution. Acceptable forms include statements like m g Δh = ∫ T(x) dx, using the work–energy theorem, or explicitly summing elastic energy in all loaded rope segments. (2) If the solution derives the maximum tension from the acceleration limit using mg − T = m a_max or T = mg − m a_max, or produces T < mg (e.g., T = 4 m g for a_max = 5 g), flag as a sign/logic error. The correct instantaneous relation when upward acceleration magnitude is a_max is T − mg = m a_max ⇒ T = m (g + a_max). (3) For setups with frictionless carabiners and multiple rope segments sharing the same tension, the solution must account for total elastic energy as the sum over all stretched segments; if this is omitted when determining L, flag the solution. The rule triggers on the absence of energy/work keywords or integrals (e.g., no mention of energy, work–energy, potential energy, elastic energy, area under stress–strain, ∫T dx) combined with reliance on a single force equation to set L, and on any occurrence of mg − T = m a_max or T = mg − m a_max in this context.

Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.title: Strain must be derived from stress via sigma = T/A and the provided stress–strain curve
Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.description: This rule validates the use of material strain in problems that explicitly provide a stress–strain (sigma–epsilon) graph for an elastic rope or cord. It flags solutions that: (1) introduce a numerical strain value (epsilon, epsilon_max, etc.) without first computing the rope tension at the relevant event (e.g., maximum allowed acceleration) using Newton’s second law and then converting to stress via sigma = T/A, followed by reading epsilon from the given stress–strain curve; (2) employ dimensionally or physically inconsistent relations linking geometry and strain, such as solving for the protective distance L solely in terms of H and epsilon (e.g., L = H/(1 + epsilon)), which omits dependence on mass m, gravity g, rope cross-sectional area A, and the rope’s constitutive law; and (3) treat strain from one segment to infer total motion without accounting for which rope segments actually contribute to the climber’s displacement and energy storage. The rule triggers when a stress–strain graph is mentioned in the problem but the solution (a) assigns epsilon arbitrarily, or (b) uses formulas that bypass sigma = T/A and the graph, or (c) derives L from epsilon in a way that ignores the required force/energy balance across the rope segments. Examples caught: epsilon_max set to a constant (e.g., 0.5) without graph-based justification; expressions like L = H/(epsilon_max + 1). The solution must explicitly show the chain: compute T at the acceleration limit → sigma = T/A → epsilon from the provided curve → apply correct geometric/energy relations for the stretched rope segments.

Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.title: Do not equate fall distance to geometric rope length in taut-rope scenarios
Elasticity and Stress-Strain Relationshi.description:
Checks solutions to rope/climbing/bungee problems where the rope is stated to be taut (e.g., phrases like 'rope always tight/taut', 'no slack', 'the segment between the clip and carabiners is always tight'). In such setups, the climber’s additional drop during arrest is produced by elastic extension of the rope (or the segment attached to the climber), not by the preexisting geometric separation to the anchor/protection. The rule flags the following patterns:
- Asserting or implying a free-fall distance equal to the rope segment length L (e.g., 'the climber falls a distance L' or setting the kinematic/energy displacement to L) when the rope is taut from the start.
- Using fall distance = L + ΔL, or using an mg L term in an energy balance before/while the rope is already exerting force, despite the no-slack assumption.
- Stating that maximum acceleration/tension occurs 'after falling L' in a taut-rope setting.
- Reusing a variable L defined as the geometric distance between the climber and the last anchor/carabiner as the arrest distance, instead of using the rope’s elastic extension (e.g., ΔL or the integral of strain over the segment attached to the climber).
The rule expects, under no-slack assumptions, that the displacement relevant for work/energy and peak-force timing equals the rope extension (e.g., Δy = Δℓ of the segment attached to the climber, or Δy = ∫strain ds), not the preexisting geometric length. Exceptions: Do not trigger if the solution explicitly states the presence of slack, intentional payout, or a mechanism delaying rope engagement before stretch (e.g., 'belayer gives slack', 'device slips until length L'). The rule is intended to catch conceptual misuse of geometric separation as fall distance when immediate rope tension is implied by the problem statement.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Incorrect initial conditions for preloaded spring-mass system
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description: Checks for modeling errors in spring-mass problems where an object is already suspended (preloading) and an additional mass is added before release. Detection criteria: (1) If the problem text indicates the heavy object M was already hanging and supported while placing m (phrases like "already suspended", "supported while placing", "then released"), then at the instant of release the spring is initially stretched by M alone. (2) If the coordinate x is measured from the spring’s natural (unstretched) length, the correct initial conditions are x(0) = (M g)/k and x'(0) = 0. Relative to the new equilibrium x0 = ((M + m) g)/k, the displacement y = x - x0 must satisfy y(0) = - (m g)/k and y'(0) = 0. (3) Flag solutions that set x(0) = 0 (or state "spring at natural length at release") or set y(0) = 0 when the scenario is sequential loading (M first, then m). (4) Also flag if the equation of motion is written for the combined mass (M + m) about the natural length, (M + m) x'' + k x = 0, while simultaneously using x(0) = 0; or if equilibrium is computed as x0 = ((M + m) g)/k but the initial displacement is taken as zero rather than - (m g)/k. Rationale: The pre-stretch by M sets the initial deflection and amplitude; ignoring it yields incorrect oscillation amplitude and subsequent contact/normal-force extrema. The rule passes if the solution either uses x from natural length with x(0) = (M g)/k, x'(0) = 0, or uses y from the new equilibrium with y(0) = - (m g)/k, y'(0) = 0.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Sign consistency for Newton’s second law in vertical fall arrest (tension vs weight)
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description: Checks that Newton’s second law is applied with correct sign conventions in vertical deceleration (fall arrest) scenarios involving gravity (mg, downward) and rope tension (T, upward). The rule targets the common mistake of writing mg - T = m a_max with a_max treated as a positive magnitude during deceleration, which implies a downward acceleration and leads to unphysical results (e.g., negative or sub-weight tension). What the rule verifies: 1) Context detection: The solution indicates a falling body being arrested/decellerated by a rope (keywords like fall, arrest, decelerate, rope/carabiner, stretch) with forces {mg downward, T upward}. 2) Acceleration direction: If the text describes deceleration of downward motion or explicitly states acceleration is upward (or uses an acceleration magnitude a_max at the instant of maximum rope force), then the acceleration used in the force equation must be upward. 3) Equation form check: For upward acceleration of magnitude a_max (>0), the correct relation is T - mg = m a_max, hence T = mg + m a_max. Using mg - T = m a_max with a_max > 0, or deriving T = mg - m a_max (or T = |mg - m a_max|) in this context is flagged. 4) Inequality check: In deceleration (acceleration upward), T must satisfy T > mg. Any result with T ≤ mg, T < 0, or a computed T like 4mg when a_max = 5g is flagged. 5) Axis convention consistency: If a downward-positive axis is explicitly used, then the acceleration value must be negative for upward acceleration (a = -a_max), so mg - T = m a must produce T = mg + m a_max. Using a positive a_max with mg - T = m a is flagged. The rule raises an error when the tension is computed as mg - m a_max or otherwise fails T = mg + m a_max for upward acceleration; it also flags negative tension magnitudes arising from sign errors.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Improper conservation of mechanical energy during kinetic-friction (sliding-to-rolling) phases
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description: This rule flags solutions that apply conservation of total mechanical energy across a phase where kinetic friction (slipping/rubbing) acts, such as when an object is spun up from non-rotating to rolling without slipping by rubbing against a surface. Detection criteria: (1) The solution explicitly invokes conservation of energy (e.g., asserts total mechanical energy is constant or uses equations like 1/2 m v_i^2 = 1/2 m v_f^2 + 1/2 I ω_f^2 + m g h) across a contact phase. (2) The same solution indicates sliding contact via terms like 'kinetic friction', 'rubs', 'slips', 'sliding', 'spin-up due to friction', 'rough surface with slipping', or describes a transition from non-rotating to rolling without slipping caused by friction. (3) No explicit non-conservative work term is included (no W_f, heat loss, or integral of friction force over slip distance), and the sliding phase is not modeled separately via impulse/torque or angular momentum about the contact point. The rule is especially targeted at rolling problems where an initially non-rotating body exits a rubbing region already rolling without slipping; in such cases, mechanical energy is not conserved during the sliding phase because kinetic friction dissipates energy. Acceptable exceptions (do not flag): (a) The solution clearly separates phases and only applies energy conservation to intervals with no kinetic friction (e.g., free-flight ascent after ejection), while handling the sliding phase with angular impulse/torque and the v = ω r constraint at the end of contact; (b) The solution justifies that only static friction acts throughout (no slipping) and accounts correctly for energy transfer or lack of dissipation consistent with the scenario. If flagged, the solver should include the work of kinetic friction or model the sliding-to-rolling transition (e.g., using frictional impulse and torque) to determine exit speed and spin before applying energy conservation to subsequent conservative-motion phases.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Do not equate frictional energy loss to gravitational potential gain in multi-stage motion
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description: Flags solutions that compute ascent height by directly setting the gravitational potential increase (m g h) equal to the energy dissipated by friction or the work done by friction during a prior contact phase, ignoring the remaining mechanical energy at separation. Detection guidance: (a) Look for equations of the form m g h = W_fric, m g h = E_loss, m g h = f_k d, m g h = μ_k N d, or equivalent statements (e.g., “height is determined by the energy lost to friction”). (b) Identify collapsed energy balances that equate frictional losses to potential gain (E_fric = m g h) without including initial kinetic energy or the exit mechanical energy (translational and rotational) as separate terms. (c) In problems where friction acts only during contact and the subsequent ascent occurs without dissipation, height should be determined from the mechanical energy the body has at the instant it leaves contact: m g h = KE_trans(exit) + KE_rot(exit) (if it comes to rest at the top). Therefore, it is incorrect to use frictional work alone to set m g h. Do not trigger if the solution properly partitions stages, e.g., KE_initial = E_fric + KE_exit and then uses KE_exit → m g h, or if KE_initial = E_fric + m g h is justified by an explicitly zero exit kinetic energy. Trigger when the height is tied solely to frictional loss or when mechanical energy conservation is misapplied by treating frictional dissipation as equal to gravitational potential gain in a multi-stage process.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Detect circular energy-conservation (tautology) without independent coupling
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description:
This rule flags solutions that apply conservation of mechanical energy in a way that produces a tautology (e.g., gh = gh, 0 = 0) because the same energy balance is reused without introducing an independent relation that couples variables changed by a non-conservative interaction. The rule checks for: 
- Presence of frictional/rolling initiation language (e.g., friction, rubs, rolling without slipping, initially not rotating) combined with an assumption of total mechanical energy conservation over that interaction interval without an explicit non-conservative work term (W_nc or work by friction). 
- Multiple energy equations over the same time interval/subsystem that are algebraically dependent (e.g., 1/2 m v0^2 = 1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 I ω^2 + mgh and a rearranged form of the same), such that substitution eliminates all unknowns and simplifies to an identity. Implementation: symbolically eliminate shared variables and test whether the resulting equation reduces to an identity (e.g., lhs - rhs simplifies to 0). 
- Missing independent coupling needed to relate translational and rotational variables created by the interaction, such as: v = ω r (rolling-without-slipping constraint at contact), angular impulse/torque relations (∫τ dt = ΔL), or an explicit non-conservative work/energy-loss term. If none of these appear while friction is invoked, and the energy equations are reused, flag as circular reasoning. 
The rule should trigger when: (1) friction/rolling initiation is mentioned; (2) total mechanical energy conservation is applied across that interval with no W_nc; (3) the set of equations used to solve for h, v, or ω is rank-deficient or reduces to a tautology upon substitution. The diagnostic indicates that an independent relation (e.g., v = ω r at ejection, or angular impulse due to friction, or inclusion of work by friction) is required to connect v and ω (and hence v0) rather than reusing the same energy statement.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Require correct spin-up relation for translation-to-rolling due to friction (no global energy conservation through slip)
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description: This rule verifies solutions involving a rigid body that enters a contact with friction while initially not rotating and exits rolling without slipping (e.g., a sphere with I = β m r^2 rubbing until it rolls). It checks that the solution: (1) does not apply global conservation of mechanical energy across the slipping (spin-up) phase, since kinetic friction dissipates energy; (2) explicitly establishes or correctly uses the necessary kinematic-dynamic relation between the post-slip translational speed v_exit and the initial translational speed v0 for a body with I = β m r^2: v_exit = v0 / (1 + β) and ω_exit = v_exit / r at the onset of rolling; (3) does not leave v_exit dependent on the friction coefficient (the result is independent of μ for constant kinetic friction); and (4) uses v_exit (not v0) as the initial speed for any subsequent conservative phase (e.g., computing ascent height via m g h = 1/2 m v_exit^2 + 1/2 I (v_exit^2 / r^2) if energy is then conserved). The rule flags solutions that: (a) set 1/2 m v0^2 = 1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 I ω^2 + m g h across the slip phase; (b) compute the height h without deriving or citing the v_exit–v0 relation; (c) use an incorrect relation (e.g., omit the 1+β factor or include μ) or fail to impose ω_exit = v_exit / r at rolling. This catches the common error of trying to determine the height from energy conservation without first finding the correct exit speed produced by frictional spin-up.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Misuse of v_cm = ω r without instantaneous center/pivot justification
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description:
This rule flags the unjustified use of the kinematic relation v_cm = ω r (e.g., v_cm = ω (l/2) for a rod) to couple translational and rotational motion in plane rigid-body problems. The equality v_cm = ω r is only valid when the body undergoes pure rotation about a stationary point (fixed pivot/hinge) or about an instantaneous center of rotation (ICR) that is at rest relative to the ground (e.g., rolling without slipping with v_contact = 0). In general plane motion (such as a freely falling or sliding rod without a fixed pivot or no-slip constraint), v_cm and ω are independent and must be related via proper constraints or dynamics.

Detection criteria:
- Identify steps where the solution sets v_cm equal to ω times a geometric length (R, l/2, l, etc.), or uses this to eliminate variables in energy/momentum equations (e.g., substituting v_cm = ω r into KE = 1/2 m v_cm^2 + 1/2 I ω^2).
- Check whether, prior to using v_cm = ω r, the solution explicitly establishes one of the following: (1) a fixed pivot/hinge at a known point; (2) a no-slip condition at a contact point with v_contact = 0, thereby defining an ICR; or (3) an explicit identification of an ICR accompanied by a statement that the chosen point’s velocity relative to the ground is zero.
- If none of these justifications are present, flag the step as an invalid kinematic constraint.

Context-specific note for impacts: Post-impact use of v_cm = ω r is permitted only if the solution clearly states that the contact point sticks (perfectly inelastic with sticking) so that v_contact = 0 immediately after impact, establishing a pivot. Otherwise, the relation must not be imposed.

Corrective guidance: Require the use of general rigid-body kinematics v_P = v_CM + ω × r_P/CM and derive any relations between v_CM and ω from actual constraints (fixed pivot, no-slip, sticking contact) or from dynamics (impulse-momentum, energy) rather than imposing v_cm = ω r by default.

Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.title: Unjustified rolling/no-slip assumption after inelastic landing
Frictionless Systems and Misapplications.description: Flags solutions that, after a rigid body undergoes a landing or perfectly inelastic collision with the ground, impose a rolling-without-slipping or no-slip constraint (e.g., use v = ωR or state "it rolls along the ground") without explicitly modeling or justifying frictional contact. The rule checks for: (1) Post-impact kinematics invoking rolling/no-slip or equating translational and rotational speeds at contact immediately after an impact. (2) Absence of a friction model: no kinetic/static friction coefficient (μ_k or μ_s) and no tangential impulse analysis (J_t) relative to the normal impulse (J_n), i.e., no check of |J_t| ≤ μ_s J_n for sticking or specification of sliding with μ_k. (3) Extended contact misuse: applying rolling to geometries that contact the ground along a line/area (e.g., a rod lying flat) where point-contact rolling is inapplicable; the correct post-impact motion should be sliding with kinetic friction unless a stick condition is demonstrated. (4) Use of mechanical energy conservation across a perfectly inelastic collision to determine the post-impact horizontal speed, instead of using impulse-momentum with frictional impulses. If any of these are detected, prompt the solver to introduce a friction model (μ_k/μ_s), compute tangential vs normal impulses to decide slip vs stick, or justify an idealized infinite-friction assumption; for rods landing flat, require modeling as sliding with kinetic friction unless sticking is proven.

Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.title: Invalid use of t = distance / single velocity when speed changes during interaction
Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.description: This rule flags solutions that compute the time an object spends traversing a medium or another body (e.g., penetration through a block) by using t = L / v with a single instantaneous velocity (initial, final, or final relative velocity), despite evidence that the speed changes during the traverse. Trigger conditions: (1) The problem statement or the solution explicitly indicates a change in speed (e.g., 'speed reduced to half'), presence of a resistive force, or any nonzero acceleration during contact; AND (2) the time inside the medium/body is computed as t = L / v_final, t = L / v_initial, or t = L / v_rel (such as L/(v0/4)) without a justified constant-speed assumption. In two-body interactions (e.g., bullet and block), the rule also checks for use of a constant final relative speed to compute time; relative speed is not constant when forces act on both bodies. Acceptable alternatives must show a correct kinematic/impulse approach: integrating t = ∫ dx / v(x), using kinematics under a justified constant acceleration (and then using average speed v_avg = (v_in + v_out)/2 or t = (v_out − v_in)/a), or deriving time from impulse (J = ∫ F dt) with a defensible model of F(t). Using an 'average force' value alone does not justify assuming constant velocity during traversal. If none of these justifications are present, the rule reports a logic error for time computation under variable speed.

Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.title: Do not compute displacement with d = v·t when speed changes during the interval
Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.description: This rule flags solutions that compute an object's displacement over an interval in which its speed changes (e.g., due to a force or momentum exchange) using the constant-velocity formula d = v·t with a single velocity value. Detection criteria: (1) The solution establishes or implies different initial and final speeds for the object during the interval (vi ≠ vf), or references a nonzero net/average force or acceleration acting during that interval; (2) The displacement over that same interval is then computed as d = v·t using either the final speed, the initial speed, or any single speed without explicitly treating v as an average velocity or integrating/using kinematic relations for variable velocity. In problems involving penetration/collision with stated 'average resistive force' or impulse, the block or target typically accelerates from its initial speed (often zero) to a different final speed while the interaction lasts; in such cases d must be obtained via v_avg·t with v_avg = (vi + vf)/2 under constant acceleration, s = vi·t + 0.5·a·t^2, or ∫ v(t) dt. Example to flag: Block initially at rest, ends with vf = v0/4 after the bullet exits; displacement inside the block computed as d = (v0/4)·t (t being the penetration time) without using average velocity or acceleration. Acceptable: Using d = ((vi + vf)/2)·t when constant acceleration is justified, or any correct integral/kinematic relation consistent with variable velocity.

Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.title: Stop at the specified event instant (no post-event accumulation)
Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.description: Checks that when a problem asks for a quantity "at/when/just as/just after/just before" a specified event, the solution evaluates the quantity up to that event only and does not add contributions from motion or processes occurring after the event. The verifier flags solutions that: (1) explicitly add distances or other quantities after the event using phrases like "after exit", "afterwards", "then it continues", "additional distance", or "plus the distance after ..."; (2) use the object's post-event speed to compute extra displacement beyond the instant (e.g., s += v_exit * t_extra on a frictionless surface); (3) integrate forces/velocities beyond the event boundary (e.g., summing over time intervals past the 'just exited' moment); (4) introduce extra additive terms unrelated to the specified interaction interval, such as appending an L/3-type segment when the requested displacement is only up to the bullet's exit. In bullet–block penetration problems, "when the bullet has just exited" means the block's displacement accumulated during penetration only; any post-exit sliding is out of scope and must not be included.

Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.title: Inconsistent gravitational potential zero after geometry/length change
Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.description: Checks for incorrect treatment of gravitational potential energy when the pivot-to-COM distance changes between stages (e.g., standing/squatting on a swing, telescoping pendulum). The rule looks for solutions that: (1) fix the zero of potential at a lowest point for an initial length r0 (often by using U = m g r0 (1 - cos θ) and setting U_B = 0 at θ = 0), then (2) change the length to r1 ≠ r0 at the same angle θ (typically θ = 0 at the bottom) and set U = 0 again using U = m g r1 (1 - cos θ), while still comparing energies across stages using the original reference. This is inconsistent because the zero level depends on r. If the reference was fixed at the original lowest point (r0, θ = 0), then immediately after changing the length to r1 at the same angle, the potential must shift by + m g (r1 - r0). The verifier flags cases where U at the post-change stage is computed as zero solely because θ = 0, despite r having changed, without adding the required offset m g Δr. Additional check: when an instantaneous radial change occurs with no external torque (e.g., at the bottom), if energy balances are written across the change, they must include both (a) the kinetic energy change from angular momentum conservation about the pivot and (b) the gravitational offset m g (r1 - r0) relative to the original zero. The rule triggers on patterns such as U_B = 0 with r = r0 and U_B' = 0 with r = r1 ≠ r0; using U = m g l (1 - cos θ) but swapping l → l + d between stages while keeping the same zero; or phrases like 'take B as zero' followed by a length change and U = 0 asserted again at θ = 0. To pass, the solution must either maintain a single potential reference across all stages and include the + m g (r1 - r0) offset when r changes, or explicitly redefine the reference and avoid mixing energies from different references in the same balance.

Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.title: Transit time L/v requires positive, nonzero velocity and stated domain constraints
Time and Displacement in Variable Veloci.description: Checks solutions that compute a traversal or dwell time using t = L / v (e.g., t = 2R / v_R for crossing a spherical shell). The rule enforces: (1) the velocity component in the denominator (e.g., radial v_R) must be explicitly defined and strictly positive at the entry boundary; (2) domain or threshold conditions ensuring v_R > 0 must be stated and used (e.g., for a repulsive charged shell, v_R^2 = v^2 − 2 k Q1 Q2 / (M2 R) ≥ 0 and specifically v^2 > 2 k Q1 Q2 / (M2 R) for entry); (3) the equality case v_R = 0 at the boundary must be handled (the particle does not enter and any finite t is invalid; time diverges), and negative or imaginary v_R indicates no entry; (4) if the solution provides a finite time without mentioning or enforcing these constraints, or evaluates t with v_R ≤ 0 or undefined, flag as a logical/domain error. This rule generalizes to any use of t = distance/velocity in the presence of potential barriers or turning points: the solution must verify that the crossing velocity is real and positive and must state the admissible parameter domain.

New Category: Pendulum Dynamics.title: Pendulum tension computed via static vertical balance (missing centripetal term)
New Category: Pendulum Dynamics.description: Flags solutions for swinging pendulum or string-constrained circular motion that treat tension using a static vertical force balance (e.g., 'T cosθ = mg', 'T = mg cosθ', 'T_y = mg', or 'vertical equilibrium') while the mass is moving. In such cases the correct radial (along-string) equation is T − mg cosθ = m v^2 / L (or equivalents like T = mg cosθ + m ω^2 L, T = mg cosθ + m L (dθ/dt)^2). The verifier should: (1) Identify contexts mentioning pendulum/string tension with a nonzero motion state (e.g., 'swinging', angle θ at release, tangential acceleration a_t, or energy change). (2) Check if the tension is derived solely from balancing components of weight without any centripetal/radial acceleration term. (3) If tangential acceleration or motion is acknowledged (e.g., a_t = g sinθ, 'begins to swing'), then any use of vertical equilibrium for tension without an m v^2 / r term is an error. (4) Also flag conclusions that directly set T = mg or T = mg cosθ at nonzero speed unless the solution explicitly states v = 0 (static equilibrium). Expected correction: include the centripetal term and use T = mg cosθ + m v^2 / L, with v obtained from energy or angular dynamics.

New Category: Pendulum Dynamics.title: Pendulum dynamics: Tension has no tangential component
New Category: Pendulum Dynamics.description:
Checks solutions of constrained circular motion (pendulum, mass on string/rod) for improper use of tension in the tangential direction. Flags the following patterns:
- Any equation that uses a tangential component of tension, e.g., "T sinθ = m a", "T sinθ = m a_t", "horizontal component of T equals tangential acceleration", or similar, where a or a_t is the tangential acceleration.
- Statements that resolve forces into horizontal/vertical and then set the tangential equation using a component of T (e.g., treating T sinθ as the driving force along the path) in an ideal, frictionless, massless-string system.
- During motion at general angle θ, setting vertical force balance T cosθ = mg (implying static vertical equilibrium) without explicitly restricting to the lowest point or static conditions.
Correct reference relations:
- Tangential equation (ideal pendulum, no tangential nonconservative forces): m a_t = −mg sinθ (plus any explicit tangential forces such as friction/air drag if present). T does not appear in the tangential balance.
- Radial equation: T − mg cosθ = m v^2/L (or m a_r), i.e., tension acts purely along the string (radially). The rule triggers when the solution violates these decompositions by assigning T a tangential component or enforcing vertical equilibrium during motion.

New Category: Multi-Component Rolling Sy.title: Use total mass in translational dynamics for multi-component rolling systems
New Category: Multi-Component Rolling Sy.description:
This rule checks that, in problems involving rolling without slipping where a system is composed of multiple components with specified masses (e.g., a chassis/body plus wheels), the translational application of Newton's second law uses the total mass of all moving parts, not just a subset. Specifically:
- If the problem statement provides separate masses for components (e.g., states that M excludes the wheels, and gives wheel masses), then the net force along the direction of motion must be written using m_total = sum of all component masses.
- For motion along an incline at angle θ, the driving gravitational component must be m_total g sin(θ), and the normal component must sum to m_total g cos(θ) when considering the entire system's external forces.
- The inertial term on the right-hand side must be m_total a, not a single component's mass times a.
- If multiple contacts exist (e.g., four wheels), the friction term in the translational equation should represent the total external friction (sum over contacts), not a single-wheel friction unless explicitly defined as total.
Flag a modeling error when the solution writes F_net_parallel = M g sin(θ) − f = M a (or analogous forms) using only a subset mass (such as the body mass) while the problem provides additional component masses that contribute to both weight and translational inertia. The correct form is F_net_parallel = m_total g sin(θ) − f_total = m_total a, where m_total includes all moving components.

New Category: Multi-Component Rolling Sy.title: Use total system mass for translational forces and F=ma
New Category: Multi-Component Rolling Sy.description: Checks that any translational force or acceleration equation (weight W=mg, ramp components mg sin(theta), mg cos(theta), normal force N, net force down the incline, and Newton's second law F=ma) uses the total mass of the system, not a partial mass that excludes subcomponents. Trigger this rule when the problem statement defines an object composed of multiple parts with specified masses (e.g., chassis mass M defined as excluding wheels, plus wheel masses). The verifier should: (1) parse mass definitions and identify phrases indicating exclusion (e.g., 'mass excluding the wheels', 'chassis only'); (2) compute the expected total mass M_total as the sum of all component masses; (3) scan the solution for translational equations involving gravity or normal reaction and for F=ma, and verify the mass used equals M_total (symbolically or numerically); (4) flag an error if the solution uses only the chassis mass or any subset of component masses (e.g., N = M g cos(theta), W = M g, F_down = M g sin(theta), or F_net = M a) when the motion concerns the entire bus including its wheels. This catches modeling mistakes where wheels or other components are omitted from the system mass in translational dynamics, even if the incorrect normal force is not used later.

New Category: Multi-Component Rolling Sy.title: Require total mass (chassis + wheels) in translational F=ma for rolling systems
New Category: Multi-Component Rolling Sy.description: When a problem states that the chassis/bus mass excludes the wheels and provides wheel masses, the translational Newton’s second law along the incline must use the total mass m_total = m_chassis + sum(m_wheels). The gravitational component and normal force must likewise use m_total (m_total g sinθ and m_total g cosθ). Verification checks: (1) If the student writes F_net = m a with m = m_chassis only, flag an error. (2) If wheel rotational dynamics (torques/inertias) are included (e.g., f_i = I_i a / R_i^2 per wheel) but the translational equation still uses only m_chassis, flag an error for inconsistent mass usage. (3) Consistency check for acceleration: for rolling without slipping with no bearing losses, a should follow a = (m_total g sinθ) / (m_total + Σ(I_i/R_i^2)). If the student’s expression replaces m_total by m_chassis anywhere in the numerator or denominator, flag a calculation error for omitted wheel mass in translation.

Pendulum Dynamics.title: Pendulum gravitational potential must use U(θ) = mgL(1 − cosθ) at lowest-point zero
Pendulum Dynamics.description: Checks solutions for a pendulum or a point mass on a rigid string/rod of length L in uniform gravity where the angle θ is measured from the vertical. When the gravitational potential energy is referenced to the lowest point (θ = 0), the correct expression is U(θ) = mgL(1 − cosθ). The rule flags the following issues: (a) stating U(θ) = mgL cosθ, −mgL cosθ, mgL sinθ, or any form lacking the additive constant needed to satisfy U(0) = 0 when the lowest point is the zero level; (b) asserting U(0) = 0 while using U(θ) = mgL cosθ (internal inconsistency); (c) using energy conservation to derive speed or tension but pairing it with an incorrect absolute U(θ) expression without explicitly defining and consistently using a different zero level. The rule also checks that energy differences are computed as ΔU = mgL(1 − cosθ) when the lowest point is the reference. If a solution derives v^2 = 2gL(1 − cosθ) but previously defined U(θ) = mgL cosθ without mentioning an additive constant or a different reference level, it is flagged as a potential-sign/zero-reference error.

Inelastic Collisions and Contact Conditi.title: Inelastic collision does not eliminate tangential velocity without friction modeling
Inelastic Collisions and Contact Conditi.description: Flag solutions that claim or implicitly enforce that a 'perfectly inelastic' (e = 0) collision with the ground makes the motion along the ground (tangential/horizontal velocity) immediately zero, without explicitly modeling frictional impulse or a stick/slip contact constraint. Verification steps: (1) Detect use of terms like 'perfectly inelastic' or 'e = 0' to determine post-impact velocities. (2) If the solution sets v_t^+ = 0, v_x^+ = 0, or tangential kinetic energy = 0 solely because the collision is inelastic, and there is no mention of friction coefficient μ, frictional impulse J_t, or an explicit sticking condition (v_rel,t^+ = 0 due to sufficient friction), flag as incorrect. (3) Also flag if the coefficient of restitution is applied to tangential components (e.g., v_t^+ = −e v_t^−) or if energy conservation across the collision is used to eliminate tangential motion. Rationale: e = 0 constrains only the normal component of relative velocity at the contact; changes in tangential velocity arise from frictional impulse during the collision, not inelasticity alone.

Inelastic Collisions and Contact Conditi.title: Consistent final-speed and proper conservation in perfectly inelastic collisions
Inelastic Collisions and Contact Conditi.description:
This rule checks solutions to rigid-body impact problems for two classes of errors: (A) mutually inconsistent numerical results for the same final speed quantity and (B) misuse of conservation principles across a perfectly inelastic collision.

What it checks:
- Contradictory final-speed values: If the solution presents multiple distinct numerical expressions or values for the same quantity (e.g., "final speed along the ground", v_final, v_ground) that are not explicitly reconciled (i.e., not shown to be algebraically equivalent or derived under clearly different, stated assumptions), flag an inconsistency. Use a numeric comparison with a relative tolerance (e.g., 5%). Examples: reporting both sqrt(3 g l)/8 and sqrt(3 g l) for v_final.
- Energy conservation misuse across inelastic impact: If the collision is stated as "perfectly inelastic" (keywords: perfectly inelastic, stick, no rebound), flag any step that equates total mechanical energy before impact to total mechanical energy after impact (e.g., mg Δh = 1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 I ω^2 evaluated post-collision or statements like "energy is conserved during the collision"). In a perfectly inelastic collision, mechanical energy is not conserved across the impact; angular momentum about the contact point may be considered during the impulse if appropriate, but not total energy.
- Inertia reference consistency at/after impact: If the post-impact rotation is modeled about the ground contact point (tip sticks), verify that the moment of inertia used is about that point. Flag use of I_cm = (1/12) m l^2 for rotation about the contact point without applying the parallel-axis theorem (I_contact = I_cm + m (l/2)^2).
- Assumption coherence: If different derivations of the same final speed rely on incompatible assumptions (e.g., one uses energy conservation across inelastic impact while another uses angular momentum about the contact point), and both are presented without resolving the conflict, flag the solution.

Detection details:
- Extract all occurrences of variables/phrases indicating the sought quantity: {"v_final", "final speed", "speed along the ground", "horizontal speed", "v along ground"}. Normalize algebraic forms; evaluate numeric equivalence within 5% tolerance. If more than one distinct value is found and no explicit equality or statement of parameter variation is provided, raise an error.
- Scan for collision-type keywords: {"perfectly inelastic", "inelastic", "stick", "no rebound"}. If present, search the local derivation for energy-conservation claims across the collision: phrases like {"conservation of energy during the collision", "total energy is conserved", "PE converts to KE after collision"} or equations equating pre-impact potential energy directly to post-impact kinetic energy. Flag if found.
- For rotational terms post-impact, check if I_cm is used without a parallel-axis adjustment when the pivot/contact point changes. If the text references rotation about the ground contact or tip, require I_contact; otherwise flag.

Outcome:
- Flag the solution if any of the above violations occur, especially when mutually inconsistent v_final values appear or energy conservation is incorrectly applied across a perfectly inelastic collision.

Inelastic Collisions and Contact Conditi.title: Post-impact horizontal speed must include kinetic friction and a complete final expression
Inelastic Collisions and Contact Conditi.description: This rule verifies solutions for rigid-body problems that ask for the horizontal speed along the ground immediately after a perfectly inelastic collision with the ground. It flags the following issues: 1) Incomplete or truncated solutions that do not present a final numerical value or symbolic expression for the requested speed. 2) Missing dependence on the kinetic friction coefficient μ_k when the problem specifies rough ground or kinetic friction; the final expression for the post-impact horizontal speed must explicitly include μ_k (unless the solution clearly and correctly justifies a special case such as μ_k = 0 or no slip with a friction consistency check). 3) Incorrect use of mechanical energy conservation across a perfectly inelastic collision (e.g., equating pre-impact potential energy directly to post-impact kinetic energy at or after impact). 4) Failure to reference collision mechanics appropriate to inelastic impacts (e.g., impulses, angular momentum about the contact point, frictional impulse) when deriving the post-impact horizontal motion. Trigger conditions: the prompt contains phrases like 'perfectly inelastic collision' and 'ground contact'; the solution lacks μ_k or any mention of kinetic friction in the final expression for horizontal speed; the solution terminates without a clear final answer; or it relies on energy conservation through the collision event.

Miscellaneous.title: Declared mass must be used consistently in dynamics and energy
Miscellaneous.description:
Checks that the mass specified in the problem statement is propagated consistently through all equations of motion and energy expressions.

What it enforces:
- Extract the declared mass expression M_decl from the prompt (e.g., "mass 2m", "mass M0", or a numeric value). If the mass is given as a scaled symbol (e.g., 2m), treat that entire expression as the mass.
- Kinetic energy: verify that any expression of the form T = (1/2)·(…)·v^2 uses (1/2)·M_decl as the coefficient of v^2 (including vector/multi-DOF forms). Flag if T = (1/2)·m·v^2 or any coefficient not equal to M_decl appears.
- Newton’s second law (all coordinate systems): verify that the mass multiplying acceleration is M_decl. Examples:
  - Cartesian: M_decl·a_x = F_x, M_decl·a_y = F_y, …
  - Polar: M_decl·(r¨ − r·θ˙^2) = F_r and M_decl·(r·θ¨ + 2·r˙·θ˙) = F_θ.
  - Momentum definitions: p = M_decl·v (and generalized momenta in Lagrangian formulations) must use M_decl.
- Lagrangian/Hamiltonian: L = T − V must use T with M_decl; Hamiltonian kinetic term must also use M_decl. Any use of a different mass symbol or missing scale factor is flagged.
- Late substitution patching: if derivations proceed with a different mass (e.g., m) and only at the end replace m → 2m without re-deriving intermediate steps, flag as inconsistent usage.

Allowed patterns:
- If the solution explicitly defines a new symbol and equates it to the declared mass early (e.g., "Let M = 2m" or "Let m (hereafter) denote the object’s mass = 2m0"), subsequent consistent use of that symbol passes.

Triggers typical of this error:
- Problem states mass is 2m, but equations use T = (1/2)·m·v^2, a = F/m, or m·(r¨ − r·θ˙^2) = F_r.
- Mismatch between mass used in radial/tangential equations and the specified mass.

Scope:
- Single-particle mechanics in any coordinate system; applies to Newtonian, Lagrangian, and Hamiltonian treatments.
- Excludes cases where reduced mass is explicitly introduced and correctly defined; if reduced mass is used, it must be explicitly tied to M_decl.

Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.title: Mis-integration of temperature-dependent power (∫P(T)dT) for cooling time/heat
Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.description:
Scope: Transient heating/cooling problems where the heat loss rate (power) depends on temperature, P(T), and the body has (approximately) constant heat capacity C. Correct physics: Energy balance gives C dT/dt = -P(T). Therefore, heat lost is Q = C ΔT, and the cooling time is t = C ∫_{T2}^{T1} dT / P(T) (signs/bounds up to convention).

Flag the following failure modes:
- The solution integrates power with respect to temperature to compute heat or time, e.g., Q = ∫ P(T) dT, E = ∫ P(T) dT, or t = (1/C) ∫ P(T) dT, t = ∫ [P(T)/C] dT. (Dimensional error: ∫ P dT has units W·K, not J or s.)
- Any time expression missing the reciprocal of P(T), i.e., the integrand for time is proportional to P(T) rather than 1/P(T). Examples: t expressed as ∫ f(T) P(T) dT with no 1/P(T), or t ≈ C ΔT / P_avg where P_avg is defined as (1/ΔT)∫_{T2}^{T1} P(T) dT (arithmetic average) instead of the correct harmonic average implied by ∫ dT/P(T).
- Statements explicitly treating heat lost as the integral of P(T) with respect to temperature (e.g., “heat lost is ∫ P(T) dT”) or equating Q from ∫ P(T) dT to CΔT.

Pass conditions (do not flag) include any equivalent correct formulation: t = C ∫_{T2}^{T1} dT / P(T) with reversed bounds and a minus sign; discrete approximations t ≈ C Σ (ΔT_i / P(T_i)); or closed forms derived from specific P(T) laws (e.g., Newton cooling with P = k(T − T0) giving t = (C/k) ln((T1 − T0)/(T2 − T0))).

Implementation hints: Parse mathematical relations. If an integral with differential dT has integrand P(T) and is used to compute Q or t, flag. For time calculations, require the presence of 1/P(T) somewhere in the integrand or equivalent algebra. Perform a unit sanity check: any use of ∫ P dT to represent energy (J) or time (s) should be marked inconsistent. Allow variable naming variants (power, heat loss rate, P, Φ, etc.) and equivalent constants (heat capacity C, thermal capacitance).

Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.title: Dimensional check: Do not integrate power over temperature to get energy or time
Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.description:
This rule verifies dimensional consistency in thermal cooling/heating solutions when power depends on temperature. It flags the following:
- Any occurrence of an integral of power with respect to temperature, e.g., ∫ P(T) dT, being labeled or used as heat/energy (Q) or work. Power P has units of W, so ∫ P(T) dT has units of W·K, not Joules; energy must be computed as ∫ P(t) dt.
- Any derivation of elapsed time that uses ∫ P(T) dT (or a quantity derived from it) directly to compute time. The correct cooling relation is dT/dt = -P(T)/C, leading to t = ∫ C dT / P(T) between the temperature bounds.
- Conflation of averages: defining an "average power over temperature" as P_avg = (1/ΔT) ∫ P(T) dT and then using t ≈ C ΔT / P_avg without justification. The correct expression is t = C ∫ dT / P(T); a temperature-averaged power is not the time-weighted average and yields incorrect results unless P(T) is effectively constant.
This rule should trigger if a solution:
- Equates Q or energy to an integral of the form ∫ P(T) dT.
- Uses any expression where the integrator variable attached to P is temperature (dT) rather than time (dt) to derive energy or time.
- Computes time by dividing C ΔT by a temperature-averaged P(T) instead of integrating C/P(T) over the temperature range.

Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.title: Cooling time must be computed via dt = C dT / P(T) using the given P(T) curve
Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.description: This rule verifies solutions to cooling-time problems where the heat-loss power P(T) is provided as a function of temperature (e.g., a plot) and the heat capacitance C is given. The correct energy balance is C dT/dt = -P(T), which leads to t = ∫_{T2}^{T1} [C / P(T)] dT (or an equivalent discrete sum t ≈ Σ [C ΔT / P(T)] using the plotted values). The rule flags solutions that: (a) compute the total heat change Q = C (T1 - T2) but then ignore it in the time calculation or proceed with unrelated plot-based quantities without forming dt = dQ / P(T); (b) treat P as constant or replace the provided P(T) curve with an assumed law (e.g., hA(T − T0)) without explicitly fitting/justifying this from the plot; (c) use t = Q / P evaluated at a single temperature or an arbitrary average P not derived from the integral ∫ [C / P(T)] dT; (d) integrate or sum P(T) over temperature (e.g., ∫ P(T) dT or Σ P ΔT) instead of integrating C/P(T); (e) omit the heat capacitance C in the time expression; or (f) produce a final quantity whose units are not time. The verifier should confirm that the final expression for time explicitly includes both C and the provided P(T) (curve, fitted function, or discrete values) inside an integral or equivalent discretization over T from T1 to T2; otherwise, the solution is flagged.

Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.title: Incorrect integration of power over temperature in cooling/heating problems
Thermodynamics - Heat Transfer and Cooli.description: This rule checks for variable-mismatch errors when integrating in thermal cooling/heating problems with temperature-dependent power P(T) and heat capacity C. Correct relationships are: dQ = C dT, total energy exchanged Q = ∫ P(t) dt, and cooling time t = ∫ [C / P(T)] dT between T1 and T2. The rule flags steps that: (1) set Q = ∫ P(T) dT or otherwise integrate power with respect to temperature to compute energy; (2) derive time t from ∫ P(T) dT or from C ∫ dT without the required division by P(T); (3) start from Q = ∫_0^t C (dT/dt) dt and substitute C(dT/dt) = P(T) to conclude Q = ∫ P(T) dT, ignoring that the integration variable is dt and a proper change of variables (dt = C dT / P(T)) is needed. Such errors obscure that energy depends only on ΔT (Q = C ΔT) while the time depends on ∫ dT / P(T). The rule triggers whenever a solution equates energy to ∫ P(T) dT or computes time without the 1/P(T) factor under a temperature-dependent power model.

Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.title: Validate thermal conductivity dimension and length-exponent contribution
Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.description: This rule checks dimensional-analysis setups that include thermal conductivity k. It verifies that k is assigned its correct SI dimensions: W m^-1 K^-1 = M^1 L^1 T^-3 K^-1. If a solution uses an incorrect length dimension for k (e.g., L^-3) or any non-equivalent dimension, the rule flags an error. Additionally, when forming the linear system for base dimensions to solve exponents (e.g., x ≈ t^α ρ^β c^γ k^δ), the rule verifies the coefficient contributed by k to the length-balance equation is +1·δ, not −3·δ. The rule also cross-checks the other quantities commonly paired with k: ρ must be M^1 L^-3, c must be L^2 T^-2 K^-1, and t must be T. If any of these base-dimension assignments are inconsistent, or if the resulting length equation uses the wrong sign/coefficient for δ due to a mis-specified k, the solution is flagged as a logic/dimensional error likely to propagate wrong exponents.

Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.title: Heat diffusion penetration depth must increase as sqrt(k t / (ρ c))
Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.description: This rule verifies the scaling of a heat penetration/characteristic length x in a homogeneous solid governed by diffusion (Fourier heat equation). It triggers when a solution proposes a dimensional-analysis scaling of the form x ∝ t^α ρ^β c^γ k^δ using time t, density ρ, specific heat capacity c (per unit mass), and thermal conductivity k. The rule enforces the physically correct diffusive scaling: x ∼ sqrt(α_th t) with thermal diffusivity α_th = k/(ρ c). Checks performed: 1) Time monotonicity: α must be positive; flag if α ≤ 0 (e.g., x ∝ t^{-1/2}). 2) Diffusive exponent: when only {t, ρ, c, k} are used, α must equal 1/2; flag if α ≠ 1/2. 3) Material parameter dependence: x must increase with k and decrease with ρ and c; require δ > 0, β < 0, γ < 0; flag if any sign is wrong. 4) Exact exponent consistency with α_th: require δ = 1/2, β = -1/2, γ = -1/2 (equivalently the dimension constraints β + δ = 0, γ + δ = 0, α - δ = 0, and -3β + 2γ + δ = 1); flag on violation. 5) General diffusion form: if the solution introduces a diffusivity-like parameter D with dimension [L^2 T^-1], enforce L ∝ sqrt(D t); flag if the proposed L decreases with t or with D. This rule catches concept errors where the penetration depth is claimed to decrease with time or scales inversely with the diffusivity/material properties.

Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.title: Detect sign-flipped exponents in heat diffusion scaling (x ∝ sqrt(k t / (ρ c)))
Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.description: This rule checks dimensional-analysis solutions for heat conduction problems where the penetration depth/length x is expressed as x ≈ t^α ρ^β c^γ k^δ. It verifies both the assigned base dimensions and the resulting exponent relations. Correct SI base dimensions are: density ρ: M L^-3; specific heat capacity c: L^2 T^-2 Θ^-1; thermal conductivity k: M L T^-3 Θ^-1. Dimensional homogeneity yields the unique scaling x ∝ sqrt(k t / (ρ c)), implying exponents α = 1/2, β = -1/2, γ = -1/2, δ = 1/2 and relations α = δ, β = γ = -δ. Flag an error if any of the following is detected: (a) k is assigned an L exponent other than +1 (e.g., M L^-3 T^-3 Θ^-1), indicating an incorrect dimensional setup; (b) the derived exponents are the exact sign-flipped set (α, β, γ, δ) = (-1/2, 1/2, 1/2, -1/2); or (c) more generally, the solution yields α = -δ and β = γ = δ, i.e., all exponents are the negatives of the physically correct ones, producing x ∝ sqrt(ρ c / (k t)) instead of the correct x ∝ sqrt(k t / (ρ c)).

Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.title: Conduction length scale must reflect dominant thermal resistance in heating of bulk solids
Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.description: This rule checks whether a solution estimating heat inflow J into a solid object (e.g., an egg in boiling water) uses an appropriate conduction length scale for the dominant thermal resistance. Trigger conditions: (a) the solution models heat inflow with Fourier’s law q = k * ΔT / Δx and multiplies by surface area to get J, and (b) the object is bulk-sized (characteristic dimension L_char ≥ 10 mm). The rule flags an error if Δx is taken as a thin shell or wall thickness that is much smaller than the object size (Δx ≤ 0.05 * L_char) without justification that the shell dominates the resistance. Justifications that prevent flagging include: (1) explicit series-resistance modeling showing R_shell >> R_internal (e.g., k_shell/k_core ≤ 0.1 or L_shell comparable to L_char), (2) convective boundary modeling indicating external convection dominates (e.g., using J = h * A * ΔT and demonstrating small Biot number), or (3) a Biot number analysis with Bi = h * L_char / k_core ≤ 0.1 supporting a lumped-capacitance approach. In typical boiling-water heating of an egg, h is large (hundreds to thousands W/m^2K) and Bi >> 0.1, so the dominant resistance is internal conduction over a length scale comparable to the egg radius (≈ 20–30 mm), not the ~0.5 mm eggshell. If the solution uses Δx equal to a thin shell thickness and omits internal conduction or Biot analysis, flag as a modeling error likely to overestimate J by one to two orders of magnitude.

Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.title: Misuse of eggshell conductivity for overall egg heat-flow modeling
Thermodynamics - Thermal Conductivity an.description: Verify that the thermal conductivity k used to estimate heat flow into an egg corresponds to the dominant heat-transfer path through the egg interior (water/protein, k ≈ 0.5–0.7 W/m·K). Flag a solution if: (1) k > 1.0 W/m·K is used while applying Fourier’s law across a bulk length scale (Δx comparable to the egg radius, i.e., mm–cm), and the shell is not modeled explicitly as a thin layer with its thickness; or (2) the chosen material for k is named as eggshell/calcium carbonate/ceramic (typical k ≈ 1.6–2.0 W/m·K) while the geometry and Δx correspond to the egg interior; or (3) no series thermal-resistance model (shell thickness ~0.3–0.5 mm + interior radius ~20–25 mm) and/or external convection is included. To pass, either use interior k in the 0.5–0.7 W/m·K range for bulk conduction into the egg or explicitly include the eggshell as a thin high-k layer in series with the interior (and convection if applicable). This rule targets modeling errors where the thin, higher-conductivity shell is incorrectly treated as controlling the overall heat transfer, inflating J.

Thermodynamics - Calorimetry and Phase C.title: Distinct specific heats for different materials unless explicitly stated
Thermodynamics - Calorimetry and Phase C.description: Check calorimetry/thermal-equilibrium solutions to ensure that each physically distinct material is assigned its own specific heat capacity unless the problem explicitly states they are identical. The verifier will: (1) parse the problem text to detect distinct bodies/materials (e.g., a liquid vs. an added solid, phases with different melting points, or different substances) and any explicit statements asserting equal specific heats; (2) inspect heat-balance terms of the form m * c * ΔT in the solution and verify that the liquid and any added solid(s) use different symbols/parameters for specific heat (e.g., C_liquid vs c_solid), rather than reusing the liquid’s C for the solid by default; (3) flag a modeling error if the same specific heat symbol is applied to different materials without justification, or if the solid’s sensible heat term is written with the liquid’s specific heat; (4) in problems involving phase change at the liquid’s freezing/melting point, also verify that latent heat terms (m_f * L) are included separately from sensible heat and that the solid’s specific heat only appears in terms for its temperature change. Example trigger: an energy balance such as m C (Th − T0) + m_f L = 2 m C (T0 − Tl) where C is used for both the liquid and a different solid without an explicit statement that their specific heats are equal. The solution passes if it introduces and consistently uses a distinct symbol (e.g., c_s) for the solid’s specific heat or if the prompt explicitly states the specific heats are the same.

Thermodynamics - Calorimetry and Phase C.title: Sign consistency when isolating latent heat from a linear energy balance
Thermodynamics - Calorimetry and Phase C.description: This rule checks for sign errors when a student solves for the latent heat (L) from a calorimetry/phase-change energy balance of the form: m_l C_l (T_h - T_0) + m_f L = m_s C_s (T_0 - T_l), where T_h > T_0 > T_l and all masses/specific heats are positive. Implementation details: (1) Identify a step where the student isolates L from a linear equation with one L-term and temperature differences. Accept algebraic variants with common factors canceled (e.g., divide by m), or with C_l = C_s = C (student using a single specific heat). (2) Compute the canonical correct isolation: L_correct = [m_s C_s (T_0 - T_l) - m_l C_l (T_h - T_0)] / m_f. (3) Normalize both sides by any common positive factors (e.g., m, C, numeric fractions) to compare forms. (4) If the student's expression equals the negation of L_correct—i.e., L_student = [m_l C_l (T_h - T_0) - m_s C_s (T_0 - T_l)] / m_f—flag a "sign inversion in isolating L" error. (5) Additionally enforce a physical sign check: under T_h > T_0 > T_l with positive masses and specific heats, L must be positive. Evaluate the student's expression under these inequalities; if it predicts L < 0 or its temperature-linear bracket has the opposite sign to the correct bracket, flag the result as physically inconsistent. Example pattern match (with C_l = C_s = C, m_f = m/6, m_l = m, m_s = 2m): correct L = 6 C (3 T_0 - T_h - 2 T_l); if the student gives L = 6 C (T_h - 3 T_0 + 2 T_l), trigger this rule. The rule is tolerant to equivalent algebraic rearrangements and triggers only when a global sign flip is detected or when the implied sign violates the stated temperature ordering.

Thermodynamics - Calorimetry and Phase C.title: Calorimetry with phase change: correct heat-capacity attribution and elimination of cold-body variables
Thermodynamics - Calorimetry and Phase C.description: This rule checks calorimetry solutions involving a liquid (mass m, specific heat C) initially at Th, a colder solid added at Tl, and equilibrium at the liquid’s freezing point T0 with some mass of the liquid freezing. In such problems, especially when two successive, identical cold bodies are added and both equilibria occur at T0 with specified frozen masses, the correct energy balances are: (i) first insertion: m*C*(Th − T0) + L*(mass_frozen_1) = (mass_solid)*c_s*(T0 − Tl); (ii) second insertion: L*(mass_frozen_2) = (mass_solid)*c_s*(T0 − Tl). For the specific case where mass_solid = 2m, mass_frozen_1 = m/6, and mass_frozen_2 = m/2, combining the two equations must eliminate Tl and the solid’s specific heat c_s, yielding L = 3*C*(Th − T0). The verifier will flag the following errors: (1) Misattribution of heat capacity—if the heat absorbed by the solid is written with the liquid’s specific heat C (e.g., 2m*C*(T0 − Tl)) instead of a distinct solid specific heat c_s. (2) Incorrect dependence—if the final expression for the latent heat L depends on Tl or c_s after using both scenarios (e.g., L proportional to (T0 − Tl) or L = 4*C*(T0 − Tl)).
