It targets errors where the reported mass does not equal n × μ after proper unit handling, or where a factor-of-1000 mistake occurs between kg and g.

Checks performed:
- Identify any stated amount of substance n (units: mol) and molar mass μ (units: kg/mol or g/mol) for the same substance, and a reported mass m with units (kg or g).
- Normalize units: if μ is given in g/mol, convert to kg/mol using 1 g/mol = 1×10^-3 kg/mol; if m is in g, convert to kg for comparison.
- Compute m_expected = n × μ (in kg). Compare m_expected to the student-reported mass (converted to kg). If the relative deviation |m_reported − m_expected| / max(m_expected, ε) > 0.05 (ε = 1×10^-12 kg to avoid division by zero), flag an inconsistency.
- If the solution explicitly states an equality like “X kg = Y g”, verify Y ≈ 1000 × X within 1% tolerance. If not, flag a unit conversion error.
- Heuristic factor check: if the ratio m_reported / m_expected is approximately 10^3 or 10^-3 (within ±10%), add a note indicating a probable kg↔g or g/mol↔kg/mol mix-up.

Example caught: n = 2.89×10^-5 mol and μ = 18×10^-3 kg/mol imply m_expected ≈ 5.2×10^-7 kg. A reported m = 5.2×10^-4 kg (0.52 g) fails the consistency check by a factor of 1000 and is flagged.

Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Behavior.title: Misclassification of molar/specific heat capacity as extensive
Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Behavior.description: This rule checks for conceptual errors that conflate intensive and extensive properties in thermodynamics, specifically for heat capacities. It flags solutions that: (1) explicitly state or imply that molar or specific heat capacity (e.g., C_{V,m}, C_{P,m}, c per mole or per mass) is an extensive property, or that it depends on the number of moles/amount of substance; (2) apply additivity of extensive properties directly to per-mole/per-mass quantities (e.g., writing C_{V,m,mix} = C_{V,m,A} + C_{V,m,B} or C_{V,m,mix} = n1*C1 + n2*C2 without normalizing by total moles); (3) label per-mole/per-mass heat capacities as “total” or otherwise suggest scaling with system size. Acceptable and encouraged relationships are C_V (total) = n * C_{V,m} and the mixture molar heat capacity C_{V,m,mix} = (n1*C1 + n2*C2)/(n1 + n2). The rule should flag a conceptual inconsistency even if subsequent algebra uses the correct relationships, whenever text claims that molar/specific heat capacity is extensive.

Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Behavior.title: Isothermal leg in ideal gas enforces equal endpoint temperature and zero ΔU on any connecting path
Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Behavior.description: This rule verifies consistency when a solution involves an ideal gas and specifies that one leg between two labeled states (e.g., B→A) is isothermal. For an ideal gas, an isothermal leg implies the endpoints lie on the same isotherm: T_A = T_B and P_A V_A = P_B V_B. Because internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, the internal energy change between those endpoints is zero for any path connecting them: ΔU_AB = v C_V (T_B − T_A) = 0. Consequently, for the non-isothermal path connecting the same endpoints (e.g., A→B), the first law must reduce to Q_AB = W_AB. The rule flags an error if the solution: (a) retains or computes a nonzero ΔU_AB term (e.g., uses v C_V ΔT_AB with ΔT_AB ≠ 0) despite an isothermal leg connecting the same endpoints; (b) fails to assert T_A = T_B or the equivalent ideal-gas constraint P_A V_A = P_B V_B for the endpoints; or (c) concludes Q_AB ≠ W_AB for the path between the same endpoints. Acceptable solutions may compute W_AB via integration along the straight line, but must set ΔT_AB = 0 and thus ΔU_AB = 0, yielding Q_AB = W_AB.

Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Behavior.title: Missing use of PV-diagram quantitative ratios and isothermal endpoint relation
Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Behavior.description: Checks solutions to PV-cycle problems that specify a straight-line segment AB and an isothermal segment BA for proper use of diagram-provided quantitative information and constraints. The rule activates when the problem references a PV diagram with labeled baseline quantities (e.g., P0, V0) or explicit ratios (e.g., halves/doubles), and states that BA is isothermal. It flags solutions that: (1) do not use the isothermal endpoint relation P_A V_A = P_B V_B to infer T_A = T_B and ΔU_AB = 0, thereby Q_AB = W_AB; (2) compute W_AB only as a generic integral or slope form without simplifying to the trapezoid area ((P_A + P_B)/2)(V_B − V_A); (3) fail to reduce W_AB (and Q_AB) to a numeric multiple of P0 V0 when the diagram provides ratios (e.g., P_A = P0, V_A = V0/2; P_B = P0/2, V_B = V0 → W_AB = (3/8) P0 V0); (4) omit the logarithmic form for isothermal work W_BA = nRT ln(V_A/V_B) = P_B V_B ln(V_A/V_B), or fail to simplify it using diagram ratios (e.g., W_BA = −(ln 2)/2 P0 V0); (5) present net cycle work W_net without combining these simplified pieces or claim the expressions cannot be simplified despite the diagram providing such ratios. The rule does not trigger if the diagram lacks quantitative labels/ratios.

Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.title: Cooling time with temperature-dependent power must integrate C/P(T) over temperature
Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.description: For transient cooling problems where the heat exchange power depends on temperature, the governing relation is C·dT/dt = −P(T). The cooling time from T1 to T2 must be computed as t = ∫_{T2}^{T1} [C / P(T)] dT (or by an equivalent solution of the ODE). This rule flags solutions that: (1) compute time using an integral of P(T) with respect to temperature, e.g., t ∝ ∫ P(T) dT; (2) compute total heat loss Q as ∫ P(T) dT over temperature (instead of over time), or use Q = ∫ P(T) dT to infer t; (3) omit or misuse the ODE linking temperature to time (dT/dt = −P(T)/C); (4) violate dimensional consistency, e.g., treating ∫ P dT (units J·K/s) as energy or time. Acceptable alternatives include deriving t via Newton’s law of cooling when P(T) = hA(T − T0), yielding t = τ·ln((T1 − T0)/(T2 − T0)) with τ = C/(hA), or numerically integrating t = ∫ C/P(T) dT from T1 to T2 using the provided P(T) data. The rule triggers whenever the integrand for time is proportional to P(T) rather than 1/P(T), or energy is obtained by integrating power over temperature.

Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.title: Misinterpreting ∫P(T) dT (power vs temperature) as energy
Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.description: This rule detects dimensional-analysis mistakes where the integral of power P with respect to temperature (or any non-time variable) is treated as energy or heat. It scans solution steps for: (a) statements like 'area under the P–T curve' or '∫ P(T) dT' being labeled as Q (heat) or energy in Joules, (b) equating or comparing ∫ P(T) dT to internal energy change (e.g., C ΔT) or to values with units J, and (c) using ∫ P(T) dT to compute cooling time. The rule checks unit consistency: power P has units W = J/s; integrating over temperature yields W·K, not J. Energy from power requires ∫ P dt. For thermal cooling with heat capacity C and power P(T), the correct governing relation is C dT/dt = −P(T), giving t = ∫ (C / P(T)) dT from T1 to T2. Trigger conditions: - Any integral ∫ P(⋅) dX where X ≠ time (e.g., temperature T) is asserted to have units Joules, is called 'heat' or 'energy', or is set equal to C ΔT or ΔU. - A step computing time using ∫ P dT or using average P multiplied by ΔT. - Units of a computed 'area under P–T' or '∫ P dT' reported as J instead of W·K. When triggered, flag the step and suggest replacing energy calculations with ∫ P dt or using the differential equation C dT/dt = −P(T) to integrate t = ∫ (C / P(T)) dT.

Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.title: Require use of provided P(T) curve for cooling-time integration
Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.description: This rule verifies that when a problem explicitly provides a plot or table of the heat exchange rate P as a function of temperature T (e.g., P(T) curve), the solution computes the cooling time using that given dependence rather than introducing an unsupported model or fabricated data. The check triggers a violation if any of the following are detected: (a) the solution defines P(T) via an assumed law such as P(T) = h·A·(T − T0), references a 'heat transfer coefficient h', 'surface area A', or other parameters not supplied or derived from the provided plot/table; (b) the solution states it will use or has used 'discrete data points from the plot' without listing the actual read-off values or showing how they correspond to the provided curve, or uses values that cannot be traced to the plot/table; (c) the solution replaces the curve with a constant or average P or a linearized P(T) without demonstrating that the parameters were extracted from the given plot (e.g., by reading a slope/intercepts). For cooling problems, the expected method is t = ∫[T2→T1] C dT / P(T) (or an equivalent discrete sum) with P(T) taken from the provided curve/table. The rule passes if the solution either: (1) explicitly reads P(T) values from the plot/table and performs an integral or sum using those values; or (2) fits a functional form to the provided curve and shows how the fit parameters were obtained from the graph. Any introduction of invented P(T) data or auxiliary parameters not supported by the provided plot/table results in a modeling error.

Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.title: Cooling time must be computed as ∫[C(T)/P(T)] dT, not ΔQ divided by average P
Cooling Time and Temperature-Dependent P.description: This rule verifies time calculations in thermal cooling/heating problems where the heat exchange power P depends on temperature T (e.g., P(T) is provided as a function or plot). The physically correct elapsed time to change temperature from T1 to T2 is t = ∫_{T2}^{T1} C(T)/P(T) dT (for constant heat capacity, t = C ∫ dT / P(T)). The rule flags solutions that instead estimate time as energy change divided by an averaged or single-value power, such as t = ΔQ / ⟨P⟩ or t = C (T1 − T2) / P_avg, where P_avg is an arithmetic mean of endpoint powers, a midpoint power, or any representative value of P(T) over the interval, without performing or approximating the integral of 1/P(T). Detection heuristics: (a) The solution forms ΔQ = C (T1 − T2) and then computes t = ΔQ / P_avg; (b) P_avg is defined as [P(T1)+P(T2)]/2, P(T_mid), or similar; (c) No integral or discrete sum of the form Σ [C(T_k) ΔT_k / P(T_k)] is present; (d) The P(T) plot/function is only used to read endpoint values. Exceptions: Approximations are acceptable only if the solution explicitly justifies that P(T) is effectively constant over the interval (e.g., demonstrates <~10% variation across [T2, T1]) or performs a proper numerical integration using reciprocal weighting (piecewise sum of C ΔT / P(T)). If these conditions are not met, the rule flags a logic error: using average power instead of integrating 1/P(T), which biases the time estimate when P varies strongly with T.

General Physics Misinterpretations.title: Incorrect inequality assertion between computed quantities
General Physics Misinterpretations.description: This rule checks for logical consistency in stated inequalities (e.g., greater/less than) between computed numeric quantities in a solution. It parses claims such as "A is less than B", "A < B", "greater than", "smaller/larger", and similar phrases, retrieves or evaluates the corresponding numeric values (including units where applicable), and verifies that the claimed inequality matches the actual numerical comparison. If units are present, it converts both quantities to compatible units before comparing. If the claim contradicts the evaluated relation (for example, stating 266000 < 7000 when 266000 > 7000), the rule flags an error. The rule also guards against sign/magnitude confusion: if the text explicitly refers to magnitude/absolute value, it compares |A| and |B|; otherwise, it compares signed values. A tolerance may be applied for near-equality claims; otherwise, clear contradictions are reported.

General Physics Misinterpretations.title: Nonlinear polyatomic Cv miscount (e.g., H2O treated as 5/2 R instead of 3 R)
General Physics Misinterpretations.description:
Checks that constant-volume molar heat capacity assignments for nonlinear polyatomic ideal gases at near-room temperature correctly include three rotational degrees of freedom when vibrational modes are neglected. Specifically: 
- Scope: Ideal-gas Cv at approximately 200–500 K ("room temperature" context). 
- Expected physics: For translational + rotational contributions with vibrations neglected: 
  - Monatomic: Cv = (3/2) R. 
  - Linear molecules (e.g., diatomic, linear triatomic): Cv = (5/2) R. 
  - Nonlinear polyatomic molecules (e.g., H2O, NH3, CH4, SO2, O3, H2S): Cv = 3 R. 
- Rule: If a solution assigns Cv = (5/2) R (or numerically ~20.8 J/mol·K) to a known nonlinear polyatomic species (e.g., H2O) under the above temperature regime without explicitly adding vibrational contributions, flag as a rotational degree-of-freedom miscount. 
- Mixtures: For mixtures, verify that the component Cv values used in the mole-fraction (or mole-number) weighted average are physically consistent with the above classification. If any nonlinear polyatomic component is given Cv = (5/2) R instead of ~3 R, flag. 
- Tolerance: Accept Cv within ±0.1 R of the expected value when expressed in units of R, or within ±0.8 J/mol·K when expressed in SI units. 
- Exceptions: Do not flag if the solution clearly accounts for vibrational contributions and justifies a different Cv (e.g., via temperature-dependent heat capacity correlations) or explicitly states and uses a data-sourced Cv close to 3 R for H2O at the stated temperature. 
- Example catch: H2O assigned Cv = (5/2) R at room temperature is incorrect; expected Cv ≈ 3 R. The rule will flag this and any downstream mixture Cv that relies on the incorrect per-species value.

Phase Change and Calorimetry.title: Steam generation enthalpy must include sensible heating and latent heat
Phase Change and Calorimetry.description: When verifying solutions that compute the mass of steam produced from liquid water using an energy balance (e.g., mass flow = input power divided by energy per kg), ensure the per‑kilogram enthalpy change includes all required terms based on the initial liquid temperature Ti, the boiling temperature Tboil at the working pressure, and the final steam temperature Tout. Specifically: (1) If Ti < Tboil, the solution must include sensible heating of liquid: c_liquid · (Tboil − Ti). (2) The phase change must include latent heat of vaporization: L_vap at the appropriate pressure/boiling temperature. (3) If Tout > Tboil (superheated steam), the solution must include sensible heating of vapor: c_vapor · (Tout − Tboil). Flag a conceptual error if the energy per kg is taken as L_vap only, or if any required sensible heating term is omitted given Ti and Tout. Do not flag if Ti ≈ Tboil (within ~1 K) or Tout ≈ Tboil (within ~1 K), or if the solution uses steam tables/enthalpy data that implicitly account for these changes. This rule targets common mistakes like computing mass rate as P / L_vap when water starts below boiling or the steam exits above boiling, which overestimates production rate.

Phase Change and Calorimetry.title: Absorbed optical power must not be set equal to incident power without losses
Phase Change and Calorimetry.description: This rule checks that a solution distinguishes between incident optical power and absorbed (Joule) power when radiation interacts with a medium or nanoparticles. Detection criteria: (1) The solution computes incident power as P_inc = S × A (or similar from intensity/irradiance and area). (2) The same quantity is then used directly as absorbed power, heat input, or for downstream thermal calculations (e.g., steam generation rate, temperature rise) without any absorption efficiency factor (η_abs < 1), absorption cross-section (C_abs), Beer–Lambert absorption coefficient (α) with path length, or explicit subtraction of scattering/reflection/transmission terms (e.g., P_abs = P_inc − P_scat − P_refl − P_trans). (3) The problem statement mentions or provides any of: fraction absorbed, scattering power P_scat, absorption cross-section/efficiency, reflectivity/transmission, or requires nanoparticle/LCR response. If conditions (1–3) hold and no loss/absorption model is applied, flag an error: "Modeling error: absorbed power improperly set equal to incident power; transmission and scattering/reflective losses must be accounted for via an absorption model (η_abs, C_abs, α, or explicit loss terms)." The rule passes only if the solution computes P_abs using an appropriate absorption model or efficiency and uses P_abs (not P_inc) in subsequent energy/heat calculations.

Phase Change and Calorimetry.title: Unjustified equal partition of incident power among absorbers
Phase Change and Calorimetry.description: Flags solutions that compute per-particle absorbed power by dividing the total incident power by the number of particles (e.g., P_abs_particle = P_incident_total / N_particles) or that set total absorbed power equal to the incident power (implying 100% absorption) without invoking absorption cross-section, absorption efficiency, geometric coverage, or an attenuation model (Beer–Lambert/optical depth). Correct methodology requires using intensity S and an absorption cross-section (and possibly an efficiency factor Q_abs): P_abs_particle = S * sigma_abs * Q_abs (or S times projected area times absorption efficiency); total absorbed power is N_particles * P_abs_particle only when the optical depth is small (tau << 1), otherwise use f_abs = 1 − exp(−tau). If a step distributes incident power evenly across particles or assumes full absorption without referencing sigma_abs/Q_abs/coverage or optical-depth modeling, mark a logic error.

Phase Change and Calorimetry.title: Require use of provided scattering/LCR model to partition incident power into Joule heating vs radiative losses
Phase Change and Calorimetry.description: This rule checks that solutions use the problem's provided scattering/absorption expressions and LCR (resonant) circuit parameters to determine how incident optical power is split between radiative losses and Joule (thermal) heating. Trigger: the problem statement includes any of the following model-specific cues: P_scat or 'scattering power', P_abs or 'absorption', LCR circuit elements (L, C, R), resonance frequency (ω0), damping/decay rate (γ), collision time (τ), Q-factor, or mention of 'radiative losses' vs 'Joule heating'. Violation conditions: (1) The solution computes incident power solely as intensity S times geometric area A (e.g., 'P_tot = S × A') and then directly equates that to heating, steam production, or temperature rise without calculating absorption/scattering via the given model. (2) The solution does not reference or use any of the provided model terms (P_scat, P_abs, σ_abs/σ_scat, L, C, R, τ, γ, Q) when determining the power available for heating at or near resonance. (3) The solution ignores the required partition between radiative and non-radiative channels (e.g., no computation of a heating fraction or branching ratio) and does not enforce energy conservation as P_in × absorption efficiency = P_heat + P_rad. Expected compliance: The solution should derive the absorbed power and the Joule-heating fraction using the provided scattering/absorption expression or LCR parameters (including τ/γ/Q), then compute heating power as P_heat = η_heat × P_abs (or equivalent), before converting to downstream quantities (e.g., steam mass rate). The rule flags solutions that bypass the provided model and assume all incident power contributes to heating.

Phase Change and Calorimetry.title: Incorrectly equating melt/intrusion volume to surface depression volume
Phase Change and Calorimetry.description: This rule flags solutions that assume the volume of a magma/rock intrusion or the volume of melted ice equals the geometric volume of a surface depression (e.g., a cone) without an energy/mass balance. Examples include statements or equations like V_intrusion = V_depression, V_melt = V_depression, or computing melted mass via m_melt = rho_i * V_depression. In temperate ice-cap problems, the depression reflects vertical motion and density contrasts (rho_i ≠ rho_w), not a one-to-one volume match. To pass, the solution must (a) derive melt mass/volume from an energy balance using available heat (Q_in) and material properties (latent heat, specific heat) before relating to geometry, and (b) acknowledge density differences between ice and water when converting mass to volume. The verifier should detect any direct use of the surface-depression volume to infer intrusion or melt volume/mass, or any equality between volumes of distinct physical domains (surface depression vs subsurface intrusion) without justification via energy and mass conservation.

Phase Change and Calorimetry.title: Require density-corrected volume change for phase change (ice ↔ water)
Phase Change and Calorimetry.description: Check that solutions involving melting/freezing (or any phase/material change) do not equate pre- and post-change volumes when densities differ. Specifically enforce mass conservation m = ρ·V across phases: for ice → water, ρ_i V_melt = ρ_w V_water, so V_water = (ρ_i/ρ_w)·V_melt and the volume deficit/void/depression is V_deficit = V_melt − V_water = (1 − ρ_i/ρ_w)·V_melt. Flag as an error if: (1) The solution sets V_water = V_melt (or uses the same geometric volume for both phases) when |ρ_i − ρ_w|/ρ_w > 0.02; (2) A depression/void volume (e.g., cone under an ice cap) is set equal to the melted ice volume rather than (1 − ρ_i/ρ_w)·V_melt; (3) Numerical results effectively assume a unity conversion factor (V_water/V_melt ≈ 1 within 3%) instead of the required ρ_i/ρ_w factor (≈ 0.917 for ice-water); (4) Densities are given in the problem, and volumes are converted between phases without using their ratio. Also check consistency: if mass for latent heat is computed from V_melt via m = ρ_i V_melt, the water volume used later must be m/ρ_w, not V_melt. This rule is generic: for any phase/material change a → b with densities ρ_a, ρ_b, enforce V_b = (ρ_a/ρ_b)·V_a and any volume deficit/excess = (1 − ρ_a/ρ_b)·V_a. Flag and suggest correction to apply the density ratio rather than equating volumes.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Zero-momentum final state assumed with nonzero initial momentum
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: This rule detects kinematic models that violate linear momentum conservation by assuming a final state with zero total momentum (e.g., products "at rest relative to each other" or a "single system at rest") while the initial state has nonzero net momentum. The verifier scans for: (1) an initial beam/target description where only one incoming particle carries momentum (e.g., a beam particle with momentum p_b and a stationary target), yielding nonzero initial total momentum; and (2) a final state described as having zero net momentum without any additional outgoing particles, recoil body, radiation, external field, or other momentum sink. If both conditions are present, the rule flags a modeling error because an isolated system cannot reduce nonzero momentum to zero. The rule also flags inconsistent particle bookkeeping where a named particle is used as the stationary initial target and simultaneously declared as part of a final bound composite at rest without specifying a mechanism that carries away the excess momentum. Exemptions: the rule does not trigger if the initial total momentum is explicitly zero (e.g., equal and opposite beams) or if an external agent or additional products are clearly identified to take the recoil. This rule is particularly applied to threshold/kinematics derivations; a correct setup must use a well-defined multi-particle initial state and conserve total four-momentum in all frames.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Misapplied energy conservation with beam energy and rest final state
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description:
This rule checks for inconsistent use of energy conservation in two-body problems involving a beam particle and a stationary target, especially when the final state is described as two particles at rest relative to each other. It flags the following patterns:
- Initial total energy omits the incoming particle's rest energy when a 'beam energy' Eb is introduced or described as small (typically implying kinetic energy). If Eb is kinetic, the correct initial energy is mp*c^2 + Eb + mΔ*c^2; writing initial energy as Eb + mΔ*c^2 (missing mp*c^2) is flagged.
- Final state is described as proton and Δ at rest (co-moving), but the total final energy is written as Ep + mΔ*c^2 with Ep treated as a free variable. In a rest final state of two separate particles, Ep must equal mp*c^2 and E_final must be mp*c^2 + mΔ*c^2 (or (mp + mΔ)*c^2 if they are bound/merged). Equations of the form Eb + mΔ*c^2 = Ep + mΔ*c^2 without explicitly setting Ep = mp*c^2 are flagged.
- Invariant-mass equality M_initial = M_final is invoked but computed incorrectly: either side expressed as a linear sum like Ep + mΔ*c^2 or rest masses only without using the invariant formula M^2*c^4 = E_total^2 − p_total^2*c^2. This is flagged unless p_total = 0 is explicitly demonstrated for that side and E_total is the sum of rest energies consistent with the stated configuration.
- Contradictory configuration statements, e.g., claiming 'final particles at rest relative to each other' while using a variable Ep for a constituent's energy or implying nonzero final momentum, are flagged.
The rule aims to ensure: (1) consistent inclusion of rest energies in initial totals when Eb is kinetic, (2) correct final energy for rest configurations, and (3) proper use of invariant mass relations rather than ad hoc sums.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Inconsistent relativistic approximations for massive beams
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: Flags solutions that apply contradictory or incorrect approximations in energy–momentum relations for massive particles, especially when the beam energy is stated to be small. The rule triggers under any of the following conditions: (1) The problem involves massive particles (e.g., variables like m_p, m_Δ appear) and the solution’s initial total energy omits the projectile’s rest-energy term (e.g., uses E_initial = E_b + m_Δ c^2 instead of including m_p c^2). (2) The solution claims or implies that m_p c^2 can be neglected compared to a small beam energy E_b, or otherwise treats E_b as dominating over rest energies when E_b is described as “small.” (3) The solution uses the ultrarelativistic/massless momentum relation p ≈ E/c (or |p| = E/c) for a massive particle (e.g., proton) without an explicit and correct justification that E ≫ m c^2; this includes using photon-like kinematics for a massive beam. (4) The solution mixes nonrelativistic energy expansions (E ≈ m c^2 + p^2/(2m)) with ultrarelativistic momentum relations (p ≈ E/c) within the same derivation, which is internally inconsistent. The rule checks text for mentions of small E_b alongside omission of rest-energy terms, presence of p ≈ E/c tied to massive particles, and simultaneous use of nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic approximations. Correct treatments should retain rest energies for massive particles when E_b is small and use the relativistic relation E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m c^2)^2 or invariant methods; this rule does not enforce a specific method but flags the inconsistent approximations.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Small-Eb relativistic kinematics: Ep must scale as 1/Eb and use invariants
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description:
This rule checks solutions that determine a projectile energy Ep in terms of mp, mΔ, and a small beam energy Eb. It enforces proper relativistic 4-vector treatment and correct leading-order scaling with Eb. The rule triggers an error if any of the following are detected: 
- Ep is derived using non-relativistic kinetic-energy partitioning (e.g., reduced-mass methods) instead of invariant 4-momentum relations. Typical red flag: p_b^2 ≈ 2 μ Eb with μ = mp mΔ/(mp + mΔ). 
- The invariant mass is misused or absent. The solution should explicitly or implicitly use s = (p_p + p_b)^2 and E^2 − p^2 = m^2 (c = 1) for each particle, not sums of scalar kinetic energies. 
- The leading-order dependence of Ep on small Eb is linear or non-inverse (Ep ∝ Eb^α with α ≥ 0). In correct two-beam kinematics near threshold, Ep should scale inversely with Eb at leading order, e.g., Ep ≈ (mΔ^2 − mp^2)/(4 Eb) up to geometry/angle factors. 
- Algebraic expansions are performed on mismatched quantities (mixing rest-mass energies and kinetic energies) to obtain p_b^2 and Ep. 
Pass criteria: The derivation references or is consistent with s = (p_p + p_b)^2 and E^2 − p^2 = m^2, avoids reduced-mass kinetic-energy splitting, and yields Ep with leading 1/Eb scaling (coefficient consistent with masses, such as (mΔ^2 − mp^2)/(const × Eb)).

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Illegal zero-final-momentum assumption with single-beam initial state
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: Checks solutions in lab-frame setups with a single incident beam and a stationary target for momentum-conservation violations caused by asserting a zero-total-momentum final state. The rule flags cases where: (1) the initial state is described as one beam particle with nonzero lab momentum (e.g., 'beam', 'E_b', 'p_b', 'target at rest', 'stationary target'), typically with p_initial = p_b != 0; (2) the final state is asserted or used as having zero total momentum in the lab (e.g., 'final system at rest', 'p_final = 0', 'proton and delta at rest relative to each other', 'form a single system at rest'); and (3) no additional momentum-balancing element is introduced (no mention of a second counter-propagating beam/head-on geometry, no additional emitted/recoil particle, no external agent). Also flags the related modeling error of enforcing E_initial = E_final without a consistent momentum balance. Guidance: In single-beam + stationary-target problems, the lab-frame final state generally carries the initial net momentum. At threshold, particles are at rest only in the center-of-mass (CM) frame, not necessarily in the lab. The correct procedure is to use the invariant s = (p1 + p2)^2; for a beam particle 1 on a stationary target 2, s_lab = m1^2 + m2^2 + 2 m2 E_b. At threshold, set s = (sum of final rest masses)^2 and solve for the requested energy (e.g., E_p) before applying small-E_b approximations. The rule triggers on textual/math cues of nonzero p_initial together with p_final = 0 (or equivalent phrasing) absent any counter-beam or extra particle, and suggests using the invariant-mass method instead.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Relativistic rocket derivation: frame consistency and momentum setup
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: Checks derivations of the relativistic rocket equation for incorrect frame choice and momentum conservation setup. The rule flags solutions that: (1) fail to explicitly work in the rocket’s instantaneous rest frame at the moment of expulsion (or an equivalent statement such as 'rocket frame'/'comoving frame'), (2) do not set the initial total momentum to zero in that frame (e.g., write p_initial = γ M_i V or γ_i M_i V1), (3) reuse the same rocket velocity symbol (e.g., V, V1) for both pre- and post-expulsion states within momentum/energy conservation equations, implying the same γ before and after, (4) mix quantities defined in the rocket frame (e.g., exhaust relative speed u) with lab-frame momentum/energy expressions without a Lorentz transformation, and/or (5) omit the correct after-expulsion balance p_rocket_after + p_exhaust = 0 in the rocket frame (equal and opposite momenta). Detection heuristics: search for conservation equations where both 'before' and 'after' sides contain the same rocket velocity symbol; identify patterns like 'p_initial = γ M_i V1' or 'γ_i M_i V1' and simultaneous use of 'u relative to the rocket'; and verify presence of statements such as 'instantaneous rest frame' and 'p_total_before = 0'. If these consistency conditions are not met, mark the setup as a modeling/frame error.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Relativistic velocity addition for exhaust in rocket problems
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: Checks that solutions using special relativity compose the exhaust velocity in the lab/inertial frame via Einstein velocity addition rather than simple linear addition. Scope: relativistic rocket problems where the exhaust speed u is defined in the rocket (proper) frame and the rocket moves at lab-frame speed V (or V1). The correct lab-frame exhaust speed is v_exhaust_lab = (V - u)/(1 - V*u/c^2) for backward exhaust (and (V + u)/(1 + V*u/c^2) for forward emission). The rule flags the following modeling errors: (1) Direct use of V ± u as the exhaust velocity in the lab frame, especially in momentum p = γ m (V ± u) or energy E = γ m c^2 with γ computed from (V ± u). (2) Any γ_exhaust computed as 1/sqrt(1 - (V ± u)^2/c^2) without the 1 ± V u / c^2 denominator from relativistic composition. (3) Conservation equations that treat exhaust and rocket velocities as if they are measured in the same frame but relate them with simple addition/difference. The rule passes when the solution explicitly applies the relativistic addition formula to transform u (rocket frame) to the lab frame before computing γ and using momentum/energy; it may also pass if the solution clearly and consistently states a nonrelativistic limit (|V|/c << 1 and |u|/c << 1) and confines the use of V ± u to that stated approximation. Otherwise, any appearance of V1 + u, V + u, or V - u as a lab-frame exhaust speed without the Einstein addition denominator should be flagged.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Frame-consistent γ usage in relativistic rocket energy conservation
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: This rule flags derivations of the relativistic rocket equation that apply energy conservation with a single, shared Lorentz factor γ for multiple bodies/states, or that fail to specify and consistently use an inertial frame (typically the rocket’s instantaneous rest frame) when balancing energy. The rule checks for any energy balance written in the form γ M_i c^2 = γ M c^2 + γ Δm c^2 (or with a single γ symbol on both sides without subscripts or frame labels), or equivalent statements implying the same γ for the initial rocket, the final rocket, and the exhaust. It also flags omission of the condition γ_i = 1 for the rocket at the instant of expulsion in its rest frame, and omission of a distinct exhaust Lorentz factor γ_e associated with the exhaust’s speed relative to the rocket. The rule requires one of the following to pass: (a) conservation formulated via four-momentum in a single frame; or (b) explicit use of the instantaneous rocket rest frame with energy balance M_i c^2 = M c^2 + γ_e Δm c^2 and momentum balance consistent with the exhaust velocity relative to the rocket. It further checks that the derivation recognizes that the exhaust kinetic energy comes from the rocket’s rest-mass decrease (e.g., ΔE_exhaust = (γ_e − 1) Δm c^2 and ΔM c^2 supplies this energy). Solutions that use lab-frame γ’s without corresponding momentum terms or frame transformations, or that conflate γ’s across different bodies/states, are flagged.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Exhaust momentum sign and relativistic velocity addition consistency
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: Checks momentum-balance sign conventions and exhaust velocity composition in rocket/exhaust models. Trigger conditions: (1) In any momentum conservation statement for a rocket expelling mass (recoil/propulsion), the exhaust momentum must appear with the opposite sign to the rocket’s forward momentum when the forward direction is taken as positive. Equivalently, in the instantaneous rocket rest frame before expulsion, the post-event momenta must satisfy p_rocket + p_exhaust = 0, implying p_exhaust < 0 if p_rocket > 0. Flag solutions that sum p_rocket and p_exhaust with the same sign (e.g., p_total = p_rocket + p_exhaust with both positive in the rocket’s direction). (2) For relativistic kinematics, the exhaust velocity in the lab/inertial frame must be obtained via velocity addition with a minus sign for backward exhaust: v_exhaust = (V - u) / (1 - V u / c^2), where V is the rocket velocity in the lab frame and u is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket (u > 0 defined backward). Flag use of plus-sign composition (e.g., v_exhaust = (V + u) / (1 + V u / c^2) or the Newtonian v_exhaust = V + u) unless the coordinate/sign conventions are explicitly reversed and consistently applied. (3) Detect explicit exhaust momentum modeled as p_exhaust = γ_exhaust m_exhaust v_exhaust with v_exhaust having the same sign as V, or written as γ Δm (V + u), and then added to p_rocket in the conservation equation. This rule applies in both relativistic and Newtonian limits: in the Newtonian case v_exhaust should be V - u, not V + u. The rule passes if the solution clearly assigns a negative sign or opposite direction to exhaust quantities consistent with the chosen axis and demonstrates correct velocity addition; otherwise it fails.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Require velocity-based justification for Lorentz factor approximations
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description:
This rule flags solutions in special-relativistic, variable-mass problems (e.g., rocket/exhaust derivations using conservation of energy/momentum) that approximate Lorentz factors (γ) without explicit velocity-based justification. Specifically:
- If the solution sets the exhaust’s Lorentz factor to γ_exhaust ≈ 1 (or treats the exhaust nonrelativistically) without explicitly demonstrating u/c ≪ 1 and quantifying the resulting error (e.g., γ − 1 ≈ ½β^2), flag.
- If the solution sets the rocket’s post-ejection Lorentz factor equal to its pre-ejection value (γ_after ≈ γ_before or γ ≈ γ_i) solely because Δm is small, an infinitesimal mass is expelled, or similar mass-based reasoning, flag. γ depends on velocity, not mass; an infinitesimal mass change does not justify neglecting Δv or Δγ.
- If approximations to γ lead to degenerate conservation statements (e.g., the momentum/energy equations collapse to a trivial or contradictory equality such as 0 = Δm·u/V1), flag as likely caused by unjustified γ approximations.
Accepted justification criteria:
- The solution must state and use a velocity bound (e.g., |u|/c ≤ ε ≪ 1 or |Δv|/c ≤ ε) and demonstrate that the neglected γ-terms are of higher order than the required accuracy (e.g., O(β^2) or O(Δγ/γ)).
- Equating γ values at different stages is acceptable only if equal velocities are explicitly shown or if a quantified small Δv makes |Δγ/γ| negligible relative to the solution’s precision.
Example violations to flag:
- “γ_Δm ≈ 1 because Δm is small.”
- “Take γ ≈ γ_i; the mass change is infinitesimal.”
- “Neglect change in γ” without bounding β or Δv.
Rationale: Lorentz factors depend on velocity, not mass. Exhaust speeds and rocket speed changes can be relativistic; mass smallness alone cannot justify γ ≈ 1 or γ equality.

Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.title: Missing derivation: jump to known final formula in SR-based rocket problems
Relativistic Kinematics and Momentum.description: Trigger when the problem statement explicitly requests a derivation (keywords: 'derive', 'show that', 'prove', 'obtain') using special relativity or specified conservation laws (e.g., 'using conservation of energy and momentum in special relativity'), but the submitted solution skips the derivation and asserts a known final result. The rule checks that the solution includes: (1) explicit setup of the relativistic conservation laws (at minimum, one momentum equation and one energy equation written with relativistic factors, e.g., p = gamma m v and E = gamma m c^2, or a 4-momentum statement), (2) intermediate algebra/differential steps connecting those equations to the target relationship (e.g., elimination of exhaust terms, relation between dm and dv, integration from Mi to M), and (3) a logically continuous sequence from setup to final expression. Flag an error if the solution presents the final relativistic rocket equation (e.g., forms involving tanh or ln(Mi/M)) or any target formula after phrases such as 'we know', 'it is known that', 'the relativistic rocket equation is', 'after some algebra/simplification', 'thus/therefore' without showing intermediate equations and manipulations. Tolerate concise derivations only if at least two nontrivial intermediate mathematical steps are shown and the conservation equations are explicitly stated. This rule is intended to catch unjustified logical jumps where a derivation is required, especially in SR rocket problems.

Energy Conservation and Approximations.title: Require x^2 terms or justified small-parameter approximation in KE ratio (v±u)^2
Energy Conservation and Approximations.description:
This rule checks solutions that compare kinetic energies (or speeds squared) in a frame where the velocity changes sign relative to a background motion (e.g., satellite moving with vs against Earth's rotation). The correct kinetic-energy ratio in the ground frame, when speeds differ by v+u and v−u, is ((v+u)^2)/( (v−u)^2 ). In normalized form with x = u/v, the exact ratio is (1 + 2x + x^2)/(1 − 2x + x^2). The verifier looks for the following:

- Pattern detection: The solution forms a ratio derived from (v+u)^2 and (v−u)^2 (or their equivalents). The expected exact expression includes the x^2 terms (u^2 and v^2 cross terms) in both numerator and denominator.
- Approximation audit: If the presented ratio omits the x^2 terms (common incorrect forms include (1 + 2x)/(1 − 2x) or linearized results like 1 + 4x), the solution must explicitly justify a small-parameter approximation by: (a) stating that |x| = |u|/|v| is small and providing a numerical estimate, and (b) quantifying the error or stating an error bound (e.g., neglected terms are O(x^2), with a bound on the relative error ≤ c·x^2 for some c). Default acceptance threshold: if |x| ≤ 0.1 and the implied relative error from dropping x^2 terms is ≤ 1% and the justification is explicit, the approximation is accepted; otherwise the solution is flagged.
- Numerical consistency: If numeric values are present, the verifier computes x = |u|/|v| and compares the reported ratio to the exact (1 + 2x + x^2)/(1 − 2x + x^2). If the relative deviation exceeds 0.5% and no explicit approximation rationale is provided, flag the result as an unjustified or inaccurate approximation.
- Instruction sensitivity: If the problem prompt asks for an exact multiplicative comparison (e.g., "how many times" without asking to approximate), using a linearized ratio is flagged unless the exact form is also given.

This rule catches errors where the u^2 term is improperly neglected when expanding (v±u)^2 in energy or speed-squared comparisons, leading to slightly incorrect ratios, and enforces explicit, quantified justification whenever small-parameter approximations are used.

Energy Conservation and Approximations.title: Misusing energy conservation and point-mass kinetic energy in distributed systems
Energy Conservation and Approximations.description: Flag solutions that compute the kinetic energy of an extended body (rod/string/beam/membrane) using a lumped point-mass formula or infer it solely from energy conservation without a velocity field. Detection criteria: (1) The problem context indicates a distributed system with spatial dependence (e.g., variables u(x,t), ε(x,t), ∂u/∂x, “rod”, “string”, “beam”, “membrane”, longitudinal/transverse modes). (2) The solution writes T = 1/2 m v^2 with v taken as a single scalar such as ∂u/∂t, ė (strain rate), ė L, or similar, and does not include a spatial integral over mass density/cross-section, e.g., no form like T = ∫(1/2) ρ|u_t|^2 dV (or for a 1D rod, T = ∫_0^L (1/2) ρA (∂u/∂t)^2 dx). (3) The solution uses energy conservation in differential form (d(T+U)/dt = 0, or dU/dt = − dT/dt) to directly infer an explicit expression for T or v(t) without first determining the spatially varying velocity field u_t(x,t) or the mode shape; i.e., energy conservation is used to replace the spatial integral with a lumped expression. (4) The solution omits justification of rigid-body motion or uniform velocity field; any reduction to T = 1/2 m v^2 is only valid if the velocity is uniform over the body and this is explicitly established. Trigger phrases/patterns to match in distributed-system contexts: “dU/dt = − dT/dt” used to solve for T or v, “from energy conservation we get T = …”, “T = 1/2 m (∂u/∂t)^2”, “T = 1/2 m ė^2 …”, absence of ∫ over x or volume when computing T. Rationale: Energy conservation constrains T+U, but does not determine the instantaneous kinetic energy of an extended body without the velocity distribution; using a point-mass kinetic energy for a nonuniform velocity field is incorrect.

Energy Conservation and Approximations.title: Misuse of coordinate time derivative and strain–velocity mixing
Energy Conservation and Approximations.description: This rule flags conceptual kinematic errors in 1D continuum (rod/string) solutions where spatial/material coordinates are treated as time-dependent variables or where strain and velocity are incorrectly combined. Specifically, it checks for any of the following patterns: (1) Use of dx/dt, ∂x/∂t, or ẋ when x (or X) is introduced as a spatial/material coordinate; in a Lagrangian description X is a fixed label (dX/dt = 0), and in an Eulerian description x is an independent spatial variable that is not differentiated with respect to time. (2) Relations that express velocity or time derivative of displacement as a product of strain and a coordinate time derivative, e.g., v = ε dx/dt, ∂u/∂t = ε ∂x/∂t, or similar forms. (3) Expressions that define strain rate as a product involving ε and dx/dt (e.g., ε̇ ≈ ε ∂x/∂t) instead of the kinematic identity ε̇ = ∂v/∂x. The correct kinematic identities to be upheld are: velocity v(x,t) = ∂u/∂t; small (axial) strain ε(x,t) = ∂u/∂x (or ∂u/∂X in Lagrangian form); and strain rate ε̇(x,t) = ∂v/∂x. The rule raises an error when a solution multiplies strain by a time derivative of a coordinate or treats a coordinate’s time derivative as a physical velocity, indicating a misunderstanding of the continuum kinematics.

Energy Conservation and Approximations.title: Misuse of rest-start kinematics with nonzero initial velocity
Energy Conservation and Approximations.description:
Checks for the incorrect use of free-fall-from-rest formulas in segments where the motion starts with a nonzero initial velocity. The verifier inspects constant-acceleration phases (e.g., after an elastic bounce) and flags if the solution: 
- Explicitly computes or states a nonzero initial speed at the start of a segment (e.g., v0 = sqrt(2 g H) after a bounce), AND subsequently uses rest-start kinematic relations such as s = (1/2) a t^2, t = sqrt(2 s / a), or v = a t for that same segment, omitting the v0 term. 
- For upward motion under gravity after a bounce, uses t = sqrt(2 h / g) to reach height h instead of solving h = v0 t - (1/2) g t^2 (or y(t) = y0 + v0 t + (1/2) a t^2 with a = -g). 
- Computes times or positions as if v0 = 0 despite prior statements or derivations indicating v0 ≠ 0 (e.g., after collision or launch). 
The rule flags these as modeling errors and suggests using the full kinematic equations with the initial velocity term for the relevant segment.

Energy Conservation and Approximations.title: Incorrect relative acceleration in an upward-accelerating elevator (using g − a instead of g + a)
Energy Conservation and Approximations.description:
This rule checks for a common modeling error when analyzing a free object inside an elevator accelerating upward. In the elevator's non-inertial frame, the apparent (effective) downward acceleration on a free object is g + a_frame, not g − a_frame. Equivalently, in an inertial frame the relative acceleration is a_object − a_frame = (−g) − (+a_frame) = −(g + a_frame), so its magnitude must be g + a_frame.

The rule flags a solution if any of the following are detected when the elevator/platform is stated to accelerate upward:
- The "relative" or "effective" acceleration of the object (nut) is modeled as g − a_frame using positive magnitudes (e.g., 9.81 − 1.22 ≈ 8.59 m/s^2), resulting in a magnitude smaller than g. For an upward-accelerating frame, the correct magnitude is g + a_frame (e.g., 9.81 + 1.22 ≈ 11.03 m/s^2).
- The fall time inside the elevator is computed using a_rel = g − a_frame (or a value near 8.59 m/s^2 for g ≈ 9.81 and a_frame ≈ 1.22), such as t ≈ sqrt(2H / 8.59) for H = ceiling-to-floor distance, instead of t ≈ sqrt(2H / 11.03).
- In an inertial-frame approach, the relative acceleration is formed as a_object − a_frame but with signs assigned so that the magnitudes subtract (−g + a_frame) for an upward frame, leading to |a_rel| < g.

Implementation notes:
- Detect context cues: elevator/platform ascending; object released/detaches; analysis "relative to the elevator" or "effective acceleration" in the elevator frame.
- Extract numeric g (~9.8–9.81 m/s^2) and a_frame; if the computed |a_rel| < g while a_frame is upward, flag the step.
- Numeric tolerance: treat g = 9.8 as acceptable; use a ±2% tolerance when matching values like 8.59 vs 11.03.
- Do not trigger if the elevator accelerates downward; in that case |a_rel| = |g − |a_frame|| may be smaller than g, which can be correct when directions align downward.

Purpose: Catch underestimation of the nut’s relative acceleration (and thereby overestimated fall time) that arises from subtracting the elevator’s upward acceleration from g instead of adding it.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Relativistic gyroperiod/gyrofrequency in uniform B must be independent of β and pitch angle
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description:
This rule verifies the correct modeling of a charged particle’s gyrofrequency/gyroperiod in a uniform magnetic field, especially in relativistic contexts (synchrotron motion). It enforces that: 
- In the relativistic regime (explicit statements like γ ≫ 1, relativistic electron, synchrotron), the angular gyrofrequency and period must be ω_g = |q| B/(γ m) and T_g = 2π γ m/(|q| B). 
- There must be no dependence on speed (β = v/c), perpendicular speed v⊥, or pitch angle φ in ω_g or T_g. Pitch angle affects gyroradius r_L = γ m v⊥/(|q| B) = γ m β c sinφ/(|q| B), not ω_g or T_g. 
- Flag as errors any expressions for gyrofrequency/period that include β, v⊥, or sinφ (e.g., T_g ∝ γ β sinφ/(qB), ω_g ∝ qB/(m γ β sinφ), or any factor of sinφ in ω_g/T_g). 
- In a relativistic context, flag the omission of γ (e.g., using nonrelativistic ω_g0 = |q| B/m or T_g0 = 2π m/(|q| B) while asserting γ ≫ 1). 
- Dimensional sanity check: ω_g must depend only on q, B, m, and possibly γ; T_g must depend only on q, B, m, and γ. If velocity-dependent factors appear in ω_g/T_g, flag the modeling error. 
- Applicable synonyms to scan: gyrofrequency, cyclotron frequency/Larmor frequency; gyroperiod, cyclotron period.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Beaming cone width ≈ 1/γ, not dependent on pitch angle φ
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description: When verifying synchrotron or relativistic emission solutions, ensure the relativistic beaming cone half-angle around the instantaneous velocity direction is stated as approximately 1/γ for γ >> 1 and is independent of the pitch angle φ. Pitch angle φ affects the rate at which the velocity direction sweeps past the observer (and thus pulse duration) via sinφ, but it does not change the beaming cone width. Flag as an error if the solution defines or uses an effective beaming angle with explicit φ-dependence, such as θ_beam ≈ sinφ/γ, θ_eff ≈ sinφ/[γ(1−β cosφ)], or θ_beam ≈ 1/[γ(1−β cosφ)] where φ is the pitch angle to the magnetic field. Also flag claims that the beaming angle scales with sinφ or cosφ. Accept formulations where θ_beam ≈ O(1)·1/γ (e.g., 1/γ, 0.5/γ) and where φ only enters timing estimates (e.g., pulse duration scaling with sinφ via the sweep rate), not the cone width.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Incorrect isotropic radiation claim in instantaneous rest frame
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description: This rule flags statements that assert or imply isotropic emission in the instantaneous rest frame of an accelerated charge (e.g., an electron emitting synchrotron/cyclotron/curvature radiation). Specifically, it searches for claims such as: (a) 'radiation is isotropic in the electron’s rest frame', (b) 'uniform over solid angle in the rest frame', or (c) 'half the power forward and half backward' in contexts mentioning electrons, synchrotron radiation, gyration, magnetic fields, or relativistic beaming. The correct concept is that in the instantaneous rest frame of an accelerated charge the angular distribution is dipolar, with dP/dΩ ∝ sin^2(theta) relative to the acceleration direction, yielding zero emission along the acceleration axis and maximum perpendicular to it; anisotropy is present even before Lorentz transformation to the lab frame. The rule does not trigger if the solution explicitly describes the sin^2(theta) pattern, a dipole angular distribution, or correctly states that emission is peaked perpendicular to the acceleration/magnetic field and is not isotropic. It also ignores contexts involving thermal or scattering processes where isotropy may be valid.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Equal-energy two-photon annihilation: lab-frame angle consistency
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description: Checks momentum-conservation consistency for problems where a moving particle (net initial momentum along a coordinate axis, typically z) annihilates with a target at rest to produce two photons of equal energy in the lab. Common error: assuming the photons are back-to-back in the lab (e.g., θ_B = 180° − θ_A or p_B = −p_A) because they are back-to-back in the COM frame. If the student imposes θ_B = 180° − θ_A with E_A = E_B while the initial longitudinal momentum p_initial ≠ 0, the final z-momentum sums to zero (p_Az + p_Bz = 0), violating conservation. The correct lab-frame configuration for equal-energy photons is same polar angle and opposite azimuths (θ_A = θ_B = α, φ_B = φ_A + π), so transverse components cancel and longitudinal momentum adds: 2 (E_γ / c) cos α = p_initial_z. This rule flags solutions that (a) claim or enforce back-to-back polar angles in the lab for equal-energy photons when p_initial ≠ 0, (b) yield p_Az + p_Bz = 0 with E_A = E_B despite nonzero p_initial_z, or (c) omit azimuthal opposition while assigning unequal polar angles for equal-energy photons. It allows back-to-back only in the COM frame (p_initial = 0), and accepts solutions that use the correct relation cos α = (p_initial c) / (2 E_γ) or explicitly set θ_A = θ_B and φ_B = φ_A + π.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Incorrect COM photon energy in e+e− → γγ (using m_e c^2 / 2 instead of √s/2)
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description:
This rule verifies the modeling of photon energies for electron–positron annihilation into two photons in the center-of-mass (COM) frame (pair rest frame). It flags solutions that incorrectly set each photon energy to m_e c^2 / 2 or treat the total COM energy as 2 m_e c^2 when an incoming particle has nonzero kinetic energy. Checks performed: 
- Scope: Problems involving e+e− → γγ where a COM-frame energy is used or implied. 
- Correct physics: The total COM energy is √s, with s = (p_e + p_p)^2. For a positron at rest in the lab, s = 2 m_e^2 c^4 + 2 m_e c^2 E_e_lab, where E_e_lab = K + m_e c^2. Each photon energy in the COM frame must be E'_γ = √s / 2. 
- Error patterns to flag: (a) Student states or uses E'_γ = m_e c^2 / 2 (≈ 0.2555 MeV) regardless of the electron’s kinetic energy. (b) Student asserts COM total energy = 2 m_e c^2 when K > 0 for at least one incoming particle. (c) The invariant s is computed using only rest masses (s = 4 m_e^2 c^4) without the kinetic-energy term. 
- Numerical trigger: If the electron kinetic energy K > 0, the correct E'_γ must exceed 0.2555 MeV; using ≈ 0.2555 MeV (within small tolerance, e.g., ±1%) or any value independent of K indicates a modeling error. 
- Outcome: If any of the above conditions are met, mark the solution as incorrect for COM energy modeling and indicate that E'_γ should be √s / 2 with s including the kinetic-energy contribution.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: COM boost must use total four-momentum (not single-particle β, γ)
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description: Checks that any Lorentz boost to the center-of-momentum (COM) frame in a multi-particle initial state uses β_cm and γ_cm derived from the total four-momentum, not from a single particle’s velocity or Lorentz factor. Required formulas: β_cm = |Σ p_i| c / (Σ E_i) and γ_cm = 1 / sqrt(1 − β_cm^2), where E_i and p_i are the lab-frame energies and momenta of all incoming particles. Flags an error if the solution: (a) explicitly sets the COM boost as β = p_j c / E_j or γ = E_j / (m_j c^2) for any single particle j when more than one particle is present; or (b) uses a β_boost or γ_boost that differs from the value computed from the total four-momentum by more than a small tolerance (e.g., relative difference > 1e−3). Special attention: for two-particle collisions with one particle at rest (e.g., e− with energy E_e and momentum p_e, and e+ at rest with energy m_e c^2), the correct COM boost is β_cm = p_e c / (E_e + m_e c^2). Using β = p_e c / E_e and γ = E_e / (m_e c^2) to represent the COM boost must be flagged. Consequence: using a single-particle β, γ for the COM transformation leads to incorrect transformed photon energies and angles; the rule prevents this modeling error.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Equal-energy claim vs COM-to-lab boost inconsistency
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description: Detects internal inconsistency in two-photon (or two massless) production solutions: if the solution asserts the two photons have equal energies in the lab, but then models the center-of-mass (COM) emission as exactly along and opposite the boost direction (θ′ = 0 and θ′ = π) and applies Lorentz energy transforms E_lab = γ E′ (1 ± β), it will necessarily produce unequal lab energies for β ≠ 0. The verifier flags cases where all of the following are present: (1) an explicit claim of equal lab energies (e.g., 'E_A = E_B' or 'equal energies'); (2) an initial state with nonzero net momentum in the lab (e.g., one particle moving, the other at rest, implying β > 0 for the COM-to-lab boost); and (3) a COM-to-lab step that sets θ′ = 0/π or uses energy expressions proportional to (1 ± β). If these conditions co-occur, the solution contains a logical contradiction. The rule also flags the pattern of setting E_A = E_B = (E_total)/2 while simultaneously deriving Doppler-shifted unequal lab energies. A consistent solution must either have β = 0 (lab = COM) or choose COM emission angles not aligned with the boost so that equal lab energies in the lab are achievable.

Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.title: Two-photon annihilation: lab-frame angle completeness and momentum check
Relativistic Electrodynamics and Radiati.description: Applies to electron–positron annihilation into two photons of equal energy when one particle (the positron) is at rest and the electron travels along the z-axis with kinetic energy T. The rule verifies that the solution is completed in the lab frame and that the angle α between the z-axis and a photon’s momentum is correctly derived using energy–momentum conservation with equal photon energies. Required checks: (1) The solution must provide an explicit formula for α and a numeric value for the given inputs. (2) It must use the lab-frame momentum relation 2 (Eγ/c) cos α = p_e, with Eγ = (T + 2 m_e c^2)/2 and p_e c = sqrt(T^2 + 2 T m_e c^2). Acceptable final forms include α = arccos[p_e c / (2 Eγ)], α = arccos[sqrt(T/(T + 2 m_e c^2))], or α = arccos[1 / sqrt(1 + 2 m_e c^2 / T)]. For T = 1 MeV (m_e c^2 ≈ 0.511 MeV), the expected numeric result is α ≈ 45.3°. The rule flags errors if: (a) α is not computed or the derivation is left incomplete; (b) the momentum relation is incorrect (e.g., missing the factor 2, using cos α = p_e c / Eγ, or assuming back-to-back z components without transverse cancellation); (c) an intermediate COM-frame transformation is used without returning to and resolving α in the lab frame; or (d) the numeric value deviates from the expected result beyond a reasonable tolerance (e.g., >2% for the given parameters).

Relativistic Flux and Doppler Effects.title: Relativistic flux must include Lorentz factor when density is in comoving frame
Relativistic Flux and Doppler Effects.description: This rule checks continuity and flux expressions in relativistic flows (e.g., AGN jets) for correct frame transformations. If the problem states that number density n(s) or mass density ρ(s) is defined in the jet/comoving/proper frame, then any particle/number or mass flux written in the AGN/lab frame must include the Lorentz factor γ(s) = 1/sqrt(1 − v(s)^2/c^2). Expected forms: particle flux Φ_N = γ(s) n_proper(s) v(s) A(s); mass flux Φ_m = γ(s) ρ_proper(s) v(s) A(s); steady continuity implies γ(s) n_proper(s) v(s) A(s) is constant along s (absent sources/sinks). Flag errors when a solution uses n(s) v(s) A(s) or ρ(s) v(s) A(s) without γ while simultaneously indicating that n(s) or ρ(s) is measured in the jet/comoving frame, or derives continuity as n1 v1 A1 = n2 v2 A2 without γ under relativistic conditions. Do not flag if the solution explicitly redefines n or ρ as lab-frame quantities (e.g., n_lab = γ n_proper) or uses four-current notation with u^μ where the γ factor is clearly included (e.g., u^x = γ v). This rule targets missing γ factors in lab-frame fluxes derived from comoving-frame densities in relativistic contexts.

Relativistic Flux and Doppler Effects.title: Incorrect Doppler frame/sign for laser–atom resonance
Relativistic Flux and Doppler Effects.description:
Checks solutions to laser-excitation of moving atoms/ions for misuse of Doppler formulas and wrong detuning sign. Triggers when the problem context involves tuning a lab laser to drive a known atomic transition in a moving atom/ion (keywords: laser, resonance, absorption, moving ion/atom, Doppler). The rule verifies the following:

- Correct resonance framing: The solution should impose the resonance condition in the particle rest frame, f_rest = f0, and relate lab and rest-frame frequencies via the relativistic Doppler transform: f_rest = gamma (1 - beta cosθ) f_lab. For head-on counter-propagating geometry (ion and laser approach), cosθ = -1, thus f_lab = f0 / [gamma (1 + beta)]. In wavelength form: λ_lab = λ0 gamma (1 + beta). Classical limit: f_lab ≈ f0 / (1 + beta), λ_lab ≈ λ0 (1 + beta).

- Error patterns to flag:
  1) Using observer/source "observed shift" formulas (e.g., λ' = λ sqrt[(1 - beta)/(1 + beta)] or f' = f sqrt[(1 + beta)/(1 - beta)]) as the required lab laser value for resonance, without inverting to solve for f_lab that makes f_rest = f0.
  2) Labeling λ' = λ/(1 ± beta) or f' = f(1 ± beta) as the classical resonance prediction for the lab laser, instead of the correct classical resonance relations f_lab = f0/(1 ± beta) and λ_lab = λ0(1 ± beta).
  3) Detuning sign inconsistency: For head-on (counter-propagating) excitation, the required lab laser must be red-detuned relative to λ0 (λ_lab > λ0). Flag conclusions that predict blue detuning (λ_lab < λ0) for this geometry.
  4) Gamma misplacement/omission: Flag relations like f_lab = f0 gamma (1 ± beta) or λ_lab = λ0 / [gamma (1 ± beta)] as resonance conditions; the correct is f_lab = f0 / [gamma (1 ± beta)], λ_lab = λ0 gamma (1 ± beta).
  5) Wrong order of relativistic correction: Between relativistic and classical resonance predictions, the leading correction is +0.5 beta^2 (i.e., ratio ≈ gamma). Flag claims of an O(beta) difference or incorrect sign for the correction.
  6) Missing explicit resonance step: No explicit statement or use of f_rest = f0 (or equivalent) when determining the lab laser frequency/wavelength.

This rule helps catch conceptual frame mix-ups where students apply observed-shift formulas (appropriate for measuring a moving source) instead of the resonance condition for tuning a lab laser to drive a transition in a moving atom/ion, leading to incorrect sign (blue vs red) and missing gamma factors.

Relativistic Flux and Doppler Effects.title: Require β^2 discrepancy when comparing classical vs relativistic Doppler; forbid 'zero error' claims at nonzero v
Relativistic Flux and Doppler Effects.description: Checks solutions that compare classical and relativistic predictions for Doppler shift (or any relativistic correction) at nonzero velocity v. Flags an error if the solution concludes 'zero error', 'exact agreement', or infers equivalence by matching only first-order terms in β = v/c. The correct reasoning is that the leading difference between classical and relativistic results appears at order β^2, and is small but nonzero for any v > 0. For longitudinal Doppler of light: lambda_rel/lambda = sqrt((1 - β)/(1 + β)) ≈ 1 - β + 0.5*β^2, whereas the classical approximation gives lambda_class/lambda ≈ 1 - β + β^2; their relative difference is ~0.5*β^2. A valid solution must either include a second-order expansion or provide an explicit error bound of order (v/c)^2 with a numeric estimate for the given v (e.g., for v = 6000 m/s, β ≈ 2e-5, so the relative difference is ~2e-10). If the solution asserts 'zero error' or compares only first-order terms to justify equivalence at nonzero v, mark it incorrect.

Cherenkov Radiation and Thresholds.title: Cherenkov threshold minimal pressure computation check
Cherenkov Radiation and Thresholds.description: This rule verifies the computed minimal gas pressure P_min required for Cherenkov emission at fixed particle momentum when the refractive index depends linearly on pressure, n(P) = 1 + aP. For each particle type with rest mass M and common momentum p, the verifier computes the speed fraction beta via the relativistic relation beta = p / sqrt(p^2 + M^2) (using natural units with c = 1; p and M may be provided in GeV/c and GeV/c^2). The Cherenkov threshold requires n = 1/beta, giving the minimal pressure P_min_expected = (1/a) * (1/beta − 1). Checks performed: (1) Numeric consistency: each learner-reported P_min must satisfy |P_min_reported − P_min_expected| / P_min_expected ≤ 0.10; otherwise flag an arithmetic/formula error. (2) Wrong-formula heuristics: if P_min_reported matches within 10% any of the common wrong forms—(1/a)(beta − 1), (1/a)(1/beta^2 − 1), (beta − 1)/a with a mis-scaling, or P_min computed using n = 1/(1 + aP)—annotate the likely cause (wrong threshold relation or inverted a). (3) Physical ordering: for fixed p and a, P_min must increase with mass (protons > kaons > pions); if the reported ordering violates this monotonicity, flag 'inconsistent mass dependence'. (4) Sanity check: P_min must be non-negative; negative values are invalid. This rule catches significant arithmetic mistakes (e.g., decimal-place errors leading to one–two orders of magnitude discrepancies) and misuse of the threshold formula in Cherenkov problems with n(P) = 1 + aP.

Momentum-Energy Relations and β Expressi.title: Check β expression from momentum-energy relation
Momentum-Energy Relations and β Expressi.description: Verify that when β (v/c) is expressed in terms of momentum p and total energy E for a relativistic particle, the formula used is β = (p c)/E in SI units, or β = p/E in natural units (c = 1). Flag any occurrence where β is written with an incorrect power of c, such as β = (p c^2)/E, β = p/(E c), β = (p c)/(E c), or generally β = (p c^n)/E with n ≠ 1. Include a dimensional check: β must be dimensionless; (p c)/E is dimensionless, whereas (p c^2)/E has dimensions of speed and is invalid for β. Accept derivations via v/c only if v is correctly given as v = (p c^2)/E, which implies β = v/c = (p c)/E. Also accept natural-unit expressions with β = p/E where c is consistently omitted. Trigger an error when the written β formula contradicts these identities, even if subsequent numerical steps effectively use the correct relation.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Consistency of Snell-law invariant and angle reference in stratified media
Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.description: Checks that in a horizontally stratified medium (n = n(z)), the conserved quantity is formed with the correct angle reference and used consistently throughout the derivation. Valid invariants are n(z) sin(θ_v) = const when θ_v is measured with respect to the vertical (layer normal), and n(z) cos(φ_h) = const when φ_h is measured with respect to the horizontal. The rule flags: (1) using n(z) sin(θ) = const while defining θ as the angle to the horizontal (should be cos for the horizontal reference), or using n(z) cos(θ) = const while defining θ as the angle to the vertical (should be sin for the vertical reference); (2) inconsistent kinematic relations between the chosen angle and the ray slope, e.g., if θ is defined with respect to the vertical, then dz/dx must equal cot(θ_v) (equivalently dx/dz = tan(θ_v)); if φ is defined with respect to the horizontal, then dz/dx must equal tan(φ_h) (equivalently dx/dz = cot(φ_h)); using dz/dx = tan(θ_v) or dz/dx = cot(φ_h) is incorrect; (3) switching angle definitions mid-derivation without updating the invariant accordingly (e.g., starting with n(z) sin(θ_v) = const and later treating θ as measured from the horizontal). This rule detects misuse of the Snell-law invariant in stratified media and mismatches between angle definitions and ray-slope relations.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Angle definition vs path-slope consistency in stratified media
Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.description: Checks that the relationship between the ray angle θ and the path slope is consistent with the declared angle reference (vertical/normal vs horizontal) and the coordinate definitions. For stratified media with n varying with height (e.g., n(z)), if θ is defined as the angle with the vertical (normal), the correct relations are dx/dz = tan(θ) and dz/dx = cot(θ); using tan(θ) = dy/dx or tan(θ) = dz/dx under this definition is flagged as an error. Conversely, if θ is defined as the angle with the horizontal, the correct relations are dz/dx = tan(θ) and dx/dz = cot(θ); using tan(θ) = dx/dz under this definition is flagged. The rule also cross-checks the chosen Snell invariant: n(z) sin(θ) = const implies θ is measured from the vertical/normal, while n(z) cos(θ) = const implies θ is measured from the horizontal; any mismatch between this invariant and the slope relation is flagged. Additionally, the rule requires explicit coordinate definitions (e.g., which symbol denotes the vertical coordinate); mixing n(z) with tan(θ) = dy/dx without declaring y as the vertical coordinate is flagged as ambiguous or inconsistent.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Incorrectly zeroing the Snell invariant due to horizontal slope or turning point
Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.description: Checks gradient-index optics solutions (n = n(z)) that introduce the continuous Snell invariant (e.g., n(z) sin(theta_v) = C for theta measured from the vertical, or n(z) cos(theta_h) = C for theta measured from the horizontal) and then set the constant C to zero solely because the ray has a horizontal tangent, dz/dx = 0, or a turning point in z(x). The rule flags any reasoning that infers C = 0 from a zero slope or from a 'horizontal segment' without demonstrating that the angle used in the invariant equals 0 degrees. In stratified media, a horizontal ray corresponds to theta_v = 90 degrees (sin(theta_v) = 1) or theta_h = 0 degrees (cos(theta_h) = 1), so the invariant equals n at that height, not zero. The rule also flags misuse of trigonometric relations that equate sin(theta_v) or cos(theta_h) directly to dz/dx; for theta defined relative to vertical, dz/dx = tan(90° - theta_v) = cot(theta_v), and for theta relative to horizontal, dz/dx = tan(theta_h). Any step that concludes C = 0 from dz/dx = 0, 'horizontal ray', or 'turning point' without the correct angle definition and mapping will be marked as a logical error.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Reflection grating equation must include incident angle unless normal incidence is stated
Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.description: Checks diffraction grating solutions (especially reflection gratings) for improper omission of the incident angle term in the grating equation. Trigger conditions: the problem/solution mentions a grating (keywords: grating, diffraction order, slit density n, spacing d=1/n) and derives/uses a diffraction condition of the form m λ = d sin β, sin β = m λ / d, or β_m = arcsin(n m λ). The rule then inspects whether the context is a reflection grating and whether the incident angle α (a.k.a. θ_i) is handled correctly. Required checks: (1) If the problem statement does NOT explicitly specify normal incidence (e.g., no phrases like “normal incidence”, “α = 0”, “parallel to the normal”), then using a simplified relation m λ = d sin β (or β_m = arcsin(n m λ)) without any sin α term is flagged as a modeling error. The correct general reflection grating equation is m λ = d (sin β ± sin α), with the sign depending on geometry. (2) If the problem statement DOES explicitly specify normal incidence, the simplified relation is physically correct, but the solution should either (a) explicitly state the assumption α = 0 before using m λ = d sin β, or (b) present the general form m λ = d (sin β ± sin α) and then set α = 0. If neither is done (i.e., the solution implicitly assumes α = 0 without stating it), flag as a minor modeling omission. (3) If the solution names a reflection grating but never addresses the ± sign/geometry selection in m λ = d (sin β ± sin α) while discussing both +m and −m orders, flag a missing sign convention/geometry discussion. Implementation notes: detect presence of incident-angle handling via terms/variables such as α, θ_i, “incident angle”, or explicit phrases like “normal incidence”, “α = 0”. Detect simplified usage via patterns: “mλ = d sin β”, “sin β = mλ/d”, “β = arcsin(n m λ)”. When flagged, report that the incident angle term (sin α) is missing or the normal-incidence assumption is unstated for a reflection grating.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Misuse of thin-lens formula for a single refracting spherical surface
Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.description: This rule flags solutions that analyze imaging by a single spherical refracting interface (e.g., a water-air meniscus or droplet on glass) using thin-lens formulas instead of the correct single-surface refraction relation. The thin-lens imaging formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v and the lensmaker equation are valid for thin lenses with two refracting surfaces and negligible thickness; they are not valid for a single refracting spherical surface between media of different refractive indices. Detection criteria: (1) The problem context indicates a single curved interface (meniscus/droplet/plano-convex cap) and objects in air (e.g., ceiling lights at ~3 m) with images observed via that interface. (2) The solution explicitly writes or invokes 1/f = 1/u + 1/v to relate object and image distances, or uses the lensmaker equation to infer focal length or radius when only one curved surface is present. (3) The solution determines R, f, or a contact angle from object/image distances without including refractive indices (n1, n2) in the imaging relation. (4) Distances are measured from an external reference (table/graph paper) rather than from the vertex of the refracting surface in the appropriate medium, or sign conventions for u, v, R are omitted/misapplied. Correct requirement: For a single spherical refracting surface between media n1 (object side) and n2 (image side), the paraxial imaging equation must be used: n1/u + n2/v = (n2 - n1)/R, with distances measured from the surface along the optical axis and proper sign conventions for R, u, and v. If a thin-lens formula is used, the solution must justify the presence of two refracting surfaces and negligible thickness; otherwise, flag as a logical/modeling error.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Confusing reflection with refraction in curved liquid surfaces
Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.description:
This rule checks for conceptual inconsistency between reflection and refraction when analyzing images or bright spots formed by curved water surfaces (e.g., a water droplet on glass acting as a plano-convex lens).

It flags a solution if it satisfies any of the following:
- The student attributes an observed image/bright spot to reflection (uses terms like "reflection", "reflected image", "mirror", "specular") while using refraction-based lens relations, such as:
  - Lensmaker's formula: 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  - Thin-lens equation with refractive index or explicit use of the refractive index n (e.g., n ≈ 1.33 for water)
  - Snell's law or statements that rays are "refracted" to a focus
- The student describes a setup where a curved transparent water surface produces a focused spot on a screen/paper below and calls it a reflection or a "reflected image" (focusing on a screen through the droplet is caused by refraction, not reflection).
- The student mixes mirror formulas and lens physics inconsistently, e.g.:
  - Uses refractive index (n) while claiming the mechanism is reflection (mirror focusing does not depend on n; for a spherical mirror f = R/2).
  - Uses mirror-based focal relations (e.g., f = R/2) while describing a transparent droplet lens or employing lens terminology.

Heuristics for detection (any trigger should flag):
- Co-occurrence within the same reasoning segment of at least one reflection keyword {"reflection", "reflected image", "mirror", "specular", "glint"} and at least one refraction/lens keyword {"refraction", "lens", "plano-convex", "focal length", "lensmaker", "Snell", "refractive index", "n =", "n ≈", "n (water)"}.
- Use of refractive index (e.g., n = 1.33) together with statements that the observed image is a reflection.
- Computation of curvature radius or focal length from a water droplet using a lens formula after labeling the phenomenon as reflection of a distant light source (e.g., ceiling lights).

Pedagogical note (for feedback): If the bright spot is on a screen or paper placed below/behind the droplet, the mechanism is refraction (lens). If discussing a reflected image of a distant source seen from above, the mechanism is reflection (mirror-like), which does not involve the refractive index for focal relations.

Optics - Snell's Law and Refraction.title: Light speed in material must satisfy v = c/n and be less than c
