Specifically, it checks for: (1) incorrect inequality direction—using ≥ instead of ≤—when mapping a constraint like 'total kinetic energy loss does not exceed 40%' (which should translate to cumulative loss fraction L(n) ≤ 0.40); (2) incorrect threshold substitution—using the complement (e.g., 0.60) instead of the stated bound (e.g., 0.40) for a loss constraint; (3) misuse of monotonicity—deriving an inequality of the form f(n) ≥ c with f(n) increasing in n, and then concluding it holds for all n or that no upper bound exists, despite the problem asking for an 'at most' count; (4) textual cues such as conclusions like 'holds for all n', 'any n satisfies', or 'no maximum' in contexts requiring an upper bound. The rule is triggered when the solution presents an inequality involving the number of collisions n where the left-hand side is a monotone increasing function of n (e.g., terms like e^(2n), n·e^2, or sums increasing with n) and the comparison is set to ≥ a threshold, or when the threshold for a '≤ X%' loss constraint is incorrectly written as (1−X%). It ensures that the solution correctly sets and uses L(n) ≤ X and resolves n_max as the largest integer satisfying the bound, rather than asserting the inequality holds for all n.

Energy and Restitution.title: Post-impact time-of-flight must use restitution (t = 2 v_up / g)
Energy and Restitution.description: Checks computations of the time between the first and second impacts (flight time after a bounce). Expected physics: after a vertical collision with the floor, the upward launch speed v_up is determined by the coefficient of restitution (c or e): v_up = c * v_down, where v_down is the pre-impact vertical speed. For a drop from rest from height h, v_down = sqrt(2 g h), so t_flight = 2 v_up / g = 2 c sqrt(2 g h) / g = 2 c sqrt(2 h / g), and the rebound height is h' = v_up^2/(2 g) = c^2 h. Flag the solution if any of the following are detected: (1) t_flight is computed as sqrt(2 h / g) (or the time to fall from rest) for the interval between impacts, missing both the factor 2 and the restitution c/e; (2) t_flight lacks the restitution coefficient (c/e) when a bounce occurs (i.e., uses v_up = sqrt(2 g h) or t_flight proportional to sqrt(2 h / g) without c/e); (3) the rebound height is set equal to the drop height h without explicitly stating a perfectly elastic collision (c = 1) or deriving h' = c^2 h; (4) v_up is taken equal to v_down without mention of restitution. This rule should scan for expressions of t_flight involving h and g and verify that the factor 2 and a restitution parameter (c, e, COR) are present, and should check rebound-height relations to ensure h' = c^2 h unless c = 1 is explicitly declared.

Energy and Restitution.title: Require restitution coefficient in post-impact vertical motion and flight time
Energy and Restitution.description: When a problem specifies a coefficient of restitution (c or e) for the ball–floor impact, any computation of the ball’s vertical motion immediately after the impact must include c. The verifier will check that: (1) The post-impact vertical speed (v_y+) is modeled as v_y+ = c * |v_y−| (upward), i.e., the normal relative velocity reverses sign and is scaled by c; equivalently, the rebound height satisfies h_rebound = c^2 * h_impact. (2) Any time-of-flight used to determine the interval until the next floor contact or the horizontal distance between impacts depends on c (e.g., t_flight = 2 v_y+/g = 2 c |v_y−|/g). (3) Final expressions for horizontal range/distance between impacts explicitly depend on c whenever the problem statement provides it. The rule flags solutions that: omit c in post-impact vertical velocity (e.g., v_y+ = |v_y−| or v_y+ = sqrt(2gh)); compute t_flight without c (e.g., t_flight = 2 |v_y−|/g or t_flight = 2 sqrt(2h/g)); or present a final horizontal distance independent of c. The check applies regardless of horizontal dynamics (e.g., frictional changes in v_x); it focuses on vertical rebound modeling with restitution.

Energy and Restitution.title: Coefficient of restitution must use justified rebound height from provided data
Energy and Restitution.description: When verifying a solution that computes the coefficient of restitution (e) for a ball-ground collision with negligible air resistance, ensure the rebound parameter used is traceable to the problem data. Specifically: (1) If e is computed via heights (e = sqrt(h_rebound / h_drop)), the initial drop height h_drop must match the given release height, and the rebound height h_rebound must be explicitly obtained from the provided figure/data (e.g., the first post-collision peak in y(t)) or derived from a stated, verifiable kinematic calculation. (2) Flag the solution if a numerical h_rebound (or post-impact speed) is introduced without citation/derivation from the problem’s figure or text (e.g., an arbitrary/guessed value like “h1 = 0.8 m” without reading from the graph). (3) Check consistency: h_rebound ≤ h_drop and e ∈ [0,1] for passive collisions; flag if violated. (4) If the problem specifies reporting precision (e.g., three significant figures), flag if the final e does not adhere. This rule targets unsupported or incorrect numerical inputs for rebound height/velocity in restitution calculations, especially when a graph is provided and must be read to obtain h_rebound.

Energy and Restitution.title: Two-body escape-speed must use reduced mass and relative energy
Energy and Restitution.description: Checks escape/binding criteria in isolated two-body gravitational problems. Trigger when a solution determines the minimum escape speed by writing the energy condition using only one body's kinetic energy, e.g., E = (1/2) m v^2 - G M m / r >= 0, or equates (1/2) m v^2 = G M m / r, without accounting for the kinetic energy of the other body. The correct criterion for escape is the relative (two-body) energy: E_rel = (1/2) μ v_rel^2 - G M m / r >= 0, where μ = m M / (m + M) is the reduced mass and v_rel is the relative speed. Acceptance conditions: the solution uses μ in the kinetic term, or works in the center-of-mass frame summing both kinetic energies and arrives at the same threshold; the solution explicitly justifies a fixed primary (M → ∞ or external anchoring) or an M >> m approximation and states the approximation. Detection details: flag if (i) the kinetic term uses m (or only one mass) instead of μ, (ii) the minimum speed scales as sqrt(2 G M / r) or sqrt(2 G M m/(m r)) instead of sqrt(2 G (M + m) / r) for the relative speed, or (iii) the text claims "total mechanical energy of the daughter/object >= 0" in an isolated two-body context without mentioning recoil/momentum conservation. Exception: do not flag if the problem statement or solution explicitly fixes one body or invokes M >> m with a stated approximation. This rule catches underestimation of escape speeds due to neglecting the recoil kinetic energy of the primary and enforces use of the reduced-mass formulation.

Energy and Restitution.title: Two-body escape must use relative energy/reduced mass, not single-body energy
Energy and Restitution.description: Checks gravitational escape problems involving two finite, free masses (attractor mass M and escaping mass m). Flags solutions that use the escape criterion on the escaping body alone (e.g., E = (1/2) m v^2 - G M m / r >= 0 or v_escape = sqrt(2 G M / r)) without accounting for the kinetic energy of both bodies via the reduced-mass formulation. The correct escape condition in an isolated two-body system is that the relative mechanical energy be nonnegative: E_rel = (1/2) μ v_rel^2 - G M m / r >= 0, with μ = m M / (m + M), giving v_rel >= sqrt(2 G (M + m) / r). The rule triggers if: (a) the derived threshold uses only m and M with v_escape = sqrt(2 G M / r), (b) energy is set to zero for the daughter alone without introducing μ or center-of-mass reasoning, or (c) the solution omits momentum conservation/COM treatment when M is not explicitly fixed or M >> m. Exemptions: do not flag if the problem explicitly states the attractor is fixed by external forces or M >> m is assumed and justified. For finite mass ratios (e.g., M = 4m), the expected minimal speed uses (M + m), e.g., v_min = sqrt(2 G (M + m) / r).

Electromagnetism and Relativity.title: Explicit derivation required for conserved J∥ in uniform magnetic field with modified momentum
Electromagnetism and Relativity.description:
This rule verifies claims of conservation of the angular momentum component along a uniform magnetic field for systems of charges (e.g., an electric dipole) by enforcing an explicit, correct derivation. It targets unsupported statements like dJ/dt = 0 and the use of incorrect linear/rotational quantities.

Checks performed:
- Trigger: The solution claims that the angular momentum component along B (e.g., J_z, J∥, (r_CM × P + L_rot)·b̂) is conserved or states dJ/dt = 0.
- Required definitions: The solution must explicitly define the conserved quantity as J∥ = [(r_CM × P_mod) + L_rot]·b̂, where b̂ = B/|B|, P_mod is the modified (pseudo/canonical) momentum appropriate for a uniform magnetic field, and L_rot is the rotational contribution (e.g., I ω or an equivalent expression derived from the body's rotation).
- Required derivation: The solution must compute dJ∥/dt explicitly using:
  - Vector identities: d/dt (r × p) = r × ṗ + v × p.
  - Equations of motion for the charges: m r̈_i = q_i (v_i × B) (plus any other specified forces), and the rotational equation of motion (torque balance) for L_rot.
  - Projection along B: The final step must evaluate the dot product with b̂ (or equivalently align axes so that b̂ = ẑ) and show term-by-term cancellation leading to dJ∥/dt = 0.
- Consistency requirements:
  - P_mod must be clearly defined and must be the appropriate modified (pseudo/canonical) momentum for a uniform B field, not merely the mechanical center-of-mass momentum. If the solution earlier defined P, that same definition must be used here; inconsistent reuse is flagged.
  - L_rot (e.g., I ω) must be consistent with the defined rotational dynamics of the dipole (correct I about the center of mass and correct torque from magnetic forces). If I or L_rot were incorrectly defined earlier, the conservation claim is invalid.
  - Units and dimensions of P_mod, L_rot, and J∥ must be consistent.
- Acceptance criteria:
  - The derivation includes d/dt of both r_CM × P_mod and L_rot, uses the Lorentz-force-based ṗ terms, includes v_CM × P_mod terms, and demonstrates explicit cancellation upon projection along b̂.
  - Alternatively, a Lagrangian/Hamiltonian derivation that constructs the correct gauge-invariant (pseudo/canonical) momentum and uses Noether’s theorem is accepted only if it explicitly identifies the symmetry and shows dJ∥/dt = 0 with the correct J∥ expression.

Flags as errors:
- Claim of conservation (e.g., dJ/dt = 0, J_z conserved) without an explicit time-derivative calculation and projection along B.
- Use of unmodified mechanical momentum for P in a magnetic field or omission of the required pseudo/canonical correction.
- Use of an incorrect or undefined moment of inertia/rotational term (e.g., arbitrary I ω) or omission of magnetic torque contributions.
- Inconsistency between definitions of P or I used in earlier parts and those used in the conservation proof.
- Reliance on qualitative symmetry/Noether arguments without constructing the correct conserved combination and showing d/dt = 0 explicitly.

Electromagnetism and Relativity.title: Lorentz factor consistency for moving electrons in photon–electron scattering
Electromagnetism and Relativity.description: This rule checks that any Lorentz factor γ assigned to an electron that is explicitly described as moving before a collision (nonzero initial momentum or speed) satisfies the relativistic bound γ ≥ 1, with equality only for v = 0. The verifier should: (1) detect contexts involving Compton or inverse Compton scattering where an initial electron is stated to be moving (e.g., p_1e ≠ 0 or v_1e ≠ 0); (2) locate any derived or asserted expression/value for that electron’s γ; (3) evaluate or simplify γ numerically or symbolically under the domain assumptions h > 0, c > 0, m_0 > 0, and wavelengths λ > 0; (4) flag an error if γ < 1, if γ ≤ 1 while the electron is described as moving, or if γ is written in a form that is strictly less than 1 under the stated domain (e.g., γ = 1 − h/(2 m_0 c λ_i)). Such outcomes are unphysical and typically indicate incorrect application of momentum/energy conservation (e.g., treating vector momentum as scalars or omitting components), which can also yield unjustified wavelength relations like λ_0 = 2 λ_i. This rule is triggered whenever a moving electron’s γ violates the bound, independent of the specific scattering angle or wavelengths used.

Electromagnetism and Relativity.title: Relativistic momentum of massive particles must not include division by c in SI
Electromagnetism and Relativity.description: Checks expressions for the relativistic 3‑momentum of a massive particle (e.g., electron) for dimensional consistency in SI. In SI units, the correct form is p = γ m v (vector), with units kg·m/s. The rule flags any momentum expressions of the form γ m v / c or γ m (v/c) that lack a compensating factor of c, which incorrectly yields units of mass (kg) rather than momentum. It also flags p = γ m β without multiplying by c (i.e., p = γ m β is incorrect in SI; p = γ m β c is correct). The rule distinguishes photon momentum (p_photon = h/λ = E/c), which is allowed to include c in the denominator, and applies only to massive particles. Context sensitivity: If the solution explicitly declares natural units (c = 1) and is consistent elsewhere (e.g., E = γ m, p = γ m v), this rule is not triggered. Indicators of SI context include use of E = hc/λ, Compton formulas with h, c, and explicit mc^2. The rule inspects the final or key stated expressions for the particle’s momentum and performs dimensional analysis; if the resulting units are not kg·m/s, it flags the error.

Electromagnetism and Relativity.title: Inverse Compton does not require photon energy > m0 c^2; enforce vector momentum conservation
Electromagnetism and Relativity.description: Flag solutions to photon–electron scattering (Compton or inverse Compton) that infer from γ>1 or from an algebraic inconsistency that the incident photon must have energy comparable to or greater than the electron rest mass energy (E_photon ≥ m0 c^2 or '≫ m0 c^2'). In inverse Compton scattering, the photon gains energy from the relativistic electron; the incident photon need not exceed m0 c^2 and is often far below it. Also verify that momentum conservation is applied as a vector equation. Trigger if the solution: (a) invokes only scalar energy conservation without writing the vector momentum balance, (b) treats momentum magnitudes additively/subtractively (e.g., |p_e| = |p_i| − |p_0|) instead of using the vector relation p_e = p_i − p_0 with directions, or (c) explains contradictions by claiming 'insufficient photon energy' or that ICS requires E_photon ≳ m0 c^2. This rule catches concept errors that misattribute inconsistencies to energy scale rather than incorrect or incomplete momentum conservation.

Force Analysis in Multi-Body Systems.title: FBD for non-attached (stacked) mass must exclude spring force and use common acceleration
Force Analysis in Multi-Body Systems.description:
This rule verifies the free-body diagram (FBD) and equation of motion for a mass that is in contact with another body attached to a spring (e.g., a small mass m placed atop a heavy mass M that is connected to a spring). It checks that the small/top mass m is not assigned a direct spring force and that its dynamics use the common acceleration of the contacting bodies while contact is maintained.

The rule flags an error if any of the following are detected:
- The force list/FBD for the top mass m includes a spring force term (e.g., kx, kΔx, F_spring) or any expression implying the spring acts directly on m.
- The equation of motion written specifically for m includes k, spring displacement x, or a spring-force variable; the correct 1D force balance for m must involve only gravity and the normal force: m a = m g − N (downward positive) or N − m g = m a (upward positive).
- The normal force N is omitted from m’s force balance while contact is assumed, or N is incorrectly set equal to the spring force (e.g., N = kx or N = kx − mg), implying spring acts directly on m.
- The acceleration used for m differs from the acceleration used for M during the contact phase (they must share a common acceleration while in contact).

Implementation notes:
- Parse body-specific equations; identify the equation labeled or contextually assigned to mass m.
- Search for presence of spring-related symbols (k, x_spring, Δx, F_spring) in m’s force balance; if present, flag.
- Verify inclusion of mg and N in m’s force balance; require that m’s EOM contains only these forces (with consistent sign convention).
- Extract acceleration symbols for m and M; require equality (a_m == a_M) during the contact interval noted in the solution.

Rationale:
- A spring exerts force only on the body it is attached to (here, M). The top mass m experiences gravity and the contact normal from M; its acceleration equals the common acceleration of the contacting bodies until separation. Assigning a spring force directly to m or using distinct accelerations violates correct FBD principles.

Force Analysis in Multi-Body Systems.title: Normal force on a riding mass must exclude spring force and depend on platform acceleration
Force Analysis in Multi-Body Systems.description: This rule verifies the force balance and normal-force expression for a mass m riding on/top of another mass M that is attached to a vertical spring. It checks that the free-body diagram of m includes only gravity (m g) and the contact normal force N, and that the equation of motion for m is written as N - m g = m a (with a equal to the vertical acceleration of the supporting platform). The rule flags the following errors: (1) Inclusion of spring force terms (e.g., ± k x) or any other forces not directly acting on m in the force balance for m, such as equations of the form N - k x = m a or N = m g + k x. (2) Expressing the normal force N(t) directly as a function of spring extension x(t) rather than platform acceleration x''(t), e.g., using N = m g - k x instead of N = m g - m x''(t). (3) Having N(t) scale incorrectly with M (e.g., N ∝ M g cos(ω t)) rather than with m, or using M as the leading multiplicative factor outside acceleration ratios for the oscillatory part. (4) When an explicit maximum is computed for the typical “released from support” SHM setup, failing the structural relation N_max = m g + m |a_min| (equivalently N(t) = m[g - x''(t)] with the maximum occurring at the most downward acceleration). The rule is intended to catch calculation errors arising from incorrect free-body isolation of m and misattribution of spring forces to m, as well as physically inconsistent dependence of N on the wrong mass or on spring extension rather than acceleration.

Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Centrifugal equilibrium pressure-gradient sign check
Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Checks that in a static fluid/gas in a uniformly rotating frame (angular speed ω) with the coordinate x (or r) increasing outward from the rotation axis, the pressure gradient balances the centrifugal body force with the correct sign: dP/dx = ρ ω^2 x (i.e., pressure increases outward). The rule activates when the solution mentions a rotating system, centrifugal force, and writes a 1D force balance along the radial coordinate using terms like dP/dx, ΔP/Δx, ρ, ω, x (or r), or expresses ΔP/Δx = β ρ. It flags errors if any of the following are found without a clearly stated alternative sign convention or additional inward body force along x: (1) A force balance written or concluded as dP/dx = −ρ ω^2 x, ΔP/Δx = −ρ ω^2 x, or equivalent, implying pressure decreases with radius; (2) An equilibrium equation −dP/dx = ρ ω^2 x followed by an interpretation that pressure decreases outward (sign-inference mistake), or any algebraic rearrangement that flips the sign relative to the stated outward-positive x; (3) A proportionality coefficient β defined by ΔP/Δx = β ρ reported as β < 0 or β = −ω^2 x instead of β = +ω^2 x for outward-positive x; (4) Qualitative statements such as "pressure decreases outward" in a purely centrifugal equilibrium. Allowed exceptions: the negative sign is acceptable only if the solution explicitly defines x increasing inward (toward the axis) or includes additional inward body-force terms in the balance (e.g., gravity along −x) that are accounted for in the final sign. The rule ensures consistency between the physical direction of −∇P, the outward centrifugal term ρ ω^2 x, and the chosen coordinate orientation.

Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Incorrectly assuming constant proportionality when balance implies x-dependence
Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Checks for solutions that treat a proportionality coefficient as a constant when the governing physics requires it to vary with position. Specifically: if a solution uses a relation of the form A(x) = β · B(x) (e.g., dP/dx = β · ρ(x)) and separately derives A(x) = f(x) · B(x) with explicit x-dependence in f(x) (e.g., from force balance in a rotating frame: dP/dx = ρ(x) · ω^2 · x, up to sign), then β must equal f(x) and therefore depend on x. The rule flags conclusions that set β to an x-independent constant (such as β = ω^2) or invoke an 'effective/average' constant without demonstrating that A(x)/B(x) is x-independent. The verifier should: (1) detect a proportionality statement A(x) = β · B(x); (2) find a derived relation A(x) = f(x) · B(x) where f depends on x; (3) if the final answer states β is constant or omits the x-dependence implied by f(x), mark as a conceptual error and recommend β(x) = f(x). Allow β to be constant only if the solution explicitly proves f(x) is constant (e.g., f'(x) = 0). Example caught: in rotating-tube hydrostatics, matching dP/dx = ρ(x) ω^2 x to dP/dx = β ρ(x) requires β(x) = ω^2 x; asserting β = ω^2 is incorrect.

Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: No gravity term along horizontal radial direction in rotating-frame balance
Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Checks rotating-frame force/pressure-balance equations written along a horizontal radial axis (e.g., a tube rotating in a horizontal plane with its axis defined as x and the rotation axis at x=0) for inappropriate inclusion of gravity or an 'effective gravity' term. In such setups, gravity acts vertically and has zero component along the horizontal radial x-direction. Therefore, the x-direction balance for hydrostatics should not include ±ρ g, g_eff, or mixtures like (g − ω^2 x). The rule flags expressions such as: -∂P/∂x = ρ(g − ω^2 x), ∂P/∂x = ρ(g − ω^2 x), g_eff = g − ω^2 x used in the x-direction, or any nonzero projection of g along x when the problem states the motion/geometry is in a horizontal plane. Allowed cases include solutions that explicitly state the axis has a vertical component (e.g., tube inclined by angle θ, using ρ g cosθ projection) or that the coordinate under consideration is vertical. Correction: remove the gravity term from the horizontal radial balance; only include centrifugal (and, if applicable, Coriolis for moving fluids) so that ∂P/∂x relates to ρ ω^2 x with appropriate sign.

Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Unjustified equation of state or assumed density profile in force-balance problems
Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Flag solutions that introduce an arbitrary equation of state (EOS) or a specific functional form for density or pressure (e.g., polytropic or ideal-gas relations) without explicit justification when the problem only requires hydrostatic/force balance to relate pressure gradient to density. Detection criteria: (1) The problem states or implies a relation of the form ∂P/∂x = β · ρ(x) (or pressure gradient proportional to density) under a known body acceleration a(x) (e.g., rotating frame with a(x) = ω^2 x), where β should be identified directly from equilibrium (β = a(x), up to sign by coordinate choice). (2) The solution assumes or derives a specific EOS or density profile that is not given or derived from stated constraints, such as P = K ρ^γ, P ∝ ρ^γ, P = ρ R T (with unspecified T), or ρ(x) = ρ0 f(x; γ, K, C), including forms like ρ(x) = ρ0 (1 + α x^2)^(-γ). (3) The solution introduces new thermodynamic parameters or constants (γ, K, n, T0, C) not present in the problem statement and uses them to compute ρ(x) or P(x) instead of determining β from ∂P/∂x = ρ a(x). (4) The solution claims an EOS is needed to find β when β follows directly from force balance. Examples to flag: mentions of 'polytropic', 'adiabatic', 'isothermal', 'P = K ρ^γ', 'P = ρ R T', or explicit profiles like ρ(x) = ρ0 (1 + ω^2 x^2 / 2C)^(-γ) in contexts where the task is only to extract β from the body acceleration. The rule does not evaluate sign conventions; it focuses on the unjustified modeling assumption that bypasses the direct equilibrium relation.

Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Disallow unjustified averaging of position-dependent beta in rotating equilibrium
Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Checks solutions where the problem defines ΔP/Δx = beta · ρ(x) for gas in a tube rotating about x = 0 with angular speed ω. In a rotating frame, the equilibrium balance is ΔP/Δx = -ρ(x) ω^2 x, hence beta(x) = -ω^2 x (position-dependent). The rule flags: (a) claims that beta is a constant (e.g., beta = ±ω^2) when the derived force balance contains explicit x-dependence, (b) steps that remove x-dependence by “averaging over the tube” or substituting x with an average/representative value without explicit instruction or justified approximation, and (c) dimensional inconsistencies (beta must have dimensions of acceleration [m/s^2]; ω^2 alone has [1/s^2]). To pass, the solution must retain beta(x) with its x-dependence (and correct sign/units) or clearly justify and quantify any approximation (e.g., small-x limit or an explicitly requested spatial average) while preserving dimensional consistency.

Mathematical Methods in Physics.title: Invalid use of first-order Taylor expansion in independent variable to locate extrema
Mathematical Methods in Physics.description:
This rule flags solutions that attempt to determine maxima/minima of a quantity f(θ) by linearizing f with respect to θ around an arbitrary θ0 and then inferring extrema from the linearized form. The following patterns are checked:
- The solution introduces a Taylor series in θ (e.g., "first-order Taylor expansion around θ0") for the quantity of interest (e.g., δθ(θ)) and keeps only the linear term in (θ−θ0).
- The solution sets the derivative of the linearized approximation to zero and concludes θ = θ0 or otherwise claims an extremum without analyzing the original function f(θ).
- The solution uses small-parameter assumptions (e.g., K_b, K_s ≪ 1) to justify linearization in θ instead of linearizing in the small parameters, with no derivation of the actual θ-dependence from the model.
- The solution does not compute d f/dθ from the original (or parameter-expanded) functional form, nor does it use second-order information (second derivative or curvature) to identify and classify extrema.
- The conclusion about the extremum is tautological (e.g., "maximized at θ0" simply because the expansion is around θ0) or based on properties of a linear function (which has no interior extrema) without reference to boundary conditions or the true functional form.
The verifier should require that extrema in θ be found by: (1) deriving f(θ) or its leading-order dependence from the model, (2) solving d f/dθ = 0 for candidate headings, and (3) confirming via second derivative or comparison of values. If only a first-order-in-θ expansion is used or θ0 is chosen ad hoc without justification, the solution should be flagged as a logic error.

Mathematical Methods in Physics.title: Misuse of small coefficients to justify linearizing in the angular variable
Mathematical Methods in Physics.description: This rule flags solutions that conflate the smallness of parameters (e.g., K_b, K_s << 1) with a need to Taylor-expand or linearize the function in the angular variable θ. Small coefficients constrain amplitude and permit dropping higher-order terms in those coefficients (e.g., O(K^2)), but they do not justify a Taylor series in θ unless θ itself is stated to be near a specific value. For extrema with respect to θ, the locations are determined by the θ-dependence (e.g., sin(nθ), cos(nθ)) via d/dθ = 0, and for single trigonometric terms the extrema occur at fixed angles independent of the amplitude. Trigger conditions include: (1) performing a Taylor expansion of δθ(θ) around θ0 solely because K_b, K_s are small; (2) asserting that the headings of maximum deviation depend on the magnitudes of K_b or K_s when the model’s angular dependence sets the extrema (e.g., sin(2θ) → maxima at θ = π/4 + kπ/2); (3) failing to analyze angular dependence (taking dδθ/dθ = 0) while using smallness of coefficients as the primary justification for finding maxima. Correct approach: keep the full θ-dependence, treat small parameters only as amplitude scalars (discard higher-order products of them if appropriate), and locate maxima/minima by differentiating with respect to θ.

Mathematical Methods in Physics.title: Chain/Product Rule Coefficient Consistency for Monomial × Powered Binomial
Mathematical Methods in Physics.description: Checks derivatives of expressions of the form v(t) = C · t^n · (A − B · t^p)^q for correct application of the product and chain rules. The mathematically correct derivative, when factoring out the same outer constant C, is dv/dt = C · [ n · t^(n−1) · (A − B · t^p)^q + t^n · q · (A − B · t^p)^(q−1) · (−B · p · t^(p−1)) ]. The verifier inspects the student's derivative and validates: (1) The inner bracket’s second term has a coefficient exactly q · B · p (with correct sign), multiplying t^(n+p−1) and (A − B · t^p)^(q−1). (2) No duplication of outer prefactors occurs inside the bracket: the inner coefficient must not include C, B^2, or extra powers of parameters (e.g., g) beyond those present in B. For example, if v(t) = −(g^2/8) · t^3 · (R^2 − (g^2/16) · t^4)^(−1/2), the correct inner coefficient is (g^2/8), not (g^4/64); including g^4 inside the bracket while also multiplying by an outer g^2/8 constitutes double-counting and triggers this rule. The rule allows algebraically equivalent factorizations but flags any derivative where the chain-rule term’s coefficient deviates from q · B · p or contains repeated outer constants.

Mathematical Methods in Physics.title: Definite integral variable/limits mismatch and missing change-of-variable
Mathematical Methods in Physics.description: This rule checks that definite integrals use a consistent integration variable with their limits and that any change of variable is properly executed. It flags expressions of the form ∫_{L}^{U} f(...) dξ where (a) the limits L,U are given in terms of a variable x ≠ ξ (e.g., r_S, r0) without an explicit substitution mapping x↔ξ and transformed limits, or (b) the integrand depends on a variable x (e.g., f(r)) while the differential is in a different variable ξ (e.g., dτ) without providing x(ξ) (or dx/dξ) and converting limits accordingly. In GR time-of-fall computations (e.g., Schwarzschild), it specifically flags attempts to compute coordinate time t with forms like t = ∫ dτ / F(r) or t = ∫ dτ · F(r) over r-limits (e.g., from ∞ to r_S) without (i) writing t as t = ∫ (dt/dτ) dτ or t = ∫ (dt/dr) dr and (ii) supplying the relation r(τ) or dr/dτ to justify the variable change and consistent limits. Example trigger: t = ∫_{∞}^{r_S} dτ / (1 − r_S/r) (limits in r, differential dτ, no r(τ) provided). The rule requires either matching limits with the differential (e.g., dr with r-limits) or an explicit, correct change-of-variable (including transformed limits) before accepting the integral setup.

Mathematical Methods in Physics.title: Validate binomial/Taylor coefficients for √(1±x) and (1±x)^(−1/2) expansions
Mathematical Methods in Physics.description: This rule checks small-parameter (|x| << 1) series expansions used in physics derivations—especially in relativistic Doppler problems—for correct second-order binomial/Taylor coefficients. It flags incorrect or swapped coefficients between √(1±x) and its inverse. Specifically: 1) For √(1 ± x), the correct expansion up to O(x^2) is: 1 ± (x/2) − (x^2/8). Using ±(3x^2/8) here is incorrect. 2) For (1 ± x)^(−1/2) or 1/√(1 ± x), the correct expansion up to O(x^2) is: 1 ∓ (x/2) + (3x^2/8). Using −(x^2/8) here is incorrect. 3) For the relativistic Doppler factor √(1 − β)/√(1 + β), the consistent combined expansion up to O(β^2) is: 1 − β + (β^2/2). The rule scans derivations that claim second-order approximations for these forms and verifies the coefficients match the above. It raises an error when the second-order terms are swapped (e.g., using +3x^2/8 in the √ expansion) or otherwise deviate from the correct values, even if the numerical impact is small (e.g., β ~ 2×10^−5). Scope: any step labeled as binomial/Taylor approximation, series expansion, or small-β approximation involving √(1±x), (1±x)^(−1/2), or their ratios. Failure condition: mismatch of the second-order coefficient signs/magnitudes relative to the correct forms.

Electromagnetism.title: Axion-induced field mis-modeled as standard toroidal field
Electromagnetism.description: Checks solutions for modeling errors where the axion-induced effective current density J = g (da/dt) B in a toroidal magnet is treated as producing the standard toroidal solenoid field inside the core rather than the axial field in the pickup-loop region. The rule triggers if: (1) the solution uses or derives B = μ0 N I / (2π r) (or equivalent Ampère's law toroid expressions) to obtain the axion-driven magnetic field; (2) the induced field at the detector/pickup loop is described as azimuthal (φ-hat) or 'toroidal' rather than axial (z-hat); (3) the field is evaluated only inside the toroid core (at radius r along the winding) instead of in the central bore where the pickup loop resides; (4) an 'effective current' I_eff is substituted into the toroid formula (e.g., I_eff ≈ ∫ J·dA or I_eff ∝ g a0 ω B A) to compute Bφ in the core. Context cues include explicit use of μ0 N I/(2π r), Ampère's law around the toroid, references to the azimuthal unit vector φ̂ for the detected field, or language indicating the flux is taken from the toroidal core field. A compliant modeling should recognize that J_eff is azimuthal within the magnet volume and sources an oscillating axial (z-directed) magnetic field in the bore/pickup-loop region; the rule flags deviations from this geometry and orientation.

Electromagnetism.title: Require ln(R_out/R_in) from 1/r field integration in toroidal/annular geometries
Electromagnetism.description: Checks solutions that compute axial magnetic field or magnetic flux produced by azimuthal currents (including effective currents like J = g·ȧ·B) in a toroidal or annular geometry. In such cases the static toroidal field inside the magnet obeys B(r) ∝ 1/r (e.g., B(r) = μ0 N I / (2π r)), and any radial integration over the annulus Rin < r < Rout must yield a logarithmic geometry factor ln(R_out/R_in). The rule flags a modeling error if: (a) the solution assumes a uniform B inside the toroid or uses a single radius (R_avg) without radial integration; (b) the final expression for the axial field or flux depends linearly on (R_out − R_in) or only on an average radius and lacks ln(R_out/R_in), ln(R2/R1), log(Ro/Ri), or an explicit ∫(dr/r) integral; (c) Ampère’s law or B(r) ∝ 1/r is invoked but the necessary radial integral over the annulus is omitted. Acceptable indicators include an explicit integral ∫_{R_in}^{R_out} (dr/r) or a final result containing the logarithmic factor. Trigger heuristics: presence of toroidal/annular geometry terms (toroid, toroidal solenoid, annulus, ring, inner radius, outer radius) and 1/r field statements (B = μ0 N I /(2π r), B ∝ 1/r). If these appear without the logarithmic factor or equivalent radial integral, flag the solution.

Electromagnetism.title: Double-counting coil turns when using B or B_max
Electromagnetism.description: This rule flags solutions that define a coil-generated magnetic field in terms of the number of turns N (e.g., B or B_max given by B = mu0 * N * I / (path length), or explicitly B_max = mu0 * N * I / (2*pi*R)), and then later present a final result that still includes an explicit multiplicative factor of the same N together with B or B_max. For a fixed magnetic field amplitude B (or B_max), measurable quantities driven by the field (e.g., axion-induced effective current J = g * dot(a) * B, induced voltage/flux in a pickup system, etc.) must not depend separately on the coil's turn count N used to generate B; N only enters through B when expressing B in terms of coil parameters. The rule checks for patterns such as 'answer ∝ N * B', 'answer ∝ N * B_max', or 'answer contains both B (or B_max) and an extra N factor' after B (or B_max) has already been defined using N. It also flags apparent double counting like 'answer ∝ N^2 I' resulting from keeping N outside B while B was set proportional to N*I. Exception: a distinct pickup coil turn count (e.g., N_pickup) may legitimately appear if it was not the N used to define the source field B; the rule attempts to match the same symbol N used in the B definition. Remediation: either (a) express the final result entirely in terms of I and N by substituting B = mu0 * N * I / (...) and remove B/B_max, or (b) keep the result in terms of B or B_max and remove the separate N factor so the scaling is not double counted.

Electromagnetism.title: Annular/Toroidal Area Sign and Consistent Use in Enclosed Current/Flux
Electromagnetism.description: This rule verifies the correctness and consistency of cross-sectional area definitions in annular or toroidal geometries used to compute enclosed current or magnetic flux. It flags: (1) negative or unphysical area expressions such as A = π (R_in^2 − R_out^2) when R_out > R_in; the correct annular area is A = π (R_out^2 − R_in^2) ≥ 0. (2) Inconsistent reuse of an area variable: if an area A is defined (e.g., annular area), subsequent steps must use the same expression when computing enclosed current I_enclosed = ∫ J · dA or flux Φ_B = ∫ B · dA; switching to a different area (e.g., π R_in^2 or π r^2) without explicit, justified change of region/geometry is flagged. (3) Misuse of A(r): if an area is defined as a constant (from fixed R_in, R_out), later steps must not treat it as a function of r; conversely, if A(r) is defined for a radius-dependent region (e.g., π r^2), it must remain radius-dependent consistently. The rule also checks dimensional consistency (area must be non-negative and have units of length^2) and raises an error if the sign or geometry of the area used in enclosed-current/flux derivations is inconsistent with earlier definitions.

Electromagnetism.title: Proper use of Ampère’s law with volume current density (no coil-formula substitution)
Electromagnetism.description:
This rule flags solutions that misuse Ampère’s law by treating a continuous current density (e.g., axion-induced J = g · ȧ · B) as if it were a discrete line current or a multi-turn coil. The verifier checks: 
- If formulas for discrete line/coil currents (e.g., B = μ0 I/(2π r) or B = μ0 N I/(2π r)) are invoked when the source is a distributed volume current density with no physical windings, flag. 
- If I_enclosed is set equal to J (A/m^2) or to J times a path length, instead of computing I_enclosed = ∫ J · dA over a surface bounded by the chosen Ampère loop, flag. 
- If the solution asserts local proportionalities like B ∝ μ0 J without specifying and justifying the Ampère loop, symmetry, and boundary conditions needed to infer field direction and spatial dependence, flag. 
- If geometric/linking factors are imported from coil analogies (e.g., using N, toroid geometry factors) when no actual turns exist, or if flux through a pickup loop is computed without integrating B over the loop area, flag. 
- Unit consistency check: substituting J (A/m^2) into equations that require I (A) without an explicit area integral leads to a dimensional mismatch; flag. 
- For axion effective currents, the field must be obtained from Maxwell–Ampère (∇×B = μ0 J_total + μ0 ε0 ∂E/∂t) or Biot–Savart with the actual geometry; relying solely on coil/solenoid analogies without a proper derivation is insufficient.

Electromagnetism.title: Region consistency in magnetic flux calculations
Electromagnetism.description: Flag solutions that compute magnetic flux through a pickup loop by multiplying a magnetic field expression valid in one spatial region by the area of a loop located in a different region. Specifically, for axion-induced currents (J = g · (da/dt) · B) in toroidal geometries: (1) Using the toroidal solenoid formula B(r) = μ0 N I / (2π r) (which applies inside the magnet core for line currents in windings) to estimate the flux through a loop placed in the central bore, and then forming Φ = B(r≈R_in) × A_loop, is incorrect and should be flagged. (2) Treating the effective current density J as a single wire current I and inserting it into the toroid formula without deriving the field in the bore from the distributed azimuthal volume current is incorrect. (3) The magnetic field used in Φ = ∫ B · dA must be computed in the same region as the loop area, with appropriate boundary conditions and source geometry; for axion searches, this means deriving the bore field from the annular, azimuthal current density rather than the core-confined field of the windings. The rule triggers when a solution mixes a core-only field expression with a bore-area flux calculation or substitutes J into B = μ0 N I / (2π r) and then multiplies by the pickup loop area without a bore-field derivation.

Electromagnetism.title: Toroidal axion-induced flux scaling: log(R_out/R_in) and independence from N
Electromagnetism.description: This rule verifies the geometric/dimensional scaling of the magnetic flux Phi_B induced by an axion-effective current in toroidal geometries. It applies when the solution computes Phi_B through a pickup loop for a toroid (or toroidal solenoid) under an axion field a(t) = a0 sin(ω t) with effective current density J = g * dot(a) * B, where dot(a) = a0 ω cos(ω t). Checks: (1) Time dependence: Phi_B must contain cos(ω t) (from dot(a)); absence is flagged. (2) Radial/geometric dependence: For a toroidal field that scales as 1/r, the radial integration must produce a logarithmic dependence ln(R_out/R_in); results that depend on R_loop^2, (R_out^2 − R_in^2), or any purely area-like quadratic radius terms without a logarithm are flagged. (3) Expected scaling: Up to order-unity geometric factors, Phi_B should scale as ~ μ0 g a0 B_max ω R_in^3 ln(R_out/R_in) cos(ω t); results missing the ln(R_out/R_in) term or the cubic inner-radius scaling are flagged. (4) Independence from winding number: If the result is re-expressed in terms of the maximum toroidal field B_max, the final Phi_B must not depend explicitly on the winding number N; any residual N-dependence is flagged. Rationale: In toroidal geometries, the effective field generated by J ∝ B produces a 1/r dependence, and the correct flux integration over r yields a logarithmic term, not a quadratic area scaling. This rule catches solutions with incorrect dimensional/geometric dependencies, such as Phi_B ∝ R_loop^2 and missing ln(R_out/R_in), or spurious dependence on N once B_max is used.

General Relativity and Cosmology.title: Comoving vs physical number density consistency and a^-3 scaling
General Relativity and Cosmology.description: Checks for confusion between comoving and physical number density in cosmology problems. The rule flags solutions that: (1) define n(t) as a physical number density (e.g., using terms like "physical number density", "n_p", or "n_phys") and then assert that "the number density in comoving coordinates remains constant" using the same variable (e.g., n(t) = n(t0)) without introducing a distinct comoving variable; (2) fail to state or use the correct scaling for physical number density with expansion, namely n_phys(t) = n_phys(t0) * [a(t0)/a(t)]^3 (equivalently n_phys ∝ a^-3) under no creation/annihilation; (3) present an explicit scaling n(t) ∝ a(t)^k with k ≠ -3 while referring to n as physical, unless n is explicitly labeled as comoving; (4) introduce both "comoving" and "physical" number density terms but omit an explicit relation connecting them, or use the same symbol for both; (5) derive radiation energy density scaling inconsistent with a^-4 (e.g., using constant n or n ∝ a^0 or n ∝ a^-2) due to incorrect number-density treatment. Detection heuristics: parse for keywords/phrases such as "comoving", "physical", "number density", "n(t)", "n_p", "n_phys", "n_comov", and statements like "remains constant" or equalities n(t) = n(t0). If a variable previously identified as physical is later claimed constant in comoving coordinates without redefining it as comoving, flag. Expected correct formulation: define a distinct comoving number density n_comov that is constant, and relate the physical number density via n_phys(t) = n_comov / a(t)^3 = n_phys(t0) * [a(t0)/a(t)]^3; for radiation energy density, require ρ_r(t) ∝ a^-4 from n_phys ∝ a^-3 and E_photon ∝ a^-1.

General Relativity and Cosmology.title: Scale-factor ratio consistency for comoving-to-physical conversions
General Relativity and Cosmology.description: This rule verifies that, in FLRW cosmology under no peculiar motion, quantities related at time t and at a reference time t0 are expressed using the correct ratio of scale factors. For a fixed comoving region, physical volume must satisfy V_p(t)/V_p(t0) = [a(t)/a(t0)]^3. Derived scalings then require: number density n_p(t) = n_p(t0) [a(t0)/a(t)]^3, photon energy E(t) = E(t0) [a(t0)/a(t)], and radiation energy density rho_r(t) = rho_r(t0) [a(t0)/a(t)]^4. The rule flags any step where absolute powers of a(t) are used without the corresponding a(t0) in ratio form (e.g., V_p(t) = a(t)^3 V_p(t0), n_p(t) = n_p(t0)/a(t)^3), or where the exponent of a(t0) does not match the expected exponent (e.g., rho_r(t) = rho_r(t0) * a(t0)/a(t)^4). It also flags expressions that leave a standalone factor of a(t0) not appearing in a ratio with a(t). The check is performed on intermediate steps and final results; even if a correct final result is stated, any inconsistent intermediate scaling is reported. To avoid false positives, the rule is suppressed if the derivation explicitly normalizes a(t0) = 1 (or declares a0 = 1), in which case ratio expressions reduce correctly to powers of a(t) alone.

Signal Processing and GNSS.title: Receiver without a clock cannot measure reception time or signal delay
Signal Processing and GNSS.description: Flag a conceptual error when a solution claims that a receiver lacking an internal clock or synchronization to the transmitter time scale can directly measure the reception time t or the signal time-of-flight Δt = t − t_i. In such setups (e.g., GNSS-like problems), the only time provided by the signal is the emission timestamp t_i and the satellite position at t_i; the receiver cannot know t or Δt_i without a local clock referenced to the same time system. The correct formulation must treat the reception time (or receiver clock bias) as an unknown to be solved simultaneously with position using range equations (e.g., c · (t − t_i) = |r − r_i| for multiple satellites). This rule should trigger if the problem statement specifies the receiver has no clock or is unsynchronized, yet the solution asserts: (a) the receiver measures Δt_i directly, (b) the receiver knows the exact reception time t, or (c) the receiver infers time-of-flight from signal content alone without introducing an unknown reception time/clock bias and solving for it.

Signal Processing and GNSS.title: Inconsistent use of measured time delay and unknown reception time in GNSS unknown counting
Signal Processing and GNSS.description:
Checks for internal inconsistencies in time-of-flight positioning (e.g., GPS-like problems) where a solution simultaneously treats the per-satellite time delay Δt_i as a measured/known quantity and also treats the reception time (or receiver clock bias) as an unknown in the unknown-counting argument. This error leads to incoherent equation/unknown counting (e.g., concluding four satellites are needed while claiming Δt_i is measured). The verifier should flag solutions that meet the following conditions:
- The solution states the receiver has no clock or an unknown clock bias (keywords: "no clock", "unknown clock", "clock bias").
- The solution claims the receiver can measure or knows the time delay between emission and reception for each satellite (keywords: "measure Δt", "known Δt", "time delay Δt_i").
- The solution also treats the absolute reception time t (or an equivalent receiver clock bias b) as an unknown and uses this to justify the number of satellites by counting unknowns (keywords: "unknown t", "four unknowns", "need four satellites").
- Optional consistency check: If Δt_i is asserted known, then the minimal unknown set is (x, y, z) and three satellites suffice in principle; if t (or clock bias) is unknown, then Δt_i cannot be directly measured without a receiver clock and should not be treated as known. Flag when both are asserted simultaneously.
The rule triggers an error when these contradictory assertions co-occur, indicating double-counting or misclassification of time quantities (t vs Δt_i) in the reasoning.

Ordinary Differential Equations.title: Incorrect exponential solution for linear ODEs with time/geometry-dependent coefficients
Ordinary Differential Equations.description:
This rule flags solutions that treat a variable coefficient in a first-order linear ODE as constant, yielding an exponential with the coefficient simply multiplied by time. It targets errors like replacing a constant k by k(t) inside exp(−k t) without integrating k(t), or using the constant-coefficient template v(t) = v_ss [1 − exp(−k t)] with k replaced by a time-/state-dependent quantity.

What the rule checks:
- Identify statements (explicit or implied) of a linear ODE of the form dv/dt + α(t) v = β(t) or m dv/dt + b(t) v = c, where α or b depends on time t or on the state via geometry (e.g., A(t) = W [L − x(t)]).
- Search the presented solution for exponential factors of the form exp(−α(t) t), exp(−b(t) t / m), or exp(−k(t) t), i.e., a coefficient evaluated at t multiplied by t inside the exponent, without an integral over time.
- Flag the specific pattern v(t) = [β/α](t) × [1 − exp(−∫? ...)] used incorrectly as v(t) = (β/α(t)) [1 − exp(−α(t) t)] or similar, unless α is explicitly constant.
- In the sliding-plate context, detect the substitution A → A(t) in an exponential decay factor derived for constant area, e.g., v(t) = (mg Z)/(η A) [1 − exp(−(η A)/(m Z) t)] followed by replacing A with A(t) inside the exponent.

Acceptance criteria for correct handling:
- For dv/dt + α(t) v = β(t), the solution must use an integrating factor with an integral: exp(−∫ α(t) dt). Any exponential decay factor must involve ∫ α(t) dt, not α(t)·t.
- If the coefficient depends on geometry through the state (e.g., α(t) ∝ A(x(t))), the solution should either:
  - correctly employ the integrating-factor method with ∫ α(t) dt, or
  - reformulate in the appropriate variable and separate, e.g., mg = η[A(x)/Z] dx/dt and integrate in x when A depends on x.

How the rule is applied:
- If a solution uses an exponential decay factor where the coefficient inside the exponent is a function of t or of the state (e.g., A(t), x(t)) without an explicit time integral, flag as incorrect.
- If a solution presents v(t) = v_ss [1 − exp(−k(t) t)] or v(t) = (c/b(t)) [1 − exp(−b(t) t/m)] with time-/state-dependent b or k, flag as incorrect.
- Provide corrective hint: Replace exp(−k(t) t) by exp(−∫ k(t) dt). If k depends on x via geometry (e.g., A = W (L − x)), recast the ODE into mg = η [A(x)/Z] dx/dt and integrate exactly in x.

Example of the error this rule catches:
- Writing v(t) = (mg Z)/(η A) [1 − exp(−(η A)/(m Z) t)] and then substituting A → A(t) inside the exponent. Correct approach: use exp(−∫ (η A(t))/(m Z) dt) or separate variables via mg = η (W (L − x))/Z · dx/dt and integrate in x.

Ordinary Differential Equations.title: Incorrect solution form for ODE y'' = k y'
Ordinary Differential Equations.description: This rule checks for misapplication of solution templates to linear ODEs where the second derivative equals a constant times the first derivative. If a solution states or implies an ODE of the form d^2y/dx^2 = k dy/dx with k constant, the correct general solution is y(x) = C1 + C2 exp(k x). Flag an error if any of the following are detected: (1) the solution uses the template for d^2y/dx^2 = a y instead, e.g., y(x) = A exp(√k x) + B exp(−√k x), or presents symmetric ± exponential terms plus a constant; (2) the exponential argument contains √k rather than k; (3) the characteristic equation is incorrectly taken as r^2 = k (appropriate for y'' = k y) rather than r(r − k) = 0 (appropriate for y'' = k y'); (4) dimensional inconsistency in k relative to the ODE: if x is a length, then in y'' = k y' the dimension of k must be 1/length; assigning k = ρ g/γ (dimension 1/length^2) while multiplying dy/dx (dimensionless) cannot produce y'' (dimension 1/length). The rule is intended to catch errors like solving u' = k u with the wrong template, using square roots of coefficients in exponentials, or presenting an unjustified pair of exponentials for an equation that admits only a constant plus a single exponential term.

Ordinary Differential Equations.title: Far-field decay and boundary-condition consistency for ODE solutions
Ordinary Differential Equations.description: Checks that all stated boundary conditions are simultaneously enforced in the final solution, especially far-field decay requirements. Applicable to linear ODE solutions that include exponential modes (e.g., terms like e^{+k x} and e^{-k x}) and possible constant offsets. The verifier will: (1) Parse the proposed solution z(x) and evaluate lim_{x→∞} z(x); if a far-field condition z(∞)=z_far is specified (commonly z_far=0), the limit must equal z_far. (2) Ensure coefficients of any growing mode (e^{+k x}, polynomial growth) are set to zero to avoid divergence if the problem requires boundedness/decay at infinity. (3) Detect non-decaying constant offsets: if z(x) contains an additive constant C or an asymptotic offset produced by an undetermined constant (e.g., z(x)=C + B e^{-k x}), then C must be fixed by the far-field boundary condition; it is incorrect to set C using a local boundary (e.g., z(0)) while leaving other constants nonzero such that z(∞)≠z_far. The rule flags solutions where the far-field boundary is violated (z(∞)≠z_far) or where constants are chosen in a way that satisfies a near-field boundary but contradicts the far-field decay (e.g., A=0 to remove e^{+k x} but C≠0 leading to a nonzero asymptote). This catches the common error of inconsistent boundary-condition application that yields a final expression not decaying to the specified far-field level.

Ordinary Differential Equations.title: Far-field boundary condition compliance (limit at infinity)
Ordinary Differential Equations.description: Checks that the final closed-form solution satisfies the stated far-field boundary condition. Implementation: 1) Parse the problem for a boundary of the form z(x) → z_inf as x → ∞ (commonly z_inf = 0). 2) Compute the limit of the submitted z(x) as x → ∞. 3) If the limit does not equal z_inf, flag a violation. This catches common errors where an additive constant causes a nonzero asymptote (e.g., z(x) = A + B exp(-x/ell) with A ≠ z_inf) or where the wrong exponential sign leads to growth. For static capillary profiles near a vertical plate with z(∞) = 0, only decaying terms are allowed; a correct minimal form is z(x) = C exp(-x/ell). The rule additionally detects typical misforms like z(x) = ell tan(theta0) (1 − exp(−x/ell)) that approach ell tan(theta0) instead of 0. Optionally, if a slope boundary at x = 0 is provided (e.g., z'(0) = tan(theta0)), verify consistency for single-exponential solutions: C = −ell tan(theta0), ensuring both the correct sign and zero far-field limit.

Trigonometry and Periodicity.title: Verify extrema classification and periodicity in trigonometric angle problems
Trigonometry and Periodicity.description: This rule checks solutions that seek headings/angles θ at which a quantity (e.g., deviation δθ) is maximized/minimized when the dependence on θ is trigonometric (such as δθ = A sin θ + B cos θ or equivalent). The rule flags two common errors: (1) failing to provide the full periodic set of critical angles, and (2) failing to verify that the identified critical points correspond to maxima (not merely stationary points). Specifically: • If the solution sets d(δθ)/dθ = 0 and obtains a condition of the form tan θ = constant, it must present the general solution θ = arctan(constant) + nπ (or the appropriate periodic family) or list all solutions over a declared domain (e.g., θ ∈ [0, 2π)). Providing only one or two specific angles without the + nπ or domain-complete enumeration is flagged. • If the solution claims angles of maximum without justification, it must include a correct extremum classification method: a second derivative test (d²(δθ)/dθ² < 0 at maxima), an equivalent neighborhood sign check, or a phase-amplitude rewrite (e.g., δθ = R sin(θ + φ) with maxima at θ + φ = π/2 + 2πn). Absence of such classification is flagged. • Acceptable evidence of periodicity includes explicit use of nπ or 2πn, or correctly listing all solutions within a stated interval. • The rule applies even when small parameters (e.g., K_b, K_s ≪ 1) are invoked, as smallness does not remove periodicity or the need to classify extrema.

Trigonometry and Periodicity.title: Symmetry-derived equality must not be replaced by a different ratio without explicit derivation
Trigonometry and Periodicity.description: This rule checks for internal logical consistency when a solution uses symmetry to assert equality between two physical quantities and later claims a non-unit ratio between the same quantities without a clear, quantitative bridge. The verifier scans for an initial statement such as "by symmetry" or equivalent reasoning that concludes A = B (or a ratio A/B = 1). It then looks for subsequent assertions that A = k·B with k ≠ 1 (e.g., A = (1/3)·B) applied to the same defined quantities. If the later change in ratio is not accompanied by explicit derivation steps—such as application of governing laws (e.g., Maxwell's equations, conservation/continuity relations), boundary-condition analysis, geometric/topological modifications, or quantified coupling arguments—the solution is flagged as inconsistent. The rule also flags the introduction of new physical effects (e.g., "shielding", "screening") not specified in the problem statement unless they are quantitatively modeled or justified by referenced properties and equations. Scope: general physics (e.g., magnetism, circuits, mechanics, fluids) where symmetry implies equal partitioning or equality. Trigger conditions: (1) symmetry-based equality claim; (2) later non-equal numeric ratio for the same variables; (3) absence of an explicit derivation or changed assumptions bridging the two claims.

General Problem Solving and Verification.title: Missing numeric final results for requested quantities
General Problem Solving and Verification.description: Checks that a solution provides explicit numeric values (with appropriate units) for all quantities the problem explicitly asks to calculate (e.g., radius of curvature R and contact angle α). The rule first identifies target outputs from the problem text by matching verbs such as 'calculate', 'compute', 'determine', 'find' and associated quantity names/symbols (e.g., 'R', 'α', 'radius of curvature', 'contact angle'). It then scans the solution for corresponding numeric assignments. A valid result must include digits and, when applicable, units (e.g., 'R = 12 mm', 'α ≈ 35°'). The rule flags as errors any solutions where: (a) the final answers for the requested quantities are absent; (b) the quantities are only expressed symbolically or as formulas (e.g., 'R = f(n_w, h, d)') without numeric evaluation; or (c) placeholders or incomplete markers are present (e.g., '...', 'TBD', 'to be determined', 'approx using lensmaker's formula' without numbers). For angle outputs, expects degrees or radians; for lengths, expects a length unit (m, cm, mm). This catches incomplete calculations where the method is described but no numerical results are produced.

General Problem Solving and Verification.title: Enforce explicit dependence and allowed symbols in final expression
General Problem Solving and Verification.description: This rule verifies that when a prompt specifies variable dependence (e.g., 'as a function of x and t') and allowed parameters (e.g., 'express all answers in terms of v0, ω, s, r'), the submitted final expression explicitly includes every required independent variable and only uses the permitted symbols. Procedure: (1) Parse the instruction to extract the set of required independent variables (e.g., {x, t}) and the allowed parameter set (e.g., {v0, ω, s, r}). (2) Parse the student's final reported expression for the target quantity and collect its symbol set. (3) Check presence: every required independent variable must appear explicitly in the final expression; if any are missing (e.g., a(t) provided without x when 'a(x, t)' was requested), flag an error. (4) Check allowed symbols: the expression must not contain disallowed symbols (e.g., k, m, μ, μ0, g) when the prompt restricts to {v0, ω, s, r}; suggest using given relations (e.g., k/m → ω², μ/μ0 → r) to rewrite. (5) Do not treat implicit dependence via auxiliary definitions (such as substituting a provided x(t) afterward) as compliant; the required variables must appear explicitly in the final expression. This catches solutions that compute a correct form in terms of time only but fail to present the final quantity in the variables specified by the prompt, e.g., giving a(t) instead of the compact a(x, t) form like a = ω² (v0 t − x + (1 − r)s).

General Problem Solving and Verification.title: Missing explicit final expression for requested quantity
General Problem Solving and Verification.description: When the problem statement explicitly asks to 'find', 'compute', or 'determine' a target quantity Q (e.g., the height h), the solution must include a final, explicit expression isolating Q on the left-hand side (Q = ...) with either a numeric value or a symbolic formula in terms of the given parameters/constants. Trigger an error if any of the following are true: (1) The solution ends with only a general or intermediate relation (e.g., a conservation law such as KE_initial = KE_final + PE_final) without solving for Q; (2) The derivation terminates mid-equation (e.g., trailing operators, incomplete lines, or ellipses like '...' or notes such as 'truncated'); (3) Q appears only inside equations but is never isolated as Q = ...; (4) The purported final line contains unresolved placeholders (e.g., KE_initial, PE_final) or undefined symbols instead of substituted expressions leading to Q; (5) The final expression references undefined placeholders or meta text (e.g., '...', 'etc.', 'to be continued') or does not restrict itself to problem-given variables/constants. If these conditions are not satisfied, flag: 'Final expression for the requested quantity is missing or incomplete.'

General Problem Solving and Verification.title: Verify mapping and validity when applying a parametric integral identity
General Problem Solving and Verification.description: This rule checks for misuse of standard parametric integral formulas (e.g., ∫₀^∞ dt (a+pt)/([(a+pt)^2+(b+qt)^2]^{3/2}) = 1/(bp−aq)(b/√(a²+b²) − q/√(p²+q²))). When such an identity is cited or implied, the solution must: (1) Explicitly define each parameter (a, b, p, q) in terms of the problem’s physical variables and show they are constants with respect to the integration variable; (2) Demonstrate the change of variables or algebraic transformation that converts the original integral to the canonical form, including correct transformation of limits to 0→∞; (3) State and verify the identity’s applicability conditions (e.g., bp − aq ≠ 0, denominator nonzero over the domain, any required sign/positivity assumptions), and confirm dimensional consistency (a and b share units; p and q share units of a per unit t); (4) Produce a final closed-form expression that matches the structure of the cited identity using the mapped parameters (e.g., dependence on 1/(bp−aq) and terms b/√(a²+b²), q/√(p²+q²)); (5) Ensure the final result has units consistent with the original integral. If the mapping, transformation, conditions, or structural correspondence are missing or inconsistent, flag a calculation error: misuse of integral identity without valid parameter identification or derivation.

New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.title: Incorrect use of Q_hot = Q_cold for maximum-work heat engine between finite reservoirs
New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.description: This rule flags solutions to problems where a heat engine extracts the maximum (theoretically allowed) work between two finite bodies/reservoirs if the student incorrectly models the process by setting the heat lost by the hot body equal to the heat gained by the cold body (Q_hot = Q_cold). In maximum-work scenarios, energy leaves the two-body system as work, so Q_hot > Q_cold and the correct criterion is a reversible process with zero total entropy change. Checks performed: (1) Context trigger: the problem mentions a heat engine operating between two finite bodies (or reservoirs) and requests maximum work/maximum mechanical energy/“theoretically allowed” work or a reversible process. (2) Correct criterion: verify the solution uses ΔS_total = 0 for reversible extraction, i.e., m_A s_A ln(T0/T_A) + m_B s_B ln(T0/T_B) = 0; for identical masses and specific heats, this implies T0 = sqrt(T_A T_B). (3) Error patterns to flag: (a) Equations or text asserting Q_A = Q_B, ms(T_A − T0) = ms(T0 − T_B), or “heat lost equals heat gained” when maximum work is sought; (b) Final equilibrium temperature T0 derived from energy balance alone, yielding an arithmetic or weighted mean, e.g., T0 = (T_A + T_B)/2 for equal m, s, or T0 = (m_A s_A T_A + m_B s_B T_B)/(m_A s_A + m_B s_B); (c) Absence of an entropy-balance derivation (no ΔS terms, no logarithmic temperature relation) in part (a) when maximum work is requested; (d) Work computed using the incorrect T0 from (a)/(b), or implicitly zero work due to Q_A = Q_B. (4) Acceptance criteria: Solutions should explicitly enforce ΔS_total = 0 and produce T0 = sqrt(T_A T_B) for equal m, s (or the general ln relation for unequal cases), and should recognize that Q_hot − Q_cold = W_max. For equal m, s, a consistent expression for maximum work is W_max = m s [T_A + T_B − 2 sqrt(T_A T_B)]. Any deviation from these criteria under the maximum-work context is flagged by this rule.

New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.title: Misuse of constant Carnot efficiency for finite reservoirs
New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.description: This rule flags solutions that treat finite reservoirs (objects/tanks with specified mass and specific heat) as if they were infinite, by using a single, fixed Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_c/T_h based on initial temperatures to compute maximum work. Trigger conditions: (a) The problem context includes two finite bodies whose temperatures change (e.g., given masses/volumes, specific heats, or a final equilibrium temperature is sought), and (b) the solution applies a constant η = 1 − T_B/T_A (or similar) to obtain W_max (e.g., W = η × Q_hot) without accounting for temperature variation. Correct requirement: For maximum work with finite reservoirs, the process must be reversible and the temperatures vary; the solution must either (i) perform an entropy balance ΔS_total = ΔS_A + ΔS_B = 0 to find the final temperature T_0 (general form: m_A s_A ln(T_A/T_0) = m_B s_B ln(T_0/T_B); for identical bodies, T_0 = sqrt(T_A T_B)), and then compute W_max = m_A s_A (T_A − T_0) − m_B s_B (T_0 − T_B), or (ii) integrate the variable efficiency as temperatures change. Failure patterns to flag include: using η = 1 − T_B/T_A with initial T_A, T_B as constants throughout; computing W_max as Q_hot × η with no entropy balance or integration; or deriving T_0 solely from energy balance (Q_hot = Q_cold) while simultaneously using constant Carnot efficiency. Exceptions: Do not flag if the problem explicitly states infinite reservoirs with fixed temperatures, or if the solution demonstrates a reversible path via entropy balance/integration of η(T) over the temperature range.

New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.title: Max work between finite equal-heat-capacity reservoirs must yield geometric-mean final temperature
New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.description:
Scope: Solutions that claim the maximum (reversible) work extractable by a heat engine operating between two finite bodies/reservoirs with equal (or proportional) heat capacities (e.g., same material, same mass m and specific heat s), initially at T_A > T_B.

What to check:
- Context detection: Look for problems stating two finite reservoirs/bodies, same material or equal heat capacity C = m s, initial temperatures T_A and T_B, and a request for the maximum (theoretically allowed) work/energy. Keywords: "maximum work", "reversible", "finite reservoirs", "two bodies", "same material", "specific heat".
- Correct equilibrium condition: For maximum work (reversible operation), the total entropy change must be zero: ΔS_A + ΔS_B = 0, which for constant C implies C ln(T_0/T_A) + C ln(T_0/T_B) = 0 ⇒ T_0 = sqrt(T_A T_B). The final common temperature must be the geometric mean, not the arithmetic mean.
- Correct work expression: The maximum work must equal the decrease in the combined thermal energy between the initial state and the reversible-equilibrium state at T_0 = sqrt(T_A T_B): W_max = C [T_A + T_B − 2 sqrt(T_A T_B)] = C (sqrt(T_A) − sqrt(T_B))^2.

Flag as error if any of the following are detected:
- The solution determines T_0 by equating heats Q_A = Q_B (e.g., m s (T_A − T_0) = m s (T_0 − T_B)) and/or concludes T_0 = (T_A + T_B)/2 (arithmetic mean) or any linear convex combination not equal to sqrt(T_A T_B).
- The solution omits the entropy balance and instead uses energy balance alone to find T_0 for a "maximum work" or "reversible" claim.
- The reported W_max depends on an arithmetic-mean T_0 or matches common incorrect forms such as W_max = C (T_A − T_B)^2 / (2 T_A) (or analogous expressions with T_A and T_B swapped), or any W_max inconsistent with C [T_A + T_B − 2 sqrt(T_A T_B)].

Acceptance criteria:
- T_0 must be explicitly given as sqrt(T_A T_B) for equal heat capacities (or the derivation via ΔS_A + ΔS_B = 0 is shown and leads to this result).
- W_max must reduce to C [T_A + T_B − 2 sqrt(T_A T_B)] = C (sqrt(T_A) − sqrt(T_B))^2. Numerical answers should be consistent with these formulas.

Notes to reduce false positives:
- Do not flag if the solver clearly states an approximation and quantifies that the arithmetic mean is used as an approximation for very small |T_A − T_B|, unless they claim it is the exact maximum-work condition.
- If heat capacities are not equal, the correct condition generalizes to C_A ln(T_0/T_A) + C_B ln(T_0/T_B) = 0; this rule targets the equal-heat-capacity case explicitly.

New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.title: Incorrect T0 and W_max for reversible engine between two identical finite reservoirs
New Category: Heat Engines and Reservoir.description: Applies to problems where a heat engine extracts the maximum (reversible) work between two finite bodies/reservoirs of the same material with equal mass m and constant specific heat s, initially at T_A > T_B, reaching a common final temperature T_0. The rule verifies the necessary reversible-process relations and flags common errors. Checks: (1) Entropy balance must be used (or implicitly satisfied): ΔS_total = C ln(T_0/T_A) + C ln(T_0/T_B) = 0 with C = m s, giving the only correct final temperature T_0 = sqrt(T_A T_B). Flags if the solution sets Q_A = Q_B or uses energy balance alone to get T_0 = (T_A + T_B)/2 (arithmetic mean) or any value not equal to the geometric mean. (2) Maximum work must satisfy W_max = C[(T_A - T_0) - (T_0 - T_B)] = C(T_A + T_B - 2 sqrt(T_A T_B)) = C(√T_A − √T_B)^2. Flags any alternative expressions lacking the square-root dependence (e.g., W_max = C (T_A − T_B), W_max = 0.5 C (T_A − T_B), or forms derived from Q_A = Q_B). (3) Heat flows must obey Q_A = C (T_A − T_0), Q_B = C (T_0 − T_B), with Q_A > Q_B and W_max = Q_A − Q_B > 0; flags if Q_A = Q_B is asserted. (4) Sanity bounds: T_0 must lie strictly between T_B and T_A and below the arithmetic mean; W_max must satisfy 0 < W_max < C (T_A − T_B); flags violations. (5) Units: W_max must be in joules (J); flags J/kg or J/K. (6) For the common numerical case with water tanks (each volume V = 2.50 m^3, T_A = 350 K, T_B = 300 K, s = 4.19e3 J·kg^-1·K^-1, density ρ ≈ 1000 kg·m^-3), the expected values are m ≈ 2.50×10^3 kg per tank, C ≈ 1.0475×10^7 J/K, T_0 ≈ sqrt(350×300) ≈ 324 K, and W_max ≈ C (√350 − √300)^2 ≈ 2.0×10^7 J. Flags if the computed W_max deviates by more than 10% from 2.0×10^7 J, uses an incorrect mass from volume, omits unit conversion from volume to mass, or leaves the numerical result unevaluated when all inputs are provided.

New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.title: Induced dipole of conducting spherical shell must be antiparallel to dB/dt
New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.description: Checks solutions for the thin-walled, nonmagnetic spherical shell in a slowly varying uniform magnetic field (quasistatic eddy current regime). The induced magnetic moment must oppose the change of the external field per Lenz's law. Specifically: (1) Context trigger: problem mentions a thin/thin-walled nonmagnetic spherical shell (radius R, thickness D) in a uniform, slowly changing magnetic field B(t) with time derivative dB/dt. (2) Expected relation: μ = -C · dB/dt, with C = (2π D R^4)/(3ρ) > 0 (ρ is resistivity). Only the component of μ along dB/dt may be nonzero; all perpendicular components must be zero by symmetry. (3) Direction/sign checks: flag if the solution states μ is parallel/same direction as dB/dt (or as B for an increasing field), omits the required negative sign in a proportional form (e.g., μ = +k dB/dt with k > 0), yields μ·(dB/dt) > 0, or assigns nonzero components of μ perpendicular to dB/dt. (4) Component check in aligned coordinates: if dB/dt is specified along a coordinate axis (e.g., y), require μ_x = 0, μ_z = 0, and μ_y = -C (dB/dt)_y; flag any μ_y with the wrong sign or any nonzero μ_x or μ_z. (5) Coefficient tolerance: allow any algebraically equivalent positive C; only the sign and direction must be as above. This rule catches concept errors where the induced μ is not antiparallel to dB/dt for the spherical shell in the quasistatic limit.

New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.title: Verify induced E-field and magnetic moment for thin spherical shell under uniform dB/dt
New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.description: Applies to solutions deriving the eddy-current-induced magnetic moment μ of a thin-walled nonmagnetic spherical shell (radius R, thickness D, resistivity ρ) in a slowly varying uniform magnetic field B(t). The verifier checks the following: (1) Induced tangential electric field: E_t must satisfy E_t = -(1/2) (dB/dt) × r on the shell surface. Using E_t = -(dB/dt) × r (missing 1/2), introducing radial/polar components, or any non-tangential direction inconsistent with (dB/dt) × r is flagged. (2) Surface current density: K must be K = (D/ρ) E_t. Any other proportionality or omission of D/ρ is flagged. (3) Magnetic moment computation: μ must be obtained via μ = (1/2) ∫ (r × K) dA over the shell. Omitting the 1/2 factor in the r×K integral is flagged. (4) Final result consistency: The closed-form expression must reduce to μ = -(2π/(3ρ)) D R^4 (dB/dt). The verifier checks sign (μ antiparallel to dB/dt), scaling (∝ R^4 and ∝ D/ρ), and numerical prefactor (2π/3). Any mismatch in sign, orientation, prefactor, or power of R (e.g., R^2 or R^3) is flagged. (5) Coordinate dependence and symmetry: For dB/dt along the z-axis, E_t must be azimuthal (φ direction) consistent with (dB/dt) × r and proportional to R sinθ on the surface. Claims that introduce θ-dependent or component choices that break spherical symmetry or yield E_t not aligned with (dB/dt) × r are flagged. (6) Faraday’s law application: The solution must use ∇×E = -dB/dt in a way that yields the 1/2 geometric factor for the sphere; directly setting E ∝ -dB/dt × r without the 1/2 for this geometry is flagged. This rule targets calculation errors in prefactors, component directions, and scaling leading to incorrect μ for the spherical shell configuration.

New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.title: Thin-film induced field must show moving image monopole (advective z–t dependence)
New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.description: This rule verifies the modeling of the induced magnetic field near a thin conducting film when a magnetic monopole/dipole is introduced above the film under the h ≫ d approximation and neglected radial derivatives. Expected behavior: Near z ≈ 0 for t > 0, the induced field satisfies an advection-type boundary condition at the film, leading to a moving image monopole that recedes with constant speed v0 = 2/(μ0 σ d). Equivalently, the induced z-component should obey ∂B′z/∂t + v0 ∂B′z/∂z = 0 and have the functional dependence B′z(ρ, z; t) = F(ρ, z + v0 t). The rule flags solutions that: (a) omit the moving image monopole description or the advective z–t coupling; (b) propose purely separable exponential decay in time and/or space (e.g., B′z ∼ e^{−γ t} G(ρ, z) or G(ρ, z) with e^{−k z}) without the z + v0 t dependence; (c) use an incorrect speed expression for the receding image (v0 not equal to 2/(μ0 σ d) in the thin-film limit); or (d) introduce spurious dependence of v0 on ρ, h, or other variables inconsistent with h ≫ d and neglected radial derivatives. Passing solutions may either state the moving image monopole with the correct v0 or present the correct advection PDE or its characteristic solution form.

New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.title: Thin-film eddy-current response: moving-image translation vs exponential decay
New Category: Electromagnetic Induction.description: For problems involving a sudden magnetic source (monopole or dipole) near a thin conducting film, the near-surface induced magnetic field should be modeled via a time-translating image source rather than a product of separate exponential decays in space and time. Specifically, the correct behavior can be expressed as an effective image monopole whose position shifts linearly with time, z_im(t) = -h - v0 t, yielding a field dependence of the form B'_z(ρ, z; t) = F(ρ, z - z_im(t)) (equivalently F(ρ, z + v0 t)), i.e., an advective translation in z.
