(2) The solution lacks an independent azimuth for the diffracted beam (e.g., ψ_m) or fails to state the groove-parallel component conservation (sin α_i sin ψ_i = sin β_m sin ψ_m) while still using identical projection factors for incidence and diffraction. (3) No explicit justification is provided that forces ψ_m = ψ_i (e.g., diffraction constrained to the plane perpendicular to grooves, in-plane geometry with φ = ψ_i = ψ_m = 0, or an explicitly stated symmetry/Littrow condition). If these conditions are met, flag the solution as conceptually incorrect. Guidance for correct structure: introduce separate azimuths ψ_i (often equal to the given φ) and ψ_m, enforce conservation of the tangential wavevector along the groove direction (sin α_i sin ψ_i = sin β_m sin ψ_m), and use the grating equation along the periodic direction, e.g., d[sin β_m cos ψ_m −/+ sin α_i cos ψ_i] = m λ (sign per convention). The rule aims to catch the specific error of assuming identical projection factors for incident and diffracted beams without justification in 3D grating geometry.

Diffraction and Crystallography.title: Require separate azimuthal projections in skew-incidence grating equation
Diffraction and Crystallography.description: Checks grating equations for reflection gratings under oblique (skew) incidence to ensure the path-difference is built from the components of the incident and diffracted wavevectors perpendicular to the grooves. For a slit density n (spacing d = 1/n), the constructive condition must be of the form m·λ = d·(sin(α_i)·cos(ψ_i) ± sin(β_m)·cos(ψ_m)), where ψ_i and ψ_m are the azimuths of the incident and diffracted beams measured from the direction perpendicular to the grooves. The rule flags solutions that: (1) use a single global factor like cos(φ) multiplying (sin(α_i) ± sin(β_m)), e.g., m·λ = d·(sin α_i ± sin β_m)·cos φ, without introducing separate azimuthal projections for incident and diffracted beams; (2) set ψ_i = ψ_m = φ or replace both cos(ψ) factors by cos(φ) without explicit geometric justification (coplanarity), or when φ is defined as the angle to the plane perpendicular to grooves; (3) omit the conservation of the component parallel to the grooves (k_parallel along grooves), which implies sin(α_i)·sin(ψ_i) = sin(β_m)·sin(ψ_m) (and, when φ is given as deviation from the plane perpendicular to grooves, correctly relates ψ_i and ψ_m to φ, e.g., cos(ψ_i) = sqrt(1 − (sin φ / sin α_i)^2) and cos(ψ_m) = sqrt(1 − (sin φ / sin β_m)^2), or an equivalent relation); (4) produce a final f(α_i, β_m, n, φ) in which the φ-dependence appears only as a single multiplicative cosine applied to (sin α_i ± sin β_m) rather than through separate projections tied to α_i and β_m. The rule accepts equivalent correct vector-form derivations and sign conventions but requires explicit, beam-specific azimuthal projections for skew incidence and reduction to the standard in-plane formula when φ = 0.

New Category: Diffraction and Synchrotro.title: Incorrect pulse duration from mixing arc length with angular beaming in synchrotron emission
New Category: Diffraction and Synchrotro.description:
This rule flags derivations of synchrotron pulse duration that improperly combine a linear arc length with an angular beaming width, or that produce the wrong Lorentz-factor scaling. It checks for the following issues:
- Use of a relation of the form Δt = L·θ_eff / v or Δt ≈ T_gyro·θ_eff (where L = v·T_gyro), which mixes a length with an angle to form a time. The correct approach is Δt ≈ θ_beam / (angular sweep rate).
- Missing light‑travel/Doppler time compression in the observed duration. For a single electron in uniform B, the observed pulse width should scale roughly as Δt_obs ∝ 1/(ω_g·γ^3·sinφ) (up to order‑unity factors), not as 1/(ω_g·γ) or 1/(ω_g·γ^2).
- Incorrect angular sweep rate: using ω_g instead of ω_g·sinφ, where ω_g = qB/(γm) is the relativistic gyrofrequency and φ is the pitch angle; the sweep rate of the velocity direction about the line of sight is reduced by sinφ.
- Incorrect gyroperiod/frequency expressions that include β or sinφ in T_gyro. The relativistic gyroperiod should be T_gyro = 2πγm/(qB) (independent of β and φ), while the perpendicular component enters the sweep rate via sinφ.
- Dimensional consistency check: any time estimate formed by multiplying an angle by a path length and dividing by a speed (e.g., L·θ/v) is flagged in this context; the correct dimensional relation is time = angle / angular rate.
The rule triggers if any of the above are detected, or if the derived γ-scaling of the pulse duration is γ^{-1} or γ^{-2} instead of the expected γ^{-3} for single-particle synchrotron pulses in a uniform magnetic field.

New Category: Diffraction and Synchrotro.title: Synchrotron pulse duration scaling with gamma, B, and pitch angle
New Category: Diffraction and Synchrotro.description: Checks the derived observer-frame pulse duration (Δt) for synchrotron radiation from a single relativistic electron in a uniform magnetic field. Scope: problems that relate Δt to the electron Lorentz factor (gamma), magnetic field strength (B), and pitch angle (phi). Expected relations: gyrofrequency ω_B = e B / (gamma m_e); gyration period T_gyro = 2π gamma m_e / (e B) (no sin(phi) or beta factors); observed pulse duration Δt ≈ 1 / [gamma^2 (ω_B sin(phi))] = m_e / (e B gamma^2 sin(phi)), up to order-unity numerical factors. The rule flags the following errors: (1) Incorrect gamma dependence: Δt scaling as 1/gamma or lacking gamma^2 in the denominator. (2) Incorrect pitch-angle dependence: sin(phi) (or sin^2(phi)) in the numerator instead of 1/sin(phi) in the denominator. (3) Incorrect magnetic-field dependence: B in the numerator or missing 1/B in the denominator. (4) Extraneous 2π factor in the Δt expression (confusing pulse duration with a full gyration period). (5) Using T_gyro directly as the pulse duration, or inserting sin(phi) or beta into T_gyro. (6) Unit consistency: Δt should have time units consistent with m_e/(e B) multiplied by dimensionless factors (1/gamma^2 and 1/sin(phi)). If any of these discrepancies are found, the solution is flagged for incorrect scaling of the synchrotron pulse duration.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Induced current: sign consistency with loop orientation and magnitude reporting
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: This rule checks solutions to Faraday-law induction problems (including sliding-rod circuits) for two linked issues: (a) consistency of the overall sign of the induced EMF/current with the stated or implied loop orientation, and (b) compliance with requests for a magnitude (absolute value). The rule triggers if any of the following are detected: 1) The problem explicitly asks for the magnitude of the induced current (e.g., phrases like "magnitude of the current", "|I|", "current magnitude"), but the submitted result for current is given as a signed expression without absolute value and can be negative over the specified time or parameter range. 2) The solution declares a loop orientation (e.g., "take counterclockwise as positive" or similar) or otherwise implies a reference direction, but the final expression for EMF/current has an overall sign opposite to that implied by Faraday’s law using the same orientation. For moving loops, the oriented EMF must satisfy ε = ∮(E + v×B)·dl = −dΦ/dt, with Φ defined by the same dl orientation. In standard sliding-rod setups with rail separation L, rod position x(t), velocity v, and uniform B(t) normal to the plane, the oriented EMF contribution should combine as ε_oriented(t) = −[L x(t) dB/dt + L v B(t)], so I_oriented(t) = ε_oriented(t)/R. If the provided expression equals the negative of this oriented result without an explicit redefinition of orientation, the rule flags a sign error. 3) If no orientation is declared and the problem asks for a magnitude, the solution must present |ε| or |I| (or state that the magnitude is taken). The rule does not flag when the student clearly uses absolute values or explicitly states that the magnitude is reported, nor when an alternative but explicitly declared sign convention is used consistently throughout.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Sign consistency of external force vs magnetic drag in sliding-rod circuits
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: Checks that, in problems with a conducting rod sliding on parallel rails in a uniform (possibly time-varying) magnetic field, the external force required for uniform motion is assigned the correct direction and magnitude. Specifically: (1) If the solution states the rod moves uniformly at constant speed in a fixed direction (e.g., to the right), the net force along the rail must be zero, so the external force must oppose the magnetic drag and have magnitude |I(t)|·L·|B(t)|. Equivalently, F_ext + F_mag = 0 with F_mag = I·(L × B) pointing opposite the motion by Lenz’s law. (2) Flag solutions that set F_ext = I·L·B(t) (or any scalar variant using the signed current without absolute values or explicit vector/sign handling) and thereby infer the external force direction from the sign of I, which can produce an external force opposite to the stated motion. (3) Implementation checks: detect the uniform motion condition and the motion direction; extract I(t) and F_ext(t); if F_ext(t) is proportional to I(t)·L·B(t) without absolute value or an explicit negation indicating opposition to F_mag, mark as sign-inconsistent. Evaluate sign consistency with representative positive parameters (B0>0, k>0, L>0, v>0, R>0, x0≥0) at t=0: if sign(F_ext(0)) is opposite to the motion direction, flag an error. Also flag if F_ext(t) changes sign within an interval where the motion direction is fixed, unless the solution explicitly justifies this with a clear sign convention and shows F_ext is along the motion direction. (4) Accept solutions that either express the external force as a magnitude with a separately stated direction (e.g., F_ext = |I|·L·|B| to the right) or use F_ext = −F_mag with a consistent sign convention that yields F_ext along the stated motion direction for the given parameters.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Incorrect constant EMF for rotating loop in uniform magnetic field
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description:
Checks solutions that compute the induced EMF/current for a rigid, closed conducting loop rotating in a spatially uniform, static magnetic field. The rule flags the following modeling errors:

- Treating the loop’s induced EMF as a nonzero constant (DC) when the loop’s orientation relative to the uniform field is changing. For a ring in a vertical plane rotating about a vertical axis in Earth’s horizontal field, the magnetic flux must be modeled as Φ(t) = A B_h cos(ω t), giving a time-dependent EMF ℰ(t) = -dΦ/dt = ω A B_h sin(ω t) with zero time average. Any result like ℰ = 2π ω R^2 B (or proportional to ω R^2 B with no sinusoidal time dependence) should be flagged.

- Misuse of the motional EMF integral ∮(v × B) · dl leading to a constant EMF in a uniform field. Common red flags include: (i) taking v = ω R θ̂ and dl = R dθ θ̂ (aligning dl with the loop tangent) for a rotation axis that is not normal to the loop, which is a geometric inconsistency for this problem; (ii) evaluating ∮(v × B) · dl as a nonzero constant in a uniform B without accounting for the loop’s changing orientation or without using the equivalence ℰ = -dΦ/dt for rigid motion.

- Assuming a DC induced current/field from pure rigid-body rotation in a uniform, steady B field (no time-varying B), instead of an AC response at frequency ω (or appropriate harmonic), and omitting any sin(ω t) or cos(ω t) dependence.

This rule expects one of the following to avoid flagging: (a) explicit use of Faraday’s law with a time-varying flux due to changing orientation (Φ(t) ∝ cos(ω t)), yielding ℰ(t) ∝ sin(ω t); or (b) a correct moving-circuit treatment demonstrating time-dependent EMF with zero mean for uniform B. It specifically flags conclusions like ∮(v × B) · dl = 2π ω R^2 B (or any constant proportional to ω R^2 B) for this geometry.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Loop field direction and vector/time-averaging in rotating ring + Earth field
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: This rule verifies correct handling of the direction and time dependence of the magnetic field produced by a conducting loop at its center when the loop is in a vertical plane and rotates about a vertical axis in Earth's magnetic field. The checker should enforce the following: (1) Direction of loop field: The magnetic field at the center of a current loop must be stated as along the loop’s normal (perpendicular to the loop’s plane). For a vertically oriented ring, this field is horizontal. Flag an error if the solution claims the loop’s field at the center is vertical or otherwise misaligned with the loop’s normal. (2) Rotation of the loop field: If the ring rotates about the vertical axis, the loop normal (and thus the loop’s field direction at the center) rotates in the horizontal plane with the same angular velocity. Flag an error if the solution treats the loop’s field direction as fixed while the ring rotates. (3) Relation to Earth’s horizontal field: The loop’s horizontal field is not generically perpendicular to Earth’s horizontal field; their relative angle changes with time as the loop rotates. Flag an error if the solution assumes orthogonality (e.g., combines fields using sqrt(B_E^2 + B_loop^2) or states B_loop ⟂ B_E,H without justification). (4) Proper vector and time averaging: The deviation angle must be based on the time-averaged horizontal vector sum of Earth’s fixed horizontal field and the loop’s rotating horizontal field over a rotation period. Flag an error if the solution averages magnitudes instead of vectors, ignores time averaging, or computes the angle from a static scalar ratio (e.g., tan(alpha) = B_loop/B_E) without accounting for the rotating, possibly sign-changing loop contribution. Detection cues for violations include phrases like “perpendicular to Earth’s field,” “vertical field at the center of the loop” for a vertical ring, using Pythagorean addition of magnitudes, or omission of any mention of the rotating loop normal and time-averaged vector sum.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Missing vector time-averaging for rotating-induced magnetic field
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: Applies to problems where a sensor/needle aligns with the average magnetic field over time (e.g., due to mechanical inertia) while a conductor loop rotates in a static external field. The rule flags solutions that (a) use the instantaneous induced field to compute deflection without performing a time average over one full rotation, or (b) perform a scalar average (e.g., averaging sin or magnitudes) instead of a vector average of the rotating field. Required checks: (1) The solution must explicitly compute the time-average of the loop’s magnetic field vector at the center over one period T: <B_loop> = (1/T) ∫_0^T B_loop(t) dt, or equivalently over 0→2π in angle. (2) If B_loop(t) has form k B_h sin(φ) n(φ) with n(φ) rotating with the loop, the vector average must use <sin φ n(φ)> = (1/2) n_perp (nonzero and perpendicular to B_h). Flag if the average is taken as <sin φ> = 0 (leading to <B_loop> = 0) or if |B_loop| is averaged instead of the vector. (3) For a circular ring with resistance R_el = ρ(2πR)/s, flux Φ = A B_h cos φ, E = −dΦ/dt, I = E/R_el, and B_center = μ0 I/(2R), the expected mean magnitude is |<B_loop>| = μ0 s ω B_h /(8 ρ) (independent of R). Consequently tan α = |<B_loop>|/B_h = μ0 s ω /(8 ρ). Flag if the final deflection lacks the 1/2 reduction from vector averaging (e.g., uses μ0 s ω /(4 ρ)), incorrectly depends on R, yields zero by averaging sin alone, or otherwise ignores the required vector time-averaging step. (4) Heuristics for detection: references to ∮ v×B·dl or instantaneous emf without subsequent time averaging; absence of any integral over a full period; language suggesting a steady/instantaneous induced field despite rotation. Accept equivalent algebraic forms that include the correct vector-averaging factor and independence from R.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Rotating conducting ring deviation angle: correct dependence and coefficient
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description:
Checks the final expression for the magnetic needle deviation angle α in a rotating conducting ring placed in Earth's horizontal magnetic field. The correct result is tan(α) = (μ0 · ω · s) / (8 · ρ), i.e., α = arctan[(μ0 · ω · s) / (8 · ρ)]. The rule validates the following:
- Accepted final forms: (i) tan(α) = (μ0 ω s)/(8 ρ); (ii) α = arctan[(μ0 ω s)/(8 ρ)]. A small-angle approximation α ≈ (μ0 ω s)/(8 ρ) is acceptable only if explicitly stated as an approximation.
- Independence from Earth's field magnitude: the final α must not depend on B_Earth; any explicit B_Earth factor remaining in the final expression is flagged.
- Independence from ring radius: R must not appear in the final expression; if R remains, flag.
- Dimensional consistency: the argument of tan/arctan must be dimensionless. The only allowed dimensionless combination of the given parameters is (μ0 ω s)/ρ; any inclusion of additional dimensional quantities (e.g., B_Earth, R, extra μ0 factors) is flagged.
- Correct numerical coefficient: the coefficient multiplying (μ0 ω s)/ρ must be 1/8 within a tolerance (e.g., relative error ≤ 10%). Common wrong coefficients such as 1/2, 1/4, or 1 are flagged.
- Monotonic limits: verify qualitative behavior—α → 0 as ω → 0, s → 0, or ρ → ∞; violations are flagged.
This rule specifically catches errors like missing the factor of 4 (e.g., tan α ≈ μ0 ω s/(2ρ)) and any spurious dependence on B_Earth or R, as well as dimensional inconsistencies in the final expression.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Motional EMF dot-product geometry consistency
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: Detects misuse of the motional-emf formula dℰ = (v × B) · dl by checking geometric consistency of vector directions. The rule triggers when a solution: (1) explicitly sets the conductor element dl parallel to the local velocity v (e.g., dl = R dθ θ̂ with v = ωR θ̂), yet proceeds to compute a nonzero (v × B) · dl; (2) claims a nonzero ∮(v × B) · dl for a circular ring rotating about its symmetry (vertical) axis in a uniform magnetic field lying in the ring’s plane, where v × B is along the axis and perpendicular to the wire tangent everywhere, making the integrand identically zero. The verifier extracts stated directions for v, B, and dl; if dl ∥ v anywhere, it asserts that (v × B) ⟂ dl at that location, so the local contribution must vanish. Any nonzero emf or current derived from such a setup via the (v × B) · dl integral is flagged as a logic error.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Incorrect flux integral: integrating along wire or using wrong area element
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: Checks magnetic flux computations through a loop/ring to ensure the integral is taken over the surface bounded by the loop (B·n dA) with correct area element and limits. Flags solutions that: (1) describe the ring as lying in the 'ρ = a plane' (a cylinder) instead of a plane z = constant; (2) use an area element like a dφ dz or integrate only over φ with a prefactor a (no radial integral), indicating integration along the wire or over a cylindrical surface; (3) include dz in dA when the surface is at fixed z; (4) omit the radial integration from 0 to a for a circular loop. For a circular loop of radius a at z = z0, the correct flux setup is Φ = ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^a B_z(ρ, z0) ρ dρ dφ. Additionally warns when an explicit flux calculation is unnecessary for a requested circuit relation (e.g., expressing emf via L, R, and i using Faraday’s law and Kirchhoff’s loop equation).

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: EMF consistency: avoid double-counting self-inductance in Faraday’s law
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: Checks for inconsistent EMF definitions when modeling a conducting loop or ring with resistance R, inductance L, and an external time-varying magnetic flux Φ_ext(t). The rule flags solutions that simultaneously: (a) define the loop EMF as ε = L di/dt + R i (Kirchhoff voltage drops across L and R), and (b) also define the EMF as ε = - d(Φ_total)/dt with Φ_total including the self-flux L i (e.g., ε = - d(Φ_ext + L i)/dt). This double-counts the self-induced contribution, often leading to contradictions such as L di/dt = - d(L i)/dt. The correct loop relation in a lumped circuit model is L di/dt + R i = - dΦ_ext/dt (equivalently 0 = R i + L di/dt + dΦ_ext/dt). The rule triggers if any equation set includes both an explicit L di/dt term and a - d(L i)/dt term as part of the same EMF definition or equality, or if ε is equated to both L di/dt + R i and - d(Φ_ext + L i)/dt. This ensures EMF from external changing flux is treated as the source, while self-induction is represented only by the L di/dt term, not also inside Φ.

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Flux through a circular loop: correct plane and area element
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: For a circular conducting ring of radius a centered on the z-axis and lying in a plane perpendicular to the axis, the magnetic flux must be computed over the disk enclosed by the ring in the plane z = z0. The surface element in cylindrical coordinates is dA = ρ dρ dφ with ρ ∈ [0, a] and φ ∈ [0, 2π], and the relevant field component is the component normal to the disk (typically B_z for a horizontal disk). The verifier should flag solutions that: (1) identify the ring's surface as the 'ρ = a plane' (note: ρ = a defines a cylindrical surface, not a plane); (2) express the flux using an area element like 'a dφ' or 'a dφ dz' (missing the ρ dρ factor); (3) reduce the flux to a line integral over the circumference, e.g., Φ = ∫₀^{2π} B_z(a, φ, z0) a dφ, without integrating over ρ; or (4) include integration over z for a fixed ring at z = z0. A correct setup should be Φ = ∫₀^{a} ∫₀^{2π} B_normal(ρ, z0) ρ dρ dφ, and if B_normal is φ-independent, Φ = 2π ∫₀^{a} B_normal(ρ, z0) ρ dρ, not 2π a B_normal(a, z0).

Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.title: Sliding conductor in B-field: require motional EMF (ε = B L v) in current/force model
Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's.description: Scope: Problems involving a sliding conducting bar or railgun accelerated by a DC source in a magnetic field (keywords: railgun, sliding bar, rails, magnetic field B, bar length L). Check for the following modeling consistency: 1) If the solution sets the circuit current as I = V/R (or I = V/R_total) constant while the bar is moving in a magnetic field, flag an error. In such systems the motional/back EMF ε_m = B L v must be included and the correct relation is I(v) = (V − B L v)/R_total. 2) If the magnetic force is modeled as F_B = I L B with I replaced by V/R (no velocity dependence) or F_B is stated to be constant, flag an error. Correctly, F_B(v) = L B I(v) = (B L V)/R_total − (B^2 L^2/R_total) v. 3) If the derived acceleration a is constant (independent of v) in a moving-conductor railgun setup, flag an error; a should depend on v via the BLv term (e.g., m dv/dt includes a term proportional to −v). 4) Also flag if the solution omits any mention of induced/motional EMF, back EMF, or a term proportional to B L v in the circuit or force equations despite using B and L and describing motion of the bar. Rationale: Ignoring ε_m = B L v violates Faraday’s/Lenz’s law and yields incorrect constant-current/constant-acceleration results. Expected correction: Use V − ε_m = I R_total with ε_m = B L v, then compute F_B = L B I(v) and a(v) accordingly.

Electromagnetic Waves and Attenuation.title: Low-loss approximation for EM attenuation coefficient α
Electromagnetic Waves and Attenuation.description: This rule verifies the small-conductivity (low-loss) approximation of the attenuation coefficient α for a plane EM wave in a weakly conducting dielectric. Given the exact form α = ω * sqrt( (μ ε / 2) * [ sqrt(1 + (σ/(ε ω))^2) − 1 ] ), with x = σ/(ε ω) and the condition x^2 ≪ 1, the correct leading-order approximation is α ≈ (σ/2) * sqrt(μ/ε). The verifier should: (1) Detect when the solution invokes the assumption (σ/(ε ω))^2 ≪ 1 (or equivalent). (2) Extract the student’s approximated expression for α and symbolically compare it to α_ref = (σ/2) * sqrt(μ/ε). (3) Flag as incorrect if the student’s α_lowloss contains: (a) ω-dependence at leading order, (b) sqrt(μ ε) in the denominator (e.g., α ≈ σ/(2√(μ ε))), or any form proportional to 1/√(μ ε) instead of √(μ/ε), (c) missing the factor of 1/ε inside the square root leading to dimensional mismatch. (4) Perform a dimensional check: α must have SI units of 1/m; α_ref yields 1/m because σ (S/m) * sqrt(μ/ε) (Ω) = 1/m. Any student expression not simplifying to 1/m should be flagged. (5) Accept equivalent correct forms that are algebraically identical to (σ/2) * sqrt(μ/ε) (e.g., using medium wave speed v = 1/√(μ ε), α ≈ (σ μ v)/2) but reject forms like α ≈ σ/(2√(μ ε)) or with residual ω factors. If the solution subsequently uses z_{1/e} = 1/α to infer depth, and α is incorrect per this rule, flag the depth result as propagated error.

Electromagnetic Waves and Attenuation.title: Check units and form of EM attenuation coefficient α in low-loss media
Electromagnetic Waves and Attenuation.description: This rule verifies that the attenuation coefficient α for a plane electromagnetic wave in a weakly conducting medium (σ/(ωε) << 1) has the correct dimensional form and magnitude. The expected low-loss approximation is α ≈ (σ/2)·sqrt(μ/ε), which yields units of 1/m because (S/m)·Ω = 1/m. The phase constant is β ≈ ω·sqrt(μ·ε) and has units of 1/m. The rule performs the following checks: 1) Dimensional analysis: Parse the user’s expression for α and evaluate its SI units using μ in H/m, ε in F/m, and σ in S/m. Flag an error if the units do not reduce to 1/m. In particular, expressions of the form α ∝ σ/(sqrt(μ·ε)) or α ∝ σ·sqrt(μ·ε) produce units S/s or S·s/m and must be rejected. 2) Pattern check for β/α swap: If α contains sqrt(μ·ε) (a signature factor of β) rather than sqrt(μ/ε), flag a likely swap between α and β. 3) Numerical sanity: When problem parameters are supplied (e.g., μ≈μ0, ε≈εr·ε0 with εr∈[3,15], σ∈[1e−5,1e−2] S/m), compute α. If |α| falls grossly outside a plausible range for GPR in soils (for these parameters typically 10^−3 to 10^1 m^−1), or if the implied penetration depth 1/α is microns to millimeters rather than meters, flag as unphysical. The rule provides corrective guidance: ensure α uses sqrt(μ/ε), not sqrt(μ·ε), and re-evaluate with α ≈ (σ/2)·sqrt(μ/ε).

Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.title: Sign consistency in steady-state Lorentz + drag for electrons (E along x, B along z)
Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.description: For a 2D electron gas with E = E i, B = B k, and linear drag Fs = -m v / τ, steady-state force balance FE + FB + Fs = 0 must yield component equations: x: -e E - e v_y B - (m/τ) v_x = 0; y: +e v_x B - (m/τ) v_y = 0. This rule verifies that: (1) the drag terms in both components carry a negative sign (−(m/τ) v_x, −(m/τ) v_y); (2) the magnetic terms follow from q(v × B) with q = −e, i × k = −j and j × k = i, giving −e v_y B in the x-equation and +e v_x B in the y-equation; (3) the electric term in x is −e E and there is no electric term in y. If the student’s component equations include sign flips such as +(m/τ) v_x in the x-equation or −e v_x B in the y-equation, the rule flags a logic/sign error in the force-balance setup, which will propagate to the computed current densities.

Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.title: Incorrect sign in current–velocity relation for electrons
Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.description: Checks that the mapping from carrier drift velocity to current density uses the correct charge sign for electrons. Verification logic: (1) Identify the carrier type mentioned (e.g., 'electrons', 'electron gas'). (2) When carriers are electrons, ensure the relation j = n q v is applied with q = -e (electron charge), i.e., j = -n e v. (3) Flag solutions that write j = n e v (or j_x = n e v_x, j_y = n e v_y) for electrons without an explicit negative sign or without defining q = -e and using j = n q v. (4) Cross-check consistency: for Drude steady state with E along +x and no magnetic field, v_x should be v_x = -(e τ/m) E; the corresponding current must be j_x = n e^2 τ/m E (positive along E). If the solution derives j_x ∝ v_x with the same sign (e.g., j_x = n e v_x) for electrons, flag a sign error. (5) In magnetotransport cases, verify that j components are opposite in sign to the corresponding electron velocity components; if j_x and v_x or j_y and v_y appear with the same sign linkage for electrons, flag. This rule targets the common mistake of using the charge magnitude e instead of the signed electron charge q = -e when converting velocities to current density.

Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.title: Verify ω = eB/m substitutions and dimensional consistency
Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.description: This rule checks algebraic substitutions and unit consistency when the cyclotron frequency ω is introduced (ω = e B / m) in magnetotransport derivations (e.g., Drude model with Hall effect). It targets errors where ω, e, B, m, and τ are combined incorrectly, leading to wrong powers or dimensions. The verifier should: 1) Detect declarations or uses of ω = e B / m. 2) Validate common rewrites: - ω τ → (e B τ) / m (unitless). - (ω τ)^2 → (e^2 B^2 τ^2) / m^2 (unitless). - 1 / (ω^2 τ) → m^2 / (e^2 B^2 τ) (units of time). Any alternate forms must be algebraically equivalent and dimensionally identical. 3) Flag explicit incorrect substitutions, especially: - 1 / (ω^2 τ) = m / (e τ B^2) (incorrect; units C·s/kg vs s). - Replacing ω^2 with (e B / m) (missing square). - Multiplying numerator/denominator by e B (or m) in a way that changes powers of B or m (e.g., turning B into B^2 or altering m^±1 to m^±2) without corresponding factors elsewhere. 4) Perform dimensional checks for each substitution: - ω has units s^-1, τ is s, so 1/(ω^2 τ) must have units s. - m/(e τ B^2) has units C·s/kg, hence not equal to 1/(ω^2 τ). If an equality relates expressions with mismatched SI units, flag as dimensionally inconsistent. 5) Verify that factors in expressions like 1 + (ω τ)^2 become 1 + (e B τ / m)^2, preserving the square on the whole ratio. 6) In any factorization step intended to simplify denominators/numerators (e.g., multiplying by e B), confirm that the resulting dependence on B, m, and e remains algebraically consistent with ω = e B / m. If any of the above checks fail, mark the step as an algebraic/dimensional substitution error and provide diagnostics indicating the correct form (e.g., 1/(ω^2 τ) should be m^2/(e^2 B^2 τ), not m/(e τ B^2)).

Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.title: Dimensionless small-parameter check (ωτ vs ω²τ)
Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.description: This rule verifies that any inequality of the form X << 1, X ≪ 1, X >> 1, or X ≫ 1 used to justify approximations employs a dimensionless parameter. In magnetotransport/Drude contexts with cyclotron frequency ω_c = eB/m and scattering time τ, the correct dimensionless parameter is ω_c τ. The rule flags occurrences such as 'ω² τ << 1', 'ω_c² τ << 1', '(eB/m)² τ << 1', or any use of X = ω^p τ^q with p ≠ q as a small parameter, since such expressions have units (e.g., 1/time) and are not dimensionless. It also flags subsequent derivations or truncations that rely on this incorrect scaling. The check includes pattern detection for '<< 1'/'≪ 1' and dimensional analysis to ensure the compared quantity is unitless; if not, it raises an error and suggests using the dimensionless parameter ω_c τ instead.

Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.title: Low-field limit (Drude) check for j_x and j_y in E⊥B magnetotransport
Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.description: This rule verifies that the derived current densities for a 2D electron gas under in-plane electric field E (along x) and perpendicular magnetic field B (along z), with a linear drag term −m v/τ, satisfy the known low-field (B → 0) limits of the Drude model. The verifier should locate explicit expressions for j_x(E,B,...) and j_y(E,B,...) and the parameters n (carrier density), e (charge magnitude or q), m (mass), and τ (relaxation time). If the solution introduces ω_c = q B / m, substitute ω_c → 0 to emulate B → 0. Required checks: (1) B → 0 limit: j_x must reduce to the Drude result j_x = σ_0 E with σ_0 = n e^2 τ / m (up to overall sign convention for current direction), i.e., j_x/E at B = 0 must be a nonzero constant equal to ±σ_0. (2) B → 0 limit: j_y must vanish, i.e., j_y(E,B→0) = 0. (3) Parity with respect to B: j_x should be an even function of B (no linear-in-B term at small B), and j_y should be an odd function of B (starts linear in B). Trigger an error if any of the following are true: j_x ∝ B (so j_x → 0 as B → 0), j_x/E at B = 0 is not equal to ±n e^2 τ/m, j_x/E depends on B in the B → 0 limit, or j_y(B → 0) ≠ 0. Accept equivalence under alternative notation (e.g., q for charge; σ_0 defined explicitly in the solution). Allow a small numerical tolerance when constants are given numerically. This rule targets modeling errors where magnetotransport expressions fail to reproduce the standard Drude behavior in the absence of a magnetic field.

Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.title: Drude magnetotransport parity and scaling of j_x and j_y
Lorentz Force and Magnetotransport.description: This rule verifies the magnetic-field dependence of the steady-state current densities in a 2D Drude model with E along x, B along z, and damping force −m v/τ. It checks that the derived j_x(B) and j_y(B) obey the known parity and scaling with the cyclotron parameter ω_c τ (where ω_c = e B / m and σ0 = n e^2 τ / m). The rule triggers an error if any of the following conditions fail: 1) Parity under B → −B: j_x must be an even function of B (no linear-in-B term), and j_y must be an odd function of B (changes sign with B). 2) Zero-field limit: as B → 0, j_x → σ0 E and j_y → 0. 3) Small-B expansion: the first derivative ∂j_x/∂B at B = 0 must be zero; the first derivative ∂j_y/∂B at B = 0 must be nonzero and proportional to ω_c τ (i.e., linear in B). 4) Functional form consistency: j_x should scale as σ0 E / [1 + (ω_c τ)^2], and j_y should scale as σ0 E (ω_c τ) / [1 + (ω_c τ)^2], up to overall constants from unit conventions. 5) Asymptotics: for large |B|, j_x ∝ 1/B^2 and j_y ∝ 1/B. The rule flags solutions that claim j_x ∝ B or j_y ∝ B^2 (or any violation of the above), indicating incorrect Hall response scaling.

Halbach Arrays and Magnetic Field Geomet.title: Halbach array: wavenumber must match rotation-per-magnet divided by spacing
Halbach Arrays and Magnetic Field Geomet.description: This rule verifies the relationship between the spatial wavenumber k, the magnet pitch (spacing) a, and the per-magnet rotation of the dipole moment Δφ in a segmented Halbach array. Scope: solutions that reference a Halbach array composed of discrete magnets, mention magnet spacing a, and discuss wavenumber k or wavelength λ. Check: If the solution states that neighboring magnets are rotated by a fixed angle Δφ per magnet (e.g., 45°, 90°, etc.), then the field’s spatial phase advances by Δφ per magnet and the fundamental wavenumber must satisfy k a = Δφ (Δφ in radians). Equivalently, k = Δφ / a and λ = 2π / k = (2π a) / Δφ. Flag an error when the student asserts λ = a, k = 2π/a, or k a = 2π for a case with Δφ ≠ 2π (i.e., when magnetization does not complete a full 360° rotation every single magnet). Special case check: For Δφ = π/4 (neighboring magnets tilted by 45°), the correct values are k = π/(4 a) and λ = 8 a; flag if a different relationship (such as λ = a or k = 2π/a) is used. Optional variant: If the solution specifies N magnets per full 2π rotation (N = 2π/Δφ), then the expected period is λ = N a and k = 2π/(N a); flag inconsistency. Tolerances: accept numerically equivalent forms within 5% relative error. Applicability: segmented Halbach arrays with uniform rotation per magnet; not intended for continuous sinusoidal magnetization profiles or non-uniform segment rotations.

Halbach Arrays and Magnetic Field Geomet.title: Halbach array wavenumber k vs magnet block size a (Inductrack)
Halbach Arrays and Magnetic Field Geomet.description: Checks the relationship used between the Halbach array wavenumber k and the lateral size a of the cubic magnet blocks in the Inductrack model. For the standard simplified Inductrack Halbach array (4-block orientation sequence), one magnetic wavelength spans 8a, so k must satisfy k = π/(4a). The rule flags solutions that: - Assert or use k = 2π/a, π/a, or any factor inconsistent with k = π/(4a). - Infer a spatial period λ = a (implying k = 2π/a) when the model context specifies the Inductrack Halbach periodicity. - Produce numeric values of k not within a reasonable tolerance (e.g., ±5%) of π/(4a) for a given a. Example: for a = 0.05 m, k should be ≈ 15.7 m⁻¹; values near 125.66 m⁻¹ indicate the incorrect k = 2π/a assumption. This rule is triggered when the solution relates k to a or substitutes a numerical k based on a; it verifies that the wavelength-to-geometry mapping (λ = 8a, k = π/(4a)) is applied rather than equating λ to a.

Halbach Arrays and Magnetic Field Geomet.title: Extraneous EMF/time-variation when deriving Halbach wavenumber from geometry
Halbach Arrays and Magnetic Field Geomet.description: This rule checks for a logical mismatch between the task of relating the spatial wavenumber k to the magnet geometry (e.g., lateral size or pitch a) in a Halbach array and the methods used in the solution. If the prompt indicates a purely spatial determination of k (e.g., fields Bx= B0 e^{-ky} sin(kx), By= B0 e^{-ky} cos(kx), or asks to relate k to magnet size/spacing) and the solution introduces time-dependent induction concepts (Faraday’s law, EMF, dΦ/dt, Lenz’s law), motion/velocity of the train (v, takeoff velocity vt), or angular frequency ω, the rule flags the solution as a logic error. The rule also flags solutions where the final expression for k depends on time, velocity, or EMF instead of spatial periodicity (k = 2π/λ with λ set by the Halbach phasing and magnet pitch/size). Key phrases that trigger flags include: “EMF,” “Faraday,” “induced voltage,” “dΦ/dt,” “∂/∂t,” “Lenz’s law,” “velocity,” “moving train,” or “propulsion,” when the task is to identify spatial periodicity only. The absence of a clear mapping between magnet size/pitch a and the spatial period λ (and hence k) further supports the flag.

Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.title: Time-varying magnetic field: do not conserve mechanical angular momentum; use magnetic moment μ as the adiabatic invariant
Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.description: Scope: Solutions involving a charged particle (e.g., electron) in a uniform magnetic field that changes slowly in time (adiabatically), typically phrased as B increasing/decreasing over a time scale much longer than the gyroperiod. Check: If the solution asserts or implicitly uses conservation of mechanical angular momentum (e.g., states L = m r v is conserved, uses angular momentum conservation to relate r and B, or infers r ∝ 1/B by holding v constant) in the presence of a time-varying B, flag as a conceptual error unless the solution explicitly accounts for the induced electric field from Faraday’s law. Rationale: For dB/dt ≠ 0, Faraday’s law (∇ × E = −∂B/∂t) implies an induced azimuthal electric field that exerts a tangential force and torque on the particle; mechanical angular momentum and kinetic energy are not conserved during the change. Correct invariant: The first adiabatic invariant (magnetic moment) μ = m v_perp^2/(2 B) remains constant when B varies slowly compared to the gyroperiod and the field is sufficiently uniform. Expected scaling: From μ = const, v_perp ∝ √B and r = m v_perp/(e B) ∝ 1/√B (not 1/B). Trigger phrases/structures to flag: 'angular momentum is conserved' for a time-varying B, 'L = m r v = const', derivations that assume v is constant while B changes, or conclusions r ∝ 1/B in this context, without mentioning induced electric field or adiabatic invariant μ. Acceptable indicators to pass: Explicit mention of Faraday-induced E and its torque/work, or use of μ as the adiabatic invariant to obtain the correct scaling relations (e.g., r ∝ 1/√B).

Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.title: Time-varying magnetic field requires induced E-field; forbid unjustified conservation of mechanical L or kinetic energy
Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.description: This rule flags solutions to problems involving a time-dependent magnetic field (e.g., B increases/decreases over time, 'adiabatically', 'slowly varying', dB/dt ≠ 0) that ignore the induced electric field mandated by Faraday’s law and consequently make unsupported conservation claims. Trigger conditions: the problem or solution mentions B changing with time (keywords such as 'time-dependent B', 'B increases', 'adiabatic', 'slowly', 'dB/dt') and the derivation either (a) uses only the magnetic part of the Lorentz force F = q v × B without the electric term qE, or (b) asserts that speed v or kinetic energy is constant because 'magnetic force does no work', or (c) invokes conservation of mechanical angular momentum L = m r v in a uniform B without addressing torques from the induced E-field, or (d) derives radius scaling (e.g., r ∝ 1/B) by holding v or L constant during B(t) changes. Pass conditions: the solution explicitly accounts for the induced electric field via Faraday’s law (∇×E = −∂B/∂t), discusses its work/torque on the particle, or correctly employs appropriate adiabatic invariants (e.g., magnetic moment μ = m v⊥²/(2B)) to relate v and r during slow B changes; alternatively it provides a quantitative justification for neglecting the induced E (beyond merely 'slowly varying'). Detection heuristics: if 'dB/dt', 'adiabatic', or 'slowly varying B' appear and terms like 'Faraday', 'induced electric field', 'E-field', '∇×E', 'μ (magnetic moment)', or 'adiabatic invariant' are absent while phrases such as 'v is constant', 'no work done by magnetic field', 'conserve angular momentum', 'L = m r v constant', or reliance solely on F = q v × B appear, flag the solution as a modeling error. Rationale: when B(t) changes, an azimuthal E-field is induced that does work and exerts torque; mechanical angular momentum and kinetic energy are generally not conserved.

Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.title: Incorrect inversion of momentum–curvature relation in magnetic fields
Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.description: Checks that solutions preserve the correct monotonic relation r = p/(|q|B) for a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field. The cyclotron radius r increases with momentum p; higher p means less curvature (larger r). Flag solutions that: (1) assert or imply that minimum momentum corresponds to maximum radius, or that higher momentum curves more strongly (smaller r); (2) apply containment/looping criteria with reversed inequalities—for a detector of radius R, to loop repeatedly inside requires r ≤ R, i.e., p ≤ |q|BR, not p ≥ |q|BR; (3) label p = |q|BR as a 'minimum momentum to loop' rather than the maximum momentum that still loops; (4) equate 'avoid looping' with p ≤ |q|BR. Trigger if text contains phrases like 'minimum momentum corresponds to largest radius', 'greater momentum gives tighter curvature', or if computed thresholds use the wrong inequality direction relative to r = p/(|q|B) and r ≤ R.

Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.title: No energy threshold for circular motion in uniform magnetic field
Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.description: Flag any claim that a charged particle requires a minimum kinetic energy, speed, or momentum to execute circular motion in a uniform magnetic field when no other constraints or forces are introduced. In a uniform B field, the transverse motion is circular for any nonzero transverse velocity; the radius is r = p/(|q|B). Energy/momentum only set the radius; there is no intrinsic threshold for circularization. Acceptable threshold calculations must be explicitly tied to external constraints (e.g., detector geometry imposing r <= R to ensure repeated looping within the apparatus, presence of electric fields, radiation reaction, or collisions). If a solution states or derives a 'minimum' energy/momentum/speed for circular motion or for curving/looping without specifying such constraints, or implies that relativistic treatment introduces an energy threshold for circular motion, flag as a modeling error. Also flag formulations that assert circular motion requires v above/below a specific value in a uniform B field alone.

Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.title: Incorrect use of relativistic E–p relation and failure to apply r = p/(qB) = R for momentum thresholds
Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.description: This rule flags logic errors in solutions that seek the minimum/threshold momentum for a charged particle to loop or be (un)measured in a uniform magnetic field with a known detector/aperture radius. The correct criterion is the geometric curvature constraint r = p/(qB) and the threshold occurs at the boundary r = R_det, giving p_threshold = q B R_det. The rule triggers when: (a) the problem context includes a uniform magnetic field (B) and a detector/aperture/field region radius (R) or mentions looping/trapping/curvature-limited detection; AND (b) the solution introduces or relies on the relativistic energy–momentum relation E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2 or extensive gamma manipulations to determine p without first or explicitly using r = p/(qB) and equating r to R; OR (c) the solution uses contradictory phrasing such as 'assuming r is minimized, set r = R' or 'minimize the radius' to define the threshold. The rule also flags if the final threshold expression for p omits R, B, or q, or includes unnecessary dependence on m or c (beyond p = γ m v) when the immediate threshold is p = q B R. Correct solutions may use relativistic relations only to convert the momentum threshold to an energy threshold after establishing p_threshold = q B R.

Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.title: Numeric minimum momentum in uniform magnetic field using p = qBR
Time-Varying Magnetic Fields and Angular.description:
Triggers for problems asking the minimum momentum of a charged particle to loop/track in a uniform solenoidal magnetic field (e.g., LHC detector scenarios). The verifier checks the following:

1) Final numeric result: The solution must provide a numerical value for the momentum threshold with proper momentum units (e.g., GeV/c, MeV/c, kg·m/s). If no numerical momentum is given, flag the solution.

2) Correct relation and geometry: The solution should use the cyclotron radius relation r = p/(qB) and set r equal to the relevant detector/tracking radius R provided or inferable from context. If r is not linked to the detector geometry (R) to determine the threshold, flag the solution.

3) Expected value consistency: When B (in Tesla) and a characteristic radius R (in meters) are present, the threshold must satisfy p_min = |q| B R. In high-energy physics units, require p[GeV/c] ≈ 0.3 × B[T] × R[m] for |q| = e. Compare the reported momentum to this value (after unit conversion) and flag if the relative error exceeds 20%.

4) Units check: Flag if the reported quantity is not momentum (e.g., energy without conversion), lacks units, or uses incompatible units for momentum.

5) Overuse of relativistic expressions without result: Discussions of γ, m, v are acceptable, but the computation must conclude with the geometric threshold p = qBR and a numeric result. If the solution introduces relativistic formulas yet omits the final numeric momentum, flag.

Example context-specific expectation: For ATLAS inner detector with B ≈ 2.0 T and R ≈ 0.55 m, p_min ≈ 0.3 × 2.0 × 0.55 ≈ 0.33 GeV/c. Solutions failing to produce a comparable numeric value or not applying p = qBR are flagged.

Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.title: Mutual Inductance Misused as Series Impedance
Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.description: Checks whether mutual inductance M between two coupled conductors (e.g., solenoid and ring) is incorrectly treated as an additive series impedance term in the single-loop equation of one conductor. Correct modeling: in time domain, L di_ring/dt + R i_ring = - M dI_other/dt; in phasor domain, (R + jωL) I_ring = - jωM I_other. Trigger this rule if any of the following are found: (1) an impedance or KVL for the ring that contains jωM multiplying I_ring (e.g., Z_ring = R + jωL + jωM, jω(L+M) I_ring); (2) a time-domain differential equation for the ring where (L+M) multiplies di_ring/dt; (3) an expression for I_ring with a denominator R + jωL + jωM or R + jω(L+M); (4) a phase difference δ computed using tan δ = ω(L ± M)/R or otherwise placing M inside the ring's impedance angle (i.e., treating M as part of self-impedance). Pass criteria: mutual inductance appears only as a driving/dependent source term proportional to the other coil's current (or its derivative), and the ring's impedance contains only R and L (i.e., M does not multiply I_ring in impedance terms). Flag as a conceptual error if violated.

Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.title: RL ring driven by mutual inductance: correct time-domain and phasor response
Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.description: This rule verifies the correctness of the current response in a single-loop RL circuit (resistance R, inductance L) driven solely by mutual inductance M from an external solenoid current I_s(t). The expected governing equation is L di_r/dt + R i_r = -M dI_s/dt. The rule flags the following errors: (1) Using an incorrect driving term (e.g., L di_r/dt + R i_r = -M I_s(t), or i_r ∝ -M dI_s/dt divided by R + L), (2) Providing a time-domain solution for general I_s(t) that omits the required exponential convolution kernel; the correct particular solution is i_r(t) = -(M/L) ∫_{-∞}^t e^{-R (t-τ)/L} (dI_s/dτ) dτ (plus the homogeneous transient C e^{-R t/L}). Any expression that reduces to i_r(t) ∝ dI_s/dt without the e^{-R(t-τ)/L} kernel is flagged, (3) For sinusoidal steady-state I_s(t) = Re{Ĩ e^{jω t}}, failing to use the phasor relation ĩ_r = [(-jω M)/(R + jω L)] Ĩ; equivalently |ĩ_r|/|Ĩ| = (ω M)/sqrt(R^2 + (ω L)^2) and the phase difference δ must satisfy δ = -π/2 - arctan(ω L/R), which implies tan δ = R/(ω L). The rule flags solutions that mix dI_s/dt with extra sinusoidal factors in steady state, or that report tan δ = ω L/R (voltage-current RL phase) instead of the correct mutual-coupling result.

Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.title: Phase relation in coupled coil and shorted ring: mutual inductance must not appear in ring impedance
Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.description: This rule verifies the phasor/impedance model for a passive metal ring (secondary) magnetically coupled to a driven solenoid (primary) under sinusoidal excitation at angular frequency ω. For a single ring with resistance R and self-inductance L coupled to a driven coil by mutual inductance M, the correct loop equation is R i_r + jω L i_r = - jω M I_s, giving i_r/I_s = (-jω M)/(R + jω L). Consequently, the phase difference δ between the ring current and the solenoid current must satisfy tan(δ) = R/(ω L) (up to sign conventions in δ; i_r lags I_s by 90° + arctan(ω L/R)). The rule flags solutions that: (a) include the mutual inductance M inside the ring’s impedance term (e.g., using Z_ring = R + jω (L ± M)); (b) produce a phase relation where M appears in tan(δ) (e.g., tan(δ) = (ω L ± ω M)/R or tan(δ) = R/[ω (L ± M)]); or (c) write the time-domain loop with (L ± M) di/dt on the left-hand side. The checker should accept expressions equivalent to i_r/I_s = (-jω M)/(R + jω L) and tan(δ) = R/(ω L), and reject any phase result or impedance model that incorporates M as part of the secondary’s reactance rather than solely as the coupling (source) term -jω M I_s.

Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.title: Mutual-inductive RL ring steady-state sinusoid consistency
Mutual Inductance and Coupled Circuits.description: Checks the final time-domain current for a single-loop metal ring (R, L) mutually coupled to a solenoid via M under sinusoidal excitation. Expected model: if the solenoid current is I_s(t) = I0 cos(ωt + φ), the induced emf in the ring is −M dI_s/dt and the ring behaves as an RL load, so the steady-state ring current must be a single sinusoid at frequency ω with amplitude |i_ring| = (ω |M| |I0|)/√(R^2 + (ωL)^2). The phase of i_ring relative to the solenoid current must be determined by the RL impedance angle and the −π/2 offset from the time derivative (i.e., δ = −π/2 − arctan(ωL/R), or equivalently the current lags the induced emf by arctan(ωL/R)). The rule flags solutions if any of the following are detected: (1) the final i(t) contains an explicit dI/dt term multiplied by sin/cos in time domain (instead of absorbing d/dt as a jω factor in the phasor/impedance), (2) the amplitude uses a dimensionless suppression factor like 1/(1 + (R/(ωL))^2) or (ωL)^2/(R^2 + (ωL)^2) not under a square root, (3) the amplitude omits ωM in the numerator or lacks √(R^2 + (ωL)^2) in the denominator, (4) the reported tan δ depends on M or I0 (it must depend only on R and ωL) or does not reflect the RL impedance angle (e.g., giving arbitrary ad hoc factors). This rule is intended to catch dimensional and modeling inconsistencies in mutual-inductive RL steady-state responses.

General Consistency and Dimensional Chec.title: EMF–passive element sign consistency in RL loop
General Consistency and Dimensional Chec.description: This rule checks sign conventions when relating the electromotive force (emf) to the voltage drops across a resistor (R) and inductor (L) in a single-loop ring. Expected relations under Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL) and Faraday’s law are: (a) if ε denotes the ring’s internal emf (i.e., the voltage drop across its passive elements), then ε = L·di/dt + R·i; (b) if ε denotes the induced/source emf from changing flux, then ε = −dΦ/dt and KVL requires ε + L·di/dt + R·i = 0 (equivalently L·di/dt + R·i = −ε). Flag a sign error if the solution asserts any of the following without explicit, correct orientation justification: ε = −L·di/dt − R·i; ε = −(L·di/dt + R·i); or labels ε as “internal emf/voltage drop across the ring” while writing ε + L·di/dt + R·i = 0. Also flag if the passive terms appear with opposite signs (e.g., ε = L·di/dt − R·i or ε = −L·di/dt + R·i) when representing the sum of passive drops. The rule triggers whenever an equation includes ε on one side and the terms L·di/dt and/or R·i on the other; it verifies that the sum of passive drops has the same sign when equated to the internal emf, and that the induced/source emf obeys ε + L·di/dt + R·i = 0.

New Category: Magnetic Drag and Cyclotro.title: Confusing path length with displacement in magnetic field with drag
New Category: Magnetic Drag and Cyclotro.description: Flag solutions to charged-particle motion with linear drag (F_d = -k v) and a perpendicular magnetic field when the solver equates the arclength (∫ v dt) to the stopping distance from the entry point. Heuristics to trigger: (1) The solution explicitly states or implies that because the Lorentz force is perpendicular to velocity and does no work, the 'stopping distance' is unchanged by B, then computes s_stop = ∫_0^∞ v(t) dt or s_stop = m v0/k and treats this scalar as the distance from the entry point. (2) The solution uses formulas like s = ∫ v dt, s = m v0/k, or ds/dt = v to represent the distance from the starting point in a case where B ≠ 0, without computing position components or accounting for trajectory curvature (e.g., no use of vector integrals for r(t) or cyclotron rotation ω = qB/m). (3) The solution matches or plugs given distances in magnetic-field cases directly into a path-length expression, or asserts phrases such as 'magnetic field does not affect stopping distance' or 'distance traveled remains mv0/k regardless of B' when the problem asks for 'distance from the entry point' or 'stopping distance from the entry point'. (4) In problems giving different distances for different B, the solution still assumes the same stopping distance due to unchanged speed decay. The rule checks for these patterns and requires, for correctness, that when B is present the solver differentiates between arclength (independent of B for linear drag) and net displacement (reduced by rotation of the velocity vector), computing displacement via vector kinematics rather than scalar speed integrals.

New Category: Magnetic Drag and Cyclotro.title: Disallow linear cyclotron-frequency factors in stopping distance with linear drag
New Category: Magnetic Drag and Cyclotro.description:
This rule verifies stopping-distance/displacement formulas for a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field with linear drag (F_d = -k v). It flags solutions that incorrectly introduce the cyclotron frequency or period as a direct multiplicative factor in a length expression. Specifically:

- Target quantity: Any claimed expression for a distance/length (e.g., stopping distance, range, displacement from entry point) under forces consisting of linear drag and a uniform magnetic field (no work by B).

- Dimensional consistency check: The final expression must have dimensions of length. If the expression includes factors with dimensions of frequency (e.g., q B / m or q B / (2π m)) multiplying a length scale (such as m v0 / k or v0 / γ with γ = k/m) without an accompanying time scale to neutralize the 1/time units, flag as an error. Example to flag: d' = (m v0 / k) * (q B / 2π m) (has dimensions of speed, not length).

- Forbidden linear B dependence in length magnitude: For isotropic linear drag, the displacement magnitude from the entry point must be an even function of B (depends on (qB/m)^2 via ω_c^2), not linear in B. If the distance magnitude is proportional to B (odd power) or includes a standalone factor qB/m or qB/(2π m) outside of a squared term or an even-function context (e.g., outside sqrt(γ^2 + (qB/m)^2), 1 + (qB/mγ)^2, etc.), flag as an error.

- 2π misuse heuristic: If the final length expression contains an explicit 2π in combination with q, B, and m forming f = qB/(2π m) or T = 2π m/(qB), and this factor multiplies a length scale to produce the claimed distance, flag for likely mixing of rotation period/frequency with displacement.

- Allowed dependence patterns: B may appear only through dimensionless groups built with the decay time τ = m/k (e.g., ω_c τ with ω_c = qB/m) and in an even-function manner (e.g., distance ∝ v0 τ / sqrt(1 + (ω_c τ)^2) or equivalent forms where (qB/m) enters squared). If B enters linearly in the numerator of a length (without squaring or even-function context), or if units reduce to speed, raise a violation.

This rule is intended to catch logic errors where rotational frequency or period is incorrectly used to scale a spatial quantity in magnetized motion with linear drag, as well as general dimensional inconsistencies arising from such misuse.

New Category: Magnetic Drag and Cyclotro.title: Stopping distance vs magnetic field under linear drag must increase when B decreases
New Category: Magnetic Drag and Cyclotro.description:
Scope: Charged particle moving in a medium with linear drag (F = -k v) and a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to velocity; gravity neglected. The magnetic field does no work (speed decay from drag only), but it bends the trajectory, reducing the net displacement from the entry point.

Physical relation used for verification: Let d0 be the stopping distance with no magnetic field, and d(B) the net displacement with field magnitude B. For linear drag, the displacement magnitude is d(B) = d0 / sqrt(1 + (qB/k)^2). Equivalently, with τ = m/k and ω_c = qB/m, d(B) = d0 / sqrt(1 + (ω_c τ)^2). This implies:
- Monotonicity: As B increases, d(B) decreases; as B decreases toward 0, d(B) increases toward d0.
- B-scaling: d is not linearly proportional to B and not inversely proportional to B; it depends on B through sqrt(1 + const·B^2).

Checks performed:
1) Monotonicity check: If a solution claims that reducing B leads to a smaller stopping distance (e.g., halving B reduces d), flag as a conceptual error. For any B2 < B1, the displacement must satisfy d(B1) < d(B2) < d0.
2) Consistency with given distances: If the problem provides d0 (no field) and d1 at B1, verify 0 < d1 < d0. If violated, flag.
3) Predictive consistency for scaled fields: If the task asks for the distance at B2 = α·B1, infer x = sqrt((d0/d1)^2 - 1) = qB1/k from the given d0 and d1. Then the predicted d2 must be d2_pred = d0 / sqrt(1 + (α x)^2). Flag if the reported d2 is not between d1 and d0 when 0 < α < 1, or not between 0 and d1 when α > 1, or if |d2_reported - d2_pred|/d2_pred exceeds a tolerance (e.g., 10%).
4) Pattern flags for incorrect proportionality: Flag statements asserting d ∝ B, d ∝ 1/B, or that halving/doubling B halves/doubles the stopping distance, as these contradict the correct sqrt(1 + c B^2) dependence.
5) No-work misconception: If a solution claims the magnetic field does no work and therefore the stopping distance is unchanged by B (d(B) = d0), flag unless B = 0.

Example application: With d0 = 10 cm and d1 = 6 cm at B1, the implied qB1/k = 4/3. For B2 = B1/2 (α = 1/2), d2 must equal 10 / sqrt(1 + (2/3)^2) ≈ 8.3 cm and must lie between 6 cm and 10 cm. Any answer below 6 cm (e.g., 3 cm) is flagged by this rule.

New Category: Average Speed and Path Len.title: Average speed in bouncing motion must use total path length, not displacement or a single cycle
New Category: Average Speed and Path Len.description: This rule verifies average-speed calculations for objects that undergo multiple bounces (e.g., a ball dropped and rebounding from the ground) over a specified time interval. It flags solutions that model the motion using only the initial drop (and possibly the first rebound) or that compute average speed from net displacement instead of total path length. Checks: (1) Context trigger: The problem mentions bounces, a coefficient of restitution, or provides a y(t) graph with multiple peaks/impacts, and asks for average speed over an interval long enough to include at least one bounce (e.g., Δt ≥ 2·sqrt(2·h0/g)). (2) Detection of improper averaging: If the solution explicitly uses v_avg = |Δy|/Δt (net displacement over time) or approximates total distance as ~2·h0 (first fall plus first rise), it is flagged. (3) Consistency threshold: If Δt ≥ 2·sqrt(2·h0/g) and the reported total distance D_total ≤ 2·h0·(1+ε) with ε ≤ 0.2, while the problem context indicates multiple bounces or a multi-arc y(t) graph, the calculation is flagged as undercounting path length. (4) Multi-bounce requirement: Average speed must be computed as total path length over the interval, i.e., the sum of absolute vertical travel segments across all falls and rebounds within Δt (D_total = Σ|Δy_segment|), not just the first cycle. The rule aims to catch underestimates of average speed caused by ignoring subsequent bounces or using displacement/time.

New Category: Average Speed and Path Len.title: Average speed must use total path length, not net displacement, in motion with direction reversals
New Category: Average Speed and Path Len.description: This rule checks computations of average speed in 1D motion over a time interval that includes one or more direction reversals (e.g., bouncing ball, oscillations). The correct average speed is total path length divided by elapsed time, where path length is the sum of absolute vertical (or horizontal) distances for each segment, or equivalently the integral of the speed (absolute value of velocity) over the interval. The rule flags solutions that: (a) explicitly compute average speed as net displacement divided by time (use of Δx/T or integral of v(t) without absolute value); (b) report an average speed equal to or within a small tolerance (e.g., 1%) of |Δx|/T while the motion exhibits at least one reversal within the interval; or (c) only count the first fall-and-rise distance (e.g., 2H/T) despite the graph or stated kinematics indicating multiple bounces or reversals within the time window. The verifier should detect reversals via the provided y(t) graph or collision timeline, assert that the total path length S must exceed |Δx| whenever a reversal occurs, and require that the student’s method sums all absolute distances of completed segments or integrates |v(t)|. This catches errors such as obtaining 0.667 m/s from an assumed 2 m path in 3 s for a bouncing ball, which ignores additional bounce segments.

Trigonometric and Transcendental Functio.title: Invalid inverse trigonometric identity or domain misuse (arcsin/arccos with cot/tan)
Trigonometric and Transcendental Functio.description:
Flags algebraic steps that incorrectly simplify inverse trigonometric expressions, especially:
- Any use of arcsin(cot(θ)), arcsin(tan(θ)), arccos(cot(θ)), or arccos(tan(θ)). These are not standard identities and are generally undefined because cot(θ) and tan(θ) are unbounded and not constrained to the [-1, 1] domain required by arcsin/arccos.
- Any step asserting arcsin(cot(θ)) = π/2 − θ, or similar complementary-angle claims for inverse trig of cot/tan.
- Simplifications like arcsin(cos(θ)) = π/2 − θ without explicit verification of the principal value and θ’s domain (this identity only holds under specific domain restrictions, e.g., θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2] or appropriately constrained to ensure cos(θ) ∈ [−1, 1] and the principal value lies in [−π/2, π/2]).
The rule checks that:
1) The argument of arcsin/arccos is within the valid range [-1, 1]; otherwise, the step is invalid.
2) Inverse trig compositions are mathematically sound: only identities like arcsin(sin(θ)) = θ (principal value) and arctan(cot(θ)) = π/2 − θ (modulo π, with principal-value caveats) are potentially valid; arcsin(cot(θ)) has no such identity.
3) Complementary-angle substitutions are applied only to correct pairs (e.g., sin(π/2 − θ) = cos(θ)) and not to inverse functions of non-bounded trig functions.
This rule will catch the specific error of treating arcsin(cot(θ)) as π/2 − θ and similar misuse in physics derivations (e.g., when manipulating Snell’s law or critical-angle relations).

Trigonometric and Transcendental Functio.title: Incorrect scaling when applying cosh^2−1 = sinh^2
Trigonometric and Transcendental Functio.description: This rule checks algebraic steps that apply hyperbolic identities with coefficients and constants, ensuring offsets are preserved. It flags transformations of the form k·cosh^2(u) − m → k·sinh^2(u) (including inside functions like sqrt or after linear scaling) that omit the necessary constant offset +(k − m). The correct relation is k·cosh^2(u) − m = k·sinh^2(u) + (k − m). If the post-step expression lacks +(k − m) and k ≠ m, the step is marked incorrect. Example: c·sqrt((c^2/a'^2)·cosh^2(τ) − 1) simplified to c·sqrt((c^2/a'^2)·sinh^2(τ)) is invalid unless (c^2/a'^2) = 1. The rule also covers misuse of cosh^2(u) − sinh^2(u) = 1: any prefactor applied to cosh^2 must be consistently applied to the constant term or compensated by an explicit offset. This detects errors where a factor multiplies only the cosh^2 term, causing unjustified cancellation or omission of constant terms.

Trigonometric and Transcendental Functio.title: Transcendental function arguments must be dimensionless (e.g., proper time in SR)
Trigonometric and Transcendental Functio.description: This rule checks for dimensional consistency when a variable with physical units is used as the argument of transcendental functions (sin, cos, tan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, ln). Specifically: (1) If proper time τ is introduced with units of time (e.g., via ds^2 = −c^2 dτ^2), then any occurrence of sinh(τ), cosh(τ), exp(τ), sin(τ), cos(τ), ln(τ), etc., is flagged unless the argument is rendered dimensionless by an appropriate scale factor (e.g., ω τ, k x, a τ / c, t/τ0, x/L) or the symbol is explicitly declared dimensionless. (2) In relativistic uniformly accelerated motion (Rindler/hyperbolic worldlines), verify that the argument of hyperbolic functions is α τ / c (or an explicitly defined dimensionless rapidity η) rather than τ alone; examples: flag t(τ) = (c/α) sinh(τ) and accept t(τ) = (c/α) sinh(α τ / c). The rule performs unit analysis on the function argument: if the argument carries nontrivial units (time, length, etc.) and no unit-canceling factor is present, it is a violation. Exceptions are allowed only when the argument variable has been explicitly defined as dimensionless (e.g., "let η = α τ / c" and then using sinh(η)). This catches errors where dimensional quantities are used directly inside transcendental functions, ensuring consistent unit handling.

Kinematics and Dynamics.title: Constant separation requires both velocity and acceleration constraints; do not infer equal speeds from zero radial relative velocity
Kinematics and Dynamics.description:
This rule detects the logical error of concluding that two bodies have equal speeds solely from the statement that the distance between them is constant or that the relative velocity is perpendicular to the separation vector at an instant. For a pair of particles with separation s(t) = |r_rel(t)| held constant over time, the kinematic constraints are: (1) r_rel · v_rel = 0 (s' = 0) and (2) r_rel · a_rel = -|v_rel|^2 (s'' = 0). Therefore, zero radial component of the relative velocity at an instant does not imply equal speeds; the relative acceleration must also satisfy the centripetal condition. The verifier will flag any solution that:
- Uses phrases like "distance is constant", "relative velocity is perpendicular to the line connecting the particles", "zero radial component of relative velocity", or "momentarily constant distance" to directly conclude "speeds are equal", "v1 = v2", or equivalent, without analyzing accelerations, forces, or angular velocities.
- Omits checking r_rel · a_rel or an equivalent dynamic constraint (e.g., centripetal acceleration condition, equal angular velocity about a common center, or force-based analysis consistent with s'' = 0).
To pass, the solution must either: (a) explicitly verify both s' = 0 and s'' = 0 (e.g., show r_rel · v_rel = 0 and r_rel · a_rel = -|v_rel|^2), or (b) provide a correct dynamics argument (forces, accelerations, or angular velocity relations) that enforces constant separation over time. In contexts like motion in a magnetic field, referencing only the perpendicular nature of the Lorentz force or the momentary geometry is insufficient to claim equal speeds; the solution must demonstrate the necessary acceleration/rotation constraints.

Kinematics and Dynamics.title: Detachment/Liftoff treated as static equilibrium in a dynamic scenario
Kinematics and Dynamics.description: Flags solutions that impose static equilibrium (sum of forces or sum of torques equals zero) at an event described as detachment/liftoff/separation in problems where the body is explicitly in motion (toppling/sliding/unstable). Detection criteria: (1) The solution mentions or targets an instant of 'detachment', 'liftoff', 'separation', 'loses contact', or 'normal force becomes zero' together with statements like 'net torque is zero', 'sum of torques equals zero', 'torque balance', 'sum of forces equals zero', or 'force balance' to solve for the angle/condition. (2) The scenario context includes motion cues such as 'toppling', 'sliding', 'unstable', 'vibration', 'starts moving', or 'dynamic' and yet equilibrium equations are used to determine the detachment condition. (3) The solution sets static friction equal to its maximum (f_s = μ_s N) at detachment without checking stick vs slip or without using the dynamic equations to determine whether friction is at its limit. Exceptions that avoid flagging: the solution derives equations of motion (e.g., Newton–Euler or energy plus kinematics), computes contact reaction(s) as functions of state (angle/velocity), and imposes detachment by setting the relevant normal reaction to zero while allowing nonzero angular velocity/acceleration; or it explicitly verifies incipient slip before using f_s = μ_s N. This rule is intended to catch modeling errors where detachment is incorrectly treated as a static equilibrium condition rather than a dynamic constraint on contact forces.

Kinematics and Dynamics.title: Misclassification of unstable linearized rotational dynamics as SHO
Kinematics and Dynamics.description: Flags solutions that treat an unstable second-order ODE as simple harmonic motion. Detection logic: (1) Parse the derived equation of motion; if a linearized form x'' = +k x (k > 0) or equivalently x'' - k x = 0 appears, classify it as unstable. Also handle nonlinear forms x'' = +k sin(x) that are then linearized to x'' ≈ +k x near the equilibrium. (2) If the subsequent analysis uses sinusoidal time dependence (e.g., x(t) = A cos(ω t) + B sin(ω t), or claims 'simple harmonic motion' with ω = sqrt(k)), flag this as inconsistent with the unstable sign. (3) Provide corrective expectation: for x'' = +k x the general solution is exponential (e.g., A e^{sqrt(k) t} + B e^{-sqrt(k) t} or A cosh(sqrt(k) t) + B sinh(sqrt(k) t)); SHO requires the stable sign x'' + k x = 0 or x'' + k sin(x) = 0. Common context includes inverted pendulum or a rod near the upright configuration where small-angle dynamics are unstable and do not oscillate.

Kinematics and Dynamics.title: Unstable toppling (inverted pendulum) time integral must be logarithmic, not SHM
Kinematics and Dynamics.description:
This rule verifies the time-to-detachment (or time-to-angle) formula for a rod/ladder toppling from an unstable near-vertical configuration (inverted pendulum about the bottom contact). It targets the common calculation error of assuming simple harmonic motion (SHM) and producing inverse-trigonometric time laws (e.g., arccos/arcsin), instead of the correct logarithmic form arising from the integral ∫ dθ/sinθ.

Scope conditions:
- The system is a uniform rod (length l, mass m) pivoting about the bottom contact after the top end has infinitesimally detached from the wall; initial angular velocity is zero near the vertical (unstable equilibrium).
- Moment of inertia about the pivot should be I = (1/3) m l^2 and the gravitational torque is τ = m g (l/2) sinθ, leading near θ ≈ 0 to θ¨ ≈ +(3g/2l) θ (unstable, not SHM).

Checks performed:
1) ODE sign check: If the solution linearizes to θ¨ + Ω^2 θ = 0 (SHM) near θ ≈ 0 instead of θ¨ − Ω^2 θ = 0 (unstable/exponential), flag as incorrect.
2) Time-expression form check: If the derived time T(θ) uses inverse trigonometric functions characteristic of SHM (e.g., T ∝ arccos(θ2/θ0), arctan, arcsin, or cosine/sine time dependence with a constant frequency), flag as incorrect.
3) Required integral check: For energy-based integration starting from rest, dθ/dt should be proportional to sin(θ/2), and the time integral must include ∫ dθ/sin(θ/2) (equivalently ∫ dx/sin x), yielding a logarithmic half-angle form. The correct canonical form is:
   T = √(2l/3g) [ ln(tan(θ2/4)) − ln(tan(θ0/4)) ].
   If the final expression for T lacks a logarithmic dependence (e.g., uses arccos/arcsin) or the prefactor is inconsistent with I = (1/3) m l^2 and τ = m g (l/2) sinθ, flag as incorrect.
4) Consistency check: If a solution claims SHM, a period, or sinusoidal evolution for the unstable toppling case, flag as incorrect even if intermediate algebra appears dimensionally consistent.

This rule catches errors where the unstable pendulum dynamics are mistakenly treated as SHM, producing T ∝ arccos(...) instead of the required logarithmic tan(θ/4) dependence.

Energy and Conservation Laws.title: Reject velocity-dependent or ad hoc geometry-based terms in potential energy for gravity-only constrained motion
Energy and Conservation Laws.description:
This rule verifies energy modeling in problems where the only specified conservative field is gravity and motion is constrained by a rigid frictionless surface (e.g., z = f(y)). It flags solutions that introduce an 'effective potential' U_eff with velocity-dependent or ad hoc geometry-based terms that are not derived from a physical conservative force. Checks performed:
- If the solution defines potential energy U or U_eff and includes any explicit dependence on velocity or initial velocity (v, v0, dot{q}), flag as incorrect. Potential energy in classical mechanics must depend on coordinates only (unless a velocity-dependent interaction is explicitly given, e.g., magnetic forces; absent such specification, velocity dependence is invalid).
- If U or U_eff contains terms of the form (1/2) m v^2/k, m v^2/k, or similar mixing of speed squared with a geometry parameter (e.g., k from z = y^2/(2k)), flag as incorrect. Geometry enters via constraints (e.g., substituting z(y) into mg z) and in force/normal/curvature relations, not as an additive potential energy term.
- Dimensional consistency check: If a proposed potential term involves v^2/k where k has dimension of length (as in z = y^2/(2k)), then m v^2/k has units of force (M L T^{-2}), not energy (M L^2 T^{-2}); flag such terms as dimensionally inconsistent in an energy expression.
- Allowable potential in gravity-only constrained motion: U(q) = m g z(q) (plus an arbitrary constant). After using the constraint, U may be expressed as U(y) = m g f(y) (e.g., m g y^2/(2k)). Any additional constant or coordinate-independent term built from v0 or k in U is invalid.
- Context safeguard: References to 'effective potential' must arise from a standard reduction with conserved quantities (e.g., central force U_eff(r) = U(r) + L^2/(2 m r^2)). In surface-constrained gravity problems, introducing U_eff with velocity or initial-condition terms without a rigorous Lagrangian/Hamiltonian reduction is flagged.
Purpose: Catch modeling errors where students add nonphysical 'potential' terms tied to speed or surface curvature (e.g., U_eff = (1/2) m v0^2/k + m g z) instead of using the correct kinetic energy T = (1/2) m v^2 and gravitational potential U = m g z with the geometric constraint.

Energy and Conservation Laws.title: Energy conservation used without detachment condition in constrained-to-free motion
Energy and Conservation Laws.description: This rule flags solutions that misapply conservation of energy in problems where a particle moves on a curved surface (e.g., parabolic bowl/track) and can lose contact when the initial speed exceeds a critical value (v_h). The correct analysis requires: (1) applying 1/2 m v^2 + m g z = constant only while the particle remains on the surface; (2) determining the detachment point using the normal-force-zero condition (N = 0 or equivalent geometric/centripetal condition); and (3) treating the motion after detachment as projectile motion under gravity to find the maximum height.
