Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.description: Checks that the normalization of the 2D point-vortex velocity field is consistent with the circulation convention stated in the problem. Detection logic: (1) Parse the problem statement to identify the circulation convention for a single vortex filament, i.e., whether it states ∮ v·dl = 2π κ or ∮ v·dl = κ. Set Gamma_expected accordingly. (2) In the solution, locate any asserted point-vortex velocity expressions, either as a vector field v(r) ∝ e_z × (r − r0)/|r − r0|^2 or as tangential speed v(d) ∝ 1/d with coefficients involving κ and possibly 2π. (3) Compute the implied circulation from the candidate field around a circle of radius d: Gamma_field = v_t(d) × 2π d. For v(r) = A × (e_z × (r − r0))/|r − r0|^2, the tangential speed at radius d is A/d, so Gamma_field = 2π A. (4) Require A = Gamma_expected/(2π). Therefore, if the problem states ∮ v·dl = 2π κ, the correct normalization is A = κ, yielding v(d) = κ/d and v(r) = κ (e_z × (r − r0))/|r − r0|^2. If the problem states ∮ v·dl = κ, the correct normalization is A = κ/(2π), yielding v(d) = κ/(2π d). (5) Flag an error when the coefficient A in the solution does not satisfy A = Gamma_expected/(2π), e.g., the presence of an extra 1/(2π) factor when the problem uses ∮ v·dl = 2π κ, or the absence of 1/(2π) when the problem uses ∮ v·dl = κ. This catches incorrect numerical factors in point-vortex velocity fields and ensures consistency between circulation quantization and velocity normalization.

Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.title: Correct method-of-images for a vortex in a 90° corner (three images with specific signs)
Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.description: This rule verifies the correct application of the method of images for a 2D point vortex or straight vortex filament near two perpendicular impermeable walls (a quarter-plane/90° corner). For an incompressible, inviscid, irrotational flow (e.g., superfluid helium) with no-penetration boundary conditions v·n = 0 on both walls (x = 0 and y = 0), a single real vortex of circulation Γ located at (x0, y0) with x0 > 0, y0 > 0 must be complemented by three image vortices: (1) at (−x0, y0) with circulation −Γ, (2) at (x0, −y0) with circulation −Γ, and (3) at (−x0, −y0) with circulation +Γ. This construction is the minimal image set that enforces zero normal velocity on both walls. The verifier should flag a modeling error if any of the following is detected in a solution that uses the method of images in a corner: (a) fewer than three image vortices are used, (b) the diagonal image at (−x0, −y0) is omitted, (c) incorrect sign assignment to any image (i.e., not the pattern −Γ, −Γ, +Γ), or (d) the resulting velocity field fails the boundary conditions (nonzero v·n on x = 0 or y = 0 when evaluated). When the task involves induced velocities (e.g., computing the initial velocity v0 of the filament), the rule also checks that the summation includes contributions from all three images with the correct signs. Equivalent constructions (e.g., complex potential formulations or harmonic corrections) are acceptable only if they yield v·n = 0 on both walls; otherwise, the solution is flagged.

Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.title: Corner vortex image distances must be 2h0 and 2√2 h0
Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.description: This rule verifies geometric consistency when using the method of images for a vortex filament (or 2D point vortex) located at equal distance h0 from two perpendicular walls (e.g., walls at x=0 and y=0 with the vortex at (h0, h0)). It checks that the solution uses the correct image vortex positions and separations: single reflections at (-h0, h0) and (h0, -h0) are at center-to-center distance 2h0 from the real vortex, and the double reflection at (-h0, -h0) is at distance 2√2 h0. The rule flags errors where the student treats any of these separations as h0, or where velocity magnitudes/denominators are proportional to 1/h0 instead of 1/(2h0) or 1/(2√2 h0) for the corresponding image contributions. It also flags direction errors arising from incorrect vector differences, e.g., using displacement vectors (±h0, 0), (0, ±h0), or (±h0, ±h0) instead of the correct (±2h0, 0), (0, ±2h0), or (±2h0, ±2h0) when computing induced velocities. Trigger conditions: the solution references two perpendicular walls, a vortex at distance h0 from each wall (often expressed as position (h0, h0)), and applies the method of images. Detection heuristics: look for distances to images stated as h0; denominators like κ/(2π h0) or 1/h0 in image contributions; or displacement vectors to images written with components of magnitude h0 rather than 2h0. Acceptable exception: if the author redefines h0 as the full separation to the image (explicitly stating h0 = 2×distance to wall), the geometry must be consistent with that redefinition; otherwise, flag.

Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.title: Exclude self-induced singular contribution when evaluating vortex drift/velocity
Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.description: This rule checks solutions that compute the velocity (drift) of a vortex filament or point vortex at its own location. If the net velocity is assembled by summing Biot–Savart (or analogous) contributions from all vortices and includes the source’s own term (self-induced field), the solution is flagged. The self-contribution is singular (e.g., proportional to 1/r or log r as r→0) and must be excluded via a principal-value limit or renormalization; it does not determine translational drift of a straight filament. In bounded geometries (e.g., walls handled via image vortices), the vortex’s translational velocity must be determined only from external flows, image vortices, and other distinct vortices. Triggers include: (a) explicit inclusion of the real vortex in the summation used to evaluate velocity at the vortex’s position; (b) use of divergent terms like κ/(2πr)|_{r=0}, ln(0), or 1/0 to set the drift speed; (c) attributing nonzero translation of a straight filament to its self-induced velocity instead of to images/boundaries. Correction guidance: compute the velocity at the filament core as a limit excluding the self-term; when curvature is present, treat the local-induction contribution separately (binormal motion) and do not use it as global translational drift.

Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.title: Point-vortex drift near two perpendicular walls: correct image configuration and coefficient
Point Vortex Dynamics and Boundary Condi.description: This rule verifies the induced drift velocity of a single straight vortex filament (2D point vortex approximation) placed at equal distance h0 from two perpendicular impermeable walls (a right-angle corner). Applicability: inviscid, incompressible (superfluid/ideal fluid) with no normal flow at walls; vortex located at (h0, h0) relative to the corner; velocity determined via the method of images. Checks performed: (1) Image configuration: three image vortices must be used to satisfy both wall boundary conditions—images at (-h0, h0) and (h0, -h0) with strength -κ, and at (-h0, -h0) with strength +κ (or an equivalent configuration by symmetry). (2) Induced drift velocity at the vortex location must be the vector sum of the three image contributions: v = (κ/(4 h0)) (1, -1), i.e., components equal in magnitude and opposite in sign; direction along the 45° bisector away from the corner. (3) Magnitude must be v0 = κ/(2√2 h0); the scaling is κ/h0 and must not include extraneous factors such as π. (4) Common error patterns to flag: results like v0 = κ/(2π h0), incorrect numerical coefficients, wrong direction (not along the bisector), or omission of the double-reflection image. The rule flags a calculation error if the final numerical factor deviates from 1/(2√2) by more than a small tolerance or if π appears in the denominator of the drift velocity for this configuration.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Series equivalent resistance must sum resistances, not reciprocals
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
This rule checks for misuse of reciprocals (conductances) when computing the total/equivalent resistance of components modeled as being in series.

What it checks:
- If a solution asserts or implies components are in series and then writes a total/equivalent resistance as a direct sum, verify that each addend has resistance units (ohms, Ω), not reciprocal resistance (1/Ω).
- Flag any expression of the form R_total = R1 + r + 1/R_V, or generally R_eq = Σ(terms) where any term is 1/R_i, R_i^{-1}, or a conductance G_i, unless the entire expression is explicitly the parallel formula 1/R_eq = Σ(1/R_i).
- Perform a dimensional consistency check on sums: reject additions that mix Ω with 1/Ω (e.g., R + 1/R_V) in a linear sum for series resistance.

Detection logic:
1) Identify the context: look for keywords/notations indicating a series model and total/equivalent resistance (e.g., 'series', 'total resistance', 'equivalent resistance', R_total, R_eq, R_Σ).
2) Parse the stated expression for total/equivalent resistance. If it is a linear sum of terms (e.g., a + b + c):
   - Verify each term has dimension Ω. If any term has dimension 1/Ω or is written as an explicit reciprocal of a resistance symbol (1/R_i), flag an error.
   - Exception: Do not flag cases where the entire left-hand side is 1/R_eq (or the entire right-hand side is within an overall reciprocal) consistent with the standard parallel relation 1/R_eq = Σ(1/R_i).
3) Examples to flag:
   - R_total = R + r + 1/R_V
   - R_eq = r + 1/R1
   - R_Σ = R + G (where G is conductance)
4) Examples to accept:
   - R_total = R + r + R_V
   - R_eq = r + (R1·R2)/(R1 + R2)
   - 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 (parallel case)

Rationale:
In a series connection, resistances add directly; including a reciprocal of a resistance (conductance) in a linear sum is physically and dimensionally incorrect unless forming the parallel combination identity 1/R_eq = Σ(1/R_i). This rule catches errors like modeling a voltmeter's contribution as 1/R_V in R_total for a series circuit.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Voltmeter reading must be the drop across the voltmeter (include RV)
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
This rule checks solutions to circuit problems that explicitly include a voltmeter with finite internal resistance RV placed in series with a source (EMF E, internal resistance r) and a series resistor R (e.g., 'voltmeter connected through a variable resistor R'). The voltmeter reading must be the voltage across the voltmeter itself: VV = I*RV, with I computed from the total series resistance. The rule flags the following:
- The voltmeter reading is expressed as the voltage across a different element (e.g., VV = I*R, VV = I*r), or textually claims 'the voltmeter measures the drop across R' or 'across r'.
- The expression for VV omits RV entirely (e.g., VV = E*R/(R + r) or VV = E*r/(R + r)).
- The current I used to compute VV is obtained from a total resistance that excludes RV when the voltmeter is in the same series branch (e.g., I = E/(R + r)).
Accepted forms include VV = I*RV and VV = E*RV/(r + R + RV), or any algebraically equivalent expression showing the drop across RV. Exceptions: Do not apply this rule if the problem explicitly models an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance connected in parallel to an element, where the reading equals that element's drop (i.e., not a series insertion scenario). Rationale: A voltmeter measures the potential difference across its own terminals; in series, it reads its own voltage drop.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Nonideal meter loading must be modeled when readings depend on external resistance
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description: This rule flags solutions to circuit problems involving a voltmeter or ammeter where the reading changes by a finite factor as another resistance is varied, but the solution neglects the instrument's finite resistance or models the topology incorrectly. The rule applies when: (1) the problem statement includes a voltmeter/ammeter without explicitly declaring it ideal, and (2) the solution either (a) asserts or implies an ideal meter (e.g., "R_V >> R, r", "neglect R_V", "ideal voltmeter", or sets R_V → ∞ / R_A → 0), (b) omits the meter resistance from the governing expressions for current/voltage (e.g., uses I = E/(R + r) and V_meter = I·R while a voltmeter is present), or (c) uses dimensionally or topologically inconsistent total resistance such as R_total = R + r + 1/R_V (adding a reciprocal of resistance or treating a parallel meter as series). Rationale: When the reading changes with the external resistor, the dependence typically arises from meter loading; a finite meter resistance must appear explicitly in the equations. Neglecting it leads to incorrect factor-change predictions and can yield contradictions (e.g., negative or infinite inferred resistances). The rule checks for explicit phrases like "neglect R_V", "R_V >> R", the absence of R_V or R_A in the derived expression for the meter reading, and misuse of series vs parallel modeling. It does not trigger if the problem explicitly states an ideal meter or if the final equations include the instrument resistance consistently with circuit topology.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Mis-modeling a voltmeter as a series element and deriving non-physical parameters
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
This rule verifies that circuits involving a voltmeter, a source with internal resistance, and an external variable resistor are modeled consistently. It flags solutions that (a) place the voltmeter’s resistance in series or (b) add reciprocal resistance terms directly to series sums, leading to dimensional inconsistencies and non-physical conclusions (e.g., negative resistances).

The rule checks:

1) Topology and placement of the voltmeter
- If a voltmeter is present, it must be modeled as a high-resistance branch in parallel with the element whose potential difference is being measured. The equivalent seen by the source should include a parallel combination with R_V (e.g., r + (R || R_V) if the meter is across R). 
- Flag any statement or equation that treats the voltmeter resistance R_V as a series element with R and r (e.g., expressions of the form R_total = R + r + ... + R_V or R_total = R + r + 1/R_V).

2) Dimensional consistency in resistance combinations
- In series combinations, only resistances (units of ohms) may be summed. Flag expressions that add conductances (1/R terms) directly to resistances without inversion (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V). 
- Suggest the correct parallel form when appropriate: R_parallel = (R * R_V) / (R + R_V).

3) Voltmeter reading consistency
- The voltmeter reading must equal the potential difference across the element it is connected across. Flag use of V_meter = I_total * R when the voltmeter is across R but the presence of the voltmeter changes the branch current (i.e., current division is ignored). 
- If the solution invokes the approximation R_V >> R (or R_V >> network) to neglect loading, require that (a) it is explicitly stated and (b) subsequent conclusions (e.g., large fractional changes in meter reading) are not sensitive to R_V. Otherwise, flag as inconsistent use of approximations.

4) Plausibility of derived parameters
- In passive DC networks, resistances must be non-negative. If algebraic results yield negative component values (e.g., R = -5 r) or the solution concludes the problem is inconsistent based on such results, flag as a likely modeling/topology error rather than a contradiction in the problem.

5) Reference structural template check (optional heuristic)
- For a source with EMF E and internal resistance r, voltmeter of resistance R_V across external R, the meter reading should be expressible as V_meter = E * (R || R_V) / (r + (R || R_V)). If the presented relations for V_meter vs. R deviate strongly from this structure (e.g., lack of any parallel combination with R_V), flag as a mis-modeling error.

This rule is intended to catch errors that lead to contradictions like R = -k r (k > 0) and claims of inconsistency arising from placing the voltmeter incorrectly in series or from adding 1/R_V to series resistances.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Voltmeter modeling must include internal resistance R_V and correct connection
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
This rule verifies that solutions involving a voltmeter correctly model the instrument and its effect on circuit behavior. The voltmeter must be represented as a high resistance R_V connected in parallel with the element or source terminals whose voltage is being measured. The voltmeter reading equals the voltage across that element/terminal, not the drop across an unrelated series resistor. The verifier should flag the following modeling errors: 
- Omitting R_V from the expressions that determine the voltmeter reading when the meter is non-ideal.
- Placing R_V in series with the circuit instead of in parallel with the measured node/component.
- Writing the total resistance as a series sum that includes 1/R_V (dimensionally incorrect) or otherwise treating R_V as a series term (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V).
- Using V_meter = I·R or V_meter = I·r when the voltmeter is connected across the battery terminals or another element, where the correct reading is the voltage across that element (e.g., V_terminal = E − I·r for battery terminals).
- Deriving relations that depend only on r (e.g., R = k·r) when the correct relation must include r + R_V (e.g., R = k·(r + R_V)) for changes in the voltmeter reading driven by the variable series resistor R.
- Dropping R_V under a "R_V ≫ others" assumption while simultaneously attributing changes in the voltmeter reading to the loading effect; unless the problem explicitly states an ideal voltmeter, R_V must appear in the governing expressions.
This rule targets consistency of circuit topology (parallel vs series), dimensional correctness in resistance sums, and proper dependence of the voltmeter reading on R_V in problems where meter loading affects the result.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Series total resistance must be a sum of resistances (no reciprocals; unit-consistent)
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description: This rule checks the modeling of total/equivalent resistance for circuits explicitly described as having components in series. It flags errors where the total resistance is written as a sum that includes any reciprocal resistance term (e.g., 1/R_V, 1/R_i), which is dimensionally incorrect (ohms plus siemens). Specifically: (1) If the solution states or implies a series connection (e.g., battery internal resistance r, external resistor R, voltmeter resistance R_V in series), then the computed total resistance must be the sum of resistances (R_total = r + R + R_V + …) with all terms carrying units of ohms; any appearance of 1/R_x inside that sum is an error. (2) The rule also flags unjustified approximations that drop a series resistance because it is "large" (e.g., claiming R_total ≈ R + r when R_V is in series), since a large series resistance increases, not decreases, the total. This rule catches dimensionally inconsistent expressions and misuse of parallel-aggregation formulas in series-circuit contexts.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Voltmeter reading must equal the drop across the voltmeter element
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
This rule detects misidentification of what a voltmeter measures in circuit solutions. It flags cases where a student treats the voltmeter reading as the voltage across some other element (e.g., a series variable resistor) instead of the voltage across the voltmeter itself.

The rule checks:
- Reading assignment: If a variable described as the "voltmeter reading" (e.g., V, V_meter, V_read) is defined as I*R or I*(R + ...), where R is a circuit element different from the voltmeter’s resistance (R_V, Rv, Rmeter), flag an error. The correct assignment in a series current path is V_meter = I*R_V.
- Dependence on meter resistance: In solutions that include a voltmeter in the current path, the expression for the meter reading must depend on R_V. If R_V is absent from the reading or the total current calculation (without an explicit, justified idealization such as R_V → ∞ in a parallel measurement), flag an error.
- Dimensional consistency of total resistance: If the total series resistance is written with a term like 1/R_V (or any 1/R term) added to other resistances (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V), flag an error for mixing conductance with resistance, indicating a likely misplacement of the voltmeter in the model.

What is flagged:
- Statements or equations equating the voltmeter reading to the drop across a non-meter element (e.g., "V = I*R" where R is the variable resistor, not R_V).
- Omitting R_V entirely from the meter reading/current expressions in a configuration where the meter is part of the series load.
- Adding 1/R terms to series resistance sums.

Rationale:
- A voltmeter measures its own terminal voltage. In any modeled current path that includes the voltmeter, its reading must be the potential drop across the voltmeter element. Equating the reading to a different element’s drop leads to incorrect dependence on circuit parameters and can produce unphysical results (e.g., negative resistance when solving). The rule enforces correct measurement mapping and dimensional consistency.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Flag unphysical negative parameters and mis-modeled voltmeter/total resistance
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
This rule checks circuit solutions involving measuring instruments (especially voltmeters) for two coupled logical/modeling errors: (1) deriving unphysical parameter values and blaming approximations instead of revisiting the model; and (2) using an incorrect circuit topology for the voltmeter and total resistance. The rule triggers when any of the following are detected:
- A total resistance expression mixes resistances with reciprocals (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V) or places a voltmeter’s input resistance R_V in series with the load when the meter is intended to measure a voltage across two nodes (a voltmeter should be modeled as a high-resistance branch in parallel with the measured element/nodes). Dimensional inconsistency (adding 1/R_V to ohmic terms) is also flagged.
- The voltmeter reading is computed as a drop across the wrong element/path (e.g., V_meter = I·R or I·(R + r)) without establishing that the voltmeter is connected across that element; for a source with internal resistance, terminal voltage across the source should be V = E − I·r, while a meter across a load should read I·R. The rule checks that the measured quantity corresponds to the nodes where the voltmeter is connected.
- Algebraic results yield a negative value for a physically nonnegative parameter (e.g., resistance R = −5r). If the solution then attributes this contradiction solely to an approximation such as “neglecting R_V” without re-examining the core modeling/measurement assumptions (meter placement, what voltage is measured, correct total resistance), the step is flagged. The rule requires that an unphysical result triggers a topology/measurement-definition review and a re-derivation before approximations are applied.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Voltmeter resistance must appear in current and reading when it is the load
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description:
Check solutions of circuit problems that include a voltmeter connected to a source (with internal resistance) through other elements (e.g., a variable resistor) to ensure the modeling includes the voltmeter's finite resistance R_V in both the circuit current and the measured voltage. Flag the solution if any of the following are detected: 
- The current is computed as I = E/(R + r) or with a total resistance that omits R_V, even though the voltmeter is part of the conducting path or is the element across which the reading is taken.
- The voltmeter reading is written independent of R_V (e.g., taken as the terminal voltage of the source or as the voltage across R or r) instead of V_meter being determined by a relation that includes R_V (e.g., V_meter = I * R_V if in series, or via a divider that contains R_V if in parallel).
- The solution explicitly assumes R_V >> R, r and then drops R_V from the model while still using a nonzero current through the meter, or uses inconsistent forms like R_total = R + r + 1/R_V and then approximates to R + r.
- In comparative/ratio questions about how the voltmeter reading changes when another resistance is varied, the final expression for the reading does not depend on R_V, despite the configuration implying that R_V determines both the current and the measured voltage.
Require that either (a) R_V appears correctly in the total resistance and in the expression for the meter reading, or (b) an ideal-meter assumption is justified and used consistently (e.g., R_V → ∞ implies zero current through the meter and appropriate open-circuit analysis). If neither is satisfied, report a modeling error: neglect of instrument resistance that determines the measurement.

Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.title: Voltmeter-in-series modeling: include R_V additively and read V = I·R_V
Electrical Circuits and Voltmeter Modeli.description: This rule checks whether a solution correctly models a voltmeter with finite internal resistance R_V placed in the only conduction path (series) with a variable resistor R and a source with EMF E and internal resistance r. Required modeling: (1) The series current must be I = E / (r + R + R_V). (2) The voltmeter reading must be the drop across the voltmeter: V = I·R_V = E·R_V / (r + R + R_V). The rule flags the following errors: • Treating the voltmeter’s resistance incorrectly in a series path, e.g., writing the total resistance as r + R + 1/R_V (dimensionally wrong) or otherwise combining R_V as a conductance. • Neglecting R_V in the series denominator on the basis that the voltmeter’s resistance is “very large” (in a series path, a large R_V increases the total resistance and cannot be dropped). • Using I = E/(R + r) or R_total = R + r when R_V is explicitly present in series. • Taking the voltmeter reading as the drop across R or r (e.g., V = I·R or V = I·r) instead of across R_V. • For ratio-based conditions involving changing R (e.g., ‘reducing R by 2/3 doubles the reading’), the model must yield V(R) ∝ R_V/(r + R + R_V) and enforce V(R/3)/V(R) = 2, which simplifies to R = 3(r + R_V); solutions that produce a relation independent of R_V, or derived from an incorrect V(R), are flagged. This rule enforces additive inclusion of R_V in series, correct definition of the measured quantity, and dimensional consistency in resistance sums.

Require Explicit Branch Selection.title: Require explicit branch selection for variables defined via max/min
Require Explicit Branch Selection.description: When a problem defines an intermediate variable using a max/min operator (e.g., v_L = max(v, v0) and ω = v_L/h), any substitution of that variable in a solution must be accompanied by an explicit determination of which branch applies. The solution should state and justify the inequality (e.g., v ≥ v0 or v ≤ v0) or perform a case split before setting v_L equal to v, v0, or an unknown critical value v_c. This rule flags solutions that directly set v_L = v_c (or v_L = v, v0) without discussing its relation to the other argument(s) of the max/min, especially when deriving thresholds (e.g., skin depth δ = d) where the resulting expression implies a relation like v_c > v0. The check passes if the solution includes a clear inequality or parameter-based reasoning (e.g., given h/d = 10 ⇒ v_c > v0 ⇒ v_L = v) to select the correct branch; otherwise it fails.

Double-counting in Physics Problems.title: Missing or incomplete final expression for requested quantity
Double-counting in Physics Problems.description: This rule verifies that a solution provides a complete, explicit final expression for the specific quantity requested by the problem (e.g., maximum height z_max). The verifier should: 1) Identify the target quantity Q from the prompt (e.g., phrases like 'maximum height', 'z_max', 'h_max', or 'z at the apex'). 2) Check that the solution contains an explicit equation of the form Q = expression or an equivalent definitive statement yielding Q. 3) Ensure the expression is syntactically complete (no dangling operators, unmatched parentheses/brackets, or truncated symbols), contains no ellipses '...' or unfinished variables (e.g., 'v0^2 y_{'), and does not end mid-derivation. 4) Verify that the final expression uses only the variables allowed by the prompt for the answer (e.g., only v0, z0, g, k if specified) and fundamental constants; it must not depend on undefined or intermediate variables (e.g., y_max, y, v_h) unless those are explicitly permitted by the problem statement. 5) Confirm that the final statement uniquely identifies a single value for Q (not just conditions, inequalities, or a procedure). Failure modes this rule flags include: the derivation stops without yielding Q; the final line references Q but lacks '=' or a complete right-hand side; presence of placeholders like 'TBD', '...', or 'to be continued'; reliance on symbols not defined or not allowed in the requested form; or expressions that are syntactically incomplete.

Double-counting in Physics Problems.title: Incorrectly summing all stage voltages for energy of a single electron in PMT/dynode chains
Double-counting in Physics Problems.description: This rule flags solutions in photomultiplier or secondary-emission dynode contexts that compute the energy to accelerate a single electron as e times the sum of all stage voltages (e.g., (n+1)eV) or assert that one electron crosses all gaps. In a PMT, each electron only traverses one gap per transit and is absorbed at a dynode; new electrons are emitted and then cross subsequent gaps. Therefore, the per-electron transit energy is eΔV for the specific gap crossed, not e times the total device voltage. The correct total energy consumption for amplifying one photoelectron is the sum over all electrons of eΔV for each gap they individually cross, accounting for δ (secondary emission gain) and collection efficiencies (η, σ). Trigger conditions include: (a) presence of PMT/dynode keywords (photomultiplier, dynode, secondary emission, η, σ, δ) and (b) expressions or statements like E_per_electron = e*(n+1)*V, energy per electron equals total tube voltage, or equivalent summations over all gaps without aggregating over the multiplied electrons and their per-gap transits.

Double-counting in Physics Problems.title: Energy in multi-stage accelerators must be weighted by traversed gaps and avoid double counting
Double-counting in Physics Problems.description: When verifying total electrical energy calculations for systems with sequential equal potential drops (e.g., photomultiplier dynode chains, multi-gap accelerators), check that the energy is computed as e times the sum over gaps of the potential drop multiplied by the expected number of electron crossings of each gap. If all gaps have the same potential V, require E_total = e * V * Σ_j N_j, where N_j is the expected number of electrons crossing gap j. Flag solutions that: (a) assign a constant eV per electron irrespective of how many gaps it traverses; (b) use sums like E_total = eV * Σ(stage electron counts) without multiplying by the number of remaining gaps for electrons produced/emitted at stage i (e.g., missing factors like (n − i + 1) for electrons going directly to the anode from dynode i); or (c) double-count electrons by summing populations at successive stages without mapping them to distinct paths and associated gap crossings. The rule also checks that branching/collection efficiencies (η, σ) are correctly used to compute expected counts along each path to the anode; omission of path-length weighting or overlap of counts triggers an error.

Double-counting in Physics Problems.title: Detect double-counted trigonometry in gravitational torque about a pivoted rod
Double-counting in Physics Problems.description: Checks torque calculations about the bottom contact/pivot for a tilted rod (or similar rigid body) under gravity to ensure the gravitational torque uses a single geometric factor. Expected: the torque magnitude from weight about the pivot is τ_g = r_cm * mg * sin(φ), where r_cm is the distance from the pivot to the center of mass and φ is the angle between the position vector and the gravitational force. For a uniform rod of length ℓ pivoted at one end: r_cm = ℓ/2 and τ_g should be mg (ℓ/2) sin θ if θ is measured from the vertical, or mg (ℓ/2) cos θ if θ is measured from the horizontal. The rule flags solutions that double-count geometry by both (a) resolving mg into a component perpendicular to the rod (e.g., F_g⊥ = mg sin θ or mg cos θ) and (b) also multiplying by a moment arm that includes another sin θ or cos θ factor (e.g., τ = F_g⊥ * (ℓ/2) sin θ), leading to products like mg (ℓ/2) sin θ cos θ, sin^2 θ, or cos^2 θ for the gravitational torque. Detection cues: (1) The torque expression for gravity contains mg and a length r (often ℓ/2) multiplied by a product of two trigonometric functions of the same angle (e.g., sin θ cos θ, sin^2 θ, cos^2 θ). (2) The text computes F_g⊥ relative to the rod and then uses a lever arm expressed with an additional trig factor of the same angle. Acceptable forms that should not be flagged include τ_g = mg (ℓ/2) sin θ (θ from vertical), τ_g = mg (ℓ/2) cos θ (θ from horizontal), or τ_g computed directly via |r × F| with a single sin of the angle between r and F. Example incorrect: τ = mg cos θ (ℓ/2) sin θ. Example correct: τ = mg (ℓ/2) sin θ (θ from vertical). The rule targets the specific double-projection logic error and should only flag the gravitational torque term; it must not penalize other forces that genuinely produce torque about non-colocated points.

New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.title: Equilibrium claim contradicts derived nonzero torque/force
New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.description: Detects internal inconsistencies where a solution derives a nonzero torque or force and later asserts equilibrium (zero net torque/force) without justification. The rule triggers if: (1) an explicit expression for torque τ or force F is presented and is not identically zero at the stated configuration (e.g., τ = −dU/dθ ≠ 0 or a summed force/torque expression with nonzero value); (2) the solution subsequently claims τ = 0 or F = 0 (via statements like 'in equilibrium', 'no torque', 'force vanishes') for the same configuration; and (3) no counteracting contributions are introduced and quantified (mechanical stops, external fields, friction, springs, etc.) to make the net zero, and no energy extremum condition is demonstrated (e.g., dU/dθ = 0 or dU/dx = 0 at that configuration). If these conditions are met, the rule flags a contradiction between the derived dynamics and the equilibrium claim.

New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.title: Sector-plate variable capacitor: capacitance must increase with overlap and use correct sector area
New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.description:
This rule verifies the modeling of capacitance for interleaved variable capacitors built from opposed double-sector plates. It targets solutions that incorrectly make capacitance decrease with the rotor angle or use the wrong overlap area. The rule applies when a solution involves N+1 fixed double-sector plates and N rotatable double-sector plates arranged alternately, with uniform separation s, radius R, sector central angle θ0 (π/2 ≤ θ0 < π), and an electrostatic constant k (Coulomb constant).

Checks performed:
- Monotonicity with overlap: If the derived C(θ) decreases with increasing overlap angle (e.g., contains 1/θ or θ in the denominator for positive θ), flag an error. Capacitance must increase with increased overlapping area.
- Correct overlap area: For sector geometry, the maximum overlap area per adjacent pair of double-sector plates is A_pair_max = R^2 · θ0. Flag use of π R^2 (full disk area) or omission of θ0 when computing area at maximum alignment. Also flag use of only (1/2) R^2 · θ0 without accounting for the “double-sector” (which doubles a single-sector area).
- Effective parallel count: In an alternately stacked set of (N+1)+N = 2N+1 plates, the number of adjacent gaps between opposite terminals is 2N. Flag models that use the wrong count of gaps (e.g., N instead of 2N) unless the per-gap area has been doubled consistently for double-sector geometry (the product 2N × A_single-sector should equal N × A_pair_max).
- Dependence on k: With k as the Coulomb constant, capacitance scales as C ∝ 1/k. Flag expressions that place k in the numerator (C ∝ k) for vacuum/air unless k is explicitly defined as a dielectric constant.
- Maximum capacitance consistency: At maximum overlap, require the scaling C_max ∝ (2N · A_pair_max) / (4π k s) = N · R^2 · θ0 / (2π k s). Flag expressions that contradict this scaling (e.g., missing θ0, using π R^2, or introducing 1/θ).

This rule is designed to catch modeling errors where C(θ) is made inversely proportional to θ and where the overlap area is incorrectly taken as the full disk area rather than the correct sector-based area for double-sector plates.

New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.title: Capacitance must scale with permittivity ε; Coulomb constant k cannot appear in the numerator
New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.description: This rule checks derivations of capacitance for electrostatic capacitors when the problem defines k as the electrostatic (Coulomb) constant (k = 1/(4π ε0), units N·m^2·C^-2). It flags a modeling error if the solution uses k in the numerator of a capacitance expression (e.g., C ∝ k A/s), or otherwise makes C directly proportional to k. Correct formulations require capacitance to scale with permittivity: C = ε A/d, or equivalently C = εr ε0 A/d = A/(4π k d) times any geometric factor. Detection criteria: (1) Identify any equation or proportionality involving capacitance (symbols like C, C_total, C_single, C_max). (2) Determine from the problem or the solution text that k is the electrostatic constant (look for phrases like "electrostatic constant k" or units N·m^2·C^-2). (3) If k appears multiplied in the numerator with area/geometry (e.g., k*A, k*geometry) or C ∝ k without an explicit inverse 1/k (or 1/(4π k)) relationship, flag an error. (4) Dimensional check: using k*A/d yields units incompatible with farads; this confirms the misuse. Exceptions: Do not trigger if k is explicitly defined as dielectric constant or relative permittivity (some texts use k for εr); in that case, C ∝ k is acceptable. Also do not trigger if k only appears inside ε0 = 1/(4π k) or as 1/(const·k). This rule is particularly relevant for parallel-plate, sector, or variable-overlap capacitors where the correct dependence is C ∝ ε and therefore C ∝ 1/k when expressed in terms of k.

New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.title: Torque evaluation for variable-capacitance systems after disconnection (fixed charge vs fixed voltage)
New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.description:
Checks solutions for incorrect treatment of electrostatic torque in systems with angle-dependent capacitance after the capacitor is disconnected from the power supply. The rule flags the following errors: 
- Using the constant-voltage energy U = (1/2) C(θ) V^2 or torque τ = (1/2) V^2 ∂C/∂θ when the text states the capacitor has been disconnected/isolated (i.e., charge is fixed). The correct energy for an isolated capacitor is U(Q,θ) = Q^2 / [2 C(θ)] and the torque is τ(θ) = -∂U/∂θ = -(Q^2 / [2 C(θ)^2]) ∂C/∂θ. 
- Concluding that the torque is zero simply because the capacitance is at or near a maximum (“equilibrium at maximum overlap implies τ = 0”). For fixed charge, the torque generally drives the rotor toward increasing capacitance; τ only vanishes at points where ∂C/∂θ = 0, not merely at mechanical limits/boundaries of θ. At a boundary maximum imposed by a mechanical stop, τ is in general nonzero and acts against the stop. 
- Claiming energy minimization with respect to θ under the wrong control variable (minimizing U = (1/2) C V^2 after disconnection). The rule expects: if connected to a source (constant V), use U(V,θ) and τ(V) = (1/2) V^2 ∂C/∂θ; if disconnected (constant Q), use U(Q,θ) and τ(Q) = -(Q^2 / [2 C(θ)^2]) ∂C/∂θ. 
Detection criteria: 
- Text mentions the capacitor is disconnected/isolated, but subsequent steps use voltage-controlled energy/torque forms or assert τ = 0 due to maximum capacitance or “equilibrium.” 
- Any explicit statement of τ = 0 at maximum overlap without checking ∂C/∂θ = 0 or acknowledging boundary constraints. 
- Inconsistent control variable: derives Q from initial charging (e.g., Q = C_max E) but then proceeds with τ formulas assuming constant V rather than constant Q.

New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.title: Sector-plate capacitor: area dependence and inverse-k scaling
New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.description: Applicable to variable capacitors built from sector-shaped plates with central angle θ0, radius R, plate spacing s, and an electrostatic constant k defined as k = 1/(4π ε0). The rule verifies that the derived maximum capacitance and the corresponding charge after connecting to a source respect the sector geometry and the correct dependence on k. It flags the following errors: (1) Using the full disk area A = π R^2 for overlap instead of sector area scaling; for sector plates the effective overlap area must scale with R^2 θ0 (e.g., A_sector ∝ (1/2) R^2 θ0 per sector), so any C_max expression that omits θ0 or replaces it with π is suspect. (2) Writing the capacitance proportional to k (e.g., C ∝ k A/s); since ε0 = 1/(4π k), parallel-plate capacitance must scale as C ∝ ε0 ∝ 1/k. If k appears in the numerator without an explicit redefinition of k to mean ε0, flag a dimensional/scaling error. (3) Computing the charge after charging with Q = C E using an incorrect C_max that lacks θ0 or has k in the numerator (e.g., Q = (N k π R^2/s) E). (4) Unit consistency: with variables (k, R, s, θ0), capacitance must have units of farads; expressions with k in the numerator typically yield incorrect dimensions. Expected form for maximum overlap is C_max ∝ N R^2 θ0/(k s) up to numerical factors (e.g., involving π); absence of θ0 or k in the denominator triggers a violation.

New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.title: Torque in variable-capacitance geometries must come from energy derivative, not F=Q^2/(2kA) with a lever arm
New Category: Variable Capacitance and T.description: This rule verifies that torque (or force leading to torque) in problems with variable overlap/angle capacitors (e.g., sector plates on a rotor) is obtained via the energy method and the correct constraint (fixed Q after disconnection or fixed V while connected). A correct solution must use τ(θ) = -∂U/∂θ with U = Q^2 / (2 C(θ)) for fixed charge or U = (1/2) C(θ) V^2 for fixed voltage, and explicitly involve dC/dθ or d(1/C)/dθ. The rule flags as incorrect the following patterns: (a) invoking the parallel-plate force or pressure formula F = Q^2 / (2 k A), p = σ^2/(2ε), or equivalent, to obtain a net force and then multiplying by an assumed lever arm to get torque; (b) assuming a single effective lever arm such as R·sin((θ0−θ)/2) or using the centroid of overlap area without justifying a full pressure distribution integral; (c) omitting the determination of whether Q or V is constrained after (dis)connecting the source; (d) producing a torque expression that does not contain dC/dθ (or d(1/C)/dθ) in any form. The rule is triggered when a solution uses area-based force formulas (Q^2/(2kA), σ^2/(2ε), ‘pressure × area’) for curved/rotational capacitor geometries, introduces ad-hoc lever arms for torque, or fails to apply τ = -∂U/∂θ with the appropriate energy for the connection condition.

New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.title: Disallow ad hoc fluid compressibility and V–P relations when model specifies rock compressibility storage with Darcy flow
New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.description: Flag solutions that introduce oil/fluid compressibility (e.g., c_o) or linear volume–pressure relations (e.g., V = V0(1 − c_o ΔP)) when the problem already specifies storage via rock compressibility c_r and provides/implicitly requires Darcy’s law for linear flow. Specifically, trigger if any of the following occur: (1) c_o (or generic fluid compressibility) appears in place of, or in addition to, c_r in the storage term when the given storage equation is q = −2 φ L^2 c_r h dP̄/dt; (2) the solution derives q from an ad hoc volume–pressure linearization rather than coupling the provided storage equation to Darcy’s linear flow q = (2 k h / μ L)(P_b − P_w) (or an equivalent Darcy expression); (3) an independent V–P relation is asserted that is not stated or derived from the given model assumptions; (4) the storage equation is mislabeled as Darcy’s law or replaced by a compressibility-based volume balance unrelated to the specified c_r. Rationale: In this setup, pore-volume change is governed by rock compressibility c_r, and depletion dynamics must come from coupling that storage relation with Darcy flow. Introducing fluid compressibility or unsupported V–P laws constitutes an inconsistent model change and should be flagged.

New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.title: Negative sign between production rate and pressure decay in depletion models
New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.description: This rule checks sign consistency between production/outflow rate and pressure decline in reservoir depletion (or any compressible storage discharge). In depletion problems where q denotes oil/gas production rate (defined positive for outflow) and pressure P (boundary or average) controls storage, mass balance requires q_out = - S dP/dt, with S > 0 the storage coefficient (e.g., S = 2 φ L^2 c_r h, or φ c_t V, etc.). The minus sign is essential: during depletion dP/dt < 0 and q_out > 0. The verifier will: (1) Identify equations of the form q = α dP/dt (or q ∝ dP/dt) where α is composed of positive storage parameters (e.g., φ, c_r or c_t, geometric factors L, h, area/volume terms) and no explicit negative sign appears. If the problem context indicates production/depletion (q > 0 by convention, no external injection), flag as a sign-convention error. (2) Check trend consistency: if the solution asserts q > 0 but derives dP/dt > 0 (or P increasing with time) during depletion, flag a sign error. Conversely, if dP/dt < 0 is used but the equation without a minus sign implies q < 0, flag. (3) Validate that S is treated as positive; introducing a negative constant to compensate the missing minus sign is not acceptable. (4) Apply to relations using boundary pressure P_b(t) or average pressure P̄(t): require q + S dP/dt = 0 (i.e., sgn(q) = - sgn(dP/dt)). Examples of incorrect forms to flag: q = φ L^2 c_r h dP_b/dt, q = C dP̄/dt (C > 0) in a depletion setting, or textual justifications like "the minus sign just indicates production" followed by its removal. Correct expectation: q = -C dP/dt so that pressure decreases over time for positive production. This rule prevents later inconsistencies such as implying P increases with time under depletion.

New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.title: Half-depletion must be defined by cumulative production; detect misuse of V–P compressibility and non-physical increasing boundary pressure
New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.description: This rule checks depletion solutions for the following conceptual errors: (1) Defining 'half depletion' by setting fluid volume (or oil in place) to V = V0/2 via an instantaneous compressibility relation (e.g., V/V0 = 1 − c ΔP or V/V0 = e^(−c ΔP)) instead of using cumulative production. (2) Inferring a constant pressure offset ΔP (e.g., ΔP = 1/(2 c) or ΔP = ln 2 / c) at 'half depletion', leading to P_b(t) = P_w + ΔP or any claim that P_b increases or remains at a fixed offset from P_w during depletion. (3) Concluding or implying a non-declining or constant flow rate q(t) due to a constant ΔP, or yielding dP̄/dt = 0 at the depletion milestone. The rule validates that: (a) half depletion must be established by integrating production rate over time, i.e., ∫_0^{t1/2} q(t) dt equals half the initial oil-in-place (or via the provided storage relation), not by an arbitrary V–P law; (b) in a depletion scenario with fixed well pressure P_w, boundary/average reservoir pressure must monotonically decrease (dP_b/dt ≤ 0, dP̄/dt ≤ 0) and q(t) should decline; (c) using the average pressure approximation P̄ ≈ (P_b + P_w)/2 to assert a constant P_b − P_w is invalid. Flag the solution if it: mentions V = V0/2 derived purely from V(P), cites ΔP = const (e.g., 1/(2 c_o) or ln 2/c_o) at half depletion, states or implies P_b(t) increases or equals P_w + const during depletion, or omits the cumulative production condition ∫ q dt = 0.5 N0 when determining the half-depletion time.

New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.title: Transient storage–flow coupling must yield a first-order ODE with exponential decay (no cancellation of dP/dt)
New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.description:
This rule checks for internal consistency when a solution combines a flow relation with a storage/compressibility relation in transient problems (e.g., reservoir depletion). Specifically, it verifies that equating the production rate from Darcy/transport (typically proportional to the pressure difference ΔP) with the storage/compressibility rate (proportional to dΔP/dt) leads to a first-order linear ODE of the form dΔP/dt = -k ΔP and thus exponential decay, rather than linear-in-time behavior. The rule flags the following patterns:
- The solution equates two expressions for q that both include a factor dP/dt and cancels dP/dt to obtain an algebraic identity between parameters (e.g., S = V0 c_o or similar), thereby eliminating the governing differential equation.
- After such cancellation, the solution still treats dP/dt (or dP_b/dt) as a constant and integrates to obtain ΔP(t) linear in time.
- Any conclusion that ΔP(t) is linear in t in a single-capacitance system with storage and flow coupling, without external forcing, instead of exponential decay.
- For half-time or depletion-time calculations in such first-order systems, the solution omits the ln(2) factor (i.e., t_1/2 must equal (ln 2) * S/k). Absence of ln(2) or linear-time scaling is flagged.
- Use of average pressure approximations (e.g., P̄ = (P_b + P_w)/2) to convert dP̄/dt into dP_b/dt followed by cancellation of dP_b/dt across both sides when equating q from storage and q from flow.
The rule triggers if any of these inconsistencies are detected, indicating the differential nature of the problem was lost (via cancellation) or the transient behavior was mischaracterized (linear instead of exponential).

New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.title: Dimensional consistency and required k/μ dependence in depletion time derived with Darcy flow
New Category: Darcy Flow and Rock Compre.description: This rule verifies time-scale expressions derived for porous-media depletion when Darcy’s law is invoked. Applicability: any solution that (a) references Darcy’s law or uses a Darcy-type relation for flow rate q and (b) presents a final formula for a time variable (e.g., depletion time, half-depletion time). Checks performed: (1) Dimensional check of time expression: The final expression for time t must have units of time [T]. Using the symbol unit metadata (e.g., φ: dimensionless, L/h: [L], k: [L^2], μ: [Pa·s], c_r: [1/Pa], q: [L^3/T], V or V0: [L^3], P: [Pa]), evaluate the units of the provided t expression. If the result is not [T], flag a dimensional inconsistency. Example of failure: t = V0/(2 φ L^2 c_r h) has units of pressure [Pa], not time. (2) Consistency with Darcy’s law parameters: If the solution relates flow to pressure drawdown via Darcy’s law at any point (e.g., q ∝ (k/μ)·(pressure drop/length)·area), then the final time expression for depletion must depend on the hydraulic resistance parameters k and μ unless an explicit constant-rate production is assumed or an explicit cancellation is demonstrated. If both k and μ are absent from the final t expression and there is no documented constant-rate constraint or explicit cancellation, flag a missing-parameter error (“Darcy flow-derived time lacks k/μ dependence”). (3) Cross-check of intermediate rate-pressure relation: If an intermediate step uses q = C · dP/dt with C having units [L^3/Pa], ensure that time is not computed solely by dividing a volume by C (which yields pressure). A valid time result requires linking q to pressure drop via Darcy’s law (introducing k/μ) or specifying q as an imposed constant with units [L^3/T]. This rule catches results where time scales are expressed only with geometric terms, porosity, and compressibility (e.g., φ, c_r, L, h) but omit k and μ despite invoking Darcy flow.

New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.title: Incorrect use of dark current to determine external photon threshold or source temperature
New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.description: Flag solutions that conflate detector dark current with the condition for external photons to excite electrons across the detector’s band gap. Specifically: (1) If the task asks for the external source temperature or photon energy sufficient to excite an electron (i.e., threshold set by the detector’s gap ΔE_g), check that the solution uses the photon energy relation (E_photon = hν = hc/λ) and the appropriate thermal-spectrum linkage (e.g., characteristic photon energy ~ a·k_B·T_source via Wien/Planck) and sets the threshold E_photon ≥ ΔE_g. (2) Trigger an error if the solution instead uses the detector’s dark-current formula (i_d = i_0·exp(-|ΔE_g|/(6 k_B T))) to solve for the external source temperature, or equates a chosen value of i_d to the condition for photon-induced excitation (e.g., "temperature at which i_d is sufficient to excite an electron"). Dark current arises from the detector’s own temperature and is independent of external illumination; it cannot determine the external source’s photon threshold. Also flag statements that mischaracterize the monotonic behavior of the provided dark-current law (e.g., claiming i_d decreases with increasing detector temperature when the given form implies i_d increases with T). The correct approach is to compare external photon energy to ΔE_g and, if needed, relate the source temperature to photon energies via blackbody spectrum relations, not via the detector’s dark-current dependence.

New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.title: Misuse of dark-current formula and implausible temperature inference
New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.description: This rule verifies calculations that use the Arrhenius-type dark current relation i_d = i_0 * exp(-|ΔE_g| / (6 k_B T)). It flags the following issues: (1) Category mismatch: If the solution applies the detector dark-current temperature T to infer the temperature of a distant radiation source (e.g., phrases like 'temperature of the source' or 'thermal photons from the source') while using the dark current formula, flag as misuse because the formula describes detector leakage as a function of the detector's own temperature, not the source’s temperature. (2) Implausible detector temperature: In JWST/ISIM context (cryogenic operation), if the computed detector temperature T is near room temperature (e.g., T ≥ 200 K) or specifically around 280–330 K (e.g., ~313 K), flag as physically implausible unless explicitly justified by provided data. (3) Incorrect or unjustified bandgap: If the calculation inserts an arbitrary ΔE_g without sourcing it from the problem statement or known detector material, flag. For JWST near-IR detectors, using a silicon-like ΔE_g ≈ 1 eV without justification should be flagged; the problem context requires using the appropriate detector bandgap value or acknowledging uncertainty. (4) Trend contradiction: For the given exponential form, dark current increases with increasing temperature (since the exponent becomes less negative as T rises). If the qualitative discussion states that i_d decreases with T, flag as a contradiction. (5) Unit consistency check: If k_B is used in eV/K, ΔE_g must be in eV; if ΔE_g is in joules, ensure k_B is in J/K and the conversion is shown. Any mismatch leading to unrealistic T is flagged. The verifier should trigger on any of these conditions when the problem context involves JWST/ISIM or similar cryogenic detectors and the dark current equation is used to estimate temperatures or interpret trends.

New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.title: Check monotonic temperature dependence for Arrhenius-type exponentials
New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.description: This rule verifies the qualitative temperature trend implied by Arrhenius-type expressions used in solutions. If a quantity Q(T) is modeled as Q(T) = Q0 * exp(s * C / (α * k_B * T)) with T > 0, k_B > 0, Q0 > 0, C > 0, α > 0, then the monotonic behavior is determined solely by the sign s in the exponent: (1) For s = -1 (e.g., Q = Q0 * exp(-E/(α k_B T))), Q must increase with increasing T (dQ/dT > 0), approaching 0 as T → 0+ and Q0 as T → ∞. (2) For s = +1 (e.g., Q = Q0 * exp(+E/(α k_B T))), Q must decrease with increasing T (dQ/dT < 0). The verifier should: (a) Detect such exponential forms with inverse temperature in the exponent, confirm positivity of parameters (energy gaps, Boltzmann constant, prefactors), and compute the implied trend via derivative sign. (b) Scan the solution text for qualitative claims about temperature dependence (e.g., 'increases with temperature', 'decreases with temperature', 'as T rises Q falls/rises', or graph interpretations). (c) Flag a conceptual error if the stated trend contradicts the trend implied by the formula (e.g., claiming dark current decreases with increasing T when using i_d = i_0 * exp(-ΔE_g/(6 k_B T))). This rule targets common misinterpretations of inverse-temperature exponentials and ensures consistency between mathematical models and qualitative statements.

New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.title: Detector bandgap consistency for JWST infrared instruments
New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.description: Check the assumed detector bandgap ΔE_g against the instrument context. If the problem references JWST or infrared detection (λ > 1 μm) and the solution uses a silicon-like bandgap (ΔE_g ≈ 1.1 eV or, more generally, ΔE_g ≥ 0.8 eV), flag a modeling error. JWST does not use silicon CCDs for science imaging; it uses HgCdTe for near-IR (typical cutoff 2.5–5 μm → ΔE_g ≈ 0.25–0.5 eV) and Si:As IBC for mid-IR (cutoff ≈ 28 μm → ΔE_g ≈ 0.04–0.05 eV). The assumed ΔE_g should be consistent with the stated spectral range via ΔE_g ≈ hc/λ_cutoff. Also flag if the implied cutoff wavelength from ΔE_g (λ_cutoff ≈ hc/ΔE_g) is < 1.5 μm while the context requires sensitivity beyond ~2 μm (e.g., NIRCam/NIRSpec/MIRI). Using a silicon CCD bandgap or naming a silicon CCD as the detector in JWST contexts will yield grossly incorrect temperature/energy thresholds and dark current estimates.

New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.title: Unjustified numeric parameter assignments without data extraction
New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.description: This rule flags solutions that assign numerical values to problem-specific parameters (e.g., i0, id, ΔEg) when those values are not explicitly provided by the problem and are not derived from the given graph, table, or earlier validated steps. If the problem references a dataset/graph intended to inform such parameters, the solution must show how the values were obtained (e.g., reading from axes, interpolation, curve fitting, or citing labeled points) or keep the parameters symbolic until they cancel. The rule marks as errors any use of approximate numbers (≈), assumed round values, or convenience thresholds (e.g., setting id to 1 e−/s) without explicit justification tied to the provided data or stated criteria in the prompt.

New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.title: Use ln(i_d) vs 1/T slope to extract ΔE_g from dark current
New Category: Dark Current and Infrared.description: When a problem provides an Arrhenius-type dark current relation i_d = i0 * exp(-|ΔE_g|/(6 k_B T)) and a dark current vs temperature graph, the solution must linearize the expression and use the graph to estimate the bandgap. Specifically: take the natural log to obtain ln(i_d) = ln(i0) - |ΔE_g|/(6 k_B) * (1/T), interpret/plot ln(i_d) versus 1/T, and use the slope m = -|ΔE_g|/(6 k_B) to compute ΔE_g. Flag a conceptual error if the solution: (a) does not mention or perform ln(i_d) vs 1/T linearization or does not extract ΔE_g from the slope; (b) asserts that i_d decreases with increasing T (contradicting the given exponential form, which implies i_d increases with T); (c) uses i_d vs T directly or ln(i_d) vs T instead of ln(i_d) vs 1/T; (d) attempts to estimate ΔE_g from a single data point rather than from the slope; (e) omits the factor 6 in the denominator when relating slope to ΔE_g; or (f) proceeds to estimate the source photon energy/temperature without first obtaining ΔE_g from the graph. The verifier should scan the solution for explicit cues such as ln(i_d), 1/T, slope, ΔE_g, and k_B; missing or misused cues trigger this rule.

New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Rotating-frame time-derivative and acceleration transform completeness
New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: This rule verifies correct application of vector time-derivative transformations between inertial and rotating frames and checks that the resulting acceleration expression includes all required terms. It targets problems involving a constant angular velocity Ω (e.g., Earth’s rotation). The rule enforces: (1) The general derivative identity must be used correctly: (dA/dt)_inertial = (dA/dt)_rot + Ω × A for any vector A expressed in the rotating basis. (2) If the solution states v = v_R + Ω × r (with r or r' as the position vector in the rotating frame), then the inertial acceleration must be written as a_inertial = a_R + 2 Ω × v_R + Ω × (Ω × r) when Ω is constant. If Ω is time-dependent, the Euler term +(dΩ/dt) × r must also be included. (3) When writing equations of motion in the rotating frame, the fictitious-force form must be consistent: m a_R = F_real − 2 m Ω × v_R − m Ω × (Ω × r) − m (dΩ/dt) × r (with the Euler term zero for constant Ω). The rule flags any of the following errors: • Misstating the derivative identity for velocity, e.g., writing dv/dt = dv_R/dt + Ω × v_R without accounting for the derivative of Ω × r. • Using an incomplete acceleration transform such as a_inertial = a_R + Ω × v_R or a_inertial = a_R + Ω × v, which omits the second Coriolis contribution and the centrifugal term. • Missing the Ω × (Ω × r) term entirely. • Incorrect coefficients (e.g., using 1×Ω × v_R instead of 2×Ω × v_R). • Wrong vector usage in cross products (e.g., using v instead of v_R in the Coriolis term). • Sign errors in the rotating-frame force form (e.g., using +2 m Ω × v_R instead of −2 m Ω × v_R). The verifier should scan the solution for the presence of these transformations and cross-product terms; if any of the required terms are missing, mis-signed, or mis-scaled, or if the derivative identity is applied to v without accounting for v = v_R + Ω × r, the solution is flagged.

New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Correct placement and coefficients of Coriolis/centrifugal terms in acceleration transformation
New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: This rule verifies the transformation between inertial-frame and rotating-frame accelerations. It checks that the relation is expressed as a_inertial = a_rot + 2 (Ω × v_rot) + Ω × (Ω × r_rot) + (dΩ/dt) × r_rot (Euler term optional and zero for constant Ω). The rule flags the following errors: (1) Misplacement of pseudo-acceleration terms onto the rotating-frame acceleration side (e.g., writing a_rot = dv_R/dt + Ω × v_R + ... rather than keeping all Ω-terms on the inertial acceleration side). Note that by definition a_rot = dv_R/dt, without additional Ω-terms. (2) Incorrect Coriolis coefficient: using Ω × v_R instead of 2 Ω × v_R, or any coefficient other than 2. (3) Double-counting of Coriolis or centrifugal terms (e.g., both Ω × v_R and 2 Ω × v_R present, or multiple Ω × (Ω × r) terms). (4) Inconsistent variable usage in pseudo-terms: the velocity and position inside Ω-terms must be rotating-frame quantities (v_rot, r_rot); using inertial v or r without explicit and correct transformation is flagged. (5) For problems specifying constant Ω, inclusion of a nonzero Euler term (dΩ/dt × r_rot) is flagged. The rule applies whether the transformation is presented via accelerations or via forces (through F_inertial = m a_inertial and F_rot = F_real − m[2 Ω × v_rot + Ω × (Ω × r_rot) + (dΩ/dt) × r_rot]).

New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Validate Coriolis term coefficient in rotating-frame dynamics
New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: This rule checks derivations that transform equations of motion between inertial and rotating frames to ensure the Coriolis term is not double-counted. In the kinematic acceleration transformation, the correct form is a_inertial = a_rot + 2(Ω × v_rot) + Ω × (Ω × r) + (dΩ/dt) × r. In the rotating-frame equation of motion, the fictitious Coriolis force must be −2 m (Ω × v_rot). The verifier should: (1) Identify the cross-product term involving the angular velocity Ω and the rotating-frame velocity (v_rot, v', or equivalent). (2) Canonically reduce occurrences of Ω × v_rot and v_rot × Ω (accounting for sign reversal) and sum coefficients. (3) Flag an error if the net coefficient magnitude on the Coriolis term is not exactly 2 in the acceleration expression or ±2m in the force expression (e.g., coefficients 0, 1, 3, etc.). (4) Additionally flag if Ω × v_rot appears more than once as separate additive terms (indicative of double counting), or if the inertial velocity v is used in place of v_rot in the Coriolis term. (5) For constant Ω (dΩ/dt = 0), ensure that no extra Ω × v_rot term arises from misdifferentiating Ω × r. This rule targets errors such as producing 3(Ω × v_rot) instead of 2(Ω × v_rot).

New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Sign check for Coriolis and centrifugal terms in rotating-frame equations
New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: This rule verifies the sign of fictitious force terms when a solution expresses motion in a rotating (Earth-fixed) frame. For constant angular velocity Ω (no Euler term), the correct relations are: (1) acceleration transform: a_inertial = a_R + 2 Ω × v_R + Ω × (Ω × r_R); (2) Newton’s second law in the rotating frame: m a_R = F_real − 2 m (Ω × v_R) − m [Ω × (Ω × r_R)]; (3) fictitious forces to add to real forces: F_fictitious = −2 m (Ω × v_R) − m [Ω × (Ω × r_R)]. The rule flags an error if the final expression for rotating-frame acceleration or force (a_R or F_R) includes the Coriolis term (Ω × v_R) or the centrifugal term Ω × (Ω × r_R) with a positive sign (e.g., m a_R = F_real + 2 m Ω × v_R + m Ω × (Ω × r_R)), or if a_R is written as a_R = a_inertial + 2 Ω × v_R + Ω × (Ω × r_R). Conversely, expressions for a_inertial are allowed to have these terms with plus signs. If an Euler term appears (dΩ/dt ≠ 0), it must carry a negative sign in the rotating-frame equation: − m (dΩ/dt × r_R). The checker should parse the final stated equation, identify terms of the form Ω × v (Coriolis) and Ω × (Ω × r) (centrifugal), determine whether the equation is for a_R or F_R versus a_inertial, and ensure the signs match the above conventions; mismatches are reported as a sign error in fictitious forces.

New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Coriolis term must use rotating-frame (relative) velocity
New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Checks derivations written for an Earth-fixed (rotating) frame to ensure the Coriolis acceleration/force uses the velocity measured in the rotating frame. In a rotating frame with constant angular velocity Ω, the Coriolis acceleration must be a_cor = 2 Ω × v_R (and the Coriolis force F_cor = 2 m Ω × v_R), where v_R is the particle's velocity as observed in the rotating frame (i.e., relative to the rotating Earth). The rule flags solutions that: (1) explicitly define v as the inertial-frame velocity (e.g., v = d r/dt in an inertial coordinate system) and then use 2 Ω × v or 2 m Ω × v as the Coriolis term; (2) use an undefined or implicitly inertial velocity symbol v in the Coriolis term when the context is the rotating frame; (3) substitute v_inertial = v_R + Ω × r directly into the Coriolis term (yielding 2 Ω × v_inertial) instead of using v_R. Acceptable forms include v_R, v_rel, v_rot, or a clearly stated 'velocity relative to the rotating frame/Earth'. This rule does not evaluate sign conventions or other fictitious-force terms; it specifically enforces that the Coriolis term depends on rotating-frame velocity, not inertial-frame velocity.

New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.title: Rotating-frame net force definition consistency (no fictitious terms inside a_R)
New Category: Rotating-Frame Dynamics.description: Checks for consistent use of the net force in a rotating frame and proper placement of fictitious forces. Trigger this rule if the solution defines F_R as m d^2 r'/dt^2 (i.e., F_R = m a_R) and then (a) adds Coriolis/centrifugal/Euler forces to F_R directly (e.g., F_R = m a_R + F_coriolis + F_centrifugal), or (b) embeds fictitious-force terms inside the definition of a_R (e.g., a_R = d v_R/dt + 2 Ω × v_R + Ω × (Ω × r)). In a rotating frame with angular velocity Ω, the only correct kinematic relation is a = a_R + 2 Ω × v_R + Ω × (Ω × r) + dΩ/dt × r, hence F_R = m a − 2 m (Ω × v_R) − m Ω × (Ω × r) − m (dΩ/dt × r). Flag if: 1) signs of the Ω-terms are wrong when moving from a to a_R (e.g., F_R = m a + 2 m Ω × v_R + ...), 2) v (inertial velocity) is used in the Coriolis term instead of v_R, 3) fictitious terms appear on both sides (double counting), or 4) the student states that “a_R includes Coriolis/centrifugal” as part of its definition. Acceptable alternatives: writing Newton’s second law in the rotating frame as m a_R = F_real + F_coriolis + F_centrifugal (+ F_Euler) is fine provided F_R is kept equal to m a_R and the same fictitious terms are not added again elsewhere. This rule is intended to catch the common confusion between defining F_R = m a_R and adding fictitious forces within a_R or to F_R, leading to inconsistent or double-counted dynamics.

New Category: Energy Accounting in Casca.title: Cascade amplification: anode count must include per-stage leakage
New Category: Energy Accounting in Casca.description: In cascaded amplification models (e.g., photomultiplier tubes) with per-stage gain δ (>1), interstage collection efficiency σ (0≤σ≤1), and initial collection η (0≤η≤1), verify that the total number of electrons collected at the terminal (anode) is computed as the sum of contributions that actually reach the anode from each stage, not as the sum of populations at intermediate stages. The expected stage model is: N₁ = η and N_{i+1} = σδ N_i for i = 1..n−1. The anode contributions must be counted as A₀ = (1−η), A_i = (1−σ)δ N_i for i = 1..n−1, and A_n = δ N_n, so that N_anode = A₀ + Σ_{i=1}^{n−1} A_i + A_n = (1−η) + Σ_{i=1}^{n−1} (1−σ)δ(σδ)^{i−1}η + δ(σδ)^{n−1}η. Flag solutions that: (a) equate the total amplified/anode electron count to η Σ_{k=0}^{n} (σδ)^k, to N_n, or to Σ_i N_i; (b) omit explicit (1−η) and (1−σ) leakage terms in the anode tally; or (c) conflate stage populations with terminal collection (e.g., modeling total anode electrons as a geometric series of (σδ)^k without per-stage leakage contributions). This rule catches modeling errors where branching losses to the anode at each stage are ignored or where intermediate-stage counts are incorrectly used as the terminal count.

New Category: Energy Accounting in Casca.title: Energy accounting in cascaded photomultipliers must include bypass fractions (1−η) and (1−σ)
New Category: Energy Accounting in Casca.description:
This rule checks energy accounting in problems involving photomultiplier tubes or similar cascaded, multi-gap accelerators with dynodes, where parameters η (photocathode-to-first-dynode collection efficiency), σ (inter-dynode collection efficiency), δ (secondary emission per collected electron), V (uniform gap potential), and n (number of dynodes) are given or implied.

What the rule verifies:
1) Completeness of branch contributions: The total energy to amplify one photoelectron must equal e·V times the expected number of gap crossings by all electrons produced. A correct solution must explicitly account for:
   a) Direct-to-anode photoelectrons: a (1−η) fraction of initial photoelectrons that bypass the first dynode and traverse all n+1 gaps to the anode, contributing a term proportional to (1−η)(n+1)eV.
   b) Bypass at each dynode: at dynode i (1 ≤ i ≤ n), a (1−σ) fraction of the δ·N_i emitted electrons that go straight to the anode, crossing (n−i+1) gaps, contributing terms proportional to (1−σ)×(n−i+1)×eV×δ×N_i (or an equivalent aggregated expression).
   c) Forward-collected electrons: the σ fraction that proceeds to the next dynode, each crossing one gap and contributing eV per stage (e.g., eV×N_{i+1}).

2) Presence of bypass factors: Flag solutions that omit (1−η) and/or (1−σ) in the energy computation, or that implicitly set η = 1 or σ = 1 without justification.

3) Parameter dependence and scaling: The final energy expression must depend on η, σ, δ, V, and n. For δσ > 1, the average energy should grow with the cascade multiplication, typically showing dependence like (δσ)^n (or an equivalent exponential-in-n growth). Flag solutions that yield energy independent of n, only linear in n without δσ multiplicative growth, or that lack δ and σ in the dominant scaling term.

4) Gap-count correctness: Verify that energy contributions weight eV by the correct number of gaps traversed (e.g., n+1 for direct photoelectrons, n−i+1 for dynode bypasses). Flag solutions that count only one gap for electrons that go straight to the anode or otherwise miscount path lengths.

5) Dimensional consistency: Energy must be proportional to e·V times a dimensionless expected count of crossings. Flag use of incorrect units (e.g., e^2, V^2) or missing e·V factor.

This rule triggers when a solution computes the average/total energy required to amplify one photoelectron in a multi-dynode system and will flag modeling errors where bypass paths to the anode are ignored or miscounted, or where the cascade multiplication and gap traversal are not properly reflected in the energy sum.

Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.title: Grating spectral resolution: resolving power and dimensional consistency
Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.description: Checks the derivation and final expression for the minimum resolvable spectral range (Δλ_min) in diffraction grating problems. The rule flags the following issues: - Use of an incorrect angular resolution formula such as Δθ = λ/(N d); the correct pathway is via the grating equation d sinθ = m λ and either resolving power R = m N (giving Δλ_min = λ/(m N)) or angular dispersion dθ/dλ = m/(d cosθ) combined with the imaging scale. - Final expressions of the form Δλ_min ≈ k · λ where k is not explicitly equal to 1/(m · N) or another dimensionless combination derived from the grating’s order m and slit count N, or lacks justification from the correct relations. - Inclusion of the grating length L in Δλ without accompanying slit spacing d or line density g (lines per length) to form the dimensionless N = L/d; using L alone leads to dimensional inconsistency. - Missing use of the correct angular–spectral mapping (no mention of dθ/dλ = m/(d cosθ) or equivalent) when converting angular separation to wavelength separation. - Non-numeric final answers when the problem provides sufficient numeric instrument parameters (e.g., pixel density like 200 pixels/mm and optical elements) and requests a concrete value. - Unit check: the final Δλ_min must have units of length; expressions yielding dimensionless or angular units are flagged.

Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.title: Incorrect Δλ–Δθ conversion for diffraction gratings
Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.description: Checks that the conversion between angular separation (Δθ) and spectral separation (Δλ) for a diffraction grating is derived from the grating equation d·sinθ = m·λ. The correct dispersion is dθ/dλ = m/(d·cosθ), so Δλ = Δθ·(d·cosθ)/m (and for small angles, cosθ ≈ 1 gives Δλ ≈ Δθ·d/m). Flags solutions that: (a) assert relations like Δλ = Δθ·cosθ, Δλ ≈ Δθ·λ, or Δθ ≈ Δλ/λ; (b) use a dispersion dθ/dλ that does not equal m/(d·cosθ); (c) produce a final Δλ expression that lacks dependence on slit spacing d and diffraction order m; or (d) infer resolving power or spectral separation from angular resolution without employing d·sinθ = m·λ. This rule targets logic errors where angular-to-spectral conversion omits the grating’s physical scaling (d, m) or uses ad hoc proportionalities.

Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.title: Use focal-length-based mapping for grating dispersion onto detector
Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.description: When a problem specifies a focusing mirror or lens that projects the diffraction pattern onto a detector, the solution must relate the diffraction angle to detector position via the focal length of that element. The correct imaging/dispersion relations are: (i) y = f · tan(β) ≈ f · β for small angles, and (ii) dy/dλ = f · m / (d · cos β), derived from the grating equation mλ = d (sin α + sin β). Flag as modeling error if the solution: (a) replaces the focal length f with an arbitrary path length, screen distance, or grating length L (e.g., uses y ≈ L · θ, y ≈ D · θ, or dy/dλ proportional to L or a propagation distance), (b) ignores the focusing element entirely when mapping angle to detector coordinate, or (c) computes linear dispersion/resolution without f appearing in the mapping to pixels. Specifically, if the problem text includes a focusing mirror/lens and a detector (e.g., CCD) but the student uses L = 10 cm (grating length) or any non-focal distance in place of f to convert angles to linear positions or to dy/dλ, this rule should trigger. The rule also expects that resolving power R = mN is used for spectral separation in wavelength space and that conversion to pixel spacing uses the focal-length-based dy/dλ combined with the detector sampling; omission of the focal-length mapping constitutes the error.

Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.title: Require computing number of slits N from grating length and spacing for resolution
Diffraction and Synchrotron Radiation.description: For diffraction-grating resolution problems where the grating length L is given and slit spacing d or line density g (lines per length) is provided (possibly in a referenced earlier part), the solution must explicitly compute the number of illuminated slits N via N = L/d or N = L × g before using any resolution relations.
